story:
I showed up early to the community center on Tuesday because I had decided, sometime between dinner and the drive over, that I was going to be serious about the violin this year. I'd been serious about it for almost four months now, which is practically a decade in my own personal economy, and I had the calluses to prove it, though Priya later pointed out that two of them were from the guitar I quit in the spring. Whatever. The point is I came early.

The multipurpose room smelled like floor wax and the leftover coffee somebody always burned in the kitchenette, and the folding chairs were already arranged in the loose horseshoe Mr. Dobbins liked for the Thursday ensemble, except today was Tuesday, so somebody had arranged them for nothing, or for us, I never found out which. Priya was there with her cello, and DeShawn, who plays clarinet and is morose about it in a way he seems to enjoy, and a new kid, Marisol, holding a trumpet like it might go off.

"Are we tuning yet?" Marisol asked. "My last teacher just had us tune to whatever the piano felt like that day."

I unlocked my phone and opened the tuner app, because that's the job I'd given myself, unofficially, three weeks ago, and nobody had objected yet, which I took as ratification. "We tune to A," I said. "Four forty."

"Forty what?"

"Hertz. The A above middle C, at 440 hertz." I set the phone on the music stand where everyone could see the needle swing. "It's an actual standard. The International Organization for Standardization formalized it. ISO 16."

"That is the saddest thing I've ever heard," DeShawn said, without looking up from reassembling his clarinet. "There's a committee for the note A."

"Standardization is why orchestras can play together," I said, and I'll admit there was a little preacher in it. This was my whole pitch that fall: that music was a rare corner of the world where everyone had agreed on something. My parents were three months into a divorce that had metastasized from a legal matter into a referendum on every decision either of them had ever made, including, in one memorable Thursday dinner, whether I should have been allowed to quit piano at nine. Meanwhile the A above middle C sat at 440 hertz, formalized, dependable, the same in Lagos and Lansing. I found that genuinely moving. Priya found it funny, I think, though she was kind enough to only say so occasionally.

We tuned. Marisol's A came in flat, then sharp, then flat again, and I watched her jaw set as she worked the tuning slide, and I remembered being there, that week when the note refuses to live inside you. DeShawn matched the app on the first try, smug as a cat. Then Priya plucked her A string and the needle hung just left of center, and she turned her peg a hair and it locked dead on, and something about watching four different instruments agree, from a phone speaker, in a room that smelled like burned coffee, made the hair on my arms stand up.

Then Mr. Dobbins came in with his violin and everything went sideways.

He didn't use my phone. He unpacked, rosined his bow like a man with all the time in the world, and played an A, and it was beautiful, and it was flat. Not by much. A few cents, maybe, whatever a cent is, DeShawn told me later it's a hundredth of a semitone but I haven't verified that and DeShawn says a lot of things. Priya matched Dobbins without comment. Marisol looked between the phone and the teacher like a spectator at a divorce. I played the app's A against his and the beating between them, that wobbling interference I'd read about, was faintly there, like two people almost agreeing.

"Jake," Dobbins said, "you're a touch sharp."

"I'm at 440," I said. "ISO 16. It's the standard."

He smiled at me, not unkindly, which is its own genre of defeat. "Some ensembles tune to 440 and some don't, and some tune to the first chair, and the first chair tonight is me, and I'm cold, because I just came in from the parking lot, and my A will drift as my violin warms up. So you can be right at 440 hertz and out of tune with the room." He nodded at the phone. "Your standard is a starting point, not a destination."

Which I wanted to argue with. I had, honestly, been building a whole cosmology on that number, a whole theory of how the world could be if people would just formalize their agreements the way the International Organization for Standardization had formalized the A above middle C at 440 hertz, and here was this man flattening my pitch and calling it the room. But I also couldn't deny the room sounded better when we were together, whatever together turned out to be. So I turned my peg down, that small surrender, and we ran through the Holst arrangement, and there's this one passage where the violin line crosses under the cello line and for two bars nobody is the melody and it's the best thing we do.

Afterward, packing up, I started composing, in my head, the speech I'd give my father about standards versus context, about how both could be true at once, how a note could be right by the book and wrong in the room, and maybe people too, et cetera. It was going to be a really good speech. Then Marisol came over holding her trumpet case and my phone, which she'd picked up off the stand for me, and she said, "Hey, your app's been on the wrong setting all night. That wasn't 440. It was 442."

She handed it back and showed me the settings screen, and there it was, plain as anything.

"Still sounded fine though," she said, and latched her case.

The community kitchen on Halstead Street smelled of scorched milk and dish steam, and by six in the evening most of the after-school crowd had cleared out, leaving Madison alone at the steel counter with two pounds of dark couverture and a saucepan of water she could not quite keep still. Her first batch, poured that afternoon into the silicone molds she had bought with her last paycheck, had come out of the refrigerator dull as river stones, breaking soft and crumbly at the edges instead of snapping. Rosa, who ran the kitchen on Tuesdays and Thursdays, had leaned over the molds and clicked her tongue.

"You going to serve that at the fundraiser?" Rosa had asked. Rosa wanted the fundraiser to impress the woman from the county grant office, who had promised to stop by near closing. "Because that looks like something you'd find in a jacket pocket in March."

So Madison had come back, after the buses, with her phone propped against a canister of flour, reading as she stirred. The trouble, the pages said, was not the chocolate itself but the fat inside it. Cocoa butter could crystallize in six different forms, and tempering aimed to make most of it set in form V, the one crystal form that gave shine and snap. Everything else she read kept circling back to that number, six, and the fifth, the good one, as if the fat were a small temperamental city with one decent neighborhood.

"Form five," she said aloud, mostly to the counter.

"Is that a boy?" Rosa called from the sink, where she was polishing the glass doors of the display case, the ones the grant officer would look through.

"It's a crystal. In the fat. There are six kinds and only one of them behaves." Madison scraped the spatula against the bowl's rim. The method she had settled on was the seeding one: melt the chocolate hot enough to erase every structure, cool it with constant stirring, then throw in a handful of already-tempered chips, chopped fine, like witnesses brought in to show the liquid what to become when it stopped moving. The physics of it, if it was physics, seemed to underpin half of what people called craft. She had always thought of baking as instinct, her grandmother's forearm and wrist, and it unsettled her a little to find a lattice of fact beneath it, as though instinct itself were a symbiosis between hands and invisible structure, each feeding the other something it could not make alone.

She worked the chocolate down through the temperatures, wrist aching, watching the surface change from glossy and loose to something thicker, matte at the edges, dragging behind the spatula in a ribbon that held its shape for a breath before sinking. The test, the pages said, was to touch a smear to your lip or the back of your hand and see whether it cooled in minutes, dull and dry, without streaks. She touched it to her knuckle and counted. It set fast. It looked matte. She dipped the tip of a knife and waited, watching the thin coat cloud over evenly, no gray bloom rising through it.

"Rosa," she said. "Come look at this."

Rosa came with a rag over her shoulder, and Madison dragged the knife edge across the dried smear so it made a sound like a fingernail on a chalkboard's quieter cousin. Rosa laughed, a short startled bark.

"That's it? That's the noise?"

"That's temper. I hope." Madison had no thermometer that went low enough, and she was honest with herself about that. She was steering by texture and by the little proof on the knife, and there was a real chance the molds would come out streaked anyway, that the heat of the kitchen or her impatience had knocked half the fat into its wrong forms. She could not see the crystals. Nobody could. She was taking the word of a smear on her knuckle that somewhere in the dark bowl, most of the fat had agreed to become the right thing.

She poured the molds in a thin, even ribbon, tapped each one against the counter to shake the bubbles loose, and carried them to the cool shelf by the window, away from the ovens, where the evening air off the parking lot had something almost boreal in it after the August day, the first small suggestion that the year was turning. Rosa stood beside her for a minute, both of them watching the filled molds as if a photograph were developing.

"If these set right," Rosa said, "I want twelve of them in the display case before she gets here. With a little card. Made on site, by volunteers."

"I'm not a volunteer. I pay for the counter time."

"You're eighteen and you're here on a Thursday night instead of anywhere else. That's volunteer enough for the card." Rosa wiped the rim of a mold with her thumb, fussing at a drip, and Madison saw that Rosa's hands were shaking slightly, the way they hadn't when she was polishing glass. The grant mattered to her. Maybe the kitchen mattered to her the way the chocolate was beginning to matter to Madison, in the specific and unglamorous way of showing up twice a week to keep something warm.

They waited twenty minutes, washing bowls, and then Madison turned the first mold over and flexed it. The bar dropped onto the counter with a hard, bright sound, and its face was so glossy it reflected the fluorescent tube above them in a single unbroken line. She snapped a corner off and the break was clean, angled, sharp-edged, with a faint gray-white fan at the surface where the crystals had fractured in the pattern she had read about and not believed.

Rosa picked up the corner Madison had broken off and ate it, slowly, the way you eat something you want to keep tasting.

"Twelve of them," Rosa said, already reaching for the little card. "And put your name on it, too."

Grandpa's den smelled of popcorn and radiator dust, and by the third quarter the room had arranged itself into its usual geography: Grandpa in the recliner, Morgan's father on the couch arm, two of Grandpa's friends from the hardware store folding into the remaining chairs, and Morgan on the floor with her laptop, half watching the game. Her cousin Dylan, who was nine, sat closest to the screen with his knees pulled up to his chin.

"See how they painted it," Dylan said during a timeout. The camera held a wide shot of the field, the yellow first-down line stretched across the grass. "They have to paint it really fast, before the play. Like with a machine."

"Nobody's painting anything," Morgan said. "The field doesn't have a line on it."

"It does. It's right there." He pointed at the television. "Yellow."

"Watch a replay," she said. "Sometimes the line goes over a player's shoe, like the shoe is in front of it. If it were painted on the grass, it couldn't do that."

Dylan squinted at the screen, and Uncle Rick laughed from the doorway and said the kid would argue about anything, which was, in Morgan's view, less an insult than a diagnosis. She opened her laptop. It was not that she doubted herself exactly; she had just never asked how the line got there, and Dylan's certainty, however wrong, had the effect of invigorating her own curiosity, which had been dormant all afternoon.

The search took four minutes. She read, scrolled, read again, then turned the laptop so Dylan could see.

"It's drawn by a computer," she said. "It's not on the field at all. The first time it was ever shown was September 27, 1998, on ESPN, and the company that did it was called Sportvision."

"Sportvision," Dylan repeated, as if tasting the word.

"That's the name. That's who broadcast it first."

Dylan leaned in toward the laptop, then back toward the television, comparing. "But it looks like it's on the grass."

"I know. That's the whole point. It looks painted and it's not." She was careful here, because she had started to say it worked by tracking the cameras, and then realized she did not actually know that, had read no mechanism, only the fact of the date and the company and the network. She stopped herself before inventing an explanation. "I don't know how it stays lined up when the camera moves. I just know it's computer-drawn and when it started."

Grandpa shifted in the recliner. "I remember when there wasn't any line," he said. "You had to guess where the marker was. Then one season it was just there, like it had always been there."

"September of '98," Morgan said.

"You and your dates." But he said it without irritation, and he did not look away from the screen when he said it, which Morgan understood as a kind of approval, one of his idiosyncrasies she had catalogued over sixteen years of Sunday afternoons in this room.

The game resumed. On third down, the running back was stopped just short, and the yellow line glowed under a pile of bodies, and Dylan stood up and shouted that he was short, he's short, look at the line, and Morgan found herself shouting too, though she had no team in this, no bet, no reason. Mr. Alvarez from the hardware store said the spot was generous, that the officials had been profligate with the yardage all afternoon, handing out inches like they cost nothing, and Grandpa told him the officials had nothing to do with the yellow line, that was the chain crew, and Mr. Alvarez said he knew that, he wasn't born yesterday.

They measured. The ball sat a chain-link's width past the line, and the crowd noise came up through the television speakers, and the den got loud in answer.

"So there's no paint," Dylan said quietly, beside her on the floor now. "Not even a little."

"Not even a little. But everyone in the stadium is looking at a real chain, held by real people, and we're looking at a yellow line that's not there. And they're supposed to match."

"Do they ever not match?"

She thought about it. "Probably. But nobody at home would know, because all we can see is the line that isn't real." That was the part that kept circling in her head, that the picture everyone trusted was the manufactured one, and the true one was on the sideline being carried by two men in orange vests.

The offense lined up to go for it. Grandpa leaned forward in the recliner, and it did not squeak, and Dylan grabbed Morgan's sleeve without seeming to notice he had done it.

"Watch the line," Dylan said. "It's not even there and I can't stop watching it."

The garage smelled of cold engine oil and old varnish, and Camille sat on an upturned milk crate with her grandfather's trumpet across her knees, not playing it. She had promised herself she would practice here, away from the apartment where the neighbors had already knocked twice, but the mute she'd ordered was cheap and the sound came through it anyway, muffled and shapeless, like someone speaking through a wall.

The trumpet had come to her in September, three weeks after the funeral, in a cardboard box with her name taped to the flap in her mother's handwriting. Inside, wrapped in a dish towel, she'd found the horn, a bottle of valve oil, and the little wooden metronome that had always sat on her grandfather's piano, its brass pendulum folded down like a bird tucking a wing. She had wound it once and let it tick itself out, and then sat very still on her bed for a long time, listening to the silence it left behind.

Her friend Priya came through the side door carrying two sandwiches and her own clarinet case, which she set on the workbench beside a jar of loose screws. "You actually practice out here. In November."

"I told you, the neighbors."

"Your neighbors need to hear you get better, that's all." Priya popped the clasps on her case. "Play me the thing. The exercise."

Camille raised the trumpet, and the metronome sat on the crate beside her, ticking at sixty, and she tried to put her notes inside the ticks. They fell out of the spaces. Her tongue hesitated on the attacks, her fingers arrived late, and when she stopped, the pendulum kept swinging, indifferent, marking out a measure of silence with the same authority it gave her playing.

"You're fighting it," Priya said.

"I know." Camille set the horn down. "He used to say that. That the tick isn't the music, it's just the fence around it." She wound the mechanism again, slower this time, and watched the weight slide down the arm. "I used to think it was ancient. Like the piano. Then I looked it up."

Priya leaned over, sandwich in hand. "And?"

"Johann Maelzel patented it in 1815. But it wasn't even his idea. It's from a design by Dietrich Nikolaus Winkel." She said the names carefully, the way she'd rehearsed them, and Priya laughed.

"So your sacred heirloom is stolen goods."

"It's not stolen. Winkel never patented his. Maelzel just got there first, legally." Camille slid the weight up the pendulum and the ticking quickened, and she found she liked knowing the number, the year, the names; it delimited something that had felt boundless. Her grandfather had seemed to her a person without a history, and now she knew that even his metronome had one, borrowed and contested, and that this made it no less his.

Her mother had wanted to sell the piano. That was the argument they'd been having since October, in the careful, exhausted voices they used now, her mother on sabbatical from the university and home too much, both of them circling the same rooms. The trumpet was a compromise Camille had proposed, thinking it was the tenable one, the smaller instrument, the movable thing; but some nights she suspected she'd only made it easier for her mother to imagine the rest of it gone.

She played the exercise again, and this time she stopped trying to land exactly on the ticks and let them pass under her like the rungs of a ladder she was climbing anyway, a little ahead or behind. Something loosened. Priya picked up the clarinet and found the key, and for four or eight bars, in a cold garage in November, they were playing together, roughly, and it sounded like music the way a drawing of a door sounds like a door, enough to know what was behind it.

The pendulum wound down mid-phrase. Neither of them stopped playing, and Camille noticed she was counting on her own now, in her chest, somewhere near where she imagined her grandfather had kept his. When they finished, Priya unwrapped the second sandwich and handed it over, and Camille took it and then reached out and lifted the little brass weight off the pendulum arm, holding it in her palm, small and heavier than it looked.

"I'm going to tell her we keep the piano," she said.

Priya looked at her. "You think she'll go for it?"

Camille closed her fingers around the weight and put it in her jacket pocket.

Brandon spread the flashcards across the picnic table before the evening could get away from him. Glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the electron transport chain: forty-one cards in his own cramped handwriting, each one a step he was supposed to have mastered three weeks ago. He had failed the test, and his mother had signed him up for the retake without asking, which stung less than the fact that she was probably right to do it. Behind him the sprinkler ticked against the fence, and above the table the last of the light came sideways through the elm.

He had made it through glycolysis twice when Marisol climbed over the back wall, the way she had since they were nine. She dropped onto the bench across from him, took a card without asking, and read it upside down. "Chemiosmosis," she said. "That sounds like a disease."

"It's kind of the point of the whole thing," Brandon said. "Glucose gets broken down, and the energy doesn't go straight into ATP. It goes into pumping protons across a membrane, and then the protons flow back through this one enzyme, and that's what actually makes the ATP." He heard himself say it and could not tell whether he understood it or had only memorized the shape of it, and the difference between those two things was exactly what had ruined him on the first test.

Marisol spun the card between her fingers. Last spring, before everything, she had gone with him to the science museum the week the biology wing reopened. He remembered standing at the display case where a model enzyme sat in a bath of green light, its lower half turning like a tiny motor while a projection of protons streamed through it from one side to the other. "It's called ATP synthase," the plaque read, and Marisol had read it aloud, and he had watched the rotor spin and felt something assemble in his mind that no diagram had ever managed. Part of the enzyme spun because the protons flowed through it, and the spinning was what built the ATP. He had stood there long enough that she left him and went to look at the tarantulas.

The twist of it was that he had almost not gone that day. His father had offered the tickets, extrinsic bribes being his father's method of late, and Brandon had debated going at all, weighing the free afternoon against what it would mean to accept anything from him so soon after the move out. He had gone, and had not called to say thank you, and now, in the backyard with the cards in front of him, he could not decide whether the trip had been a mistake or one of the last good things they would share. His instinct was to dichotomize, to sort every memory of his father into the years before and the year after, but the truth was more tangled than that, and he knew it.

"The mitochondria," Marisol said, flipping the card over. "You said that word like forty times that day at the museum. Like it was a celebrity."

"It kind of is." He picked up a stick from under the table and drew two lines in the dirt beside the bench, a membrane, then an arrow. "The protons pile up on this side, like water behind a dam. When they flow back through, they make part of the enzyme spin. The spinning builds the ATP." He turned the stick like a rotor. "All that glucose, all those steps, just to spin a wheel."

Marisol watched the stick turn. "So the dam isn't the energy. The spinning is."

He stopped the stick mid-turn, because she had said in six words what his teacher's slides had failed to say in thirty, and because he could not tell whether he had known it already. Discernment, his English teacher liked to say, was knowing the difference between what you believed and what you merely repeated, and right now Brandon was short on it. He looked at the arrow in the dirt, the crude membrane, the protons he had drawn as dots, and he thought of the model turning in its green light while his father stood a few feet behind him, also watching, neither of them saying anything.

His phone buzzed against the table. It was his father: Did you pass the retake yet? Then, a second message: I still have the museum stub on my desk. Brandon set the phone face down between the flashcards and the stick. The sprinkler had gone quiet, and the elm had gone dark against the last gray band of sky.

"Are you going to answer?" Marisol asked.

Brandon turned the stick in the dirt one more time, slow, like something flowing through it.

The porch swing at Abuela's house had a specific creak, one Annabelle could set a metronome to, and she had been listening to it for three days while she tried to argue about water rights entirely in Spanish for five minutes. The assignment was due Monday. Her debate coach had said the point was not winning but fluency under pressure, which Annabelle understood to mean that she would lose, and in a second language.

She had filled eleven pages of a spiral notebook with arguments. The reservoirs were overdrawn. The farmers had senior rights under a treaty older than the state. The cities needed the water or they would die of thirst, and the letters, if translated, would go on for pages. Abuela brought out lemonade and set it on the railing without interrupting, the way she did, and went back inside through the screen door that clapped twice.

It was Abuelo who ruined the notebook, though he did not know he was doing it. He came out after his nap, lowered himself into the wicker chair, and asked her in Spanish what she was writing so fiercely. Annabelle attempted an answer, stumbled on the word for reservoir, and switched to English to explain the assignment. He listened with his whole face, the way he listened to everything, and then he said, "Ethos, pathos, logos. Aristotle named three means of persuasion. Ethos is the speaker's credibility, pathos is the audience's emotions, and logos is the logic of the argument."

He did not say anything else about it. He asked whether she wanted more lemonade, and when she said no, he went to check on the tomatoes. Annabelle sat very still and looked at her eleven pages, which were, she now saw, nothing but logos. Every line was a fact, a number, a clause of a treaty. If she delivered them perfectly, her audience, whoever they were, would know that reservoirs were overdrawn and would feel absolutely nothing about it.

The problem was that pathos in Spanish terrified her. In English she could do it; she knew how to slow down and let a silence sit. In Spanish, every emotional register belonged to Abuela's kitchen, to arguments about whether Annabelle was eating enough, to the bellicose tone of her tío René at holidays, loud and wonderful and not at all what a debate judge wanted. She did not know yet how Spanish sounded when it was quiet and serious. She had not acclimated to the language's soft rooms, only its loud ones.

She found Abuela shelling peas on the back steps, dish towel over her knee, and asked her, in Spanish, careful and slow, to tell her about the year the wells went dry. Abuela had grown up two hours east, in a town that had nearly emptied when the aquifer dropped. Annabelle had heard fragments of this her whole life but never in full, and she had never thought of it as something she could use. Abuela talked for a long while, her hands never stopping, and the story was not about aquifers or measurements. It was about her mother washing clothes in a washtub with water hauled from a neighbor's well, and how the neighbor eventually put a lock on the spigot, and how the two women did not speak for a year after that, and how the neighbor came to the funeral anyway and stood in the back and cried.

Annabelle did not take notes. She sat with her hands in her lap and let it land on her, and then she asked Abuela one more thing: whether she would say some of it again, slowly, so Annabelle could repeat the phrases back. Abuela looked at her for a moment, surprised maybe, or pleased in a way she did not announce, and then she said it again, the washtub, the lock, the funeral, and Annabelle repeated each sentence after her like learning a song. The Spanish was simpler than her notebook's Spanish. It did not need the subjunctive. It needed the word for lock and the word for cried, and Abuela corrected her gently, twice, and made her tea without being asked because the evening had turned cool.

That night Annabelle cut the notebook down. She kept the treaty clause and the reservoir numbers, because logos still had a job to do, but she moved them to the end, and at the beginning she put Abuela's sentences, the washtub and the spigot. Then she added a middle section she had not planned, something about who her audience was supposed to trust, and she realized she had almost no ethos of her own. She was sixteen, she was not from that town, and her Spanish had a gap in it like a missing tooth. So she wrote a line that admitted it: that she was a granddaughter repeating what her grandmother told her, and that the grandmother was in the kitchen, and that anyone could go ask her themselves.

She timed it on the porch the next morning, five minutes, twice through, with Abuelo listening from the wicker chair and pretending to read his paper. He did not say whether it was good. At the end he folded the paper in half and said, "Your accent wanders." Then he said, "It wanders less when you talk about the washtub." Annabelle looked at him, and then through the screen door at Abuela, who was drying a dish and had definitely been listening the whole time, and she turned back to her notebook and drew a small star next to the line about the funeral, just so she would not lose it on the bus.

The porch light at Granddad's came on with the last of the afternoon, and Sienna spread her laptop, a notebook, and a cold mug of lemonade across the kitchen table where he did his crosswords. Her assignment was due at midnight: build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods, then test it. She had never written a class before tonight, only loose snippets copied from the board, and she kept rereading the prompt as though a hidden instruction might surface the fourth time through.

"A class," she said aloud, because Granddad liked to hear what she was doing, even when he understood none of it. "Like a blueprint. You write the blueprint once, and then you can build as many actual things as you want."

"Like a cookie cutter," he said, not looking up from his puzzle. "The cutter isn't the cookie."

That was closer than he knew, she thought. She typed the outline her teacher had given: the word class, a name, curly braces. She wanted to model something real, so she chose a bird, because Granddad's feeder outside the window had its whole diurnal schedule, chickadees at dawn, cardinals by late morning, and she gave her class a name and a field called song, marked private, which apparently meant the outside world couldn't just reach in and grab it. It had to ask politely, through a getter. There was something appealing in that, a rule of manners built into the language itself.

The trouble came with the constructor. Her notes said a constructor was a special method that ran when an object was created, setting up its fields, and the class needed one so the bird was born already singing. She wrote it the way she wrote every other method, with void in front, because methods that returned nothing got void, and surely a constructor returned nothing. She wrote her test, a small main method that built a bird and printed its song, pressed run, and got null. Not an error, not a complaint. Just null, a polite nothing, as if she had asked the bird to sing and it had never learned how.

She stared at the screen. Either her test was wrong, or the class was wrong, or both, and the clock on the microwave said 9:14. Granddad asked whether she was winning. "I don't know," she said. "That's the strange part. Nothing's broken. It just didn't happen."

She tried changing the test, and it changed nothing, which told her something important: the test was probably fine, and the problem lived where the object got built. She looked at her constructor again, line by line, the way Granddad looked at a crossword clue he suspected was a trick. It had the name of the class. It had parentheses. It had a body that set the field. Then she noticed, really noticed, that little word void sitting at the front like a hat on the wrong head. Her teacher's example on the board, she now recalled, had nothing there at all. No void, no anything. She had assumed the teacher was being sloppy, skipping a word the way people skip words in speech, and she had fixed it, added what was missing. She deleted the void and pressed run.

Song of the Sparrow, the screen said, exactly what she had put in the constructor. She sat back and let out a breath she hadn't measured. So that was the rule, and it wasn't sloppiness, it was the language being exact where she had been generous: a Java constructor has the same name as its class and no return type, not even void. "The word void," she told Granddad, "was turning it into just another method. A regular one. So it never ran." He nodded as if this were obvious, which in a way it now was, and asked, "So what do you call the thing that runs when it's born?"

"A constructor," she said. "It's called a constructor."

She added a second field, a private one for the bird's feeding time, and a getter for it, then a second test, and ran everything twice, because once felt like luck and twice felt like knowledge. It was 10:40 when she submitted, and she sat afterward not celebrating but introspect, turning the evening over in her mind. She had arrived believing that code was a place where you followed the rules you were given, and she still half believed it, but the night had also shown her the other half: the rules had to be discovered, guessed at, tested against a stubborn machine that answered only in nulls and prints. Which half was truer, she couldn't yet say, and she was honest enough with herself not to decide tonight. It would have been a travesty of the whole evening to pretend the void had been her only mistake; there was also the assumption, the quiet certainty that the teacher had left something out rather than that the language meant exactly what it said.

Granddad closed his puzzle and stood. "Cookie cutter," he said, patting her shoulder on his way to the kettle. "Next time you'll check the cutter before you blame the dough."

The library's third floor smelled like warm toner and old carpet, and David had claimed the corner carrel by the window since seventh period, when Ms. Okafor had told him the principal wanted to see the editorial before it ran. He spread out his notes: the school board race, the two candidates for the open seat, the student paper's unanimous decision to endorse Marina Reyes. He had written four hundred words defending the endorsement on the merits. Mr. Hadley wanted to read it first. Nobody had said the word "censor," but nobody had to.

"You look like somebody stole your backpack," said Priya, dropping into the chair across from him with her own laptop. She was the managing editor, which meant she had been in the room when Hadley's assistant delivered the request in that soft, cheerful voice, as though asking for a favor. That insouciant tone had bothered David more than the request itself; if the administration was going to interfere, the least they could do was look uneasy about it.

"He wants to vet it," David said. "Vet, review, approve. Whatever you want to call it."

"Preview," Priya offered. "He'd probably say preview." She pulled up the paper's shared drive. "My dad calls that kind of word a dysphemism dressed up as a euphemism. A word that makes something sound worse than it is, except it's pretending to make it sound better."

David laughed without meaning to, then stopped, because the thing still sat in front of them. He turned to the library database instead of answering. He had a vague memory of something, a real newspaper, a fight over an endorsement that had made the news itself, and he wanted the details before he argued with a principal armed only with a student's outrage. He typed "newspaper endorsement blocked by owner" into the search field and waited while the results loaded.

There it was. In October 2024, the Los Angeles Times did not endorse a presidential candidate after its owner blocked the editorial board's plans, and several board members resigned in protest. He read the paragraph twice. He had expected to feel vindicated, the way you do when history hands you a club to swing, and for a moment he did. The Times was a giant, and even a giant could be stopped by one person with ownership. Then the feeling complicated itself. The board members had resigned, which was brave, but the paper still hadn't endorsed anyone, which meant the readers had still lost. Leaving was a way of refusing to cooperate. It was not a way of winning.

"Find something?" Priya asked, craning to see his screen. He read the sentence aloud, quietly, because the third floor had rules and because it felt like the kind of sentence that deserved a lower register. She was quiet for a moment too. "So even there," she said, "the people who did the work couldn't publish what they'd decided. And the ones who left, they left. They didn't get it printed."

"They got the story out anyway," David said. "Everybody found out why. The resignations were the story." He was thinking of his own position now, testing it the way you test a bridge before driving across. He believed the paper should run the endorsement without Hadley's approval, and he believed that refusing to show it to him was its own kind of power play, one that would let the administration call the students reckless for the rest of the year. He believed both things and they did not fit together neatly, and he was tired of pretending they should.

"Here's what I keep circling around," he said slowly. "If we just run it, we're insubordinate, and next year's editors inherit a war. If we let him read it, we're inured to it. It becomes normal that he reads everything, and it's easier for him every time after the first." Priya nodded at the word. She understood it; her grandmother's generation had stories about things becoming normal that way. "So maybe the move is in the middle. We show him the editorial, in print, at a meeting, with a recorder running, and we tell him what we found today. The Times. The resignations. We say we'd rather not make him into that story."

"That's a threat in a nice jacket," Priya said, but she was smiling. She started a new document and titled it "Meeting Agenda" while David copied the citation into his notes, the whole sentence, dates and all, in case he needed to read it aloud. Then he closed his laptop, slid it into his backpack, and stood up. "Come on," he said. "Let's go see if Hadley's still in his office."

The bell over the door of Kessler's Corner Store had a crack in it, so it rang flat, and Nicholas had come to know that sound as the start of his shift. He stacked the chip bags along the top rack while Mr. Kessler counted the till, and between customers he slid his calculus notebook onto the counter beside the register. He had a test on integration in two days, and the shop's dead hours, three to five, were the only quiet ones he got.

His uncle thought he was wasting the summer. "A boy your age should be outside," his uncle had said at dinner, describing the riparian trail along the creek where he fished, the shade, the water smell. Nicholas had said nothing, because the truth was awkward: the area under a curve felt more like a real place to him than the creek did. You could walk into it, in a way. You could measure it.

The problem on his page was from Tuesday's math club, and it had gone wrong in a way nobody had caught at the time. Priya had gotten one answer and Danny had gotten another, both working the same region between a line and a parabola, both showing complete work. Mrs. Okafor had been out of the room, and by the time she came back the club had moved on to voting on T-shirt designs, and the two answers had sat in Nicholas's bag all week like a splinter.

He remembered Danny at the whiteboard, marker squeaking, drawing the line above the parabola on the interval and then writing the parabola minus the line anyway, because the parabola's equation came first on the handout and he had subtracted in the order he'd copied them. Priya had subtracted the other way and gotten a negative number, then flipped its sign at the end without saying why. Both of them had laughed it off. Danny, who everyone would lionize the moment he got into his engineering program, had shrugged and said, "Sign's just a detail." Nicholas hadn't been sure it was.

A customer came in for milk and a lottery ticket, and Nicholas rang her up, made change, watched the door swing shut behind her. Then he drew the two curves again in his notebook, roughly to scale, and looked at them instead of at the algebra. The line sat above the parabola across the whole stretch between the crossing points. That was just a fact of the picture. He shaded the sliver of region between them with the side of his pencil, light, so he could erase it if he was wrong.

And then he saw it, or thought he did. The region had a size, one size, whichever equation you liked better. If the line was on top, then the way to get that size was to integrate the line minus the parabola over the interval where they stayed in that order. Danny had reversed it and had gotten the negative of the true area. Priya had gotten the negative too, but then she'd silently turned it positive, which was like guessing the right answer for the wrong reason. Nicholas wrote both procedures out side by side and found where they diverged, and his pulse did something small and embarrassing.

Mr. Kessler came over to refill the coffee station and glanced at the notebook. "That look like good news or bad news?"

"Good," Nicholas said. "I think." He turned the notebook so the shaded sliver faced his boss. "The area between two curves. You take the upper one minus the lower one, over the part where they're stacked that way." He tapped the line, then the parabola beneath it. "Danny had it backwards, so everything came out negative. Priya just flipped hers without knowing why, which happens to work here, but I don't know if it always works." He stopped, hearing himself pile uncertainty on a man who sold lottery tickets. "Sorry. That's probably not interesting."

Mr. Kessler studied the page longer than Nicholas expected. "My brother surveyed wetlands," he said. "Forest biome, swamp, whatever. He had a whole thing about boundaries. Said the argument was always about where you drew the line, not what was inside it." He went back to the coffee, and Nicholas sat with that, deciding whether it meant anything or whether it was just something an old man says near a notebook.

At five, Priya came in for a soda before her shift at the pharmacy next door. Nicholas slid the notebook across the counter, open to the two columns, before he could talk himself out of it. "From Tuesday. You were negative because of the order, not because of a mistake. Danny's the one who reversed it." She set the soda down and read, and her face did the thing faces do when someone is checking your work and finding you less wrong than they'd assumed.

"So why did flipping it work for me?" she said.

"That's what I can't promise," Nicholas said. "It worked here because the sign was the only thing off. If the curves crossed inside the interval, I don't think you could fix it with one flip. You'd have to split it up. But I haven't done that part yet." He pulled the notebook back and wrote her number at the bottom of the page, then Danny's, and drew a box around the difference so he'd look at it again on the bus.

Priya took her soda and pushed two quarters across the counter. "Text me if the crossing thing breaks," she said. "I want to be there when it does."

The bell rang flat behind her, and Nicholas turned the page and drew a parabola slicing through a line, twice.

The backyard smelled of cut grass and the vinegar his mother used on the fence, and Thomas had until sundown to make the launcher work. Regionals were Saturday morning. Two days before that, this evening, his engineering notebook was due to Mr. Okonkwo, and the notebook was supposed to contain a prediction: given the launch angle and the spring setting, exactly where the ball would land. He had the equations. He had the ball. He had a target circle drawn in chalk on the far patio, thirty-two feet from the firing line.

He set the launcher on the picnic table, cranked the spring six turns, and tilted the barrel to forty-five degrees, because forty-five was the textbook's sacred angle, the one his physics teacher defended with such certainty that Thomas's older brother called that classroom a theocracy, a place where one law held and no questioning was tolerated. Thomas had laughed at that, mostly, though he privately thought the brotherhood of students who'd failed the last quiz were disaffected for good reason, and he did not want to join them.

The math was not the hard part. He broke the launch speed into pieces: the horizontal component, which stayed constant and carried the ball forward, and the vertical component, which gravity pulled down on, slowing the rise and hurrying the fall. Two motions stacked on top of each other, two clocks running at once. He worked it on the patio in pencil, winded a little by how clean it was, how the world could be split like that and then rejoined. The numbers said 11.2 meters. Thirty-two feet was 9.75 meters. He adjusted the spring to four and a half turns, recalculated, and wrote 9.9 meters in the notebook with a satisfaction he would remember later as premature.

He fired. The ball rose, hung against the pale sky, dropped, and hit the concrete a full pace short of the chalk circle, bounced once, and rolled to rest against the recycling bin. Thomas stood over it. He checked the angle. He checked the spring count, counted the turns twice. He measured the actual distance with the tape measure, dragging it through the grass, and got 8.7 meters. More than a meter short of what the equation promised.

His neighbor Dana leaned over the fence, elbows on the rail, a popsicle in one hand. She was on the quiz team with him and had already submitted her own notebook, which was why she could afford to look this relaxed. "Your prediction wrong, or your launcher broken?"

"The launcher's fine. I checked everything." He turned the notebook toward her so she could see the columns, the separated components, the careful recombination. "The math says 9.9. It landed at 8.7. Every time." He had fired four more shots while measuring, and all four had landed in the same wrong place, which was almost worse, because it meant the world was consistent about contradicting him.

Dana came around through the gate and knelt at the landing spot, studying the scuff mark the ball had left. "So the equation lies."

"The equation doesn't lie." He heard how it sounded even as he said it, like a small-town sheriff defending the law. He wanted it to be true, that was the honest problem; the cleanliness of the method had seduced him, and now the ball sat there in the grass contradicting his notebook, and Mr. Okonkwo wanted a prediction with an explanation of the error, and Thomas had until dark to produce one. He had already decided that if he couldn't explain the gap, he would rather withdraw than hand in a guess, though he also suspected that wanting to expiate a bad prediction by quitting was its own kind of vanity, a way of punishing himself instead of doing the work.

He fired again, this time standing to the side, watching the whole arc. The ball seemed to sag near the top, just slightly, a hesitation the parabola on his page didn't have. He thought about everything the equation left out: it treated the ball as if the air weren't there at all, as if it flew through nothing. He crouched and looked at the ball, scuffed and grass-stained, an actual object shoving through actual air. "The calculation ignores the air," he said slowly. "Air resistance slows real projectiles. So the ball lands shorter than the math predicts. That's the gap."

"So write that," Dana said, licking the popsicle stick. "Judges love a known limitation."

"It's not a limitation of the math, it's a limitation of what I put into it." He took the notebook back to the table, sat on the bench, and began writing beneath the prediction: the predicted range, the measured range, then the sentence about air resistance slowing real projectiles, and after it a line he underlined twice, that the model and the yard disagreed, and that the disagreement was in the yard, not the model. Then he crossed out "in the yard" and wrote "in the world outside the model," because precision mattered now more than rhythm. The light was going amber at the fence line. He looked at the chalk circle, still empty, still thirty-two feet away.

"One more shot," he said, and cranked the spring to five and a half turns.

Jordan had until Monday to write two thousand words on how views of the French Revolution had changed since 1800, and by Saturday afternoon he had a page of quotes and no argument. His mother had dropped him at the city history museum with a notebook and forty minutes on the parking meter, because the essay required a primary source and the museum's special exhibit, "Remembering Revolution," had a case of nineteenth-century histories under glass.

He found the case in the back room, past a wax figure of a sans-culotte and a scale model of the Bastille. Behind the glass lay four leather volumes, their spines cracked, opened to a frontispiece portrait of a narrow-faced man with heavy eyelids. The label read: Adolphe Thiers, History of the French Revolution, published 1823 to 1827. Jordan copied the dates into his notebook. He knew Thiers's name from somewhere and could not place it, which bothered him the way a word on the tip of the tongue bothers you, so he read on.

"Thiers praised moderate leaders such as Mirabeau and Lafayette," the label continued, "and condemned radicals such as Robespierre." A footnote, smaller, added that Thiers would later help govern France himself. So the man had written the history before he ran the country. Jordan stood with his pen stopped against the page. He had been planning to open his essay with Carlyle, who treated the Revolution like a force of weather, and now here was somebody with a stake in the aftermath, drawing the line between respectable men and monsters while the ashes were still warm.

A girl about his age came in holding a museum map folded into a triangle. She stopped at the case and read the label over his shoulder. "Mirabeau and Lafayette," she said. "I did them last year. Our teacher called Thiers a moderate, if you can believe that."

"Why wouldn't I believe it?"

"Because look at the portrait. He looks like a man grading his own exam." She turned the map over in her hands. "I'm Priya. I'm here for the same reason you are, probably. Summer seminar, historiography paper, Monday."

Jordan showed her his page of quotes, and she laughed at the Carlyle plan, not unkindly. "You can't start with the grandiose ones," she said. "Start with the moderates. Thiers lionized Mirabeau, and everyone after him had to decide whether to agree."

They took the exhibit quiz together at the touch screen by the exit, mostly to use the stools. The quiz asked which figure was blamed for the Terror, and Jordan tapped Robespierre. Priya tapped the Committee as a whole. The screen told them both were defensible, which Jordan thought was a dodge until he considered that the whole exercise of the essay might be that: not who was right, but how each generation picked its villains. He wrote that down, then crossed out "villains" and wrote "losers," because Thiers's radicals had lost, and the moderates had lost more slowly.

In the rotunda, on the way out, they passed a bronze plaque of museum donors, and Priya pointed out that half the wing was named for one family. "Same problem," she said. "The people who pay for the building get the nice portrait. Thiers wrote the first big history before he ran France, so he got to decide who looked reasonable. Somebody's always holding the pen."

Jordan looked at his watch. Twenty minutes left on the meter, and he had a thesis forming that he did not entirely trust: that accounts of the Revolution split between those written close to the fear and those written from a safe distance, and that the close ones, like Thiers, told you as much about what frightened the author as about what happened. But Thiers had also read documents no one else had, and Priya had a point about the donors, and he could not prove that distance made anyone more honest, only less invested. He was honest enough with himself to leave a line in his notes: distance gives verisimilitude, not truth, and he was not sure yet what to do with that.

In the parking lot his mother was already at the car, engine running. Priya waved from the museum steps and said she'd see him Monday, or she wouldn't, and either way they were both writing about a dead Frenchman's eyelids this weekend. In the passenger seat Jordan opened his notebook on his knee and underlined Mirabeau, Lafayette, Robespierre, and then, in the margin, the question he could not answer yet: who is holding the pen now?

Liam sat cross-legged on the living room carpet with a notebook, a pencil, and the growing suspicion that his own life contained nothing worth staging. The assignment from drama camp was due in five days: a ten-minute play about a moment from his own life, written and staged by him alone. His mother kept drifting past the doorway with laundry, pretending not to hover, which was its own kind of theater.

The moment he'd chosen, tentatively, was the afternoon in seventh grade when he'd told his best friend Marcus that Marcus's overdue library book was "a pretty parochial concern," a word Liam had just learned and badly misused, and Marcus had laughed so hard he fell off the bleachers and split his lip. It was funny, but it was also, underneath, the afternoon Marcus stopped telling him things. Liam couldn't tell if that was the play or just the guilt.

Priya arrived at four with a grocery bag of grape soda and her drama camp binder flapping open. She dropped onto the couch, kicked her shoes into the corner, and said, "The pyramids of Giza took twenty years and you can't write ten minutes." She handed him a soda, which he shook, on purpose, before opening.

"Freytag," Priya said, when he'd mopped soda off his chin and the notebook. She flipped to a napkin she'd drawn on at camp, a lopsided pyramid labeled in gel pen. "Gustav Freytag described dramatic structure as a pyramid of exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution. In his 1863 book on drama technique." She tapped the peak of the triangle, where she'd drawn a tiny screaming face. "Your climax goes here. Ten-minute play means your climax is like minute six. So where's yours?"

Liam looked at the napkin. His instinct was that the climax was the fall, the split lip, the blood on the concrete, because that was the loudest thing. But he tried placing it at the peak and found that everything after it went flat: Marcus walked to the nurse, Liam followed, the end. Falling action with nothing falling. "Maybe the climax isn't the blood," he said slowly. "Maybe it's the second before, when I open my mouth. When I could still say something else."

From Priya's side of the room, watching him, the change was visible the way weather is visible: he stopped chewing his pencil and started writing without looking up, which for Liam was practically a medical event. She read over his shoulder as two versions of the scene took shape on the page. In one, the boy said the fancy word and the friend laughed and bled. In the other, the boy swallowed the word and said something plain instead, and the friend told him the thing he'd been about to tell him, which was that his parents were separating. The second version was quieter. It was also, she thought, harder, because nothing exploded and nobody got to be right.

"That one's better," she said, "but you can't stage it. Nothing happens."

"Something happens," Liam said. "It just doesn't happen out loud."

They argued about it through half a grape soda each, Priya pacing and acting out the falling-off-the-bleachers version with a couch cushion, which debilitated her for a full minute of laughing on the floor. "Fine," she gasped. "Do your quiet one. But you have to be the one who plays the friend, because if you play yourself you'll just stand there looking like a misanthrope who's sorry about it." Liam said that a misanthrope wouldn't have a best friend to write a play about, and Priya said that a misanthrope absolutely would, one, and would write a play about ruining it.

His mother drifted past the doorway again, slowed, and drifted on, which they both noticed and neither mentioned.

On the night of the performance, in the same living room with the lamps rearranged, Liam staged the quiet version. He played Marcus, and Priya, in a hoodie that was meant to be Liam's, said the plain sentence instead of the parochial one, and then sat very still while the other boy, given the opening, finally said the thing about his parents. The audience of nine included Marcus himself, who had been sent a text three days earlier with only the time and the address. When the lights came back up, Marcus didn't say whether it had really gone that way, or whether the other version, the falling, the blood, was the true one. He just picked up the gel-penned napkin from the coffee table, studied the little screaming face at the peak, and said, "You put me at the top of a pyramid."

The party had spilled from the Kowalskis' kitchen onto the lawn, and Isabella stood near the fence holding a cup of punch she hadn't touched, watching her classmates invent dances that would embarrass them by August. Someone had strung lights between the porch and the maple. Everyone she could see was going somewhere in the fall: state schools, a conservatory in Boston, one gap year that nobody believed would last only a year.

She found Devon by the cooler, turning a can of soda in his hands without opening it. "You counted the yard yet?" he asked. "Like a census. I keep doing it without meaning to."

"Counted what?"

"Who's here." He nodded toward the lawn. "Four hundred and six of us started ninth grade together. Or close to that. There are maybe three hundred backdrops back there."

Isabella did the subtraction in her head and didn't like the remainder. "Some moved. Some went private. Marcus went to that academy in his dad's city."

"Sure," Devon said. "But not all of them." He popped the can, took one sip, and set it on the fence post like evidence he intended to return to. "I looked it up last night, because I couldn't sleep. The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in 2021-22. Eighty-seven. I kept saying it to my ceiling."

"That's the whole country, though. Not us."

"We're not special," Devon said, and wandered off toward the music, leaving her with the number.

She followed the fence line, and the arithmetic walked with her. Thirteen percent somewhere, distributed across four years, invisible until you stood in a backyard and noticed the absences the way you notice a missing tooth. Her younger self had assumed that everyone who started simply kept going, the way a river does, and the correction felt less like information than like a debt she hadn't known she owed.

In her back pocket, her phone held a message she'd received in March and never answered. She stepped behind the garage where the music thinned and read it again, the way she'd read it a dozen times. It was from Renata, who had sat beside her in biology sophomore year and then, by junior year, sat nowhere. "i know this is weird. i'm getting my GED in june instead of walking. i didn't drop out, i want you to know that, it just looked exactly like dropping out from the outside. my mom got sick and somebody had to be home. anyway. you were the only person who noticed i stopped coming. you don't have to reply. it just felt wrong to graduate without telling anyone why i wasn't there." Isabella had drafted four replies and deleted each one, afraid that sympathy would sound like pity, afraid that silence was its own verdict. Now she typed the simplest true thing: "i noticed. i'm at a party and it's strange and you should know you're the reason it's strange. GED in june is graduating. come find me after." She pressed send before she could litigate the sentence further, and watched the word delivered appear beneath it.

The Kowalskis' dog, a belligerent little terrier who had spent the evening defending the sandbox from toddlers, streaked past her and hurled himself at the fence, barking at nothing on the other side. She watched him and thought that everyone at this party was standing on some substrate they never examined, the four quiet years of attendance and passing grades, and that Renata had been standing on something too, just a different and harder material, one that didn't come with a ceremony.

Devon reappeared at her elbow with two cups of punch and handed her one. "You look like you found a name in the missing column."

"Renata Alvarez. Junior year. Her mom got sick." Isabella took a drink, and the sweetness surprised her. "I'm not sure that's all of it either. But it's part of it."

"You going to track the rest down?" He said it lightly, but she understood he was asking whether she intended to turn the evening into an accounting, a ledger of everyone the cohort had quietly set down along the way, or whether she could hold both things at once: the joy of the lit yard and the fence-line of people who should have been in it.

"I don't know," she said. "Maybe some. Probably not all." The lights hummed above them; someone had put on a song from freshman year, and the whole lawn shouted the chorus like a promise made in the dark. Her phone buzzed once against her hip, and she reached for it.

Elijah arrived at the community center gym twenty minutes early, the way he had every Tuesday since October, and found Marcus already there, shooting free throws with his back to the door. The league was a patchwork thing, six teams of boys who mostly did not go to school together, and their team, the one sponsored by Delgado's Hardware, had started the season 4 and 1. Then they lost three in a row, and the losses had a sound to them: Marcus yelling at Dev for not passing, Dev calling Marcus a ball hog, the younger kids going quiet on the bench. Elijah wanted one thing, which was to finish the season with a team that still liked each other. He was not sure this was the same thing as winning, and he kept trying to decide whether it was.

The fight that night started over a screen. Marcus set it late, Dev's defender slipped under it, Dev turned the ball over, and on the walk back up the court Dev said, "You want forty shots a game, just say it." Marcus said, "I want to win, which is different from what you want." By the time they got to the locker room, Coach Reyes had stopped trying to forestall it. He stood in the doorway with a folded piece of paper and put it on the bench where Marcus could not miss it.

The note was short. Elijah read it over Marcus's shoulder: "Storming. Look it up. Practice Thursday." Marcus crumpled it and threw it into the corner, which was its own kind of answer, and left. Elijah picked the paper back up, smoothed it against his thigh, and took it home.

At his kitchen table he typed the word into his phone. What came up was a psychologist named Bruce Tuckman, who proposed in 1965 that groups develop through four stages: forming, storming, norming and performing. He read it twice. The names sounded like something from a worksheet, but he recognized the shape of it immediately, the polite first weeks, then the arguments, and something after that he could not picture yet. He texted his older sister at college, because she was studying psychology and he wanted to check that the internet had not invented it.

"Real thing," she wrote back. "They made us memorize it. Forming, storming, norming, performing. Tuckman, 1965. Why, did your team finally start fighting?"

"Coach left it on a note," Elijah typed. "Marcus threw it out."

"Of course he did," she wrote. "Wanting to be the guy who scores is its own philosophy. Everything Marcus does has a logos. The question is whether the team's is the same one."

Elijah set the phone down and thought about Marcus's want, which was not a mystery: Marcus believed he was the best player on the floor, which was true, and believed that this meant the offense should run through him, which had stopped being true the moment teams started doubling him. Dev wanted touches, the younger kids wanted minutes, and Elijah wanted whatever held all of it together, though he could not have said in one sentence what that was. On Thursday he brought the note to practice and left it on the bench again, unfolded this time.

Dev found it first. "What's forming, storming, norming, performing?" he said, reading it aloud, pronouncing the words carefully like a list he was being tested on. Marcus came over and looked at the paper, and Elijah said, "Some psychologist, Tuckman. He says groups go through it. We're supposed to be in the storming part." Marcus read the screen of Elijah's propped-up phone for a long moment, then said, "So we're normal," and walked back out to the court. It was the closest thing to an apology anyone had offered all season.

The norming happened without ceremony. Dev started calling screens early so Marcus could hear them, and Marcus started throwing the skip pass he had hoarded all year, and the younger kids got their minutes in a blowout against the church team that they won by nineteen. The performing, if that was the word, arrived on a Sunday in December, the last scheduled game, against the league's best team: they ran a set play with four passes and no words, and Elijah, who had not scored all afternoon, cut to the basket and laid it in at the buzzer. In the locker room afterward the noise was all of them at once, and Reyes stood in the corner with the box scores and a new piece of paper.

"League's folding," he said. "Center lost the gym rental budget in the county vote Tuesday. We already played the last game." He held up the paper, which was a flyer for a winter clinic at a gym across town, and Marcus took it from his hand and folded it into his pocket before anyone else could move.

Sarah spread the ocean current map across the picnic table, weighting the corners with her mother's gardening stones because the wind in the backyard had opinions about paper. The map came from Mr. Okafor's class, and Monday she had to stand up and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe, which was a strange thing to be asked to do in a town four hundred kilometers from any ocean.

The arrows on the map curved like rivers made of color. Some were red, fat and confident, sweeping up out of the tropics. Others were blue, thinner, dragging down the eastern edges of continents. Sarah had assumed, on first glance, that red meant fast, the way red on a speedometer means you are about to ruin your day. It was a reasonable guess, and it was wrong, and the wrongness had already cost her. On Thursday's quiz she had written that the Gulf Stream must be the speediest current in the Atlantic because its arrows were the reddest, and Mr. Okafor had written in the margin, in his dour red pen, "See me. You are reading the colors as speed. They are not speed."

Her cousin DeShaun was sprawled on the grass with his phone held above his face like a man watching his own private sky. "You've been staring at that table for twenty minutes," he said. "Is the map going to confess?"

"It lied to me," Sarah said. "Or I lied to myself. One of those."

She texted her friend Priya, who kept every handout from every class in a color-coded binder that mesmerized the entire honors track. The message she composed lay in the grass beside DeShaun, drafted three times: "Priya. Ocean map emergency. If the red arrows don't mean speed, what do they mean? Because I told Okafor the Gulf Stream was the fastest current in the Atlantic and he looked at me the way you look at a pigeon that has flown into a window. Answer fast, I am outside and the wind is trying to eat my homework."

Priya's reply came in pieces, as her replies always did. First a photo of the legend from her own map, zoomed in so close it was mostly pixels. Then: "look at the KEY sarah." Then: "the key at the bottom. bottom left. i can see your soul from here."

Sarah found the key. It was small and polite and had been sitting there the whole time, under her thumb print of potato chip grease. Warm currents, red arrows. Cold currents, blue arrows. Temperature, not speed. She read it twice, then a third time, and felt the specific embarrassment of someone who has confidently explained to a room that the moon is a lamp.

"Okay," she said out loud. "Okay, so the red arrows are warm water."

"Congratulations," DeShaun said, without lowering the phone. "You're a scientist."

"Warm water moving north." She traced the Gulf Stream with one finger, up along the coast of America, then curving east across the Atlantic toward Europe. The line of it was almost elegant, like a delivery route drawn by someone who cared about beauty. Warm water, traveling north, arriving at places like Britain and Norway, which by latitude should have been far colder than they were. That was the assignment: explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe. And suddenly the explanation wasn't a paragraph to memorize, it was this red river on the paper, carrying warmth the way a train carries passengers.

"But how fast is it, actually?" she asked. "The map doesn't say. Red could be slow and warm. Blue could be fast and cold. I don't know the speeds at all."

"So find out," DeShaun said. "Or don't. Say 'the map shows temperature, and the speed is a separate question,' and be the only person in class who admits it."

Sarah considered this. Half the kids on Monday would recite whatever the first search result said, smooth and certain. She could be certain too, easily, and be wrong the way she'd been wrong about the red. Or she could stand up there like a small dissident against false confidence and say: this is what the map shows, warm currents in red and cold in blue, this is the warm river crossing to Europe, and this is where my knowledge ends.

She flipped the map over and wrote on the back in pencil, drafting her Monday speech in the flattest language she could manage, then crossing out the flattest parts. DeShaun wandered over, read over her shoulder, and tapped one line. "You wrote 'the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe' twice in two sentences."

"It's the assignment. It bears repeating."

"It's repetitive is what it is." He picked up one of the gardening stones and set it on her pencil, a small dour monument. She shoved him and he laughed and sat back down in the grass.

The wind picked up again, tugging the map's corner free so the whole thing snapped like a sail. Sarah pressed it flat with both hands and looked at the red arrows one more time, the warm river running north and east, toward countries she had never seen, carrying heat across an entire ocean. Then she took a photo of the map with the key circled in her thumb, and sent it to Priya with one word: "Monday."

Jordan had until five o'clock tomorrow to submit a written critique of a Frida Kahlo painting for the community studio's youth show, and the studio had decided, in its mysterious apportionment of good and bad luck, that his assigned painting was the one with the wounded deer.

He'd spent the evening sprawled on the paint-spattered couch with a print of it, feeling torpid, while Priya across the room worked on her own critique with the smug efficiency of someone who had already finished a draft. "You could just describe it," she said. "Deer, arrows, ocean, done."

"That's a list, not a critique." He held the print at arm's length, then closer, then tipped his head sideways until Priya laughed at him. "Ms. Okafor wants formal analysis. Colour, composition, symbolism. Three paragraphs, apparently, or the universe collapses."

"So write the paragraphs."

The problem, which he could not explain without sounding like an idiot, was that he had two ideas about the painting and they refused to sit in the same paragraph. One idea was technical: something about how the greens of the forest and the red of the deer's wound and the sky's streaks pushed against each other, so the whole surface seemed to hum. The other idea was about Kahlo putting her own face on a pierced animal, which was either the saddest self-portrait ever made or a joke at the expense of everyone who expected women to paint flowers. He couldn't tell which idea was the real one, and every draft he started collapsed into either art-vocabulary soup or feelings with no evidence.

The deadline was real because the youth show opened Saturday and the critiques would hang beside the paintings. Priya had already read hers aloud twice, partly to help him and mostly, he suspected, to aggrandize herself, since her critique of the Diego Rivera print contained the phrase "monumental dignity of labor" four times.

"You're overcomplicating," she said. "Pick the hummingbird. Write about the hummingbird."

"I can't just pick symbolism. It has to connect to how the painting is built." He flattened the print on the table and squinted at the deer's neck, where the wound ran red against leaves so green they looked lit from inside. Something about that pairing kept snagging him. He dragged out the studio's big wooden colour wheel, a wheel Priya called the pizza of knowledge, and spun it until he found what he was looking for. Red sat directly across from green, opposite each other on the wheel.

"Complementary colours," he said. "They sit opposite each other on the wheel, like red and green."

"So?"

"So look." He held the wheel beside the print. "She puts them side by side everywhere. The wound against the leaves, the ribbon against the branches. And when they're side by side they make each other look brighter. That's why the painting vibrates. It's not just blood, it's blood made louder by green."

Priya came over, which he counted as a victory. She looked, really looked, tilting her head the way he had, and said, "Huh," in the tone of someone annoyed to be interested. "So the hummingbird's not just a symbol, it's also red hanging in green."

"Right. Or, wait." He turned the print over and back, as if the back might hold the answer. "It's both. The colour makes you look, and then what you're looking at is the wound. The brightness is the argument. Kahlo builds a glowing painting so you can't look away from the thing that hurts." He said it out loud and heard, for the first time, his two ideas snapping together like magnets.

He wrote fast, filling the margin with crossed-out words, while Priya read over his shoulder and periodically said "monumental dignity" to annoy him. At one point she leaned on his arm mid-sentence and he wrote "grn" by accident and had to fix it.

By eight, he had a draft with a real thesis: that the composition led your eye in a circle, down the neck, through the ocean, back up the antlers, so the deer never got to rest, and the complementary reds and greens kept the whole loop humming. In his last paragraph he admitted the thing he still couldn't settle, which was whether the deer was despair or defiance, and argued that the painting refused to choose, and that maybe refusing to choose was the point. Priya read that part twice.

"It's better than mine," she said. "Don't tell anyone I said that."

He printed it at the front desk, folded it, and put it in his backpack. Then he turned the colour wheel idly with one finger, watching red and green chase each other around and around, until Priya pulled his sleeve and said, "Come on, they're locking up," and he left it still spinning.

Hayden stood in front of the Trajectory Table at the science museum for the fourth time that afternoon, feeding tokens into the coin slot like a man paying a debt in installments. The exhibit was simple: a pneumatic launcher at one end of a six-meter table, a row of movable cups down the far edge, and a dial that set the launch angle. A brass plaque claimed that a ball fired at twenty degrees would land in the fourth cup, and Hayden had watched three balls sail over that cup and bounce off the table's rim, which was the closest thing to proof he'd had all week that the universe was willing to contradict authority.

He had failed the projectile quiz on Tuesday. Not a graceful failure, either; he'd solved for the landing distance by multiplying the launch speed by the flight time, which had felt like common sense and had earned a red circle and the word "components" in the margin. The problem, he'd gathered since, was that the ball's speed wasn't one thing going one direction. It was two things at once, sideways and vertical, and the sideways part didn't care about gravity at all.

"You're hogging it," said a voice behind him. A girl about his age stood there with a museum volunteer badge clipped crookedly to her jacket, though the badge belonged, judging by the photo, to someone named Dolores. "I mean, you can hog it, it's your token. But my break's in ten minutes and I've been trying to beat this thing for a week."

"Priya," she said, when he stepped aside. She fed a token, set the dial to twenty degrees, and watched the ball clear the fourth cup by a full handspan. "See? The plaque's wrong. I told the floor manager and he said the plaque was reviewed by an engineer, so." She shrugged, a small visceral gesture of someone who had lost an argument with laminated paper.

Hayden told her about the quiz. He told her about the red circle, and, because it seemed relevant, about the time in seconds that the ball spent in the air, which the exhibit printed helpfully on a small screen after every shot: 0.62 seconds. "So if I knew how fast it was moving sideways," he said slowly, "the horizontal distance it travels would just be that constant sideways velocity multiplied by the time it's in the air. Multiply once, and you get where it lands."

Priya pulled a phone from her pocket. "It says launch speed is 6.2 meters per second. So times 0.62 is," she paused, tapping, "3.8 meters." She walked the table with her arm extended, counting meters aloud from the launcher, and stopped at a point well past the fourth cup and just short of the sixth. "But that's using the whole speed as if it's all going sideways. Your red circle says no."

"Right. At an angle, some of it's going up." Hayden crouched at the table's edge, trying to see the ball's path as two arrows instead of one diagonal. "At zero degrees, all of it is sideways. At ninety, all of it is up and it just drops. Twenty degrees is somewhere between." He had no protractor, no calculator, no sine table, and the museum was not going to provide trigonometry. But the cups were movable, and the flight time was printed, and the launch speed was fixed at 6.2. He could run the experiment the universe was already running.

They fired at five degrees, ten, twenty, thirty, calling out the landing cup after each shot while Priya logged it, and Hayden noticed something that made the back of his neck warm: the printed flight time shrank as the angle rose, exactly as it should if more of the speed were being spent upward.
