He had the landing distances and the times. What he lacked was the sideways speed at twenty degrees, but between ten degrees and thirty degrees, the ball had landed in cups five and seven, and twenty sat between them. "I can't compute it," he admitted, "but I can interpolate. Somewhere near cup six."

At twenty degrees the ball struck the lip of the sixth cup and dropped in. Priya cheered loudly enough that a docent looked over, and Hayden laughed, an unguarded sound he hadn't produced in a physics classroom all year. "The plaque says four," Priya said, snapping a photo of the ball in the cup with the wrong brass plaque in the frame. "The plaque says four, and the logos of the whole thing, the actual logic, says six." She wrote on the museum's comment card in careful block letters: PLAQUE WRONG. CHECK SIXTH CUP. SLOW MOTION VIDEO IF YOU DON'T BELIEVE US.

"You know they might just throw that out," Hayden said.

"Then I'll fill out another one next Saturday." She fed one of her own tokens, set the dial, and stepped back. "Twenty degrees. Call it."

"Cup six," Hayden said, and gripped the table's railing as the launcher hissed.

The email arrived on Tuesday afternoon, and Alexander read it three times before showing it to anyone. The community hall confirmation read, in cheerful administrative font, that Room B was reserved for Thursday evening, April 13th, for the Feldman family Seder. His grandmother had handed him the task in January, the way she handed him things now, without ceremony, as if he had already agreed. You're old enough to run it, she'd said. Your grandfather's hands shake. Your father will help but you'll lead. He had spent two months learning the order of the evening, the fifteen steps, the blessings he'd mumbled through for years and now had to actually know, and somewhere in those months he had also, confidently, filled out the hall reservation form.

He found his father in the garage, sanding a drawer he had no intention of finishing. "Dad. The hall. I put down the wrong night." His father set the sandpaper down. "What do you mean, the wrong night?" Alexander turned the phone toward him. "The thirteenth. I booked the thirteenth." His father looked at the screen for a long moment, and then he laughed, one short syllable that did not quite presage disaster but wasn't comfort either. "You did what your grandfather did in 1987," he said. "He showed up a day late for everything for the first year he kept it."

Alexander stood there feeling the ground shift slightly under a fact he had somehow never assembled, though it had been in front of him his whole life. Every Seder he could remember had happened in the evening, and it had never once occurred to him to ask why the first Seder and the second Seder fell on what the secular calendar called different days, or why his grandmother lit candles at dusk on Fridays and called it the start of Shabbat. He said, slowly, testing it, "So the holiday starts at sundown. The evening that starts it, not the evening that ends it." His father nodded. "In Judaism, a day begins at sundown. So the Seder is the night that begins the holiday." Alexander heard his own voice repeat it back, and the sentence settled into place like a key turning.

The problem was concrete and getting more so by the hour. The first Seder was Wednesday night. It was Tuesday. The hall was booked for Thursday, and the office closed at five, and his cousin Talia was flying in from Chicago expecting a table, and his grandmother had already cooked enough food for an army of epicures, brisket and kugel and the chicken soup she refused to let anyone else season. Alexander called the hall and was told, by a woman who sounded genuinely sorry, that Wednesday was taken by a baptism rehearsal. He called his uncle, whose apartment could maybe hold fifteen people if nobody breathed. He sat on the garage steps with his phone dark in his hand and thought about telling his grandmother she'd been right to give this to someone older.

Instead he went back inside and made a judicious call, the kind his grandmother would have made: he asked his aunt Rena, who lived four blocks away and had a dining room she was vain about and had not been asked because of some argument nobody could remember the origin of. She picked up on the second ring. "Aunt Rena. I booked the hall for the wrong night and I need your table and I'm asking you first, before Dad suggests it, because it should be my asking." There was a pause long enough that he counted his own heartbeat. "Fifteen people," she said. "Sixteen with Talia's girlfriend. I have three tables. Come at four and help me move them."

Wednesday morning his grandmother stood at the stove and did not step aside. Alexander washed vegetables beside her, and when he asked whether she wanted to lead the four questions, since his grandfather always had, she said, "You're leading. I'll correct you when you're wrong, that's different." At four he carried chairs down Rena's street, two at a time, his arms aching in a way that felt like part of the work. Talia arrived at five with her girlfriend, Mara, who had never been to a Seder and asked Alexander, while he arranged the seder plate, why they were doing this tonight instead of tomorrow. "Because the day starts at sundown," he said. "So this evening is the one that begins the holiday. That's the whole thing. Tomorrow is the second night, a second Seder." Mara nodded slowly and said, "That's actually beautiful," and Talia said, "Don't tell him that, he's unbearable already."

The candles were lit at 7:41, the exact minute printed on his grandmother's fridge calendar, and he watched the flame and felt the evening tip from preparation into the thing itself. He poured the first cup, lifted it, and began the kiddush in a voice that shook on the second word and steadied by the fourth. His grandfather's eyes were closed, his lips moving along. When Alexander stumbled on a phrase, his grandmother said the correct word once, quietly, without opening her eyes, and he took it up and continued.

Between the blessing and the washing, Aunt Rena caught his eye across the table and raised her glass a fraction of an inch. Later, during dinner, she would tell him the argument that had kept her from these tables was stupid, and he would tell her he'd known that for years, and they would both laugh. But for now he was standing at the head of the room, sixteen people waiting, the afikoman already hidden somewhere in the house by his youngest cousin. Alexander broke the middle matzah in two, held up the larger piece, and said, "Hide this well, Dov. I'm counting on you to make it hard."

The kitchen clock said 9:40, and Charlie had until 8 a.m. tomorrow to understand something she had pretended to understand for three weeks. She spread her notes across the counter between the toaster and her mother's bread dough, which was rising under a damp towel and filling the room with a warm, yeasty patience she did not share. The retake was her last chance to stay eligible for the spring research program, and Mr. Osei had underlined one problem type in red: given mass, find moles of product.

Her brother Theo sat on the floor by the sink with a flashlight, investigating the pipes. "This copper's all bent," he reported. "That's because it's ductile. It bends without snapping. I learned it for my thing."

"What thing?"

"My museum thing. Saturday. I have to explain an exhibit for ten whole minutes." He aimed the flashlight upward. "I'm going to be a virtuoso of explaining. Like the guy in the video."

Charlie pulled her calculator toward her and copied the equation from her notes onto the back of a grocery receipt: 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O. Then, because Theo was watching and because counting was the only part she trusted, she counted the atoms out loud, tapping the pen. "Four hydrogens on the left. Four on the right. Two oxygens, two oxygens. Okay. So two moles of hydrogen gas react with one mole of oxygen gas, and you get two moles of water." She said it twice more, quietly, the way she used to recite locker combinations.

"Wait," Theo said, standing up. "That's my exhibit. The hydrogen wall. There's this big equation and you burn hydrogen and water comes out. The guy in the video says it and then there's like a little flame and the beater gets foggy."

"The beaker?"

"Whatever. Can you do it? Mom has matches."

"Mom has a quiz tomorrow and no lab." But she looked at the equation again, and something small shifted in her, the way a knot loosens before you actually pull it. The equation wasn't a decoration. It was a ratio. Two to one to two. If she knew how much hydrogen she had, the equation told her how much water she'd get, the way a recipe told you how many loaves came from a bag of flour. She found the molar mass of hydrogen gas in her notes, 2.016 grams per mole, and wrote it on the receipt.

"Let's say you had eight grams of hydrogen," she said, mostly to herself. "Eight divided by 2.016, that's about 3.97 moles. And the equation says two moles of hydrogen gives two moles of water. Same number of moles." She worked the division twice, got 3.97 both times, and felt the steadiness of it, a floor under her feet where there had been a drop. "So 3.97 moles of water. That's it. That's the whole problem."

"Is that a lot?" Theo asked.

She weighed it out in her head. "A mole of water is about eighteen grams, so around seventy grams. Half a glass, from something you can't even see." She looked at the glass by the sink, ordinary and clear, and then at the dough rising under its towel, and thought that everything in the kitchen was like this if you stopped to ask. Her body would metabolize the bread tomorrow, break it into pieces too small to name, and no one would call that a miracle either.

"You could come Saturday," Theo said. "The video guy says people who explain things to someone else get way better. Like a hundred percent."

"I have to be honest, I don't know if explaining it makes me a virtuoso or just someone who got one problem right on a receipt." She folded the receipt into her pocket anyway. "But you can quiz me. Say the equation."

He squared his shoulders, held the flashlight like a microphone. "Two moles of hydrogen gas react with one mole of oxygen gas to form two moles of water."

"Good," she said, and turned the page to the next problem.

The radiator in Room 214 clanked all through sixth period, and Violet had stopped hearing it until the question on the board made her hear it again. Predict the effect of an increase in temperature on the reaction below, Ms. Okafor had written, and beneath it, N2 + 3H2 goes to 2NH3, with a note in parentheses: exothermic. Violet's pencil hovered. She could do pressure shifts, concentration shifts, the whole tidy logic of Le Chatelier, the system pushed one way and pushing back. But temperature had always slid past her. Temperature was not a substance you could add. It was everywhere at once, like weather, like her mood since March.

Around her, pens moved. Marcus, two seats over, was already underlining something with the flat certainty he brought to every answer, right or wrong. Priya had her hand half raised, then lowered it, then raised it again, and Ms. Okafor said, "Hold your thoughts, everyone. Lab partners, compare. I want arguments, not answers." Violet turned to the boy beside her, Daniel, who was re-copying the equation as though neatness might make it confess.

"It shifts left," Daniel said. "Heat speeds things up, so it makes more product, but then it makes less, but the forward reaction is exothermic so..." He trailed off into the shape of his own confusion, and Violet felt a small, unwelcome warmth toward him for being honest about it. She had spent most of the semester protecting the opposite impression, that she understood everything, which had disenfranchised her from the one thing she actually needed: the right to ask a dumb question.

"If you can't add it," she said slowly, "then what does 'adding temperature' even mean." The radiator clanked. She thought, without warning, of her grandmother's kitchen in February, the stove going all afternoon, and of the evening she had sat there with this same textbook and no Wi-Fi, snow sealing the road, her grandmother humming over a pot of something that needed to simmer. She had been so bored that week, a damp, subterranean ennui, that she had resorted to the homework she'd brought to avoid doing. Same chapter. Same equation. And she remembered what she had done, because it had felt almost criminal at the time.

"Give me your pencil," she told Daniel, and he surrendered it warily. On his paper, beneath the equation, she wrote: N2 + 3H2 goes to 2NH3 + heat. Daniel frowned. "You can't just add heat to the equation." "Watch me," she said. "It's exothermic. So heat is a product. It's like the ammonia, it comes out of the reaction." She held the pencil still, testing the idea against the week in her grandmother's kitchen, where it had first appeared to her as a way of making an unsolvable problem solvable, a trick she had trusted only because nothing else had worked. "And if a reaction is endothermic instead, heat is a reactant. It goes on the left. It goes in."

"Okay," Daniel said, but his voice was careful, the voice of someone deciding whether to be convinced or embarrassed. "So if heat is a product and you raise the temperature." "You're adding product," Violet said. "The system shifts away from it. Left, toward the reactants." She looked at what she had written and felt the ground of it, solid in the way her grandmother's kitchen floor had been solid, tile warmed all afternoon by the stove. Heat as a product, heat as a reactant; the whole slippery question of temperature suddenly had handles.

Ms. Okafor drifted past their desk and paused at the penciled equation. Violet braced for correction, for the eraser, for the phrase "you can't just." Instead Ms. Okafor read it twice and said only, "Say that to the class, Violet," and moved on, which was its own kind of verdict, though Violet noticed she did not say whether the trick was a real method or a useful lie, a model that happened to work, and that question stayed with Violet longer than the answer did. She had lived inside models before. Last spring she had modeled herself as fine, cheerful, recovered, and the model had worked right up until the day it didn't, which was March, which was why her mood was weather now. She knew better than to trust a model completely. She also knew that a model that got her through the problem was not nothing.

When Ms. Okafor called on her, Violet stood with Daniel's paper still in her hand, its rewritten equation facing her like a small window. "Exothermic means heat is a product," she said to the class, her voice steadier than she expected. "Endothermic means it's a reactant. So raising the temperature is adding it, and the system pushes the other way." Marcus looked up from his underlining with an expression she couldn't read, possibly defeat, possibly interest, possibly the recalculation of everything he'd written. Ms. Okafor wrote "shifts left" on the board and then, beneath it, drew a long arrow pointing to the right.

"What's the arrow for?" Priya asked.

"That," Ms. Okafor said, capping her marker, "is next semester."

The kitchen table had disappeared under Mia's science fair supplies by four o'clock: agar plates, a borrowed scale, a box of cotton swabs, and a two-pound bag of table salt with a nutrition label she had read four times without understanding. Her project was supposed to answer whether salt slowed the growth of bacteria she'd swabbed from the kitchen counter, and the article Mrs. Okafor had printed for her kept using the word epidemiology, describing researchers who tracked illness through populations the way Mia was tracking colonies across a grid of plates. She liked that idea, that a kitchen counter could be a small country and she its mapmaker.

The trouble was her procedure sheet. At the bottom, in Mrs. Okafor's tidy handwriting, it said: convert your salt masses to moles before you record them. Mia had read the sentence so many times it had gone smooth and meaningless, like a stone handled all winter.

"You're going to need the good scale, not the kitchen one," her brother Danny said, sliding onto the chair across from her with a granola bar. He was twelve and considered himself her lab assistant by right of proximity.

"The kitchen one measures grams. That's fine." She tore a paper towel, set it on the scale, and zeroed it. Then she poured salt until the display read 175.0. The plan called for three concentrations, and this was the first. She copied the number onto her data sheet and then sat staring at the blank column beside it, the one labeled moles.

"Like the animal," Danny said, mouth full.

"No." She pulled her chemistry textbook toward her, flipped through the chapter on quantities in reactions, and found the periodic table with the atomic masses printed beneath each element's name. Sodium, 22.99. Chlorine, 35.45. She added them on her calculator twice because the first answer seemed too plain: 58.44. She checked the textbook's example and saw the same number there, printed beside the formula NaCl. Sodium chloride, table salt, molar mass 58.44 grams per mole.

"Say that again?" Danny leaned over the book.

"Sodium chloride. Fifty-eight point four four grams per mole." She wrote it at the top of her notes in capital letters so she would not lose it, and then did what she always did with a number she did not trust: she asked it a question. If one mole weighed 58.44 grams, then 175 grams was not one mole, and it was not two. She divided, 175.0 by 58.44, and got 2.99. Almost exactly three. She stared at that small, unlikely neatness, then divided again and got 2.9946, which was less neat and somehow more believable.

Her mother came through with groceries and paused at the table. "How much did that kit cost?"

"Twenty dollars. But the plates are sterile and the swabs are reusable, so I can amortize it," Mia said. "Danny can use the leftovers next year for his mold bread thing."

"I will not be doing mold bread," Danny said, with dignity.

Mia weighed the second sample, 58.4 grams, and wrote one mole beside it, checking her own confidence like a loose tooth. She was honest enough with herself to know the conversion was arithmetic, not understanding; she could not yet say why chemists wanted moles at all, only that they counted substances by weight and that this was how. Somewhere between the bag of salt and the textbook there had been a small tectonic shift in her thinking, the plate of it moving quietly, and she could feel that something had resettled even if she could not name the new terrain.

She weighed the smallest sample last, 29.2 grams, and wrote half a mole, then sat back. On the counter beside the stove, the first agar plate waited with its lid on, and the article on epidemiology lay folded to a page about rates and populations, and outside the window the light was going the color of weak tea. Mia picked up the cotton swab, rubbed it once along the cutting board, and lifted the lid of the plate.

"Ready?" she said.

Danny leaned in, granola bar forgotten.

I did not care about the showcase, which is why I stayed up past lights-out rewriting my critique for the third time. The art shed at Camp Wanoka had one good lamp and a wasp nest above the door, and I claimed the desk every night that last week of July because it was quiet, not because I wanted to win. That's what I told Marisol, anyway, and she rolled her eyes at me, which I chose to ignore.

The workshop was Ms. Petro's idea, though she mostly sat by the fan and let us fight. Twelve of us, reproduction prints taped to the plywood tables, learning to say why a painting worked instead of just whether we liked it. I had always been a liker. I liked sunsets, I liked dogs, and by Wednesday I understood that none of that counted as thinking. Marisol, who was doctrinaire about formal analysis in a way that made her insufferable and right, kept saying, "Colour first, then composition, then symbolism. In that order. Feelings last, if there's room." I thought that order was a cage until I got inside it and found it was actually a ladder.

My print was The Broken Column. I'd picked it because everyone else wanted the one with the monkeys, and because on the first day I'd looked at it for ten seconds and had to look away, which I did not admit to anyone, including myself. I told the table I picked it for the palette. The desert greens, the cracked earth, the grey of the corset. "Good," Marisol said, without looking up. "Say something about the nails."

There were nails in the painting, driven into the figure's face and body, and tears running down her cheeks. That much I could catalog. What I couldn't catalog, what kept sending me out to the wasp nest for air, was that despite all of it she looks straight at the viewer. The eyes don't ask for anything. They don't even accuse. They just meet yours, and then you're the one who has to decide what to do with your own face. I wrote three paragraphs trying to explain my discomfort and deleted all three, because they were about me, and the assignment, annoyingly, was about her.

Thursday night Marisol found me in the shed at eleven. "Petro says you're folding," she said, dropping onto the stool. "She said you called your draft garbage."

"I called it garbage because it is garbage. It's a list. The tears symbolize pain, the column symbolizes her spine, it reads like a fortune cookie."

"So stop maligning your own draft and fix it. You have the whole fact on the page and you're hiding behind it." She tapped my notebook. "Nails through the face and body, tears on the cheeks, and she's looking straight out at us. You wrote that like it's the setup. It's the whole thing. The discomfort you keep not admitting is data."

"That's not data, that's me being weird."

"Then be weird on purpose." She stole my grape soda and left, which is how you know she cares.

So Friday, at the showcase, when Petro called my name, I stood in front of everyone with my notecards and did not use them. I talked about the green of the valley against the dry pale sky, how the vertical split of the body pulls your eye down the way the column does, how the corset straps cut the canvas into bands. I talked about the tears and the nails as symbols you could name without explaining away, the way you can name a wound without knowing who struck it. And then I said the true part, the part I'd decided to keep. "Every critique I wrote before this one tried to figure out why her gaze is unbearable, and I don't think that's a question with an answer. She's pierced everywhere, she's crying, and she still looks straight out at you. When you meet her eyes, the painting stops being about her pain and becomes about your looking. You want to glance away and there's nowhere to glance. I'm telling you I don't know what to do with that, and I don't think a formal analysis is supposed to solve it. I think it's supposed to stand there, the way she does."

The applause was thin, because it was 90 degrees and half the camp was asleep, but Marisol nodded once, hard, like a referee calling a point. Petro did not pick my critique for the yearbook page, the thing I supposedly did not care about; she picked a boy named Devon's essay on the monkeys, which was tidy and had a thesis. Marisol was furious on my behalf, which was more satisfying than winning would have been, though I planned to keep pretending otherwise.

After the showcase I walked down to the lake with the last grape soda and sat on the dock. Marisol came and sat beside me and didn't say anything for a while, which for her was practically a sacrament. Somewhere behind us a counselor was rounding up stragglers, and I felt the particular ennui of the last night of anything, when you're too tired for what's ending and it hasn't ended yet.

"Devon's essay was better organized," I said.

"Devon's essay would've been fine about a shoe ad." She nudged my elbow. "You going to do this in college? The whole looking-at-things-till-it-hurts thing?"

"Undecided," I said, and she laughed, and out on the water a fish rose and fell, one silver circle widening and then gone.

Mrs. Okafor's living room smelled of burnt popcorn and peppered chicken, and every seat was taken by the time Zoe arrived with her father, carrying the drinks she'd been sent for. The neighbor had opened her house to half the street for the semifinal, and the television, usually reserved for cooking shows, had been angled toward the couch like an altar. Mr. Kessler held the best chair by right, as he did every tournament, and was holding forth about the striker he had lionized since the man was nineteen, some genius of the penalty box who, in Mr. Kessler's telling, had never once dived in his life.

Zoe sat on the floor near the coffee table, where the screensaver of her phone showed a referee's whistle. She had refereed under-twelves for two seasons, until a father in a raincoat had followed her to the car park shouting that she'd cost his son a trophy, and she had handed in her badge the following Monday. Nobody in this room knew that. She had told her father it was the early mornings. He had said, "Fair enough," and that had been the end of it, which was its own small wound.

In the eighty-eighth minute, the striker went down in the box under a challenge that looked, from the low camera angle, like nothing at all. The referee waved play on, and Mr. Keller stood up so fast his chair tipped. Zoe, before she could stop herself, said, "He's checking it." The screen had already cut to the referee standing with a hand pressed to his ear, his face blank, the whole stadium waiting on a man in a room somewhere watching replays.

"Checking what?" said Mr. Kessler. "He said no penalty. It's done."

"Not anymore." She was surprised by how steady her voice came out. "This World Cup, it's the first one with VAR. Video assistant referees. Russia, this year. They can look at goals, penalties, straight red cards, and if he booked the wrong player, even that."

Mrs. Okafor's nephew, Daniel, who was taking a gap year and considered himself the room's authority, scoffed from the doorway. "It's only for offsides," he said. "They announced it before the tournament."

"It's goals, penalties, reds, mistaken identity," Zoe said. "Four things. That's all four things." She had read the coverage in June, twice, mostly because she wanted to know whether the job she'd quit was about to become a different job. Daniel took out his phone, typed, and went quiet in a way that made three people laugh at him.

The wait stretched. Someone turned the popcorn bowl upside down over the coffee table and found only kernels. Zoe watched the referee's face and thought about the raincoat man, about how many of his grievances would have survived a camera. She had liked the whistle because it was precise, because it rewarded being certain, and she had quit on a night when she couldn't be. Whether the game was better now, whether anything was, with the final judgment pulled out of one person's head and into a replay room, she genuinely did not know. It felt like fairness and it felt like a smaller kind of courage, both at once, and she could not get the two ideas to lie flat together.

The verdict came in letters on the screen. No penalty. Mr. Kessler sat down heavily, and for a second Zoe thought the room's disappointment was the whole event. Then the referee pointed, unhurried, to the spot anyway, and the graphic resolved: the original challenge was still under review, and it had been judged a foul inside the area. A penalty, against her side, in the ninety-first minute.

The room erupted in a noise with no agreement in it at all. Daniel was saying, "That's not what you said, that's not one of the four," and Zoe was already answering, "Penalties, it's literally penalties, review the penalty decision itself," while Mr. Kessler stood with both hands on his head, decrying the end of football as his striker argued with a decision made by a person none of them would ever see.

The kick was taken while half the room still mid-protest. The keeper went the wrong way. Zoe stayed on the floor, hands flat on the carpet, having been right about the rules all the way down and wrong about everything that mattered to her, and Mrs. Okafor leaned over and said, "You knew all that off by heart?"

The room smelled of dry-erase marker and the oranges Ms. Ferrante left on the back table every Tuesday, though she never stayed. Math club was student-run, which meant Derek ran it, and Derek had written three problems on the board before most people had their backpacks off. Kyle sat near the window, third row, where the radiator clicked and the October light came in low enough to warm the back of his neck. He wanted the last problem. It was a polynomial, some arch of a function, and the question asked for its maximum, and Kyle had never once in his life found a maximum on purpose.

"You know calculus," Derek said, not looking at him.

"I know it exists." Kyle uncapped his pen. "That's the whole of my knowledge."

Priya slid into the seat beside him, already turning her notebook sideways so he could see. She had done the first derivative in four lines, fast, her handwriting tilting like it was running downhill. Kyle copied the setup slowly, term by term, watching how each power dropped and each coefficient multiplied. When he tried it himself on the second function, his hand kept wanting to skip steps, and twice he lost a sign and had to go back.

The room argued in the background. Tyler, who took everything as a personal contest, was insisting on something at the front, and Marcus was shaking his head with the sardonic patience of a boy who had been Tyler's lab partner all through chemistry. Kyle tuned them out until their voices got sharp enough to cut through.

"I got the derivative first," Tyler said. "You copied it wrong."

"I did not copy it. Look." Marcus turned his notebook toward the board. "Same problem, same derivative. Different original function. You dropped something."

Kyle leaned over. Tyler's function ended with a plus seven. Marcus's didn't. Otherwise the two lines were identical, and when each of them differentiated, they had arrived at exactly the same result, and now they were circling the same maximum on the same downward slope and calling each other's work garbage.

Kyle looked at his own page. He had the plus seven version. He differentiated it, term by term, and reached the same derivative Marcus had, and the difference between their original functions was just that seven, sitting at the end like a signature. He set the derivative equal to zero, solved, and got a clean number for where the arch peaked. Then, because it was there, he differentiated the constant by itself. Zero. He wrote it down, crossed it out, wrote it again. The seven vanished when you took the derivative, every time, the way a stone disappears when you throw it in the air and only the throwing is left.

"Wait," he said. Both of them looked at him. "The derivative of a constant is zero. That's why you got the same thing. Adding seven just moves the whole graph up and leaves the derivative alone." He slid his notebook into the aisle between them. "You're both right. You just drew the same hill at different heights."

Marcus took the notebook. Tyler read it twice, jaw working, the way he did before chess moves. "So who made the mistake?"

"Nobody. Or the textbook did, printing two versions." Kyle heard how thin that sounded. "Or one of us miscopied the board. I can't tell that part."

Derek came back and stood over the notebooks, and for a moment nobody said anything, and the radiator clicked twice. Tyler pulled out his phone and photographed the board, then his page, then Marcus's page, lining them up like evidence. He wanted a verdict. Kyle understood the want, felt it himself, the itch to force the world into a right answer and a wrong one, and he also understood that what he had found was narrower and stranger than a verdict: a rule that held no matter who was at fault. The maximum didn't even care. It sat at the same horizontal spot on both graphs, Tyler's floating seven units above Marcus's, two peaks stacked invisibly in the same column of air.

Ms. Ferrante's oranges had gone unclaimed again. Kyle got up, took one, and set it on Tyler's notebook like a gavel. Marcus laughed, short, and Tyler didn't, but he stopped arguing.

"Speciation," Priya said, peeling her own orange with her thumbnail. "This is how it happens in biology. One population drifts apart, and both of them survive."

"They're not species, they're arithmetic," Derek said.

"They're both true and they can't merge." She split the orange and handed Kyle half without asking.

Kyle sat back down and worked the maximum again from scratch, his way, slowly, and it exhilarated him more than he wanted anyone to see, the way the peak emerged from the algebra without his having to guess at it. At the top of the arch the function flattened, the derivative went to zero, and for one clean instant the thing stopped climbing and had not yet started falling. He wrote the coordinate in the margin and underlined it, then wrote beside it, in smaller letters, one version or both. Outside, the sun had dropped below the roofline, and the radiator ticked on.

"Same answer tomorrow?" Marcus asked, zipping his bag.

"Bring your own orange," Tyler said.

The screen door clapped shut behind Brayden, and the smell of his grandmother's house met him the way it always did, coffee and lemon polish and something faintly like peppermint from the tin she kept above the fridge. He had brought The Great Gatsby in his backpack, its spine cracked, its margins already tattooed with pencil, because Grandma's book club met on Thursdays and she had decided, unilaterally, that he was joining this month. He was sixteen and had plans that involved his phone and none that involved three women in their seventies discussing a novel he'd been assigned for English, but she'd made peach cobbler, and there was no real disincentive strong enough to compete with that.

"You read the whole thing?" Mrs. Okafor asked him before he'd even sat down. She had a way of asking questions that assumed yes.

"Twice," Brayden said. "The second time slower."

"Why slower?" Grandma set down the teapot.

"Because the first time I believed everything Nick said. The second time I kept catching him at stuff."

Mrs. Okafor's eyebrows rose, interested. She flipped her copy open to a page already flagged with a torn envelope. "Then you're ready for this. In The Great Gatsby, published in 1925, the narrator Nick Carraway says, 'I am one of the few honest people that I have ever known.'" She let the sentence sit there like a coin on a table. "Now. Your teacher wants an essay on the unreliable narrator. So tell me, is he?"

Brayden reached for his cobbler and then put the fork down, because his hands wanted to gesture. "That's the thing. That line is right before he's about to break up with Jordan, and he doesn't tell her the whole truth about why. He softens it. He narrates his own cowardice and calls it honesty in the same chapter."

Mrs. Prasad, who had said almost nothing, leaned forward. "So he's lying?"

"No," Brayden said, and then heard how certain it sounded and pulled back. "I don't think it's lying. It's more like..." He tried a few words in his mouth. Inchoate, that was the one for the feeling, a suspicion still soft at the edges. "He hides things. He doesn't mention that he's from money until it matters. He says he reserves judgment and then judges everybody. He's mad at Tom and Daisy for smashing things up and retreating into their money, but he shakes Tom's hand at the end. He's the only one who actually shows up for Gatsby's funeral, which is supposed to prove something, but he's also the one telling us it proves something."

Grandma poured his tea without asking whether he wanted it. "When I was your age I thought Nick was the only good person in that book."

"And now?"

"Now I think he wanted me to think that."

Brayden laughed, and then stopped, because the idea opened up under him like a trapdoor. "That's it, though. That's what I couldn't figure out for my essay. If he's unreliable, why do I still trust him when he says Daisy's voice is full of money? Why do I believe his descriptions of the parties?" He turned his fork over. "It's like he sutures you to his side. Every scene is stitched through his eyes, so even when you catch him bending something, you've already been seeing what he sees. You're in the wound with him."

Mrs. Prasad tapped the table. "So what's your thesis?"

"That's my problem," Brayden admitted. "Half of me thinks Nick is a liar who doesn't know he's lying, so the claim about honesty is dramatic irony. The other half thinks he does know, that he's confessing the whole time, hiding his failures in plain sight and hoping we won't look. And I can't decide, because Fitzgerald doesn't decide for you. Maybe both are true at once." He rubbed the back of his neck. "Can an essay end with 'I'm not sure'?"

"Mine did, in 1968," Mrs. Okafor said. "My professor wrote 'coward' in the margin. I kept it anyway."

Grandma carried the dishes to the sink, and through the window Brayden watched the light go long and gold over her tomato stakes, the same light, he thought, that fell on Gatsby's lawn at the end of that summer. He got up, found his pencil, and opened the book to the page with the envelope flag still tucked in it. At the top, above the famous line, he wrote in the margin: he says this right before he fails to be honest. Prove or complicate.

"Better than 'I'm not sure,'" Mrs. Prasad said, reading over his shoulder.

"Same thing," Brayden said, and underlined it twice.

The pen was chained to the clipboard, which struck Loic as an insult, as though a person filling out paperwork at a restaurant called Verdur might sprint for the door with a ballpoint. He had told Mr. Basset, the owner, that he had two years of serving experience. He had said it in a calm voice, with his hands still on the table, and Mr. Basset had nodded and slid the clipboard across. That was forty minutes ago. Since then Loic had carried out three baskets of bread, refilled four waters, and convinced himself that the lie was a minor one, the kind of thing everyone did, the kind of thing that barely counted as a lie at all.

The paperwork was the problem. The first sheet asked him things in a language he did not speak, allowances and withholding and filing status, and he had written his name and address and then stalled. He could not ask Mr. Basset, because Mr. Basset believed he had done this twice before. Under the counter, in the gap between the register and the wall, he thumbed a text to his mother: they gave me a form, tax thing, no idea. He watched the dining room while he waited. It was cosmopolitan for their town, olive oil in dark bottles, a menu that used the word "farro" without apology, and Loic liked that about it, liked imagining himself explaining the menu to strangers in a low, knowledgeable voice.

His mother's reply arrived as he was stacking water glasses. It's called Form W-4, she wrote. It's how your employer knows how much federal income tax to withhold from each paycheck. Fill it in as single, one job, and sign it. He read it twice, then a third time, because the sentence had a shape he wanted to keep, something orderly in it, a form for a form, a system that already knew he existed. He copied the words onto the sheet in his most careful handwriting, and when Mr. Basset passed, Loic said, "W-4's done," and Mr. Basset said, "See, you're an old hand," and Loic smiled as though this were true.

Then the Saturday crowd came in, and Loic discovered that he was not an old hand at anything. The first table of four ordered the farro and the braised shorts, and when the woman asked whether the shorts were beef or pork, Loic said, with total confidence, pork. He did not know. He had never known. But some part of him had decided on the first night of his new life that he would be a person who knew things, and that part of him spoke without consulting the rest. He delivered the food, pork that was beef, and stood against the pass believing firmly that nobody at that table would notice, that the difference was small, that he was, on the whole, doing well.

He was not doing well. The cooks knew it; they had begun to look at him the way you look at weather you don't trust. A second table waited nine minutes for menus. He dropped a fork and picked it up and put it back on the table, and only afterward understood what he had done, and stood in the middle of the floor holding a tray of nothing. He tried to contextualize the evening, to place it inside some larger story of first nights and learning curves, but the framing kept slipping, because there was a simpler structure underneath: he had lied to get in the door, and every mistake since then had flowed from the need to protect the lie. He had always distrusted neat causality, the idea that one act produced one result, but tonight the chain was so visible he could have counted its links.

At nine, a party of six came in, and Mr. Basset put them in Loic's section. "You've handled big tops before," he said, and Loic said, "Sure," and walked toward them with his notepad feeling like a stolen object in his pocket. They ordered drinks, four lemonades, a wine, a sparkling water, and the man at the head of the table asked him what he recommended. Loic opened his mouth to invent. He felt the sentence forming, something confident about the pork, and behind him he heard the first table's woman saying to her husband, quietly, "This isn't pork."

He took the order to the kitchen, and then, instead of returning, he stood there. The cook raised an eyebrow. From the doorway he could see both tables, the six waiting on his recommendation, the two waiting on an explanation, and Mr. Basset at the bar polishing a glass with no idea that his new server's entire résumé was fiction. There was a version of the next hour where he kept talking, kept knowing things, and it ended with him fired in a week, probably, or worse, never fired, just slowly understood. There was another version that required walking toward Mr. Basset right now, before the six got their food, and saying a sentence he had never practiced.

He walked toward the bar. "Mr. Basset," he said. "I have to tell you something before it gets worse. I haven't done this before. Any of it. No two years, no two months. I made it up in the interview because I wanted the job." His voice was lower than he expected, and steadier.

Mr. Basset set the glass down. He looked at the party of six, then at the first table, then at Loic for a long moment. "Table four's been waiting for their check and table nine needs a recommendation. You're going to tell nine the truth about what's good, which is the farro, and you're going to apologize to four about the pork, and Monday you're going to redo that W-4 in front of me so I know your handwriting wasn't borrowed too." He pushed the tray into Loic's hands. "Go. You already know the pork's beef, so say that much honestly."

Loic crossed the floor, stopped at the party of six, and said, "The farro, honestly. It's the one thing here I can actually vouch for."

Riley had booked the library's makerspace kiln for four o'clock, and by three forty he had eleven pieces laid out on the rolling cart, glazed and bone dry, waiting like patients in a corridor. The showcase opened in the county annex tomorrow at ten. Everything had to be fired tonight or not shown at all, and the librarian at the desk, Mrs. Okafor, had made it clear that the kiln was his until nine, after which the room was reserved for a coding club that would not be moved. He counted the pieces again, though counting changed nothing.

Ten of them were the terracotta bowls and tiles he had been making since September, low-fired work, orange and honest, stamped on their undersides with the pattern of his grandmother's lace tablecloth. He had pressed that lace into the clay the week she moved into the memory care unit, when his mother said something about patrimony, about things that get handed down or lost, and Riley had decided, without saying so, to operationalize the feeling. A pattern pressed in clay was a pattern that survived. The eleventh piece was a porcelain cup, translucent-edged and thin as a promise, thrown two weeks ago by Dana from his art class, who had asked, that morning, whether she could share his kiln slot because the school kiln was down and the showcase mattered to her too.

"Of course," Riley had said, because it was the right answer, and because Dana had taught him to center clay on the wheel in October and had never once made it feel like charity. Now he stood in front of the cart with her cup in his hands and a knot forming somewhere behind his sternum that he could not name precisely. He had fired terracotta before. He had never fired porcelain. He set the cup down and went looking for the binder.

The makerspace kept its manuals on a shelf beside the button maker: kiln schedules, glaze charts, a photocopied textbook with a cracked spine. Riley sat on the carpet under the fluorescent light and turned pages with the melancholic patience of someone who suspects the pages will confirm his problem. They did. Earthenware, he read, was normally fired below about 1,200 degrees Celsius. Porcelain needed more: between about 1,200 and 1,400 degrees Celsius. He read the two sentences four times, as if repetition might reveal an overlap, a temperature where both would vitrify, but the numbers sat there without mercy. One clay wanted less. The other wanted more. There was no load that loved them equally.

He did the arithmetic of it aloud, alone in the room. If he fired hot enough for Dana's cup, his bowls would slump or bloat or crack in ways the book described with clinical calm. If he fired cool enough for his bowls, her porcelain would never fully mature, would stay porous, would weep water from its walls at the showcase like a thing that had failed to become itself. He looked at the clock. Four hours and forty minutes. One kiln. Two makers. He thought about asking Mrs. Okafor to bump the coding club, and knew before he stood up that he wouldn't ask, because the club was nine kids learning to build something too, and their claim was as real as his.

Dana arrived at four fifteen with her cup wrapped in a dish towel, hopeful in a way that made everything harder. Riley showed her the binder instead of explaining, which felt more honest, and watched her read the same two sentences, watched her lips move slightly around the temperatures. "Earthenware under twelve hundred," she said. "Porcelain above it." She closed the binder and put both hands flat on it, as if holding it shut might hold the evening together. They were quiet for a while. Down the hall a printer chattered out someone's tax forms.

He could fire her cup and his two best bowls. That was the compromise the numbers permitted: the load sized for porcelain, his least important work sacrificed to temperature. Or they could split the slot, cool firing first for his bowls and a second, hotter load after for her cup, which would run right up against nine o'clock and the coding club, with no margin for a kiln that cooled on its own schedule and no guarantee the cup would be cool enough to handle by morning. Dana said the second option was fairer. Riley said he didn't want fair, he wanted her cup in the show, because it was better than anything he'd made. She said that wasn't true, and they both understood they were not arguing about pottery anymore, and neither of them said what they were arguing about.

They chose the split. They loaded his bowls at four thirty, and while the kiln climbed, they sat on the counter eating vending machine crackers and arguing about whether the lace pattern was too sentimental, Dana saying it wasn't, Riley saying it probably was and he'd pressed it into the clay anyway. At seven the kiln finished, and they opened it at seven forty, burned-orange bowls glowing against the shelf like small suns, all ten intact, every lace mark sharp. It was eight fifty when they reached for the cup, and Mrs. Okafor appeared in the doorway with the coding club behind her, and Riley, holding the cup up to the light one last time before loading it, saw the hairline crack running down from the rim, thin as the lace itself. "It was already there," Dana said. "From the trimming. I was going to tell you if it survived."

Jordan had told his mother, twice, that explaining things was basically his gift, which was why he had volunteered to make a five-minute video for the college's incoming-freshman science page on how greenhouse gases trap heat. He regretted this. He regretted it most at his grandfather's house, where he'd been sent for the weekend with a printed graph of carbon dioxide over the last century and a phone camera he hadn't turned on once.

The graph lay on the kitchen table beside a bowl of pistachios. Jordan squinted at the jagged line, which rose overall but undulated as it climbed, small teeth inside a long slope, and he could not for the life of him say why it wiggled. His grandfather drifted past in slippers, glanced at the paper, and said, "That looks like my heartbeat monitor. Am I dying?" Jordan said he was not dying, probably, and Grandpa took a pistachio and drifted out to the sun porch to listen to a baseball game with the sound off.

Jordan's cousin Priya arrived around noon, ostensibly to return a casserole dish but actually, as she admitted within ninety seconds, because her mother had heard Jordan was making a fool of himself with a camera and wanted to watch. "You said you'd start filming at ten," she said, settling into the chair across from him. "It's twelve forty. That's not a filming schedule, that's a hostage situation."

"The problem," Jordan said, "is the wiggle. If I can't explain the wiggle, the whole thing looks like chicanery. Like somebody drew a scary line on purpose." He traced the little rising teeth with his finger. "People will think it's a trick."

"People think everything's a trick," Priya said. "My chemistry teacher says you could show some people a sunrise and they'd ask who painted it." She pulled the graph closer. "Also, and I say this with love, what are greenhouse gases even for? Aren't they just bad? That's the whole assignment, right? Gases bad, planet sad, the end."

That was, in fact, more or less the script Jordan had drafted in his head the night before, and hearing it out loud he found he didn't like the sound of it. It had the shape of a slogan, not an explanation. He went looking for something better, which in this house meant the sun porch, where his grandfather kept forty years of old astronomy magazines in unstable towers. Grandpa watched him dig without comment except to say, "Don't topple the one with the eclipses," and Jordan, sneezing twice, found a tattered issue with a sidebar about Earth's heat balance. He read it standing up, one hand on a tower of magazines to keep it from avalanching.

"Okay," he said, coming back in with the magazine open like a waiter with a menu. "So. Without its natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius instead of roughly 14 degrees Celsius." Priya mouthed the numbers back at him slowly. "Fourteen is what we actually have. Minus eighteen is the version with no greenhouse effect at all."

Priya frowned at the magazine, then at the window, where the February yard sat brown and thawed. "So it's not bad. It's the reason I'm not wearing a spacesuit right now." Jordan said the natural effect was the reason, yes, and what he had to figure out was how to hold both things at once, that it kept the planet livable and that the line on the graph kept climbing, and he'd have to be honest in the video about which parts he understood cold and which parts he was still shaky on. The wiggle, for instance. He was still shaky on the wiggle. Priya said the wiggle might be seasons, plants breathing in and out across a year, and when Jordan asked how she knew, she said she didn't know, she'd guessed, which was different, and he should verify before he said it to actual strangers.

Grandpa shuffled in, looked at the two of them hunched over the table, and tapped the long climbing line with one finger. "Whichever way you explain it," he said, "say it like you're telling me why the furnace kicked on. Minus eighteen out there, I'd be a popsicle in my own porch." Jordan felt something settle, visceral and quick, the difference between fourteen and minus eighteen no longer a pair of numbers but the gap between this kitchen and a dead white field, and he propped the phone against the pistachio bowl and pressed record.

The essay was due Friday, and Colton had written nothing except his name, because every time he tried to argue about Heathcliff he heard Marisa Vasquez asking whether Nelly's dislike of certain characters coloured how she told their story, and he could not unhear it.

That had been Monday, in fourth period, Room 114, the desks arranged in their crooked horseshoe so that everyone could see everyone else's annoyance. They had been on Chapter 34, the chapter with the hair and the locket and the digging, and Ms. Okafor, who never answered anything directly, had asked them who was speaking. Marisa had her book open flat on the desk and she'd said, without raising her hand first, "The whole thing is Nelly Dean talking, right? She's telling it to Lockwood, the visitor, and he's the one writing it down. So it's her story more than anyone's." She'd paused, tapping the page. "And she doesn't like some of these people. Does that change what we're allowed to believe?"

Colton had disliked the question immediately, mostly because his half-formed essay was about Heathcliff as a villain, and if Marisa was right, the villain might be partly a construction, assembled by a housekeeper with grievances. He'd spent that evening reading back through the early chapters, and there it was: he was not watching Catherine and Heathcliff on the moors at all. He was standing in a kitchen at Wuthering Heights, years after everything, listening to a woman narrate. Everything reached him through her, and then through Lockwood, who had his own biases, his own vanity, his own reasons for shaping what he copied down. Two sets of hands on the story before it ever touched his.

The problem was that Marisa's question had two answers, and they didn't fit together. In one, Nelly was an unreliable narrator, and the reader's trust had to be earned chapter by chapter, checked against her inconsistencies, her convenient lapses of memory, the moments where she intervened in events and then reported on them as though she were a window rather than a participant. In the other, the novel knew all this, had built itself out of it, and the unreliability was the point: Brontë had published the thing in 1847 with this structure intact, layers of telling inside telling, and to strip Nelly away to get at some truer story underneath would be to abrogate the whole design. You couldn't fire the narrator and still have the book.

He tried the argument out on his brother, Danny, who was home from his first semester at State and eating cereal at eleven at night. "So imagine a guy tells you about a fight he was in," Colton said, "and then you find out his buddy rewrote the guy's account before you read it. What do you actually know about the fight?"

"Nothing," Danny said, milk dribbling back into the bowl. "You know about the two guys."

Colton sat with that. Danny hadn't read the book and had still put his finger on the thing. Maybe what the reader knew was the tellers. Maybe sentience in that novel didn't belong to Catherine or Heathcliff at all, not really, not directly; it belonged to Nelly, watching, judging, deciding what to reveal, and to Lockwood, misreading everything and writing it down anyway. The characters had inner lives, sure, Colton wasn't going to pretend they didn't, but he only ever got them as Nelly chose to render them. Heathcliff's depths were an inference. Nelly's mind was the evidence.

Thursday night he wrote the essay in one sitting, and it was strange, because the act of writing it made the inchoate position suddenly definite on the page even though it still felt soft in his head. He argued that the double narration made trust itself the subject of the novel. He argued that Nelly's biases didn't corrupt the story so much as constitute it. Then, three-quarters through, he wrote a paragraph he hadn't planned: that he could not finally decide whether Brontë meant readers to distrust Nelly or to accept that distrust was all readers ever got, and that the honest conclusion was that both readings survived the text. He handed it in Friday with that paragraph still in, feeling like he was confessing to a crime he hadn't committed.

Monday, Ms. Okafor handed the essays back facedown. Marisa turned hers over, glanced across the horseshoe at him, and held up her paper so he could see the grade circled at the top. He turned his over. The same number, more or less, which felt like either a tie or a joke. At the bottom of his last page, in green ink, she'd written a single line: "Good. Now defend the part you gave up on."

He looked at it for a long moment, then at Marisa, who was already arguing with the boy next to her about whether Lockwood counted as a narrator at all if he mostly just listened.

"He counts," Colton said across the room, before he'd fully decided to say anything. "Everything's coming through both of them. That's the whole book."

"Prove it," Marisa said, and turned her desk a few degrees toward his.

Mathis stood at the edge of his own graduation party with a paper cup of sparkling cider and listened to his uncle describe his five-year plan for him, which began with engineering and ended, apparently, with a corner office Mathis had never asked for. The yard behind the house had been strung with white lights, and someone's playlist was shuffling through pop songs his younger cousins kept voting down. He had managed, so far, to preempt every direct question by refilling the chip bowl, but the bowl was full now and his uncle had cornered him near the fence.

"You're good with numbers," his uncle was saying. "That's not nothing. My father worked the mill his whole life and died owing money. You get to choose."

"I know," Mathis said. He did know. The choice was the problem, or rather the way everyone kept insisting it was a choice between two clear things, when inside his head it was more like a fog with a few lit windows.

His cousin Talia rescued him with a question aimed past him. "Whose idea was the march?" She pointed at the speakers, where the playlist had landed, for reasons no one could explain, on a slow brass processional that Mathis recognized at once. He had walked to it that morning, across a football field in a rented gown, sweating through his shirt.

"It's from graduation," he said. "Pomp and Circumstance. Everyone walks to it."

"I know it's from graduation. Whose is it?"

"Elgar," said a voice from the picnic table, and Dev walked over balancing a paper plate of potato salad. Dev had been in his English seminar, the one where they read the tragedies. "It's Elgar."

"Like the guy who wrote it," Talia said.

"The title's older, though," Dev said, and looked at Mathis the way he did when he was about to make someone lose an argument. "You want to guess where he got it? Anyone?"

Talia's little brother shouted something about kings. Mathis turned the phrase over in his mouth, silently, feeling for its rhythm. Pride, pomp, and circumstance. He had heard that cadence before, that swelling three-beat line, and it had not been at a commencement. It had been in a room with desks in a circle and Ms. Okoye's poster of the Globe Theatre, a man talking about losing everything he had made of himself.

"Othello," Mathis said. "It's Othello. When he loses his rank. He talks about the pride, pomp, and circumstance of glorious war going away." He heard the whole line in his own voice and checked it against memory, and it held.

Dev pointed his fork at him like a referee confirming a goal. "Glorious war. And then they play it at graduations so teenagers can walk in a circle."

"Because it sounds like victory," Talia said.

"It sounds like loss," Dev said. "That's the joke. The march is gorgeous and it's a man mourning."

Mathis looked at the speaker wired to the fence post, the brass still climbing, and thought about his uncle's corner office and his own lit windows in the fog. He had spent the spring being told, by adults who meant well, that commencement was a beginning, pure and simple, and that his job now was to pick a door and be decisive. But the music itself was double, and nobody minded. The same sound carried grief and ceremony at once, and four hundred people had sat in bleachers and felt both without needing to choose.

"It's not a joke, exactly," Mathis said slowly. "It's more that the music can hold both. Othello loses the war part, the glory part, and the pomp still means something when the graduates walk. It's like the ceremony is a synecdoche for whatever it is you're leaving, and whatever you think you're starting. It's not one or the other."

Talia squinted. "You lost me at the middle of that sentence."

"Same," said her brother.

"I'm saying I don't have to decide tonight whether the fog is bad," Mathis said. "I might go in for engineering and I might go in for literature, and the honest thing is I don't know yet which door is real, and it might be that neither one is the whole door."

His uncle had gone quiet during the Othello exchange, and now he set down his cup. "The mill didn't give you options," he said, but softly, without the corner office behind it.

"I know it didn't," Mathis said. "That's why you want me to be sure. But Elgar wasn't sure either, or the play wasn't, or something. The march works because it's both things."

Dev was already drifting toward the dessert table, and Talia's brother had begun conducting the brass with a plastic fork. The song reached the passage everyone knows, the one that swells and then folds back on itself, and Mathis found himself conducting too, just slightly, cup in hand. His uncle watched him for a moment, then raised his own cup toward the speaker.

"To the indigent guy at the mill," his uncle said. "He'd have liked this part."

"He would've," Mathis said, and kept conducting until the song was over.

The open house on Fenwick Road smelled of new paint and old carpet, and Blake stood in the hallway holding a printed flyer while strangers drifted past him into the kitchen. His mother had sent him alone because she was working the late shift, and he was supposed to judge whether the flat was worth the train fare she'd paid for him. He was sixteen, and until this morning he had never thought about what it actually cost to stand inside a room and call it yours.

A letting agent named Dominic was holding court by the window, telling a young woman in a green coat that the property was a rare opportunity, an expression Blake had already heard twice about two different flats. Dominic had a grandiose way of describing radiators, as though central heating were a moral achievement, and Blake watched the woman nod along while clearly doing arithmetic behind her eyes.

"Rent is eleven hundred a month," Dominic said. "And we'd need a deposit upfront, plus the first month's rent. Two months' rent for the deposit, so twenty-two hundred, then eleven on top of that. Plus a holding fee while we do the referencing."

The woman, whose name turned out to be Amira because Dominic said it twice with false warmth, asked him to write it down. Blake drifted closer under the pretense of inspecting the boiler, which was indeed in the kitchen, boxed in like something the flat was embarrassed by. He liked numbers the way some people liked football, quietly and without permission, and twenty-two hundred plus eleven hundred was already thirty-three hundred before the invisible fee.

"I thought there was a cap," Amira said, scrolling on her phone with her thumb. "On deposits. For renting."

Dominic sighed the sigh of a man who found rules a personal inconvenience. "There are exceptions," he said, and began to pontificate about administration and risk and how landlords had to protect themselves, his voice rising into a rhythm that was meant to end all questions. "In this market, two months is standard practice."

Blake had moved to the doorway of the sitting room, where a couple was measuring a wall for a sofa that would not fit. Amira was reading her screen with her lips slightly parted. "It says here the Tenant Fees Act 2019," she said slowly, not looking up. "It caps most tenancy deposits at five weeks' rent when the annual rent is under fifty thousand pounds."

The silence that followed was brief but real. Dominic opened his mouth, and Blake, who had been quiet since the front door, heard himself say, "Eleven hundred a month is thirteen thousand two hundred a year. That's under fifty grand." He hadn't planned to say it. The words had simply arranged themselves, the way they did in maths class when a problem opened up in front of him.

Dominic looked at him for the first time, taking in the school jacket and the flyer held like a shield. "You're here to view the property?" he said, in a tone that made viewing sound like trespassing. "Perhaps the adults could handle the details."

"He's right though," said the man with the tape measure, not turning around. "Five weeks, not two months. My sister just went through this in Leeds." Amira was already doing the calculation on her phone's notes app, multiplying eleven hundred by five and dividing by four point three, whatever that gave, and then announcing, "About twelve hundred and seventy-nine. Instead of twenty-two hundred. That's nearly a thousand pounds I'd still have."

What happened next was less a confrontation than a slow deflation. Dominic retreated into phrases like "subject to verification" and "I'd have to check with the landlord," which Blake understood, watching him, to mean that the number would quietly become correct once enough people had looked at it. Amira thanked the man with the tape measure. The couple left. Blake stayed to look at the second bedroom, which was barely bigger than the bed in it, and thought about the way his mother kept a jar labelled DEPOSIT on top of the fridge, into which she put notes from every shift.

He didn't know whether she knew about the cap. He didn't know whether the jar was for a mortgage down payment someday, which a man at another viewing had once described to him as the five percent that got you through the door, or for a rental deposit like Amira's, the money you handed over and hoped to see again. The two systems ran on the same word, deposit, and meant different things, and Blake stood in the small room understanding for the first time that his mother had been navigating both, alone, without anyone to check the arithmetic. Her savings had a kind of asceticism to them, the jar and the skipped things and the brand of tea she bought only when it was on offer, and he had mistaken it for preference until this afternoon.

On the train home he texted her: deposit can't be more than 5 weeks rent if yearly rent is under 50k, tenant fees act 2019, look it up before you sign anything. Then, after a pause: the flat had a good boiler. It was not much of a verdict. It was, for now, what he had.

She replied with a thumbs up and then, a minute later, a second message: jar's at 1900. He looked at the number for a long moment, the fields going grey past the window, and typed back, want me to make a spreadsheet of the flats we've seen? Rents, deposits, all of it. I can do the maths. The three dots appeared on her side of the screen, stopped, and started again.

The suit jacket had been his grandfather's, and it smelled faintly of the cedar closet, and Anthony sat in the back seat of the car with his arms crossed so he wouldn't have to touch the sleeves. His father drove. His mother rode in front with the directions to the funeral home printed out, though the funeral home was twenty minutes away and they had been there twice already, once for the viewing and once to settle the paperwork. The service was at eleven. It was ten twenty, which meant there was time, which meant there was time to think, which was the problem.

"Uncle Ray wants you to say something," his mother said, turning around at the red light on Delmar. "Just a few sentences. During the open part."

"I don't have anything."

"About your grandfather. A memory."

"I know what it's about." He hadn't cried yet. That was the thing he kept returning to, the thing he examined the way you probe a tooth you suspect is wrong. His grandfather had died on a Tuesday; it was now Saturday; in between, Anthony had gone to school on Wednesday and Thursday, had laughed at Marcus's impression of their chemistry teacher on Friday, had eaten three meals a day and slept, mostly, through the night. Somewhere he had picked up the idea that grief had stages, that you moved through them in order like checkpoints, and if you skipped one, if you laughed four days out, you were doing it wrong. The car behind them honked, gently, and his father went.

His backpack was on the floor by his feet. In it was the AP Psychology textbook he'd been reading before any of this happened, chapters assigned for the fall semester he was supposedly preparing for, and he pulled it out now because there was nothing else to do with his hands. He hadn't planned to look anything up. He turned to the index, found bereavement, then grief, then loss, and followed a page number to a section on mourning.

His mother watched him in the visor mirror. "Homework? Today?"

"It's not homework." He read the page twice. A psychologist named George Bonanno had followed bereaved people over time, the book said, and what he found was that resilience was common, more common than anyone had assumed, and that there were no mandatory stages that everyone must pass through after a loss. Anthony read the sentence again. No mandatory stages. He had been operating for four days on the belief that there was a correct way to do this and that he was failing at it, and here was a man with a clipboard, apparently, who had watched actual widows and actual grandchildren and found that most of them functioned, laughed, kept eating, and that this was not a defect in them.

"That face you're making," his father said. "What?"

"Nothing. This chapter." He almost put the book down. Then he didn't. "Did you cry?" he asked the back of his father's head. "I mean. When. You know."

His father changed lanes before he answered, which was a kind of answer itself. "At the hospital. And once at the diner, weirdly, when the waitress brought his usual coffee order without being asked." He cleared his throat. "Why, you haven't?"

"No. I mean a little at the viewing. Not since."

"There's no schedule, Anthony."

"I know that now. That's what I'm saying. I found it." He held up the book as though it were evidence, which it was. "This guy studied it. Resilience is actually common. People just keep going and it's normal. There's no set of stages everybody has to pass through." Saying it out loud changed something; the fact had been true on the page and became true in the car.

His mother was quiet for a long moment. "Your grandfather would have liked that you looked it up. He never trusted anything he couldn't check himself." She smiled at the window. "He spent an hour once with a mechanic arguing about the etiology of a rattling noise. Where it started, what caused it. He loved that word. Everything had an etiology with him."

The car turned onto the parkway, and the light through the trees strobed across his father's hands on the wheel, and Anthony watched it, half mesmerized, thinking that even Bonanno's finding had limits. It told him resilience was common; it didn't tell him whether his own resilience was real or just delayed, whether the crying was coming in a week or a month or whether it wasn't coming at all, and whether that would be worse. He could hold both ideas now. He was probably fine, and he did not entirely know yet. Both could be true. His grandfather, the most honest man he'd known, would have approved of stating it exactly that way, with the uncertainty left in.

"He paid for my first semester of books," Anthony said suddenly. "I never told you. He handed me an envelope in March and said don't make it altruistic in your mind, I'm not being generous, I'm investing, you'll owe me conversations when you're in college. That's what I could say. At the open part."

His mother turned around again, and his father's eyes found him in the mirror, briefly, before returning to the road.

"Say that," his father said. "Say exactly that."

They pulled into the funeral home lot at ten fifty-two, gravel popping under the tires, his uncle already standing on the steps in a tie the color of a plum. Anthony put the textbook back in the bag, straightened the jacket that smelled of cedar, and got out of the car.

The paycheque came in a thin envelope with the week's schedule, and Noah read it standing in the passageway between the kitchen and the washrooms, where the smell of fryer oil was thickest. He had worked sixty-one hours over two weeks at fourteen dollars an hour, which he had already calculated on his phone three times, but the number on the line marked NET PAY was smaller by an amount that made his stomach tighten. Above it, in smaller print, sat a column of deductions: income tax, CPP, EI. He folded the envelope into his back pocket and went back to clearing table nine.

He was saving for a ticket to London. His brother Marcus had moved there in September, and their mother had said, in the flat voice she used for things she couldn't change, that if Noah wanted to see him before Christmas, he'd be paying his own way. The cheapest flight was six hundred and eighty dollars, and the envelope in his pocket brought his total to five hundred and eleven. Two more pay periods, if nothing went wrong. He stacked plates and did the arithmetic again, as though the deductions might have shrunk.

At table four, a woman with reading glasses was interrogating her bill. "Why is it a hundred and two dollars when the menu said eighty-nine?" she asked her husband, and Noah slowed his bussing to half speed, the way Priya had taught him, so he could listen without seeming to.

"Tax," the husband said. "It's not on the menu prices. Thirteen percent, added at the end."

"That's absurd. In London it's just in the price."

Noah's ears went hot. Marcus had sent him a photograph two nights ago, a receipt from a café near his flat, and Noah had spent twenty minutes on it with the calculator app, confused, because nothing on it looked like the bills at the restaurant. The total was simply the total. He had texted Marcus and gotten back only "VAT," which told him nothing.

Priya was folding napkins behind the host stand when he came around the corner. "The woman at four says in England the sales tax is already in the price."

"It's called VAT," Priya said, not looking up. "My cousin in Manchester goes on about it."

He looked it up on his phone in the dry storage room, between the sacks of rice. Value added tax, the standard rate in the United Kingdom, had been twenty percent since January 4, 2011. He sat on a crate and worked it backwards on the calculator: if the tax was inside the price, then a receipt for twelve pounds carried two pounds of tax already paid, quietly, invisibly, the way salt is already in the bread. At the restaurant, the tax arrived at the end like a verdict. Same money leaving, different theatre. He caught himself thinking it was a difference of semantics, then corrected himself, because it wasn't just the words; it was what you could see and what you couldn't, and he wasn't sure which he trusted less.

That night, closing, he counted his tips at the far end of the bar while Priya ran the till. Cash tips were endemic to the place, the owner pretended not to know about them, and Noah had been adding them to his flight fund in a jar at home, three and four dollars at a time. He had counted forty-eight dollars tonight. It wasn't enough, and he knew it wasn't enough, and he pushed the bills around on the bar as though rearranging them might breed.

"Your till's out," Priya said suddenly, in a low voice, from the register.

"How much?"

"Over. Twenty-two dollars and forty cents." She held the tape up, then lowered it. "That's the table four bill exactly. The woman paid cash and I never closed it."

Noah stood very still. Twenty-two forty, sitting in the drawer, money that wasn't hers and wasn't his, money that would close the gap between him and January by one more shift. Nobody would ever know; the woman was gone, the owner was gone, and Priya was looking at him the way people look at you when they've decided to let you decide.

He thought about the receipt with the tax buried inside it, everything already settled before you saw it, and he thought about his paycheque's neat columns, everything itemized and still somehow opaque. Two ways of arranging the same unavoidable losses. He had liked to believe the visible one was the honest one. He wasn't sure he believed it anymore, and he was honest enough with himself to leave that question open.

"Run it as a payment on account," he said. "We'll tell Marco in the morning and refund it if she comes back." Priya nodded once and turned to the till, and Noah swept the last of the napkins off the bar into the bin.

Jaxon found his mother at the kitchen table with three novels fanned out in front of her and a legal pad covered in her slanted handwriting. "Book club's at seven," she said without looking up. "And I'm supposed to lead it, and I still don't know what I think." The clock above the stove read 4:40.

He set his backpack down slowly. His AP Literature teacher had spent the last two weeks on critical lenses, and tomorrow morning, first period, Jaxon had to turn in an essay applying a feminist lens to a passage from Jane Eyre. He had a photocopied page in his bag, flagged with a pink sticky note, and he had nothing written yet.

"Which book?" he asked, pulling out a chair.

"Pride and Prejudice. We're arguing whether Elizabeth Bennet's choices are really hers." She rubbed her eyes. "Deb thinks Lizzy marrying Darcy is true love and self-determination. Priya says it's just the best deal available to a woman with no money and no sons. It's my job to keep it from becoming a shouting match."

Jaxon spread his photocopy on the table beside her legal pad. The passage was the one where Jane agrees to marry Rochester, all tremor and submission. "We could trade problems," he said. "You help me with my essay, I help you with your debate."

His mother laughed, a short tired sound, but she slid her chair around to his side of the table. He could smell the orange peel she'd left on a saucer, and the radiator ticking under the window carried the smell of dust going warm.

"Okay," he said, reading aloud. "So the feminist lens. My teacher says you ask who has power in the scene, and who's doing the looking, and who's being looked at." He paused.
