"Rochester keeps saying he'll dress Jane in jewels and silks. She keeps saying no. That part's easy. What's hard is that Jane wants the marriage too. So is her wanting hers, or is it the wanting she was trained to have?"

His mother pulled the legal pad closer and started writing. "That's exactly Priya's argument about Lizzy."

"Wait." He got up and went to the bookshelf in the hallway, the low one by the coat rack, where his mother kept the books from her college years, their spines gone soft. He ran a finger along them and pulled out a thick one, its cover a faded gray. He'd seen it once when he was ten and thought it looked boring. Inside the front cover his mother had written her maiden name and a date. He carried it back to the kitchen.

"The Second Sex," his mother read off the spine. "Simone de Beauvoir. That's from 1949." She flipped through it, pages whispering. "There's a line in here. 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.' I underlined it. Look, it goes through everything, society, childhood, all of it, that's her whole argument, that society shapes womanhood."

Jaxon copied the line onto his legal pad, pressing hard. "So if that's true, then Jane's wanting isn't fake, exactly. It's real wanting, but it's built wanting. She lives in a world where marrying Rochester is the biggest thing a woman can do, so of course the biggest feeling she has points at him."

"Then Lizzy's love isn't a lie either," his mother said slowly. "It's just that she fell in love inside a very small room."

"Priya's going to malign Darcy's proposal no matter what," Jaxon said. "And Deb will act like money is a peccadillo compared to passion. You could say they're both right about half of it."

His mother looked at him. "Say that again."

"Say what again?"

"The small room. Say it the way you just said it." She wrote it down, word for word, and he watched her do it, and something in his chest went loose and warm.

The clock said 5:25. He still had four paragraphs to draft and she had to make the pasta salad she'd promised Priya. She stood, filled the big pot, set it on the burner, and while the water heated she read his opening paragraph out loud, stumbling once over "patriarchal gaze," and he crossed it out and wrote "who does the looking" above it instead.

"One thing I can't figure out," he said, watching the water shiver toward a boil. "De Beauvoir says society makes the woman. But Jane still says no to the jewels. If she's fully trained, where does the no come from?"

His mother grated cheese into a bowl, knuckles working. "That's a good question for your essay. You don't have to answer it. You just have to be honest that it's open." Steam climbed the window and blurred the streetlight coming on outside.

At 6:40 she left, cake carrier in one hand, legal pad in the other, calling back through the door, "Text me if your conclusion is any good." Jaxon sat alone with the pot cooling and the gray book open on the table. He read the underlined line twice more, then wrote his final paragraph and left the last sentence hanging on a question. He took a photo of it and sent it to his mother, then closed the book and set it back on the low shelf, spine out, where he could find it again.

The cones were set up behind the grocery store, in the far corner of the lot where the cart returns never quite reached, and Madison's father had promised that if she could park between them three times in a row, he would take her on the highway that same afternoon. She had backed in twice already, each time crooked but inside the lines, and now she sat with her hands at ten and two, breathing on the windshield, studying the gap in the mirror.

"Third one," her father said from the passenger seat, eating sunflower seeds he'd bought inside. "You've got more room than you think."

"That's what people say to make you feel better about having less room than you think."

He laughed, shells clicking against his teeth. She reversed slowly, turned the wheel hand over hand, and came to rest close enough to the rear cone that she could have touched it through the open window. Not perfect, but legal. She left the engine running and looked at him until he shrugged.

"Fine. Three in a row. Highway it is."

The on-ramp near the store was short and steep, the kind that gave you about eight seconds to get up to speed, and Madison had been dreading it for two weeks. Her instructor at school, a pugnacious retired cop named Mr. Vasquez who seemed to take personal offense at hesitation, had told her class that merging was where people failed, not because they couldn't drive but because they trusted their mirrors. She'd written it in her notebook without really understanding it.

Now she accelerated down the ramp, watching the side mirror, which showed a lane of empty gray asphalt, and she began to drift left. Her shoulder turned for a half second, a reflex she hadn't planned, and there was a sedan beside her, silver, close enough that she could see the driver's coffee mug on the roof of her own mouth-shaped reflection in its window. She pulled back level in her lane, heart going like a dropped metronome.

"There was a car there the whole time," she said.

"Yep." Her father cracked another seed. "Mirrors leave blind spots beside and behind you. That's why you look over your shoulder, every time. Vasquez didn't cover that?"

"He covered it. I just didn't believe him."

"It's not a matter of belief," her father said, in the mild tone he used when he was enjoying being right. "It's geometry. Or physics. One of the sciences."

She merged properly at the next opening, chin over her shoulder, signal on, and it was almost anticlimactic, how easy it was once she actually looked. The highway unrolled ahead, bland and sunlit, big-box stores giving way to pines. She held her speed and let the wheel settle.

What interested her, driving home in the right lane, was that both things were true. The mirrors were useful; they showed her most of what was behind her, and she would not give them up. And they were incomplete in a way that mattered exactly when it mattered most, in the seconds before a decision. Mr. Vasquez had wanted her to distrust the mirrors entirely, as if they were out to deceive her, and her father wanted her to trust the shoulder check with the same blind faith she'd wrongly given the glass. She thought neither position was quite right, though she couldn't yet say what the right one was, except that it involved looking twice and believing once.

Back at the grocery store, her father went in for more sunflower seeds and she stayed in the car, rearranging the mirrors, small adjustments, tilt and angle, until the view in the glass overlapped better with the view over her shoulder. It didn't fix everything. There would still be a wedge she couldn't see, and she accepted that now instead of resenting it.

Her phone buzzed. A text from Priya, who had failed her test twice: how was the highway. Madison typed back that it was fine, then deleted it, then typed the truth: almost merged into a silver car, mirror looked empty, shoulder check saved me. Do the shoulder check. Priya.

When her father came out with the seeds and a receipt he'd been examining like a document that might impugn him, a gallon of milk charged twice, she started the engine. He pointed at the cones still standing in the far corner of the lot.

"One more," he said. "For complicity's sake. I was the one who said you had more room than you think."

"You were right, though."

"I know. That's the worst part."

She backed in on the first try, straighter than the others, and sat there a moment with the engine idling, looking from the mirror to the window and back again, seeing two slightly different pictures of the same quiet lot.

Juliette took the last seat in the bank's waiting area, between a man talking too loudly into his phone and a woman rocking a stroller with her foot, and pulled the folder of papers her grandmother had thrust at her that morning into her lap. The folder smelled of lavender and pencil shavings. Inside were the deed to a small brick house on Felton Street, a statement from a savings account opened in 1968, and a sticky note in her grandmother's slanted hand: Ask about the equity. And don't let them charm you.

She was third in line. The man beside her was arguing with someone about a deposit that hadn't cleared, and the word "deposit" kept landing like a small hammer. Juliette had learned the word at fourteen, when she'd handed a cashier a jar of birthday money for her first checking account and watched the teller type it into a machine as though it were nothing. Money going in. That was all a deposit meant, though she'd felt, at the time, that something larger should happen, some ceremony.

"Number forty-one," the speaker announced, and the stroller went up. Then forty-two, the loud man. Juliette smoothed the folder on her knee and thought about the argument from last night, which was really the argument from every night that week. Her grandmother wanted to sell the Felton Street house and give Juliette the proceeds toward a down payment on an apartment, since Juliette was starting at the university in September and the campus rentals were devouring her part-time wages. Her mother said it was too much, that Grandmere had earned that house, that Juliette should take the student loans like everyone else and stop letting an old woman rearrange her whole life around a girl who hadn't even picked a major.

Grandmere's neighbor, Mrs. Okafor, had sold her own house on the same street in the spring, and Juliette had been at the kitchen table when Grandmere heard what Mrs. Okafor walked away with. It was less than anyone expected. "She still owed on it," Grandmere said, tapping the table with two fingers. "The bank took its share first." She'd looked at Juliette then with an expression that demanded understanding, and Juliette, not wanting to admit she had none, had nodded and gone home and looked it up at midnight in the blue light of her laptop: home equity is the home's current value minus what is still owed on the mortgage. She'd read it three times. Then she'd found a forum where a man in Ohio complained that he'd owned his house for nine years and still had almost no equity, and a woman replied that ownership was a ladder you climbed slowly, and Juliette had closed the laptop feeling both informed and vaguely cheated, as though the ladder had been advertised as an escalator.

"Number forty-three." She stood too fast and her chair scraped. The teller was younger than expected, maybe twenty-five, with a name tag that said DARA and a pen she was already spinning.

"I need to know what my grandmother's house would actually give her," Juliette said, laying out the deed. "She owns it outright. No mortgage. And I need to know what a down payment on an apartment would look like, because she wants to give me the money and my mother thinks it's chicanery, her word, of the emotional kind."

Dara stopped spinning the pen. "Emotional chicanery. That's a good phrase." She pulled the deed closer. "Okay, so if there's no mortgage, then the equity is the whole current value. Every dollar of the sale price, minus fees, is hers. Your neighbor, if she still owed money, she'd only keep the value of the house minus what was still owed on the mortgage. That's the difference. Your grandmother keeps more because she owes nothing."

Juliette wrote this down even though she knew it, because writing it down made it true in a way that knowing it at midnight hadn't. Dara, warming to the subject the way people do when someone under twenty actually asks, explained that a down payment was usually some fraction of the price, that the mortgage covered the rest, and that rent, by contrast, was money that never came back to you at all. "You're paying for the right to exist in the space," Dara said. "Which is not nothing. I rent. I exist in a very nice space above a laundromat." She grinned. "It smells like dryer sheets and I've learned to love it."

The dryer sheets line startled a laugh out of Juliette, loud enough that the stroller woman looked over and almost smiled herself. "The thing is," Juliette said, quieter, "I don't know if I should take it. She sold her wedding rings two years ago to cover the property tax. My mother says taking the house money makes me the kind of person who lets people sell their houses for her."

"Or it makes you the kind of person who owns something at nineteen instead of paying rent into a hole until you're forty." Dara slid a pamphlet across the counter, then pulled it back. "Actually, don't take the pamphlet. Pamphlets are where hope goes to die. Talk to a mortgage officer, that desk over there, and talk to your mother tonight, not on the phone, at the table." She stamped something on a slip of paper and handed it over. "That's a referral, not a decision."

Outside, the afternoon had the hot metallic smell of July pavement. Juliette sat on the bank's wide stone steps and called her grandmother, watching a pigeon commandeer a sandwich crust from a smaller pigeon with total impunity. "Well?" Grandmere said before hello. "What did they say?"

"That you'd keep almost everything," Juliette said. "Because you don't owe anything on it. The whole value is yours."

There was a silence on the line, long enough that Juliette could hear the kitchen radio, the one that only got the classical station. "Then come to dinner," her grandmother said finally, "and bring your mother, and bring that face you make when you've decided something and won't say it." Juliette looked at the slip of paper in her hand, at the referral, not a decision, and at the pigeon now eating like a king on the steps below her. "I haven't decided," she said. "I'm working on it."

Madeline had circled the help wanted sign in the window of Hartwell's Hardware twice on her walk past, once in the morning and once after her interview, as though the circling itself might hold the position open. The manager, a wide, deliberate woman named Ruth, had asked her three questions, none of them about hardware, and then said she would call by Friday. That left four days for Madeline to want the job with an intensity that embarrassed her a little, since the work was stocking shelves and mixing paint on Saturdays.

She told her cousin Dara about it that night over video, because Dara, nineteen and already working at a warehouse in Ohio, had opinions about everything and a phone plan that made the calls free. "So did your boss seem normal?" Dara asked, chewing something off camera, a gourmand even from a bag of gas station trail mix, narrating each handful.

"She seemed fine. Quiet."

"Quiet's fine until it isn't. My old supervisor got quiet and then fired Jayden on a Tuesday because he was in a bad mood. That's it. That was the whole reason." Dara leaned closer to the lens. "Bosses can just do that here. Fire you for nothing."

Madeline said she didn't think that was true everywhere, and Dara said name one place, and neither of them could, so the argument dissolved the way theirs always did, into a bet of ten dollars and a promise to look it up, which Madeline suspected Dara would forget by morning.

She didn't forget. She sat on her bed with her laptop and found it in twenty minutes, scrolling past forums full of people who were certain and wrong. Her mother had been from Billings, and the summer Madeline was nine she'd spent three weeks there while her parents sorted things out, a month of dry grass and her uncle's loud kitchen. She remembered her uncle saying, once, over burgers, that out there a job was a job, they couldn't just toss you off it, and she'd assumed at nine that this was a feeling, not a law. It was a law. Montana, the one state in the country where, after a probationary period, an employer generally needed good cause to fire someone. There was even a name for it, the Wrongful Discharge from Employment Act, from 1987, printed in plain type at the top of the page. Everywhere else, the sites agreed with Dara in the flat tone of settled fact. She texted her cousin the link and the ten dollars became a question of honor.

On Friday, Ruth called while Madeline was slicing a mango badly at the counter, and offered her the Saturdays, and then paused in a way that made Madeline grip the knife handle. "One thing. It wouldn't be just stocking. Saturdays we run the paint counter, and I lost my mixer in April, so you'd be on your own by June. It's a lot of standing there with nothing happening, and then a rush. Some people find the dead air desensitizes them to customers, honestly, they stop seeing the person and just see the can. I need someone who doesn't do that."

Madeline said she didn't think she would. She was thinking of her mother, actually, who had waited tables for years and could still, at forty, ask a stranger what they needed in a voice that made the question real. She wanted to be like that, though she understood even as she thought it that wanting a quality and having it were separated by years of Saturdays she hadn't worked yet.

Ruth was noncommittal, in the way of a person who had heard promises before, and said to come Monday at eight. When Madeline hung up, she texted Dara the news, and Dara replied with a wall of congratulations and then, forty minutes later, a separate message: "okay so my friend tomas just got let go from the warehouse. for nothing. I checked. we're in ohio." Madeline read it twice, sitting on the floor with mango juice drying on her fingers, and felt the fact settle somewhere between triumph and uselessness, a rule that protected exactly one state's worth of cousins, hers included, since her mother had come from the one place it counted.

On Monday she arrived at seven forty. Ruth was already at the paint counter, teaching herself something from a laminated sheet, and she looked up when the bell rang and pointed at the aprons on the hook with her chin. Madeline took the smallest one, still too big, and tied it while Ruth slid a can of eggshell white across the counter toward her and said, "Mix me this. And tell me why you're standing like you're about to apologize."

The craft cabin smelled of pine sap and turpentine, and by Wednesday afternoon Kaitlyn had painted the same gray sky four times. The assignment for Friday night's exhibition was simple enough: a landscape of the lake and the ridge behind it, any medium, done by suppertime or it didn't hang. Her problem was stranger than the deadline. On the left side of the canvas, where the gray met the orange of a sun-baked rock face, the sky looked warm, almost dusty rose. On the right, above the blue water, the identical gray, mixed from the same jar in one sitting, looked cold and faintly blue-green. She had not touched the paint between them. She leaned close until her nose almost grazed the canvas, then stepped back to the doorway, and the sky kept splitting into two skies.

"Your gray's dirty," said Rosa from the next easel, without looking up from her clay owl. "You probably didn't clean your brush."

"I cleaned it." Kaitlyn held the brush up like evidence in a trial. "Same water, same rag, same everything. It's the same gray."

"Then your eyes are dirty." Rosa smiled to show she was joking, mostly. Kaitlyn let it go, because arguing would impugn nothing except Rosa's certainty, and Rosa's certainty was not the sort of thing that yielded. Still, she covered the right half of the sky with a scrap of paperboard and stared at the left. Warm. She moved the paperboard. Cool. She did this five times, quickly, like a magician proving there was no trick, and each time the gray changed its mind.

The camp's bookshelf, four sagging planks of mildewed paperbacks behind the ping-pong table, was nobody's idea of a library. But the art counselor, who was off driving the van to town until five, kept a few of her own books there, and Kaitlyn went looking with her hands still tacky with paint. She found a fat volume with a cracked spine, half biography and half color plates, about a French chemist named Michel Eugène Chevreul. She read standing up, one hip against the shelf, while two boys argued over whether the top of the ping-pong table was legally a desk. Chevreul, she read, had published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839, and the law said that a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it. She read the sentence twice. She looked at her own hands, then at the window, then at the page again.

From the doorway of the rec hall, Deb Chen watched the girl with the paint-stained fingers stand absolutely still over a book for what had to be ten minutes. Deb had come in for the ping-pong paddles and had stayed because stillness like that was rare at the camp, rarer than loons. She could see the open page from where she stood: a diagram of small squares nested inside larger squares, gray inside orange, gray inside blue. The girl, Kaitlyn, Deb remembered, from the awkward first-night name games, touched one small square with one finger, very carefully, the way you'd touch a moth. Then she closed the book, tucked it under her arm without asking, and walked out fast, heading for the craft cabin, and Deb picked up the paddles and thought no more about it, except that she hoped somebody would hang that book back up eventually.

In the cabin, Kaitlyn dragged her canvas into the light by the window. The complement of orange was blue; the complement of blue was orange. So her gray, sitting beside orange rock, drifted toward blue, which should have made it cooler, not warmer. She frowned at that. Maybe she had the complements backwards, or maybe the shifting worked in some way the sentence didn't say, because the sentence only said toward the complement of the neighboring color, and her gray was neighbor to orange on one side and blue on the other, and it looked warm on the orange side. She did not know which part she was getting wrong. What she knew was that the gray was not one thing, and that the painting could use that, if she had the nerve to let it.

Rosa came over at six, carrying her finished owl, which had a metamorphic look, as though it might at any moment become a different and better owl. She stood in front of the canvas while Kaitlyn worked a thin line of violet into the rocks.

"It's called simultaneous contrast," Kaitlyn said, not stopping. "Chevreul, 1839. The gray shifts toward the complement of whatever's next to it. That's why it's two colors."

"That's the same gray?"

"Same gray."

Rosa was quiet for a moment. "You're not going to fix it, then."

"I don't think it's broken." Kaitlyn stepped back and looked at the sky, warm over the rocks, cool over the water, one gray doing the work of two. Whether the painting was honest or whether it was an accident she had decided to call a plan, she could not entirely say, and there was no time to decide before Friday. The show started at seven. She picked up the paperboard scrap, held it over the left sky one more time, and watched the warmth go out of the gray like a tide pulling back from shore.

"Hand me the violet," she said, and Rosa did.

The practice rooms at Halloway Concert Hall were in the basement, below the stage, and you could hear the floorboards flex when the orchestra rehearsed above. Logan had claimed room four every Tuesday since September because it had the piano with the least dead keys. He spread his staff paper on the music stand and set his pencil down crosswise, the way his older sister had shown him years ago, though she had stopped playing before she finished high school.

The assignment was sixteen bars, a melody with chord changes, written in standard notation by Friday. His teacher, Mr. Okafor, had said only that endings matter more than beginnings, because a listener forgives a weak first phrase but remembers a weak last one. Logan had written fifteen bars that he almost liked. The melody rose through the first eight, settled in the middle, and by bar fifteen it had walked itself home to a C major chord. It should have felt finished. It felt like a door closing on a room with nothing in it.

He played the fifteen bars through, then the last chord, then sat with his hands in his lap. In the key of C, he had been using C, F, and G chords, the ones every beginner used, and the melody sat on top of them the way a cat sits on a warm car, comfortable and going nowhere. Above him the orchestra had stopped. A tuba player laughed at something in the hallway.

Theo knocked and came in without waiting. Theo was a second-year composition student who wore the same green coat in every season and who agreed, in Logan's experience, with whatever the last person in the room had said. Logan had privately labeled him a sycophant and felt some guilt about it, since Theo's flattery was at least sincere, unlike the kind that wants something.

"Sixteen bars," Logan said. "Mine ends on C and it sounds like the melody just got tired."

"Maybe tired is honest," Theo said, and then, when Logan said nothing, "or maybe it's not. Could be both." Everything Theo said was equivocal, but he played piano better than Logan did, so Logan slid over on the bench.

"Play bars fourteen and fifteen." Theo played them. The melody's last phrase ended on an E, held over a C major chord, and then silence. Theo played it again and this time, without being asked, added a G chord under the second-to-last melody note and put an F on top of it with his right hand. Suddenly the final C chord did not just arrive. It received something.

Logan pulled the staff paper toward him. "What did you add? Tell me the notes."

Theo spread his right hand so Logan could see. "G, B, D, and F. It's a dominant seventh, on G." He said it as if naming a sandwich he'd ordered a hundred times, then added, "People put it before the end all the time. You'll hear it in practically anything upstairs." He stood, checked his phone, and left with a compliment about Logan's bar nine that Logan did not believe and accepted anyway.

Logan wrote the four notes into bar fifteen, stacked in the notation he had learned that month, stem directions checked twice. He played the ending with the new chord, and the sound of the G, B, D and F pulled his ear forward into the C major chord the way a held breath pulls toward release. He did not fully understand it. He had been told his whole life that music theory was a set of rules, and this felt less like a rule than a fact about gravity he had stepped off a curb and noticed. He wrote the chord symbol above the staff and drew a bracket from it to bar sixteen.

At the Thursday rehearsal, Logan sat in the last row of the concert hall with the paper on his knee. The student orchestra was running a slow piece that ended with four repetitions of a final phrase, and on the third one the strings dropped low and the horns took a chord that he recognized by shape, that same tilted, leaning sound. The whole audience, he could feel it, leaned with it. Whatever the chord was doing, it did not need to be understood to work, and Logan found this both reassuring and slightly annoying, because it meant his earlier endings had failed in a way he hadn't been able to hear until tonight.

In room four on Friday morning he made a choice. He kept the dominant seventh in bar fifteen, but he also kept a version on a second sheet without it, labeled with the date, filed in the folder under his sister's old exercise books. When Mr. Okafor collected the sixteen bars that afternoon, he played Logan's ending once, said "Better," and moved to the next student's paper. Logan sat in the basement afterward with the folder open on the piano lid, both endings side by side, and played them alternately until he could no longer decide which one he preferred, and then played the version with the added note one more time.

The gymnasium smelled of floor wax and folding chairs, and Lucas arrived early enough to claim a seat near the microphone that stood at the center aisle. He had come with a page of notes he'd copied out the night before, though he'd told his mother he was going for the free pizza the student council had promised. The town hall meeting had been called to debate a resolution asking the state legislature to adopt a recall provision for local officials, and Lucas, who had spent three weeks arguing about impeachment in his government class, intended to speak. He wanted, more precisely, to be right in public, which felt different from being right in a classroom where only Mr. Okafor was listening.

The council members sat behind a long table draped in gray felt, and beside them, as a guest, sat a woman introduced only as Ms. Reyes, visiting from Ottawa. Lucas noticed her because she took notes in a small green book while everyone else typed on phones. When the mayor opened the floor, an old man in a barn coat was first to the microphone, saying that if the council could not remove a bad road commissioner, then the whole structure was a farce. People clapped in the scattered, uncertain way of crowds who agree with a sentiment but not yet with its consequences.

When Lucas's turn came, his palms were damp against his notes. He said that removing a leader should be hard, that the founders of presidential systems had made it deliberately difficult. "In 1868 the Senate acquitted President Andrew Johnson by one vote," he said. "Thirty-six senators voted to convict, one short of the two-thirds needed. So even when a president is hated, the bar stays high." He let that sit, pleased with the weight of it, and then added, "If we make removal too easy, every loser of an election will try to overturn it."

Ms. Reyes raised her hand, and the mayor, seeming relieved to have something to do, called on her. She stood without leaving her chair, holding the green book. "A parliamentary system works the other way," she said. "The head of government stays only as long as the legislature supports him. If his own party turns, a simple vote removes him. It is designed to be easy." She said it lightly, as if offering weather, and sat down. Lucas felt his argument tilt beneath him, because he had never actually thought about why two systems would choose opposite assumptions, only about which one was correct.

The old man in the barn coat came back to the microphone. "Young man," he said, and Lucas braced for dismissal, "you said thirty-six. It was thirty-five. I teach this, retired now, but I have transcribed that roll call more times than I care to admit. Thirty-five voted to convict. One vote short." He paused. "Edmund Ross was the one everyone remembers, but the number is thirty-five." Lucas looked down at his notes and saw his own handwriting, the six written in a fast, sloppy loop, and could not remember whether he had miscounted or miscopied. The veracity of everything else on the page suddenly seemed provisional. "Either way," he said, and heard how weak it sounded, "one vote decided it."

"That's exactly the point," Ms. Reyes said from her seat, and several people laughed, not unkindly. "One vote, in both directions." Lucas stood there with the microphone still live and the whole gymnasium waiting, and instead of defending his six, he found himself thinking about what the two systems disagreed on. A parliamentary system trusts the legislature to judge constantly, in real time, without ceremony. A presidential system trusts the fixed term more than it trusts any majority, and so it raises the bar until removal becomes almost metamorphic, something that almost never happens, and when it does, it changes everything. He could not decide which mistrust was wiser. He suspected the answer depended on what you were afraid of.

"I got the number wrong," Lucas said into the microphone. The old man nodded once, like a judge accepting a plea. "But the number being close is the interesting part. Maybe the bar is too high. Maybe a prime minister can be removed too easily, by a bad week. But it can't be both." He looked at Ms. Reyes, who was writing in her green book again, and he wondered what she thought of a town arguing about a road commissioner as if it were the fate of a nation. Someone called out that they were debating a county drainage board, not the presidency, and the room laughed properly this time.

The mayor moved the resolution to a vote of the council, and Lucas sat down and watched the hands. The clerk read the tally slowly, as though she too understood the weight of margins. Five in favor. Six against. It failed by one vote, and the old man in the barn coat stood up, put on his hat, and said loudly enough for the first three rows to hear, "Well. History repeats." Lucas stayed in his seat while the chairs were stacked, copying the corrected number onto a fresh page in his own notebook, pressing hard enough that the five came through onto the next sheet.

On his way out, Ms. Reyes was waiting by the door with her coat over her arm. "You changed your mind up there," she said. "Most people don't." Lucas shrugged, still unsure whether that was a compliment or a diagnosis. "I changed one number," he said. "The mind part's still out for deliberation." She smiled and held the door open for him, and the cold outside hit his face like a splash of water.

Sophie knelt in the frozen grass between her mother's shoes and the headstone with the name HAMIDI chiseled deep enough to catch shadow, and she said, "Tell me again how she did it." Her mother's breath came out in slow white clouds. "She didn't do anything, that was the thing. She just sat there and everyone knew where to stand." Above them the January sky was the flat gray of an unwashed window, and the cemetery held only the two of them and a crow that kept landing on the fence and leaving, as if it couldn't decide.

The plan had come out of the November kitchen, out of the last iftar before her grandmother died. Sophie had been seventeen for a month and a half, and her aunts had been passing the dates over her head all her life. During Ramadan the whole family broke each day's fast at sunset with the meal they called iftar, and it always began the same way, with one date, the way the Prophet Muhammad had done it. Her grandmother had kept the dates ready for the moment the sun went down, every single evening of every Ramadan for fifty years, and when she died in December, nobody had said out loud who would take it over. Sophie had asked for it the way you ask for something you're afraid will be refused: quickly, at the sink, with her back turned. Her mother had said, "You know it's not just food. It's the timing." Sophie had said she knew.

Now it was her problem, and the problem had a shape she hadn't expected. Half the family wanted the iftar held the old way, at the house on Delancey Street, with the prayer before the dates and her uncle calling the adhan from the hallway because the speaker had broken years ago and nobody had fixed it, which had somehow become tradition itself. The other half, the younger half, had proposed something at the community center, catered, efficient, with a printed schedule so the fast could be broken on time without anyone standing in a kitchen all afternoon. Sophie had listened to both sides over a holiday dinner that was not the holiday dinner, and had understood that the argument wasn't really about venue. It was about whether a thing survived by staying exactly where it was or by being allowed to move.

She had come to the cemetery because the argument needed a third opinion and the third opinion was under the grass. "You'd tell me to stop being dramatic," she said to the headstone. Her mother laughed, a short sound, startled out of her. "She would. She'd say, feed them, the rest follows." Sophie looked up at her. "But that's the part I don't know. Does it?" Her mother pulled her scarf tighter and didn't answer, which Sophie had learned, recently, was its own kind of answer, the recalcitrant silence her grandmother had also used when a question was better left to ferment in the person asking it.

The concrete task was this: Sophie had to have the dates ready at the second of sunset, not ten minutes after, and she had learned, testing herself, that she could not trust her own eyes to know when the sun had gone. She'd looked up the calculation instead, and had spent a full afternoon in her room with the prayer times and the compass on her phone, until her aunt caught her at it and said, "You're doing what your grandmother did, the week before Ramadan, every year." That had been a strange comfort, that the worry was inherited, that her grandmother had also once sat somewhere with a piece of paper and no idea what she was doing. It might have been happenstance that the woman who became the family's keeper of iftar was the one who worried hardest, but Sophie didn't think so.

She had also gotten something wrong, and found out at the worst time. Last week, at the trial run she'd organized for the cousins, she had put out dates and water, and she'd watched the second hand of the kitchen clock tick past the calculated minute, and she had let everyone eat, and then her cousin Yusuf had looked at his own phone and said, "It was two minutes ago. The sun's been down." Two minutes. Nobody had made it a crime, but Sophie had felt it like one, because the whole point of the date was the moment, the first thing to touch a fast that had lasted since dawn. She had redone the calculation that night and found her mistake, a daylight savings setting she'd overlooked, and had sworn at her phone in a whisper in the dark.

The two sides of the family argument came together in her head on the walk back down the cemetery path, not because she forced them but because the frozen ground made her walk slowly and the walking did it. The community center people were right that a thing can be carried. The Delancey Street people were right that some things soak into walls. What she settled on, and she knew settled was too strong a word, was the house, the old way, but with the schedule printed anyway, taped to the refrigerator where the adhan speaker used to be, because the adhan could come from a phone now and a wrong clock could not be allowed to happen twice. Her mother walked beside her with her hands in her pockets and offered nothing, which Sophie understood as permission of a kind, though she could not have said of what.

The evening before the first fast, Sophie stood in the Delancey Street kitchen alone, the way she imagined her grandmother had stood, with the box of dates open on the counter and the small glass plates laid out, one for each person, eleven in total. She picked up a date and turned it in her fingers, this unremarkable brown thing that had to be in a hand at the second the light left. From the hallway her mother called, "Are you ready for tomorrow?" Sophie set the date back in the box, on top, where she would see it first. "The sun sets at 5:47," she said. "I'll be standing right here at 5:46."

Megan had chosen the bowling alley herself, mostly because it was impossible to be awkward somewhere that smelled like rented shoes. Her date, Daniel, had suggested a coffee shop, and she had countered with Tuesday night league lulls and half price games, and now here they were under the black lights, holding shoes in two plastic bags like trophies from a very small war.

The first game went well. Daniel bowled a respectable gutter ball and laughed at himself without performing the laughter, which Megan logged as promising. They talked about orientation schedules and roommates and the cafeteria's alleged burrito bar, and the conversation moved at the pace of two people testing a bridge with one foot on each plank.

By the second game, the planks ran out. Daniel asked what her major was, and she had already told him. She asked if he had siblings, and he had already said two, a younger sister, and a brother in Denver whose whole personality was apparently the Broncos. Megan watched the pins reset themselves with a mechanical clatter and tried to resuscitate the small talk, which lay between them on the lane like something that had been left out too long.

Then Daniel said, "Okay, I have an idea, but it might be weird." He wiped his palms on his jeans. "My psych teacher told us about this study. Arthur Aron, 1997. Pairs of strangers took turns asking each other thirty six questions, and the questions got gradually more personal, and afterward the pairs felt closer than pairs who just made small talk." He let that sit for a second. "We're out of small talk. I'm just saying."

"You want to run a psychology experiment on our first date."

"I want to cheat, technically. Same thing."

Megan pretended to consider it, though she had already decided, the way she decided most things, quickly and then slowly after. Her mother would say it was rushing intimacy, that closeness you built out of a questionnaire was a house with no foundation. Her brother would say the foundation was the questionnaire, that anything that worked was real the moment it worked. Both of them were probably a little right, which was the most annoying possible arrangement.

"Fine," she said, picking up her ball. "But we bowl between questions. And I go first. Question one, and I'm starting easy. What's your actual worst fear, spiders excepted?"

"You said starting easy."

"Spiders are the universal exception."

He answered while she rolled a seven, something about being forgettable, which was a better answer than the question deserved. Then his turn, and his question came while the ball was still traveling: what she would save from her childhood bedroom if it burned. She said her grandmother's recipe box, then admitted she had never cooked anything from it, and Daniel said that somehow made it mean more, not less, and she felt the consonance of that, two notes she hadn't expected to line up.

The questions climbed the way the study apparently promised, one rung at a time. Somewhere around question eleven, which Daniel delivered in the tone of a person defusing something, Megan realized she had told him about her parents' divorce, a subject she usually rationed out over three months of friendship, and that he had told her about his brother in Denver being sick last year, the real story, not the Broncos story. She also noticed she had stopped keeping score. The screen was keeping score anyway, indifferent and accurate, flashing her losses in orange while she failed entirely to mind.

By the last frame, the questions had reached a place where the answers had weight to them, and Megan found herself thinking that her mother and her brother were describing the same bridge from opposite banks. The closeness wasn't fake just because the questions came from a study, and it wasn't guaranteed just because a study said strangers had felt it before them. What stayed uncertain was the part no experiment covered, which was what happened after the thirty six ran out and you were left with only whatever you'd built. She didn't say any of this. She was eighteen, not a fortune cookie.

"Question thirty six," Daniel said. "Last one. The study doesn't say what it is, so I'm making it up, which I feel is within the spirit of the thing." He stood at the line with his ball, not bowling, waiting. "If this goes horribly, statistically we still had a better night than the small talk couples. And if it doesn't go horribly, what do you want to do next Saturday?"

Megan looked at the pins, ten of them, white and patient under the black light.

"Gutter ball decides nothing," she said, and rolled.

The biology test was on Friday, and Sadie had promised herself she would stop memorizing and start understanding, though she could not have said what the difference would feel like until she found it. On Wednesday, Ms. Okafor moved the whole class outside to the community garden behind the science wing, where she had taped letters to the tomato stakes: A, U, G, C, strung along a fence like laundry. She held up a shoebox full of index cards.

"Each of you is a transfer RNA," she said. "You carry one amino acid and you have a three-base anticodon. Find your match on the messenger RNA."

Sadie drew a card. AUG was written across the top in Ms. Okafor's cramped hand, and beneath it, in smaller letters, a single word: methionine. She stood there turning the card over while the rest of the class scattered along the fence, reading stakes, comparing letters.

"What if I can't find mine?" Dev asked. He was holding a card with UAC on it and had walked the entire fence twice.

"Then look harder," Ms. Okafor said, which wasn't an answer, and everyone knew it. Sadie thought Ms. Okafor liked to equivocate like that when she wanted them to do the finding themselves, offering a reply that sounded like help but committed to nothing.

She walked the fence slowly. The stakes spelled out a message in triplets, base after base, and she stopped at the first three: UAC. Her card said AUG. She stood between the stake and the tomato vines, which had gone turgid and heavy after the morning watering, their stems thick and firm enough to hold the weight of the fruit without sagging. She held her card against the stake. UAC. AUG. She matched them, base by base, and felt something rearrange in her head, quiet and total, like a door she hadn't known was closed.

"It pairs," she said. "UAC pairs with AUG."

"So give me the amino acid," Dev said, and she realized he was the ribosome, standing there with his hand out, waiting. She handed him her card and he clamped it between two fingers. "One amino acid, one codon," he said. "Next."

Priya came forward with GGC in blue ink and found the CCG stake, and gave Dev her card, which said proline. Marcus matched his CGA to a GCU stake, wavered, asked Ms. Okafor whether he was right, and got only a shrug for his trouble. Sadie watched him do it and couldn't tell whether his pairing held. She looked at his card, looked at the stake, and decided it did. He gave Dev alanine. The chain grew in Dev's hand, amino acid by amino acid, and Dev read them off in order, and Ms. Okafor had a chart on her clipboard that translated the sequence into something else entirely.

"It says a word," Dev announced. "It spells something."

Sadie leaned over to see. The chain of amino acids they had assembled corresponded to a short peptide, and Ms. Okafor had rigged the messenger RNA on the fence so that the finished protein, according to her chart, was real: a fragment of insulin. The thing that kept people alive, that her own grandmother injected every morning, had been built in front of her by eleven teenagers passing index cards in a garden.

Later, at the picnic table by the compost bins, she argued with Priya about whether it meant anything. Priya said the cell had a purpose, that this was the whole point of the machinery, that insulin existed in order to regulate sugar. Sadie wasn't sure. The tRNA didn't know what insulin was. The card in her hand hadn't wanted anything. It had matched AUG to UAC because the shapes fit, and the chain had grown because each carrier did one small thing, and the insulin had fallen out of the accumulation the way a sentence falls out of grammar. She said something like that, less smoothly, and Priya called it bleak.

"It's not bleak," Sadie said. "It's just not teleology. It's not designed toward an end. It's a lot of small matches."

"Then why does it work so well?"

"I don't know." She turned her card over in her fingers, the AUG side down now, methionine facing up. "That part I can't explain. Maybe someone can. Maybe it's the long version of what we just did, and I'd need another shoebox."

Priya laughed at that, short, and stood up. Sadie stayed at the table with the card, matching it once more against the letters in her head, UAC against AUG, because she wanted to be sure it would still be there tomorrow.

"Keep it," Ms. Okafor said from the fence, gathering stakes. "You earned that one."

The print lay flat on the table between Julia and Priya, propped against a stack of art history textbooks, and the assignment sheet beside it asked for something Julia did not yet know how to give: a formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism, two pages, due Thursday. Ms. Okafor had said the word "formal" as though it were a door she was holding open for them, and Julia had spent three days standing outside it. The painting was The Broken Column, and Julia had chosen it because everyone said it was famous, and she was beginning to suspect that this was a bad reason.

"Why is there a building inside her?" Priya asked, leaning over the print with her chin in her hand. It was a fair question. The figure in the painting stood alone in a cracked, parched landscape, and where her torso should have been solid there was an opening, and through the opening her spine showed, painted as a cracked Ionic column, the kind with the scrolled capital, the kind from ancient Greece, split down the middle.

"Maybe it's a metaphor," Julia said, and hated the word even as she said it. She had used it in English essays the way other people used salt, to cover whatever she couldn't taste. Priya gave her a look that said she had noticed.

The classroom had emptied after last bell except for the two of them and Marcus, who was arguing with a paintbrush at the far table, and the radiator ticking under the window. Julia turned the print toward herself. She had read somewhere, in the first frantic hour of research, that the painting was a self-portrait, that the artist had painted it after years of hospital beds and corsets, but Ms. Okafor had circled a line on Julia's rough draft in red pen: "You are telling me what the painting means. I want you to show me what the painting does." Julia did not yet understand the difference, and the not understanding sat in her chest like a held breath.

"Okay, forget meaning," she said aloud, mostly to herself. "Colour first. That's formal, right? Look at the blues." The sky behind the figure was a flat, cold blue cut by sharp white fissures, like the ground. The flesh was pale, almost grey. And running down the figure's cheeks were the tears, which were the only thing in the whole canvas that shone.

"They're not sad tears," Priya said slowly. "I mean they are, but they're painted like glass. Like they'd cut you."

Julia wrote that down, because it was better than anything she had. Then she looked again at the column where the spine should be, and the question Priya had asked came back to her with the force of an actual problem rather than a rhetorical one. A Greek column, inside a human body. She thought of the fluted stone pillars in the textbook chapter on the Parthenon, all symmetry and civic order, and she thought of the split running down this one, and something shifted in her without settling.

"Wait," she said. "Ionic. That's the style with the scrolls at the top. She didn't just paint any column, she painted that one." Priya leaned in again. "So the composition is like, her body is the facade, the front of a building, and it's torn open, and what's holding her up is architecture, but it's broken architecture." Julia was writing fast now, the pen skipping. "The straps, too. Look, all those white straps around her, like the painting won't let her fall apart completely."

Marcus had drifted over from his table, wiping his hands on a rag, and stood at the edge of their light looking down at the print. "My grandmother had a back brace," he said, not to either of them in particular. "After her surgery. She used to make us kids sign the cast, like a fun thing, but the brace part, she never let us touch it." He tapped the edge of the table twice, an apology for the interruption, and Priya moved the print a few inches toward him so he could see.

Julia thought about how easy it would be to ascribe all of this to pain and stop there, to write two pages that said the painting was sad because the painter was sad, which was true the way a weather report was true. But the tears were glass, and the column was Ionic, and the composition held the figure upright in the centre of the frame as though refusing to let her slump, and these were choices, made with a brush. Maybe that was what Ms. Okafor meant by what the painting did. It took a broken thing and made it stand in the open, in daylight, facing out.

She worked on the draft that evening at her kitchen table while her mother dried dishes behind her, and she found the sentence she had been looking for only by writing badly past it: the tears and the column are made of the same hard material, and the painting makes you look at both without letting you decide which is the wound and which is the support. She sat with that sentence for a long time. She could not tell if it was insight or decoration. In the space between her certainty and her doubt, which felt like a kind of interregnum, she underlined it anyway, in pencil, so it could still be argued with.

The next morning she found Priya at the lockers and handed over the draft, and Priya read the sentence, and read it again, and said, "I don't know if that's right." Julia said, "I don't either," and Priya said, "Then put it in. That's the good stuff," and pressed the pages back into Julia's hands, and Julia went down the corridor toward Ms. Okafor's door holding them the way Marcus's grandmother must have held the brace she never let anyone touch.

Dev's basement smelled like the inside of a hockey bag, and the couch had a crater in the middle that pulled anyone who sat in it toward the floor. Joshua lowered himself into the crater anyway, balancing his laptop on his knees, because the couch had the good outlet behind it and Dev had claimed the only chair before Joshua even got his shoes off.

"So explain it to me like I'm your grandmother," Dev said, spinning a lacrosse ball on his finger. "Why is your search better than just, you know, walking through the list?"

"Because the list is sorted," Joshua said. "Ten million numbers, all in order. If I walk through it, I check the first one, then the second, then the third, and maybe I find my target on the millionth try, or maybe I never find it and I check all ten million. That's a linear search. It works, but it's dumb about the work it does."

"And yours is smart."

"Mine cuts the problem in half every single time." Joshua pulled up the code. "I look at the middle number. If my target is bigger, I throw away the whole bottom half and look at the middle of what's left. Then I do it again. Ten million becomes five million becomes two and a half million, and pretty soon I'm down to one number. A handful of steps instead of a million."

"Like guessing a number between one and a hundred," Dev said. "You'd say fifty first."

"Exactly. High, low, then middle." Joshua tilted the screen toward him. "You keep a low pointer and a high pointer, and the middle is low plus high, divided by two. Then you move the pointers depending on which half you throw out."

Dev squinted at the midpoint line the way he squinted at bad refs, which was a compliment of a kind. "That looks fine."

"It looks fine," Joshua agreed, and pushed Run, and the test data went through like a greased puck. Two hundred numbers, target found on the fourth comparison. Joshua did a small drumroll on the crater's armrest.

The competition dataset was another animal. Dev had downloaded it that afternoon, the full thing, some monstrosity with indices so large they didn't fit comfortably in Joshua's head, let alone anywhere else. Joshua's program chewed on it for four seconds and then crashed with an error he had never seen before, something about a value that couldn't be represented, sitting right there on the screen like a rat in the kitchen.

"Oh no," Dev said, delighted. "Your smart search is dumb."

"It's not dumb, it's..." Joshua scrolled up. The crash pointed at one line, and he stared at it, and stared at it, and then felt the specific embarrassment of a person who has been confidently explaining something for ten minutes. "Low plus high divided by two. On the huge data, low and high are both enormous. Adding them together goes past what the numbers can hold, and the whole thing breaks."

"So don't add them."

"I have to find the middle somehow." Joshua got up, because he thought better standing, and paced past the drying rack of ping pong paddles, mouthing the arithmetic. Low plus high, over two. The same as low plus half of the difference between high and low. He stopped mid-stride. "Wait. The distance from low to high is just high minus low, and that's small even when both of them are huge. So the midpoint is low plus high minus low, divided by two. Same middle, no giant addition, no crash."

"That's it?"

"That's it." Joshua sat back down into the crater, deleted one line, and typed the new one. The fix looked almost insultingly small on the screen, a few characters rearranged, like fixing a bridge by moving one bolt. He hit Run again. The giant dataset scrolled past, the target came back correct, the program exited cleanly, and Joshua exhaled so hard the lacrosse ball wobbled on Dev's finger.

"So your grandma explanation," Dev said. "You'd have to add 'unless the list is astronomically big, then write the midpoint a different way.'"

"I'd say it in a nicer way than that." Joshua saved the file twice, which was a habit he wasn't going to defend. He was also, he admitted to Dev, still not one hundred percent sure he could explain why the overflow had picked that exact moment to happen rather than some other moment; he understood the shape of it, the way he understood that his car needed oil, without being able to reify the whole engine on demand. "The theory I can do. The weird edges of it, I find those by crashing."

"That's why you keep me around," Dev said. "I download the catastrophic data. Off-by-one errors are endemic to you people, you know. It's like a colloquialism among programmers. 'Works on my machine.' Works in your basement, you mean."

"Throw me the ball," Joshua said, and held up the laptop as a mitt.

The essay was due in forty-one hours, and Olivier had written one sentence. He read it again on the laptop screen: "Historians have interpreted the French Revolution in different ways." He deleted "in different ways" and typed "differently," then deleted that too, and went downstairs in search of the kettle.

His grandfather had moved in with them in March, and his boxes were still stacked in the guest room, smelling faintly of pipe tobacco that nobody was allowed to smoke anymore. Olivier had been told to keep out, but the kettle lived in the kitchen, and the guest room sat between the stairs and the kitchen, and through the half-open door he saw his grandfather asleep in the armchair with a book open on his knee. The book was thick and cloth-bound, its spine gone the color of weak tea. Olivier reached for it carefully, the way you take a glass from a sleeping person's hand.

On the title page, in faded copperplate: The French Revolution: A History. Thomas Carlyle. He turned to the front matter and found the date, 1837, printed small and certain. "Grand-père," he said, and the old man woke without a start, as though he had only been waiting to be needed.

"That was my father's," his grandfather said. "Take it if it's useful. Mind the foxed pages, they tear." He closed his eyes again before Olivier could ask what foxed meant.

Upstairs, Olivier spread the book beside his laptop and began taking notes. The problem, he discovered within twenty minutes, was that Carlyle did not write like a historian at all. He wrote like a man describing a thunderstorm from inside it. There was a chapter that opened with the King trying to flee the country in disguise, and Carlyle lingered not on the economic pressures or the political factions but on the faces, the sweating postilions, the moment a postmaster recognized the King from his profile on a coin. Olivier underlined a line about the Queen at the window and wrote in the margin, melodramatic?, then felt slightly ashamed of himself.

The books from the library were stacked on the desk, and he worked his way through them alongside Carlyle: a Marxist account in which the Revolution was moved by class forces the way weather is moved by pressure systems, a revisionist study that dismantled that argument almost gleefully, a recent synthesis full of caveats. The Marxist treated individuals as instruments of larger processes, interchangeable, replaceable. Carlyle treated the Revolution as though it had been caused, at every turning point, by somebody choosing. Olivier sat back. His tea had gone cold in the crepuscular light coming through the blinds, and he turned the desk lamp on, and the two stacks of books looked, in the sudden brightness, like counsel for opposing sides.

He called his classmate Manon, who was also writing the essay and had already written, she claimed, nine hundred words, though she admitted under questioning that four hundred of them were the introduction. "What's your thesis?" she asked.

"I don't have one yet. I have a fight." He told her about Carlyle, about the coin-profile recognition scene, about how the modern books kept dissolving people into structures. "It's like Carlyle thinks history is a series of moral choices," he said, "and the others think it's forces. And the annoying thing is that the scene works either way. The postmaster recognizes the King because of a coin, which is a policy, which is a structure, and then he decides what to do about it, which is a choice."

"That's not a thesis, that's a hedge," Manon said, but she said it without conviction, and then she asked him to read the recognition scene aloud, and when he finished she was quiet for a second. "Read that part again," she said. "The part about the coin."

He worked until midnight, drafting and cutting. The sentence he kept building toward was one that refused to come out clean: that Carlyle's insistence on individual moral choice in 1837 was itself a historical position, that even a refusal to see impersonal forces was a way of seeing. He distrusted it because it felt clever rather than true, and he distrusted his distrust because the clock in the hall, which his grandfather had wound every Sunday since March, was telling him it was one in the morning and the essay was due at noon.

In the morning he found his grandfather at the kitchen table with toast and the newspaper, the empty space on his knee where the book had been. "Did it help?" his grandfather asked.

"I don't know yet," Olivier said. "I might be arguing he was wrong and right at the same time."

His grandfather buttered his toast and considered this. "My father would have said that was the only honest kind of argument," he said. "But he also thought utilitarianism was a disease, so weigh that accordingly." He folded the newspaper in half and slid it across the table, open to the crossword, and took out a pencil. Olivier poured his coffee and sat down across from him, essay still unfinished in his head, deadline still ticking, and picked up the pencil anyway.

"Seven across," his grandfather said. "Four letters, 'period of decline.'"

"Decay," said Olivier.

The printer at the back of the Fairview Public Library took quarters, which Ryan had, and gave instructions, which he ignored. He had twenty minutes before the climate club meeting and one design, a drawing of a drowned street sign he had inked at two in the morning, and a plan he described to himself as "figure it out at the machine." The library enfranchised anybody with sixty cents into the whole world of publishing; that was how he thought of it, anyway, since the art room at school now required a permission slip for the paper cutter.

He had quit art class in March. Not dramatically, in the way he sometimes rehearsed quitting things, but by simply not turning in the self-portrait, and then not turning in the apology for the self-portrait, and then letting the weeks accumulate like silt until Ms. Okafor stopped asking. The portrait had been honest, which was the problem. It showed his face the way he actually suspected it looked to other people, and the class had gone quiet in the wrong way. His mother said he'd traded one kind of honesty for a cheaper one. He was still deciding whether that was fair.

The poster was, in his private taxonomy, the first thing he'd drawn since. Flyers were their own phylum of object, halfway between litter and art, and he wanted this one to be art that was not afraid to become litter. He fed a sheet of A3 into the tray and pressed the button for 100 percent, because scaling felt like a negotiation he wasn't qualified for.

The sheet came out with the drowned street sign floating in too much white. Behind him, a kid of about eleven watched over his shoulder with the frank entitlement of someone who intended to comment.

"It's too small," the kid said.

"It's A3."

"What's A3?"

"Big paper," Ryan said, and immediately felt the answer was beneath both of them.

He tried again at a larger percentage, but when he asked the machine for A4, something happened that he stood looking at for longer than he would admit. The shrunken printout was the same drawing, and the shape of the page was the same shape. He held the A4 up against the A3 against the window, where the late light lay alluvial across the tables, and the edges lined up corner to corner, the big page exactly a doubled version of the small one. He cut the A3 in half with the blunt library scissors, and the two halves were A4, and each half matched the printout's proportions exactly.

"Those are ISO 216 sizes," the kid said, with the air of someone reciting something off a cereal box. "The sides are one to the square root of two. Cut it in half, you get the same shape again."

Ryan looked at him. "How do you know that?"

"My dad's an engineer. He cries at paper."

What the kid's father apparently wept over, Ryan now tested: he printed the poster at A4, and it matched the half of the A3 perfectly, and the half of the half, an A5 he cut with growing confidence, matched again. One drawing, descending through sizes like a set of nested spoons. The small versions were not degraded copies. They were the poster, fully themselves, asking nothing of the big one. He thought, without wanting to, of the self-portrait, which had existed at exactly one size, in exactly one room, in front of exactly one audience, and had died there.

The club's co-president, Dara, arrived with a USB drive and an agenda. She wanted forty flyers by Saturday and had assumed they'd photocopy his design "whatever size, whatever, people will get it." Ryan laid his cut sheets in a row on the table, A3 to A5, and said the design would hold at any size, that a flyer could be folded into a smaller flyer and still be true, and Dara said, "Ryan, it's a street sign, not a manifesto," which was fair.

Then came the part he hadn't planned. Ms. Okafor was at the next table, returned books stacked beside her, and she had been watching the row of diminishing pages for some time. She didn't say anything about March or the portrait. She picked up the A5, held it at arm's length, and said, "This one. Print this one forty times."

"The small one?"

"The small one," she said, and put on her reading glasses. "It looks like you finally stopped apologizing for the size of things."

He didn't know if that was true, or if a drawing could apologize, or whether quitting in March had been cowardice or just a kind of waiting. What he knew was that the machine took quarters and he had four, and that the kid was still there, and that some truths could be cut in half forever without changing shape.

He fed the tray and pressed the button.

Annabelle's mother had been in bed since Tuesday with something the doctor called a slow virus, a thing that would debilitate her for a while without ever quite becoming dangerous, and so the kitchen had become Annabelle's by default. The first three dinners had been eggs, toast, and a bag of frozen peas eaten standing at the counter, and by Friday she had decided this was beneath her, or at least beneath the situation. She wanted to do the week properly: a plan, a shop, five meals cooked on Sunday and reheated on the nights that followed. She had read about it online at one in the morning, scribbling a list in the margin of her chemistry notes, and on Saturday morning she took the bus to the farmers' market with sixty dollars and a canvas bag that had once held library books.

The market occupied a parking lot behind the old cannery, rows of white tents along the harbor, the stalls closest to the water selling littoral things Annabelle had no plans for: buckets of steamers, bundles of dulse, a man shucking oysters with a short blunt knife. She walked past all of it toward the tables of vegetables, because her list began there. The list itself had taken her two hours. At first she had planned seven dinners, then realized she would be cooking for two and eating lunch at school, then cut it to five, then argued with herself about whether Wednesday's chili and Thursday's chili were the same meal. She had settled on the position that they were different meals separated by a night of rest, though she suspected the argument was mostly semantics.

At the tomato stall she counted out eight Romas, then put two back, then took them again. The farmer, a woman with gray braid and soil in the creases of her knuckles, watched this with open amusement. "Deciding something?" she asked.

"I'm planning a whole week," Annabelle said. "It turns out deciding is most of the work."

The farmer laughed and gave her a ninth tomato for free, which felt like a grade. At the next stall Annabelle bought a bag of carrots, a bunch of kale, three sweet potatoes. At the egg stand she waited behind a man buying four dozen while she tried to remember whether her mother's rice was the short-grain or the long-grain, and finally bought a bag of jasmine because she liked how it smelled when the water came up to the boil. At the butcher's trailer she asked for a pound and a half of ground pork, and the butcher asked her what she was making, and when she said rice bowls and soup and a chili she was mostly inventing, he nodded as though she had said something wise.

The problem revealed itself slowly, over the course of the afternoon, in her own kitchen. She cooked the rice in the biggest pot, all four cups of it, and browned the pork, and roasted the sweet potatoes on one sheet pan while the kale wilted in a skillet. By five o'clock the counter held six containers, labeled in her careful hand, and she felt something close to triumph. Then, spooning a test bowl for herself, she stopped. The rice had been sitting in the pot, then in a container, then in the microwave, and somewhere in the back of her mind was a fragment from a food-safety unit in eighth grade, half remembered and shaped like a warning. She had read, too, in one of the batch-cooking articles, that a thermometer was not optional equipment. Her mother owned one. It lived, she discovered, in the drawer with the dead batteries and the birthday candles, a thin metal probe with a small dial.

She had never used it. She microwaved her test bowl again, longer this time, until the edges of the rice scalded her thumb, then pushed the probe into the center of the pile and watched the needle crawl. It stopped at what looked like a hundred and forty. She pulled the phone from her back pocket and searched, and there it was, plain as a bus schedule: the USDA advises reheating leftovers to an internal temperature of 165 degrees Fahrenheit, which was 74 degrees Celsius. She looked at the dial, which had both scales printed on its face, the Celsius numbers smaller, inside. A hundred and forty was nowhere near. She had been about to eat it.

"Fine," she said out loud to the empty kitchen, feeling both foolish and, strangely, more competent than she had all day. She stirred the bowl so the cold center and the scalded edges traded places, put it back in the microwave for another minute, and probed it again. This time the needle eased past the mark, 74 on the inner ring, 165 on the outer. She held it there a moment to be sure the number stayed. Then she ate her dinner standing at the counter, rice and pork and a fried egg she had added because she deserved it, and it was good, and hot all the way through in a way she could now feel as a fact rather than a guess.

She texted her friend Priya, who had laughed at her earlier in the week for the eggs-and-peas dinners. Making real food now, she wrote. Reheated rice at 74 Celsius, verified. Priya sent back a thumbs up and a question mark, and Annabelle did not explain, because explaining would have turned it into something smaller than it was.

On Monday she carried a container to her mother's room, reheated in the kitchen first, probe through the center before she would let herself climb the stairs. Her mother was propped against pillows, gray faced but hungry, and she ate half the bowl while Annabelle sat on the end of the bed and pretended not to watch.

"It's good," her mother said. "When did you learn to cook?"

Annabelle considered the truthful answer, which was two days ago, in a kitchen full of steam and a drawer full of dead batteries, and the other truthful answer, which was that she hadn't learned yet, not really, that Thursday's chili was still an open question and Wednesday's might be a disaster. "I'm working on it," she said, and took the empty bowl back down to wash.

The choir room at St. Brigid's smelled of dust and old hymnals, and on Thursday afternoons it belonged to Natalie and Mrs. Okafor, who had played the organ there for thirty-one years and had agreed, after some coaxing from Natalie's mother, to teach her composition instead of piano. "You already play," Mrs. Okafor had said at the start. "What you don't know is how a song gets built. So we will build one. Sixteen bars, chord changes, written properly. Not memorized. Written."

Natalie sat at the scarred upright piano with a staff notebook open on the music rack, and her problem sat there with her: the melody in her head would not come out. It arrived whenever she was walking home from school or lying awake, a line that rose and then settled, and by the time she got to the choir room it had thinned to nothing. She had four bars written, in the key of G, and she could hear exactly how the fifth bar should end on a long held note under a D chord, a note that would hang in the air the way the last note of the offertory anthem hung in the sanctuary on Sundays. But she could not figure out how long to make it.

Mrs. Okafor was at the organ bench across the room, running a quiet scale with the swell shades half closed, and she had a rule about questions. "Ask the piano first," she would say. "Then ask me what the piano told you." So Natalie played the four bars through, then stopped at the edge of the fifth, and held the G she wanted, counting under her breath. One, two, three, four. A whole bar. In the time signature at the top of her page, the four told her the bar held four beats.

She looked at what she had written and saw the trouble. The bar before ended with a quick note on the fourth beat, a pickup into the held G, so the G began on beat one and she wanted it to last through the whole bar and then some, to spill into the next measure the way a held note in the anthem seemed to. She wrote a half note, two beats, and played it, and the silence afterward felt like a hole. She wrote a whole note instead, four beats, and that swallowed the pickup she wanted in the next bar. Neither was the note in her head.

Her phone buzzed against the bench. It was her brother Marcus, three hundred miles away at his first semester of college, who had taught himself guitar from videos and had opinions about everything.

"Are you still doing the church thing?" he'd texted. "Don't let the organ lady turn you into a hymn machine. Church music is all rules. Rules circumscribe you. You should be writing whatever comes out, like me. I don't even read notation."

Natalie typed back, "you circumscribe yourself by not reading notation. you can only play what you can copy." Then she put the phone face down, because she was not sure that was true. Mrs. Okafor's rules had felt like walls when Natalie started, but lately they had started to feel like the walls of an instrument itself, something you touched to make sound. Marcus made whatever noise he pleased and it all sounded like other people's noise. She didn't want to say that to him, though. He was the one who had shown her a video of a jazz pianist last spring, the performance that had been, for her, seismic, the moment she understood that a person could make music that hadn't existed five minutes earlier. Without Marcus there would be no Thursday afternoons at St. Brigid's at all.

She turned back to the page. The held G. She looked at the dotted rhythms elsewhere in her melody, where a dot after a shorter note stretched it a little, and she thought, for the first time, about what the dot was actually doing. A dot after a note adds half the note's value. She said it to herself the way she rehearsed French vocab, then tested it against her fingers. A half note was worth two beats. Half of two was one. Two and one made three. She penciled in a dot beside the half note, making a dotted half note, and played the bar, counting: the G held for one, two, three, and then a short note filled the fourth beat and lifted her into the next measure exactly the way the anthem did, the way the line in her head had done all along. Three beats out of the four. She sat very still, then wrote the next two bars without stopping.

"You found something," Mrs. Okafor said from the organ bench. She had stopped playing.

"My bar kept coming out one beat short," Natalie said. "Every time I counted it. I put a dot on the half note and now it's three beats and it works."

Mrs. Okafor came over and looked at the page for a long moment. "Sing it for me," she said, and Natalie did, and Mrs. Okafor nodded once, which was the most she ever gave.

That evening Natalie sat on her bed with the notebook, eight bars done, and found another text from Marcus: "fair point about notation lol. maybe I'll learn to read this summer. send me what you wrote?"

She photographed the page, the pencil marks, the small dot she'd had to press twice to make dark enough, and then she held her thumb over the send button. The melody was half invented and she didn't know if the second eight bars would match the first; the rules had given her one honest bar and then handed the rest back to her. She thought about Mrs. Okafor saying ask the piano first, and she set the phone down unfinished, picked the notebook back up, and played the eighth bar into the tenth, slowly, counting.

Chase sat at the kitchen table with his chemistry notebook open, a calculator warm in his hand, and the strong suspicion that his answer was ridiculous. The problem wanted grams of ammonia from 51 grams of hydrogen reacting with nitrogen, and his result, 289 grams of product, sat on the page like an accusation. Nothing weighs more coming out than going in, not when the other reactant was a gas in the same tank. He checked his work three times and kept arriving at the same number, which was either a sign of consistency or of a single error faithfully repeated.

His mother set a cup of tea beside his elbow without asking whether he wanted one, which was her way of noticing a boy who had been staring at the same page since dinner. "Bad homework or bad day?" she said.
