"Bad homework." He turned the notebook toward her, knowing she'd look anyway. "I'm supposed to figure out how much product I get from a starting amount, and my number's impossible."

She tapped the balanced equation he'd copied from the board. N2 plus 3 H2, arrow, 2 NH3. "That part looks tidy. That's as far as my chemistry goes." She squeezed his shoulder and went back to the sink, leaving him with the tea and the puzzle.

He texted Priya, who was doing the same assignment across town. Her answer came back in a photo of her page: 289 grams, identical to his, with a triumphant little star beside it. Chase frowned at it, then at his own paper, and did not feel triumphant at all. Two wrongs arriving together was not verification; it was a conspiracy. He texted back, doesn't that seem high? She replied with a shrugging emoji and went quiet, presumably to finish the rest of the set.

His little sister Nora wandered through the kitchen hunting for the good scissors, found them in the drawer where they always were, and paused at his elbow long enough to read his equation aloud in a dramatic voice. "En-aitch-three. It's the smelly one, right?"

"Ammonia. Yes." He was about to wave her off when he stopped, because she had read the equation as if it were a sentence, and it was a sentence, and he had been reading it wrong. The big 3 in front of the hydrogen and the 2 in front of the ammonia were speaking in a language he hadn't bothered to translate. He had taken 51 grams, divided by the mass of one hydrogen molecule, and then multiplied by the 2 over the 3 straight from the equation as though those numbers were talking about amounts of stuff, grams of stuff, the stuff you could weigh on a scale.

"What?" said Nora, who could sense when someone stopped listening.

"Nothing. You actually helped." He pulled the calculator closer. "Hey, do me a favor. If I tell you the numbers in the front of a recipe mean batches, not cups, what would you do first?"

"Convert to cups," she said, in the tone of someone humoring the slow. "Obviously. Batches and cups aren't the same thing." She took the scissors and left, and Chase sat very still, because that was it, that was the whole error, sitting in the open where a nine-year-old had stepped over it. The coefficients in the balanced equation were a ratio of moles that reacted, not a ratio of masses, and he had been dividing grams by grams while pretending the numbers meant what he needed them to mean. It was a kind of casuistry, honestly, an argument that sounded rigorous all the way down to the last digit while resting on a quietly swapped premise.

He started over. Molar mass of hydrogen first, grams converted into moles, and only then the 2 over 3 applied, and then back out through the molar mass of ammonia into grams. The answer came out to 289, and his stomach dropped, and then he saw the dropped digit in his long division and corrected it and got 289 anyway, which sent him hunting through the arithmetic until he found the place where he had divided by 2 instead of multiplying by it. On the third pass the answer settled at 289 grams, unchanged, immovable, and he put his head in his hands.

Then he laughed, because the number was fine and the number had never been the problem. He texted Priya again: our answers are wrong the same way. The coefficients are moles, not grams. You have to convert first. The reply came in bursts: a string of exclamation points, a photograph of her crossed-out work, and finally, wait, so the whole class got this wrong? Chase looked at the time, weighed the judicious option of waiting for morning against the small cruelty of letting thirty people turn in a shared error, and opened a group chat for the class, typing before he could talk himself into caution.

Nora came back through with her scissors and a half-finished paper snowflake, watched him type, and asked what he was doing. "Sharing a correction," he said. "Somebody might still be up." The message sent. Somewhere across town a phone on a bedside table lit up, and Chase, still not certain whether anyone would thank him in the morning, closed the notebook and took his cold tea upstairs.

The hardware store sat at the end of the plaza, sharing a back hallway with the grocery next door, and Sofia learned this in her first ten minutes of work because Mr. Aldrich, who owned both, walked her through the doorway with a key on a stretchy coil around his wrist. He had hired her on the strength of one interview and a note from her neighbor, who bought birdseed here every Saturday. Her job, he said, was the register, the seed rack, and restocking shelf paper for the paint department. She had spent the night before the interview reading the federal child labor rules on her phone, not because anyone told her to, but because she could not sleep and reading regulations felt like a way of holding still.

Her foreboding about the job had been vague until then, something about register codes and being trusted with money, and by noon it had faded into ordinary nervousness. She sold a woman three packets of beefsteak tomato seeds and a trowel. Behind her, Denzell, the other part-time hire, a seventeen-year-old who had been working here since June, was organizing the seed display by packet color. He held up two packets of the same variety and said the plants would still come out different, all that phenotypic variation, genes plus weather plus whatever the soil was doing. Sofia said she had not thought about tomatoes that way. He said nobody did, that was the problem.

At two o'clock Mr. Aldrich came through the back hallway fast. Rosa, the deli woman at the grocery, had called in with a flooded basement, and he had a line of lunch customers. He looked at Denzell first, because Denzell was older, and asked him to run next door and cover the slicer until Rosa showed up. Denzell did not move. He said he could work the register, the produce scale, the coffee machine, but not the slicer. Mr. Aldrich said it was a deli, not a chemistry lab, and that a slicer was a slicer.

"Under federal child labor rules, workers under eighteen can't operate power-driven meat slicers," Denzell said. "Even in a grocery store deli or a restaurant."

Mr. Aldrich stood there with his hand still raised, halfway through pointing at the hallway. Then he turned and looked at Sofia, and Sofia felt the question arrive before he said it, and she heard herself say the same thing Denzell had said, that under eighteen meant under eighteen, that she had read it the night before and it had not seemed like information she would ever need. She was surprised by how steady her voice came out.

Mr. Aldrich did not argue. He went to the office and came back with a laminated federal poster, the same one Sofia realized she had passed in the hallway without reading, and stood under the light with it, moving his finger down the lines. A man came in for pipe tape and Sofia sold it to him while Mr. Aldrich read. When the man left, Mr. Aldrich said, to nobody in particular, that he had been nineteen when he started and had run slicers since, and that he had not known a rule could reach all the way into a small store like his. He said he supposed that was the point of rules. He put the poster back.

Then he called his sister-in-law, who was forty-one, and while the phone rang he stood in the doorway between the two stores with his shoulders lower than they had been all day. Sofia could not tell whether he was angry. He had every reason to be annoyed at losing an hour of coverage, and instead he had lost it twice, once from Denzell and once from her, and she had volunteered her refusal without being asked, which was either loyalty or something worse. She thought of the way Denzell had said no, flat and fast, like a coin dropped on a counter, and the way she had said it, testing each word as it left. One of them had been sure. She was not sure she was the one.

Denzell went back to the seed rack. He lined up the tomato packets in pairs, two beefsteaks side by side, and said the plants would come out different anyway, even from the same packet, even in the same yard. He said his bio teacher would be proud of him for using the word twice in one day. He said the slicer thing had come up in June, his first week, when Rosa had asked him to cut a pound of turkey and he had stood there until she laughed and did it herself, and after that he had looked the rule up on his phone in the break room so he would have it ready.

Through the open hallway door Sofia could hear the sister-in-law arriving at the deli, her keys, her voice asking what was still needed. Mr. Aldrich came back through and stopped at Sofia's register. He put a roll of quarters on the counter, the float for tomorrow, and slid it toward her. "Same time Saturday," he said. "You'll take the early shift, and if Rosa's out again, I'll be the one cutting the turkey."

Dylan counted the numbers on the napkin three times before he was willing to believe them, and even then he believed them the way you believe weather forecasts, provisionally, with a coat. He had worked nineteen hours at Marzano's at nine dollars an hour, which should have been a hundred and seventy-one dollars, and the check in his hand said one hundred fifty-two. He turned it over as though the missing nineteen dollars might be hiding on the back, perhaps with an apology.

"Take it up with Rosa," said Marcus, the shift lead, who was extruding dough through the pasta machine with the calm of a man who had done it ten thousand times and intended to do it ten thousand more. "She does the payroll. But fair warning, she'll make you do the math yourself. She thinks suffering teaches."

Rosa was in the back office, which was really a closet with ambitions, filing receipts into a binder that looked older than the restaurant. When Dylan asked about his check she didn't look up. "How much did you expect?"

"A hundred seventy-one."

"How much is on it?"

"A hundred fifty-two point oh six."

"Then the difference is?" She still hadn't looked up. Dylan did the subtraction on the receipt paper. Nineteen dollars, give or take. Rosa finally raised her eyes, which were amused, and pointed at the pay stub's tiny print. There, in a line smaller than the ingredients on a gum wrapper, was the word Social Security, and next to it a number. He divided. Six point two percent, almost exactly.

"They take six point two percent off the top," Rosa said. "Every check. Up to a limit on how much you make in a year, and you, my friend, are not remotely close to that limit." She snapped the binder shut. "So it's not theft, it's the government being your extremely patient savings account. An annuity, more or less, for when you're old and obsolescent like me."

"I'm not going to be old," Dylan said. "I'm going to be a legend."

"Legends still pay in," said Rosa, and shooed him out with the binder.

He texted his sister Priya that night, because Priya was a college sophomore and therefore, in the family mythology, an oracle. He wrote it out carefully: my check was 19 bucks short, it's 6.2 percent withheld for Social Security, but only up to a yearly wage limit, which I will apparently never reach at a pasta place. Her reply arrived in installments, as her replies always did, each bubble a thought she had not finished editing.

"congrats you have discovered taxes," the first said. "also welcome to the workforce, where the paycheck is a lie the hours tell." The second: "but actually think about it this way. you're paying for your future self, who you currently don't know and might not like. grandpa gets a check every month because of people like you. it's a chain letter, but nice." The third, after a long pause: "or it's a promise other people made before you were born and you're stuck keeping it. depends on the day. anyway did they feed you."

They had fed him, as it happened. Staff meal at Marzano's was whatever the kitchen had misjudged that evening, and on Friday it had been an entire tray of garlic bread that nobody ordered because of a printer error Dylan himself had caused. He had eaten six pieces. He told Priya this and she sent back a single thumbs up, which in her language meant she was done being an oracle and had gone back to her homework.

The thing Dylan could not stop turning over, on the walk home and then lying on his bedroom floor with the ceiling fan clicking overhead, was that both of Priya's versions felt true at once. The money was his, earned hour by hour, and the money was also a promise he had inherited, somebody else's grandfather's monthly check, paid forward whether he had agreed or not. He could hold both ideas, one in each hand, like the two halves of a breadstick, and he could not make them into one idea, and maybe that was fine. Seventy years from now some version of him would get a check, or wouldn't, and that version was a stranger he was choosing to tip now.

On Monday he asked Rosa to put him down for a double shift, "for the annuity," and she laughed so hard she had to set down the knife.

"Wash your hands," she said, and slid the apron across the counter to him.

Jake's mother had left for a six-week rotation at the hospital in Kelowna, and before she went she taped a list to the fridge that read, in her cramped handwriting, "Feed yourself. Real food. Not cereal." She had also left forty dollars in an envelope and a standing offer of amnesty for whatever he had done to her cast-iron pan two months ago, which he had not confessed to and did not intend to. Eighty dollars a week, then, for seven dinners and whatever lunches he could assemble from the wreckage.

His plan, formed at one in the morning with three browser tabs open, was to cook in batches on Sunday: a pot of chili, a tray of roast vegetables, a pot of rice that would hold in the fridge and reappear, transformed, in fried rice on Thursday. He had read that this was what people with foresight did. He was prepared to become a person with foresight.

The farmers' market occupied a parking lot beside the rec center, forty stalls under white canopies that snapped in the wind. He bought onions, carrots, a paper bag of potatoes, and a jar of honey because the man selling it called him "chief" and Jake found he could not walk away. At the fish stall, a woman with sunburned forearms was filleting salmon and talking to a customer about the season. "Littoral fish, mostly," she said, laying a fillet on the scale. "Caught close in along the shore. Smaller boats, shorter trip, better fish." Jake nodded as though this confirmed something he had long suspected, then bought two fillets because they were on for less than the farmed ones, and because he wanted to be the kind of person who knew what littoral meant.

The stall after that sold eggs, tomatoes, and a wheel of cheese that cost more than his entire budget for Tuesday through Friday. He looked at the tomatoes, then at the grocery store across the road, and made the first genuinely adult decision of his life: he would buy the beans, oats, and canned tomatoes at the supermarket, and everything else here. A mixed economy, he thought, and was pleased with himself.

At the supermarket he pushed the cart to the cereal aisle and then past it, to the oats. There were two bags. The large one was nearly twice the size of the small one and cost more in total, and he reached for it automatically, on the principle that big meant cheap, the principle that governed every purchase his grandfather had ever made. Then he noticed the small print on the shelf label, below the price. There was a second number, smaller, labeled per 100 g. He looked at the small bag's label. It had the same kind of number, and the number was lower.

"Unit price," said a voice beside him. A woman about his mother's age was comparing two bags of flour. She was not talking to him, exactly; she seemed to be talking to the aisle. "The shelf label's unit price shows the cost per gram, litre, or item. It lets you compare packages of different sizes fairly." She put the smaller flour bag in her cart and moved off toward the baking supplies, and Jake stood there holding the big bag of oats, which was, he now understood, a worse deal.

The strange part was that he had almost wanted the big bag to win. There was something satisfying about hauling home a sack of oats like a settler. Instead he took the small one, plus the cheap one, because the unit price on a third bag, a store brand he had been ignoring out of brand loyalty he could not explain, was lower than both. He did the same arithmetic at the canned tomatoes, at the rice, at the olive oil, where the comparison was per litre and where the fancy bottle turned out to cost nearly double per litre what the plain one did. He had been walking past the plain one his whole life.

Sunday he cooked. He had to exhume the big pot from the back of the cupboard above the fridge, a space where his family stored appliances that had stopped being used but had not been formally dismissed, and he found the pot nested inside a steamer, inside a colander, like an archaeological dig of good intentions. The chili took two hours because he kept stopping to read the recipe on his phone, which sat on the counter slowly accumulating a fine dusting of cumin. He browned the onions too fast and they went dark at the edges, and he stood over the pan deciding whether this was a disaster or "caramelized," and chose caramelized, which turned out to be roughly correct. The rice he got right on the first try, which he found suspicious.

By evening the fridge held four containers, labeled in marker because the website had said to label them: CHILI, RICE, VEG, SALMON (WED). He ate a bowl of chili standing up, then another sitting down, then a third watching a video about knife skills that he would not need until Saturday. He was not sure the batch system would survive contact with Wednesday, when he had practice until six and would want nothing but toast. He was not sure the money would last the six weeks, or that he would keep choosing the store-brand oats once nobody was watching the unit prices with him. The salmon sat in its container, looking expensive and perishable, and he moved it to the front of the shelf so he would not forget it. Wednesday needed him, and he intended to be ready.

Sadie had promised herself she would finish the chapter before dinner, but the margin of her paperback was filling up faster than the pages were turning. Her assignment was due Monday: read Chapter 7 of Pride and Prejudice through either a feminist or a Marxist critical lens, then write a page about what the lens revealed. She had picked Marxist because it sounded more trenchant, more like something a graduate student would say at a party, and now she was stuck on the first paragraph, pencil hovering.

The problem was that she did not actually know what a Marxist reading did. Her class notes said something about class and money, which seemed obvious in a novel where the whole plot was men with estates, but obvious was not an essay. She dragged her laptop closer and typed the question into the search bar, then deleted it, embarrassed, as though Ms. Okafor might somehow see the search history and know that Sadie had spent two class periods nodding.

"You're making a face," said her brother Theo, dropping onto the other end of the couch with his own book, which he held upside down for effect. He was eleven and considered this comedy.

"I'm working."

"You're glaring at a book that's older than Grandma."

She ignored him, but her eyes had caught on something in the page she'd just read, a sentence about the Bennets sending for a servant, or rather about a servant doing something in the background while Elizabeth and the others talked. The servant had no name. She flipped back through the chapter and found another one, carrying letters, holding horses. Also no name. She sat up straighter and grabbed a pencil.

"Can I see your notebook?" Theo asked, because he had learned that when Sadie sat up straighter, interesting things sometimes happened, like the time she'd mapped every meal in a book about famine.

"Get your own." But she slid her spare pencil across the cushion without looking.

She started a tally in the back margin. Every time a servant appeared, she made a mark; every time a servant was given a name, a circle; every time a servant actually spoke, a star. By the end of the chapter she had a long column of marks, two circles, and no stars at all. The chapter was full of people whose labour kept the characters fed, dressed, driven and comforted, and the novel mentioned them only in passing, never letting them say a word. She read her own tally back and felt something shift in her chest, the way a room looks different when a light comes on in a corner you'd stopped seeing.

"So a Marxist reading," she said slowly, to the couch cushions, to Theo, to nobody, "asks whose labour makes everyone's comfortable life possible. Like, literally. Whose work is underneath all this tea and letter-writing."

"Is that your homework?"

"That's my whole essay, maybe." She was already writing it, half sentences, arrows. The servants made the Bennets' leisure possible and the novel could not see them; the critic's job was to look where the novel didn't. She wanted to write that Austen was a classist monster, and then she stopped herself, because it wasn't that simple, either. The novel was also slyly funny about money, about women needing to marry it because they couldn't earn it, and that felt like the other lens, the feminist one, pressing in from the side.

"That was a smart face," Theo observed.

She tried holding both ideas at once: the book was blind to the people downstairs and clear-eyed about the desperation of the women upstairs. Maybe the two lenses weren't rivals but a pair of eyes. She wasn't sure. She wrote "I think" in the margin and did not cross it out.

Their mother came through with a basket of laundry, saw the tally of marks, circles and stars, and paused. "That looks grim."

"It's kind of grim. I counted how many times the servants in the chapter are named and how many times they speak. Two named. Zero speaking."

"Out of how many?"

"Seventeen appearances." Sadie tapped the column. "Seventeen times they're in the scene doing things, and they never get a single line."

Her mother set the basket down. "My grandmother was in service before she married. She'd have had something to say about that. Mostly she'd have said nothing, that was the job." She picked up the basket again, then stopped. "Don't let your tea desiccate into that mug again, Sadie. It's like archaeology in there."

"I'll wash it." Sadie looked at the cold tea, the brown ring at the bottom, and then at her page. She added a sentence: the silence of the servants might be the most accurate thing in the chapter, if silence was what the system produced. She didn't know if that was true. She underlined it anyway, because not knowing felt more honest than pretending the tally had settled anything.

"Read me some," Theo said, so she did, the part about the twenty-five servants and two named and none speaking, and when she finished he frowned and said, "So who made all that food they keep eating?" and Sadie looked at the page, at all her careful marks, and began to draw a new column in the margin.

Tyson had been told the blackbox rehearsal hall would be different from the mainstage, but nobody had said how, so he walked in with his blocking notebook under his arm and his confidence arranged the way it had been on the thrust stage: entrances left, exits right, all of it facing one way. The community theatre had moved the one-act festival into the annex because the auditorium floor was being refinished, and when he pushed open the door he found not a stage at all but a bare rectangle of gray floor with chairs on all four sides.

"There's no front," said Priya, who was playing the sister. She stood in the middle of the space and turned in a slow circle, and every direction she faced left three other directions looking at her back.

Tyson opened his notebook anyway, out of habit, and looked at the diagrams he had drawn two weeks ago. The play was about two siblings dividing their dead father's belongings, and he had staged the arguments like a chessboard, each of them planted behind their furniture and firing lines across an open middle. It had worked when the audience sat in one place. Now he tried to picture it from the north chairs, and what he pictured was the backs of two people talking at an audience across the room. He closed the notebook.

"Okay," he said. "New plan. We can't stay still. If we stand in one spot, some section only sees our backs." He said it out loud partly to hear whether it was true, and it was, and it changed everything. On a stage where the audience sits on all sides, the actors have to keep moving, rotating through the space, so no section is stuck looking at shoulder blades for a whole scene.

They started over. He walked the diagonal from corner to corner himself first, feeling how strange it was to have no darkness to back up into, no wings, no place where he was invisible. Everywhere was seen. He moved the father's trunk to the center and made the sister circle it while the brother crouched and unpacked, and then he reversed them, and the simple act of orbiting turned the scene into something he hadn't written in the margins of his script. "You're like two planets," he said, and Priya said, "Don't get poetic, just tell me where to stand," but she was grinning.

The second problem was subtler. Movement for its own sake looked like traffic, and by Thursday's run-through the actors were drifting in anxious little loops, always in motion, never meaning anything. Tyson sat in the south chairs and watched an entire argument between two people who might as well have been pacing a bus station. He had learned one rule and mistaken it for the whole job. So he tried an experiment: he gave each movement a reason grounded in the objects, the trunk, the coat on its hook, the friable old letters that crumbled when Priya gripped them too hard during the reading, and let the stillness fall where it fell, as long as it fell facing outward. When it worked, a pause could face one section for a moment, because the turn that followed would bring it around to everyone else.

The play itself kept beguiling him in ways he hadn't expected from his own material. There was a monologue about the father's hometown, a dry grassland town on the steppe that he had written as an exotic nowhere, and when Marcus delivered it center-floor, slowly rotating through the compass points so that every section of chairs received one image of the place, the words stopped being set dressing. Marcus turned toward the east chairs and said the town had no landmarks, that distance was the only thing you could see, and Tyson, sitting in the west chairs, felt the line arrive at him like something carried around the room by hand.

On Saturday, the night before the performance, the director of the theatre stopped by the annex, watched ten minutes from the aisle, and afterward asked Tyson what he would change if the room had a front again. Tyson started to answer and then didn't. Part of him wanted the thrust stage back, the safety of a single audience to please, a geometry where you could hide. But the rectangle had taught him something he couldn't fully put into sentence form, something about how attention moves, and he was honest enough with himself to admit he didn't yet know whether the in-the-round version was better or only newer to him.

"I honestly don't know," he said. "Can we run the last scene once more?"

The chairs sat dark on all four sides. Priya picked up the crumbling letters, Marcus began his slow turn, and Tyson moved a folding chair into the north row to watch.

Amy had taped the paper to the refrigerator so she couldn't avoid it, which was the whole point. On it, in her brother Dex's blocky handwriting, ran a string of letters: CCAAUGGUACCGUAA. Below that, a code table mapping every three-letter combination to an amino acid, and a question in red marker: WHAT PROTEIN DOES THIS MAKE? The prize, according to Dex, was that whoever solved it first didn't have to take out the recycling for a week.

"You realize you've invented homework for fun," Amy told him, holding the door open with her hip while she carried in the groceries. "Voluntary homework. Scientists will study you."

"Scientists will study you," Dex shot back from the counter, already pulling the cereal box out of the bag before she'd set it down. "You're the one losing to a seventh grader."

She was, in fact, losing to a seventh grader, and that was the irritating part. Amy had spent an hour at the kitchen table with the string of letters and the table of codons, splitting them into threes the way you'd slice a loaf of bread. CCA, AUG, GUA, CCG, UAA. She'd looked up each one and written out the amino acids in a neat column, and the column had come out looking like a ransom note: proline, then something, then something, then nothing useful at all. When she tried starting from the very first letter instead, she got an even worse jumble, letters grouped as CAA, UGG, UAC, CGU, AA, the last one too short to even count. It was like she was reading a sentence that had been shuffled, or like she'd picked up a book and started reading from the middle of a random page.

There was a memory she kept circling back to, from the fall, when she'd still been deciding whether to commit to molecular biology at all. She'd gone with her mother to the insurance office to sort out the car policy, and while they waited, her mother had flipped through a brochure and said, half joking, that they could amortize the cost of the better plan over the year so it wouldn't sting all at once. Amy had liked the word so much she'd written it on her wrist. Later that week, sitting in on a college lecture video with a borrowed password from her cousin, she'd watched a professor fill a whiteboard with the alphabet soup of DNA and RNA and felt the same click: big things, paid out in small installments. A genome, parceled into letters, parceled into threes.

"Stop philosophizing at the fridge," Dex said now, drifting past with the cereal and a spoon. "You're staring at it like it owes you money."

"It does owe me money. I paid for your science fair poster board."

"You want some?" He rattled the box at her. "Dry cereal, straight from the bag. It's basically hedonism."

"It's basically dust." But she took a handful anyway, and stood there chewing, eyes on the letters, and something about the second grouping she'd tried kept snagging. AUG. She'd looked it up and gotten that first amino acid, the one that started with M, methionine, and then a word she'd heard in the lecture video surfaced whole: start. Not the beginning of the string, but the beginning of the reading. AUG wasn't just an amino acid in the middle of the lineup. Translation usually begins at the codon AUG, she remembered the lecturer saying, pointing at it with the cap end of a marker, which also codes for the amino acid methionine.

"Wait," she said out loud, spraying a little cereal dust, which she regretted instantly.

"Charming," said Dex.

"Shut up, shut up, this is it." She grabbed the pen off the counter and circled AUG on the paper, ignoring her brother's protest that she was defacing official science fair property. From there she re-sliced the rest: AUG, GUA, CCG, UAA. Methionine, valine, proline, and then the last one, UAA, which the table listed under a column of codons that coded for nothing at all, a full stop, the end of the sentence. She'd been reading the strand like it began at the left edge, like a line of text, when really the front of it was padding, a runway. The CCA before AUG wasn't the start of anything. It was scenery.

"So what's the protein?" Dex demanded, craning to see her scribbles.

"Methionine, valine, proline, stop. A four-piece protein. Tiny, but real." She tapped the table. "The trick is the AUG. That's where translation begins, and it happens to code for methionine, so every protein you build this way starts with the same amino acid. Like how every movie starts with a logo."

"Every movie starts with the logo, but the logo isn't in the movie," Dex said, and then paused, frowning at his own sentence. "Wait, no. It's in the movie. Bad example. Yours is better."

"You're admitting mine is better?"

"I'm admitting nothing. I'm acknowledging a temporary competitive setback." He picked up the pen, added a note to his poster materials, and then, in the small voice he used when he actually wanted to know something, asked, "So if I put a bunch of junk letters before the AUG, people would still find it?"

"That's the whole point of the junk," Amy said. "That's what it's for."

Their mother came through with the recycling bag and set it down between them like a verdict. "One of you is taking this out, and I believe there was a wager."

"There was a wager," Dex said gravely, "and I have been defeated by the start codon." He hefted the bag over his shoulder with theatrical grief, and Amy watched him go, then looked back at the refrigerator, at the circled AUG, small and ordinary among all the other letters, waiting to be found.

The instructor arrived in a gray hatchback with a magnetic sign on the door, and the first thing he did was not get out of the car. Alexia stood in the driveway of her mother's house, keys already warm in her hand from the kitchen counter, and watched him through the windshield as he pointed, twice, at her hip. She looked down. The belt was not across her. It was not even in her hand.

"We're not moving," Mr. Rudd said through the rolled-down window. "Not one foot."

"It's the driveway," Alexia said. "I could see the mailbox from here if I fell over."

"Not one foot," he said again, and folded his hands on the dashboard in a way that suggested he had done this before, possibly many times, possibly this morning.

Her father would have liked Mr. Rudd. Her father spent his working life calculating what a company owed people after the worst day of theirs, drafting language to indemnify them, as he put it, though he was careful to add that money never actually indemnified anybody. He was in Lisbon now, on a sabbatical he had described over the phone as a year of not being an actuary, which so far seemed to consist of sending her photographs of tiled walls. When she was nine he had taught her to ride a bike by first explaining, on graph paper, the statistical case for helmets. She had worn one. She had also, in the same year, stopped telling him about the time she fell off in the culvert by the Hendersons' field, because she had not been wearing it then, and the numbers felt different when they were about her.

Her mother held the opposite position, stated flat over dinner: if it's your time, it's your time, and a strap of nylon is not going to argue with God. Her mother said this about seat belts, about the water tower, about a cousin who survived a combine accident in 1994 and one who hadn't survived a much smaller thing. Alexia had grown up between these two voices, one with a spreadsheet and one with a shrug, and had mostly solved the problem by never needing to choose between them, because at seventeen she had never yet been in charge of anything that could kill her.

She took out her phone. Mr. Rudd watched her type, unbothered, as though this were part of the curriculum. She found the CDC page on her third attempt, past a forum and a site that looked pernicious in a way she couldn't quite name, all caps and exclamation points about government overreach. She read the line twice to herself and then out loud. "Wearing a seat belt reduces serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half."

"About half," Mr. Rudd agreed, as if she had read him a weather report.

"So that's it? That's why the driveway standoff?"

"That's why the driveway standoff."

She thought about how to file this. Her father would say half was an enormous margin, that no one sane declined those odds. Her mother would say half was also not all, that people died belted every day of the week, which was true, and useless, and somehow comforting to her, the way a locked door is comforting even though doors get kicked in. Alexia did not know yet which of them she was, or whether she had to be either, or whether at some point you just picked the way of thinking you could live inside and stopped auditing it. She pulled the belt across her chest and clicked it home, and the sound was smaller than she expected.

"Good," Mr. Rudd said, and got out, and came around to the passenger side, and handed her nothing at all, because she already had the keys.

The car started on the second try. She backed out slow enough that a turtle could have passed her, turned onto the county road, and held it at thirty while the gravel shoulder unspooled beside her and the Hendersons' culvert came up green in the distance. Mr. Rudd adjusted the mirror on his side, entirely at peace.

"Twenty years I've done this," he said. "The ones who buckle without being told are never the ones you worry about."

"Is that in the statistics?"

"It's in my knees. Turn here.

The community studio smelled of turpentine and burnt coffee, and Megan claimed the stool by the window because the light there made the reproduction pinned to the easel legible, or at least that was the reason she gave herself. The assignment, printed on a half sheet and taped to the wall, asked for a formal analysis of a Frida Kahlo painting: colour, composition, symbolism, in that order, though her instructor had said the order didn't matter as much as the looking. She had chosen the double self-portrait, the one with two Fridas seated on a bench, one in white lace, one in Tehuana dress, their exposed hearts joined by a single thread.

She had been looking for forty minutes. What she had written so far was that the sky behind the figures was stormy on the left and calm on the right, and that the artery the European Frida clamped shut with her own fingers bled onto her white skirt in three deliberate drops. She didn't know yet whether that was analysis or just inventory.

"You're frowning at it like it owes you money," said Deshawn, dropping onto the stool beside her with his own reproduction, the one with the deer. He was doing the same assignment for a portfolio he needed by November.

"I can describe it," Megan said. "I can't say why it works. There's a difference and I can hear my professor hearing the difference."

"Then say the colors first. That's the whole formula, isn't it." He wasn't mocking her, exactly. He was mocking the formula, which was a distinction she appreciated.

She tried it aloud. The warm terracotta of the dress against the cold white, the repetition of red in two hearts and one small portrait held in the hand, how the vertical line of the thread divided the canvas almost, but not quite, down the center, so the painting was off balance in a way your eye kept trying to correct. That felt closer to something. Deshawn nodded slowly, and then, because he was incapable of leaving a silence alone, he asked how old Kahlo had been when she painted it.

"Twenties, I think." Megan turned to the binder of photocopies the studio kept on the shelf by the sink, the one with the coffee ring on the cover. She flipped past the biography section looking for the date of the double portrait, and instead found a timeline with a photograph above it, a teenage girl in a family portrait with an unsmiling, level gaze.

September 17, 1925, the timeline said. A streetcar crashed into her bus. Kahlo was eighteen. The injuries caused her pain for the rest of her life.

She read it twice, then a third time, because the number refused to sit still in her head. "She was my age," she said, and heard how the sentence came out, half statement and half complaint, as though the timeline had done something to her.

"How old when what?" Deshawn leaned over, peering at the page.

"When the streetcar hit her bus. September 17, 1925. Eighteen. And it left her with injuries, pain for the rest of her life, and the paintings came after." Megan closed the binder, then opened it again. She had spent the morning thinking the exposed hearts were a symbol she had to decode, some puzzle with an answer key, and now the thread joining the two Fridas looked less like a code and more like a claim: this is what a body does after that, it splits and it connects and it clamps its own artery shut to keep from bleeding out.

"I was going to write that the doubled figure was about identity," she said. "Like, indigenous versus European, which half she chooses. My grandmother would call the Tehuana half the true one and the white one a reactionary costume, backwards-looking in the wrong direction." She paused. "But that's me expatiating on ideas I got secondhand. The blood is specific. The clamp of her own fingers is specific. I keep wanting the painting to be an argument I can referee instead of a person my age showing me where it hurts."

Deshawn was quiet for a moment, which from him was nearly a concession. "So write both. Say the identity reading, then say the accident, then say you don't know how the two fit together. That's allowed, isn't it? In a critique?"

"It's allowed," Megan said. "It just isn't tidy." She thought of her own grandmother again, the apartment with the saints and the plastic-covered couch, how the old woman had once called Megan's art school indigent charity dressed up as opportunity, and how Megan had not argued because part of her feared it was true, and how the fear had never once stopped her from going. Sitting here with the binder open, she suspected Kahlo would have understood that particular doubleness better than any of her textbooks did.

She pulled the assignment sheet toward her and wrote a first line: The painting is off balance by design, its two figures joined by a thread that the eye follows the way it follows pain, toward the hand that is already trying to stop it. Then she crossed out the last clause, then wrote it again.

Deshawn held up his reproduction of the deer, arrows and all. "Nine arrows," he said. "I counted them for you, since you like specifics."

The assignment was due Monday and Owen had until the library closed at nine. Mrs. Prasad had given them a single question, "Who owns the news?", and refused to say anything more, which everyone agreed was a power move and which Owen privately admired. He wanted an A. More than that, he wanted to beat Dana Okafor, who had already told the class, with terrible confidence, that the answer was "nobody, that's the whole point of journalism."

He spread his materials across the long table by the microfilm machines: two laptops, one his and one borrowed from the front desk because his kept dying, and a stack of newspapers he'd pulled from the periodicals room. His father had texted him twice from the dinner table, which was a thing his father did, texting people in the same house. "Ask the librarian about the LA Times," the first message said. "Your uncle says the rich guy saved it." The second message said, "Your uncle is wrong, obviously."

Owen's uncle Ray had come for dinner Sunday, and the argument had gone nuclear over the roast chicken before Owen could even eat his drumstick. "A billionaire bought the LA Times," Ray had said, tapping the table. "Patrick Soon-Shiong. 2018. Five hundred million dollars, plus he took on the pension obligations. That man saved that paper." His father had set down his fork. "That man bought a megaphone." His mother had said, "Can someone pass the peas," and nobody had.

So Owen had a problem and, possibly, a thesis. He opened the library's newspaper database and searched Soon-Shiong's name, then did the thing he'd learned from Dana, of all people, which was to read the same story in two places. The LA Times piece about a water contract read one way. A smaller paper's piece about the same contract read another. He couldn't have said exactly where they diverged; it was less a lie than a tilt, like a shelf that looked level until you set a marble on it. He copied both URLs into a document and titled it MARBLE.

The librarian, a grad student named Priya who worked the reference desk on Thursdays, came by to collect the laptops that hadn't been used in an hour. "You're the third kid this week on that assignment," she said. "One of them cried." Owen asked her whether a rich owner saves a newspaper or controls it. She stacked a laptop onto her cart. "I can't do your thinking for you. But the ownership records are public. Third floor, the big red binders." Then she paused. "Also, whoever's at table four has been watching you for twenty minutes, so either you're famous or your girlfriend is here."

It was Dana. Dana sat down across from him without asking, which was Dana's way, and looked at his screen. "MARBLE," Dana read aloud. "Cute." Owen covered the document reflexively, then uncovered it, because covering it looked worse. "Your answer was nobody," he said. "Nobody owns the news." Dana pulled one of his newspapers toward her. "I said no one person owns it. Which is different." Outside the window the streetlights came on all at once, the way they did, like a decision being made somewhere.

They worked mostly in silence after that, which was its own kind of conversation. Dana read the database entry aloud without being asked: "Los Angeles Times, acquired 2018 by Patrick Soon-Shiong for five hundred million dollars, plus assumption of pension obligations." She said "pension obligations" the way people say a phrase they've just learned, carefully, holding it out to see if it broke. "That's a lot of money to spend on something you don't want anything from," she said. "Or a lot of money to spend keeping people's retirements safe," Owen said, and heard his uncle's cadence in his own voice and disliked it.

He tried to hold both ideas at once, the way you'd suture two edges of a torn page, and found they didn't quite meet. A man who spends five hundred million and takes on the pensions could be a rescuer. The same man could be an owner. The database couldn't tell him which, and he suspected the database was itself owned by somebody, which opened a door he decided to stand near without walking through, at least tonight. For the essay, he wrote a sentence he half believed: that ownership and rescue were not opposites, and that a paper could be saved and bought in the same motion, by the same man, on the same day.

At the announcement that the library closed in fifteen minutes, Dana was reading existentialism in a dictionary someone had left on the shelf, for no reason she would explain, and Owen was looking at the two articles about the water contract. "The LA Times runs alluvial soil testing the other paper doesn't run," he said. "The other paper runs quotes the Times doesn't." Dana closed the dictionary. "So what do we write?" Owen began stacking the newspapers, squaring the edges. He slid MARBLE, the printout, across the table to her. "I don't know yet," he said. "Read the marble first."

The guitar had lived in Grandpa Ray's closet for thirty years, and it came to Sara still holding whatever tuning he had last left on it, which was nothing recognizable. Her teacher, Ms. Okafor, had a studio above a dry cleaner on Miller Street, a room that smelled faintly of starch and rosin, with a poster of Andrés Segovia glaring down like a man conducting a plebiscite against sloppy practice. Sara carried the old guitar up the stairs in a garbage bag because the case had disintegrated, the vinyl flaking off like dead skin.

"Before we play a single note," Ms. Okafor said, "we tune. An out-of-tune guitar teaches your ear lies." She plucked the lowest string and let it wobble in the air, sour and ashamed. "In standard tuning, from the lowest string to the highest, it's E, A, D, G, B, and E again. The E repeats, an octave up. Say it back to me."

"E, A, D, G, B, E," Sara said. It sounded like a spell, or a password to a club she wasn't sure she belonged to.

Sara had wanted to learn guitar since the previous spring, when Ray sat on the porch of the house she'd known all her life and played three songs from memory, his fingers stiff but sure. That was the last month before the diagnosis got loud. He gave her the guitar in June, in the hospital, wheeled down to the lobby because he refused to have the handoff happen in a room with a television in it. "It's a piece of junk," he told her, which was false, and they both knew it was false, and that was the joke. "You'll have to tune it. I haven't touched it since your mother's wedding." Then he made her promise not to learn anything sappy.

Now she sat with the tuner app glowing on her phone, propped against Ms. Okafor's metronome, and turned the first peg. The string climbed, wavered, climbed. When the app flashed green and the word E, Sara felt a small ridiculous pride, the kind you feel for tying a shoe correctly at age seventeen. The second string went sharp and she brought it back. A, said the phone. D, said the phone. Her fingertips were already hurting, the old strings coarse as fishing line, but she kept going, G, then B, then the high E, which snapped up to pitch with a ping that startled them both.

Ms. Okafor laughed. "You jumped like it bit you."

"It kind of did." Sara flexed her fingers. The tips had gone pale with grooves pressed into them, little trenches, and she understood suddenly that this was the tax. The instrument would take her hands and transfigure them, callus by callus, into something that could hold down these strings without complaint, and there was no way to pay in advance. You just kept hurting until you didn't.

Ray had described it differently, that day on the porch. He'd called practice "drudging through the pelagic deep," and when she'd asked what that meant, he'd said, "Vast, cold, and no shore in sight. Then one day you look up and you can play, and you can't tell anyone how you got there." She'd thought he was being pretentious. Now, tuning her sixth string for the second time because she'd overshot the first, she suspected he was being accurate, which was worse.

They worked through a two-chord song, E minor to G and back, and Sara's transitions were slow enough that Ms. Okafor started calling the gap between chords "the pause for reflection," which was her polite way of saying it was a mess. But near the end of the half hour, one change landed clean, both chords ringing together without a buzz, and for two seconds the room held a sound Sara had never made before, round and full, rising through the floorboards from the dry cleaner's machines and the street noise below like it had always been there, waiting.

"Better," Ms. Okafor said. "Practice twenty minutes a day. Tuning first, always. Even the days you hate it."

Walking home with the guitar in its garbage bag, Sara played the strings silently against her sleeve, pressing the shapes of E, A, D, G, B, E into her memory like passwords, and pulled out her phone at the bus stop to call the hospital. Ray answered on the fourth ring, his voice thin.

"I tuned it," she said. "All six. Want to hear?"

The line at city hall wound past the marriage license desk and a vending machine that offered only grape soda, and Clara stood in it with a voter registration form going soft in her hand. She had turned seventeen three weeks ago, which meant she could register now, though she could not vote until after the next election, whenever that turned out to be. The clerk ahead of her was arguing with a man about a parking permit in the patient, flat voice of someone who had argued about parking permits every day for a decade.

Behind her, two students from the debate team were rehearsing something at each other. The taller one, Dev, kept saying "in a parliamentary system" the way other people said "in theory," and the shorter one, Priya, kept saying "so the president is elected separately, that's the whole difference," and neither of them seemed satisfied. Clara, who knew them slightly from a Model UN conference where everyone had argued about whales, drifted backward until she was accidentally in their conversation.

"In Britain the prime minister isn't elected by the voters at all," Dev was saying. "The party picks the leader, and if the party loses the parliament, the head of government just goes. A president sits there for four years no matter what."

"Unless he's impeached," Priya said.

"Which almost never happens and takes forever when it does. That's my whole case. A vote of no confidence is faster."

Clara said, "How much faster," and then regretted it, because Dev turned to her with the expression of someone handed an audience.

He had a notebook, of course. He flipped through it and found a page with a date circled twice, which she thought was a lot of confidence in one's own handwriting. "March 28, 1979," he said. "James Callaghan, the British prime minister. His government lost a vote of no confidence by a single vote. Three hundred eleven to three hundred ten. One vote, and it forced a general election. The whole government, gone."

"One vote," Clara said. She looked at the form in her hand, at the line where her name went, and did the arithmetic she had been refusing to do for three weeks: her vote, one; a national electorate, some large number she couldn't precisely name. She had been telling her mother that registering was mostly symbolic, and her mother had said, "So is a flag," in a tone that Clara had filed under things to think about later.

"I'm arguing that the parliamentary way valorizes accountability over stability," Dev said. "The president can't be removed by the legislature in a normal vote, so you get gridlock. The prime minister can, so you get responsibility."

"Or chicanery," Priya said. "Oppositions can manufacture a crisis to force an election they think they'll win. That's my case. It's not accountability, it's opportunism with better manners."

The line moved forward. The marriage license couple left arm in arm, and the clerk waved Clara up, and she laid the form on the counter thinking about how a prime minister could fall in an afternoon and a president couldn't fall at all without something like a trial, and how neither system seemed to promise that the person holding the office would be good at it. The clerk, a woman with reading glasses on a beaded chain, looked at the form, then at Clara.

"You're not going to be able to vote this cycle," the clerk said. "You know that."

"I know," Clara said. "I want to be on the rolls anyway."

"For one vote," the clerk said, stamping it, and it sounded like a small joke and also like a fact, and Clara could not entirely tell which, which seemed to be the condition of the whole morning. Dev, still behind her, said, "It was one vote in 1979," as though this settled the matter, and Priya said, "It was also 310 votes against," as though that settled a different matter, and both of them were somehow correct at once, a thing Clara suspected she would spend the next several years getting used to.

She signed her name and the pen skipped on the r, so it looked briefly like someone else's signature, hers if she were slightly bolder. Outside on the steps the air smelled of bus exhaust and cut grass, noxious in the specific way of cities in early summer, and she sat down to wait for her bus with the registration receipt in her pocket and the two systems still arguing in her head, neither one winning. A pigeon landed near her shoe and considered her with one orange eye. "You don't get a vote either," she told it, and it walked away.

Sofia sat on the hood of her mother's Corolla with her cap in her lap, picking at the tassel, because the ceremony had ended twenty minutes ago and the parking lot had turned into a slow parade of trunk decorations and relatives taking photographs of other relatives. She had wanted to leave early. She had not left early.

"Congratulations," said Danny, appearing beside the car with his hands in his pockets. He had not been at the ceremony, which was the kind of thing nobody said out loud.

"Thanks. You could have come."

"I had an interview." He said it lightly, the way he said most things now, and then ruined it by adding, "Third one this month," which was not light at all.

Danny had left school in November, junior year, to work at his uncle's shop, and then the shop had closed in the spring, and since then he had been applying to places Sofia had never heard of, distribution centers and a bakery at four in the morning. She had listened to a lot of it over the phone, lying on her bedroom floor with her chemistry notes open to a page she was not reading.

"Any luck?"

"They keep saying they'll call." He leaned against the car next to hers, a Honda with a FOR SALE sign that had been there so long it had faded to pink. "My cousin keeps telling me the economy's great. Three point nine percent unemployment, he says. For people twenty-five and up with a diploma. I looked it up, because I didn't believe him. He's right, that's the real number, 2023. Meanwhile the ones without one, that's me, we're at five point six. Same year. So the economy is great for people who are not me."

"That's a gap," Sofia said, and immediately regretted the phrasing, like she was grading him.

"That's a gap," Danny agreed, and grinned, which was worse.

Her grandmother's maxim, delivered over many Sunday dinners, was that school was for people who lacked imagination. Grandma had come from a city Sofia pictured as permanently lit and cosmopolitan, had built a dress shop from nothing, and had never once filled out a form that asked about education. Sofia had grown up hearing this the way other kids heard blessing before meals. Then, in tenth grade, a guidance counselor had told her, without ceremony, that college graduates earned more and worried less, which had sounded less like wisdom and more like a warning label. She had been carrying both sentences around for three years without deciding between them, the way you carry two keys when you only have one lock.

Danny gesticulated at the parking lot, at the balloons sagging off a minivan, at the whole assembled apparatus of celebration. "Look at this. Four years of worksheets and you get a polyester robe and a party in a parking lot."

"It's not a party. It's tailgating with grief."

He laughed at that, really laughed, and she remembered November of junior year, before he dropped out, when he had stayed after class to argue with Mr. Reyes about whether logarithms had personalities. Danny had insisted they did, that some were friendly and some were hiding something, and Mr. Reyes had given him a B-plus for the semester mostly, Sofia suspected, out of respect for the argument. That was the Danny she kept expecting to see at school every Monday after he left, glancing at the empty chair two rows over like it was going to fill itself.

"Are you going back?" she asked. "For the GED, or whatever."

"Maybe." He kicked a bottle cap across the asphalt. It skittered under a truck and stayed there. "My cousin says five point six isn't that bad, statistically. I told him to go be a statistic."

"It isn't that bad," Sofia said. "But it's worse than three point nine. That's the whole thing, isn't it. It's not hopeless, it's just harder, by exactly the amount they measure."

Danny looked at her for a second. "That's the most tassel-cap thing you've ever said."

"I'm wearing the tassel. It does things to me."

Her mother came out of the crowd then, holding her phone up sideways, filming, calling Sofia's name in the voice she used at airports. Sofia slid off the hood and stood next to Danny for the picture, and her mother said, "Danny! Good, get in, get in," and he did, still grinning, throwing an arm around Sofia's shoulders like graduation was something he had narrowly escaped and she had narrowly survived.

Later, when the lot had emptied and Danny had driven off in the pink-sign Honda, which turned out to be his uncle's, Sofia sat in the Corolla's passenger seat waiting for her mother to stop saying goodbye to Mrs. Odum. She held her phone and did not open it. She was going to college in August, on a scholarship that covered tuition and not much else, and she was going because three point nine was better than five point six and because her grandmother had been wrong about imagination, probably, and because Danny had been right about logarithms, which had personalities, some of them hiding something.

Her mother got in, started the car, and said, "Mrs. Odum wants a copy of that photo."

"Send her the one where Danny looks like he's graduating too."

"I will," her mother said, and pulled out of the spot, past the sagging balloons, past the truck with the bottle cap still underneath it.

The parking lot behind the shuttered Kmart had been repainted once and then abandoned, so the lines wandered, and Savannah's father said that was good, because nobody would be filming her mistakes. He was a defense attorney, home between trials, and he had offered to come along to her first lesson the way he offered to come along to everything, briskly, as though her childhood were a case he still had standing to litigate. The instructor, a wiry woman named Ruth, checked the mirrors and said they'd start with the wheel alone.

For an hour it was only that: ignition, gear, the creep of the car across chipped asphalt, the wheel turning in her hands with a heaviness she hadn't expected, like steering something asleep. Her father sat in the back with his coffee and made occasional trenchant remarks about her overcorrections, and Ruth said, "Let her find it," in a voice that closed the subject, and Savannah, flushing, found it, more or less, the car settling into something like a line.

Then Ruth directed her out through the gap in the curb and onto the frontage road, which was nearly empty too, a Sunday morning stretch of strip malls and streetlights. There was one other car, a blue hatchback ahead, and Savannah kept glancing at it. Every time she looked down at the speedometer and back up, the hatchback had grown larger, filling the windshield, and each time she eased off the gas as though she'd been caught at something.

"You're riding up on him," Ruth said, mildly.

"I didn't mean to. I wasn't even going fast."

"That's the trick of it. Speed sneaks. Watch when he passes a sign."

A green sign for a hardware store was coming up on the right. The hatchback drew level with it, then passed it, and Savannah, without deciding to, began to count, one-one-thousand, two-one-thousand, and she was still on two-one-thousand when her own hood slid past the sign. Too close, then. She tried the next lamppost. One-one-thousand, two-one-thousand, and this time she crossed the lamppost's shadow just as the second second ended, and the hatchback ahead had loosened, had become a car again, a normal object at a normal distance, and she could see its whole back window and the bumper sticker on it, faded, unreadable.

"It's called the two-second rule," Ruth said. That was all.

Savannah's father leaned forward between the seats. He wanted to know whether two seconds was a legal standard or a rule of thumb, whether it would hold up if you had to litigate a rear-end collision, whether the driver in back was automatically at fault or whether you could subpoena the other car's data to show a brake-check. Ruth let him run and then said, "It's not about court. It's about having room to be wrong." Savannah turned that over while she drove. Room to be wrong. In the back seat her father was already drafting the counterargument, something about how following distance created a moral hazard, how you couldn't run a life on cushions, and she caught herself agreeing with half of it, because she had grown up on his version: close, precise, no wasted margin. But the margin, she was discovering, was not waste. The distance between her and the hatchback was distance in which things could happen, the driver braking for a dog, Savannah's foot arriving a beat late, the world being imperfect, and the imperfection simply absorbing into the gap. Her father was right that you had to show up close to anything that mattered. Ruth was right that arriving and colliding were separated by almost nothing.

The blue car turned off at a pharmacy and the road ahead was hers alone, and she was surprised by how the emptiness felt less like freedom than like the loss of a ruler. Without the hatchback there was nothing to measure against, and she let the speed drift up until Ruth said, "What's your limit?" and Savannah said, "Whatever it is, I don't want to find out from a ticket," and brought it back down herself. That was the whole morning, she thought, in miniature: not one doctrine but two, held at the same time, her father's exactness and Ruth's allowance for error, and her not sure yet which one to keep at which distance, only sure that the counting had worked, and that the counting was a kind of law she had chosen to obey rather than been made to.

They looped back through the Kmart lot, and her father got out first to take a call, pacing by the cart corral with his phone at his ear, free hand already arguing. Ruth wrote something small on a card and handed it over: the date of the next lesson, and under it, in blunt pencil, "two seconds." Savannah slid it into the pocket with her permit, put the car in drive, and, alone behind the wheel for the first time with Ruth watching from the curb, counted the front wheel slowly across a crooked white line, one, two.

The phone store smelled like floor cleaner and warm plastic, and Vanessa had been standing at the display wall long enough that the greeter had stopped greeting her. Behind the counter, her cousin Deshawn was helping a man in a paint-spattered jacket, sliding a box across the glass. When he came over he wiped his hands on his apron of lanyards and said, "Your mom's battery finally did it, huh."

"She says it won't hold a charge anymore."

"That happens." He picked up her mother's phone, which she'd brought in a sandwich bag like something dead, and turned it over. "This thing's from like 2019. The battery's basically desiccated. You could replace it, but honestly, at that age, you'd be paying to keep a rock alive."

She wanted to say something light back, but the number on the price tag she'd been circling with her eyes for ten minutes had dried out her voice. Two hundred eighty-nine dollars, or thirty-one dollars a month on the installment plan, which was the part that interested her, because thirty-one a month was what she could cover from her café shifts without touching the account. The account was for after June. The account was for a bus ticket and a damage deposit in a city six hours from here, and her mother did not know its exact size, only that it existed, only that Vanessa had said "I'm saving, it's fine" enough times that the words had stopped meaning anything specific in their kitchen.

Deshawn ran the financing on his tablet and turned the screen toward her. "So here's the thing. The installment plan isn't free money. There's a monthly rate, and it stacks. What you borrow costs more the longer you take to pay it back. Pay it off early, you pay less. Stretch it out, more."

"How much more?"

He tapped. "Depends on how fast you pay. Here, look, this is the total cost over the whole term versus the sticker price."

While he loaded the numbers, she drifted, the way she did in any store, toward the credit union kiosk wedged between the accessories wall and the refrigerator of trading-card machines. The credit union shared the building with the phone store, some zoning arrangement nobody could explain, and a young teller sat there under a poster of a mountain meadow so green it looked manufactured. A bank of demo phones beside the kiosk ran a slideshow of stock wallpapers, one of them a montane landscape, pines and scree and a lake, clearly chosen for verisimilitude, though nothing about it resembled an actual Tuesday.

The kiosk had two savings brochures fanned out like playing cards. She picked up both. Teen Savings, it said on one, interest compounded monthly. On the other, Regular Savings, compounded yearly, same rate. Her account was in the second one. She had opened it at sixteen with a signature that still looked forged and had never thought about the word "compounded" since.

At the bottom of the brochure, in type so small it seemed embarrassed of itself, was the formula. A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt). She read it twice, then a third time, mouthing it. She took out her own phone and typed it into the calculator, guessing at the letters, and then flipped the brochure over and found the key printed on the back like an answer to a riddle. "n is how many times per year interest is added," she said, half to herself, and the teller glanced up and nodded without breaking her stride on a deposit slip. Vanessa sat down on the demo bench and worked it. Same P, same r, same t. Twelve for n, then one for n. Monthly came out slightly larger. Not by a life-changing amount, on what she had. But larger, and larger in a direction that ran all one way, the way water runs downhill and never checks with you first.

She thought of her account compounding once a year like a plant watered annually, and of the financing plan running the same machinery in reverse, quietly and patiently taking a little more from her the longer she owed. Two systems, one giving and one taking, both powered by the same indifference. She could move the savings to the monthly account, that was a phone call. She could take the installments and pay them off fast. Or she could pay for the phone outright from the account and lose a chunk of the escape fund in one afternoon, which was the option her chest kept suggesting and her head kept refusing.

"Hey," Deshawn called. "You still want the gray one? I got one left in the back."

The teller looked up again, this time at her, and Vanessa realized she'd been staring at the meadow poster while the calculator glowed in her hand. Thirty-one a month. Twelve months, roughly, plus whatever the interest added, and the savings moved to monthly compounding to make up a piece of the difference, and her mother's phone in its sandwich bag on the counter with the cracked screen and the dead battery and two years of photos Deshawn said he might be able to transfer if the thing would hold a charge long enough.

"Can you move her photos onto the new one?" Vanessa asked. "It's her birthday Friday. She thinks I'm just getting the battery looked at."

Deshawn grinned and pulled the box out from under the counter. "Then let's not tell her the battery news," he said, and slid the sandwich bag toward himself like it was evidence.

The bread was gone before the peanut butter, and somehow that was the thing Camille finally understood. It happened in the cafeteria at eleven forty, forty minutes before the quiz she had every reason to fail, with a sandwich disassembled on a napkin in front of her.

The trouble had started in September, when Ms. Okafor's chemistry class crossed from the periodic table into stoichiometry. Camille had been fine with molar mass; she could add atomic weights with a calculator like anyone. But then the problems changed shape. Given so many grams of reactant, find the grams of product. The textbook laid out a method like a city ordinance, rigid and posted on every page: grams to moles, moles across the bridge of the balanced equation, moles back to grams. She followed the ordinance and still arrived at wrong answers, off by factors she couldn't name, and the wrongness had begun to feel personal, a message about what she was and wasn't cut out for.

"You're doing it again," said Priya, sliding her tray across from Camille's. "The face. The face you make when a number has insulted your family."

"Twenty-five grams of sodium reacts with chlorine gas, find the mass of sodium chloride produced. I got point nine. Devon got thirty-eight point something. One of us is insane."

Devon set down his own sandwich, which he had built with the grim efficiency of someone who habituated to cafeteria lines years ago and no longer looked at the food. "I don't get it either," he said, with a cheerfulness that made it worse. "I just move the numbers until they look right."

Priya, who would not take the quiz because she had tested out, had been watching Camille disassemble her own sandwich into components: two slices of bread, a mound of tuna. She had started doing it without thinking, arranging the slices like a diagram. "Okay," Priya said. "How many sandwiches can you make?"

"Out of this? Two. Obviously."

"Now say there's tons of tuna left in the kitchen. A whole barrel."

"Still two. I only have two slices of bread."

"So what's limiting you?"

Camille looked at the bread. Something rearranged itself behind her eyes, slowly, the way furniture moves in a dream. "The bread runs out first," she said. "So that's it. The bread decides everything. The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first, and it sets the greatest amount of product the reaction can make." She said it to the sandwich, then looked up, almost embarrassed, as if she'd been caught talking to it.

"That's what my brother called it last night," Devon said. "I thought he made the word up."

"No, it's real. It's in chapter nine." Camille was pulling her notebook out of her bag, pushing the sandwich aside. The grams, the moles, the conversion: none of it was the point. The point was that every problem had a bread, a thing that ran out first, and the answer was never bigger than what the bread allowed. Her wrong answer of point nine suddenly had a shape. She'd divided somewhere she should have multiplied, or used the wrong molar mass, or treated sodium chloride as though it were just sodium. She couldn't tell which yet, and that bothered her, honestly and specifically: knowing that a mistake existed was not the same as finding it.

In the lab room, the clock gave them ten minutes of review, and Ms. Okafor wrote a fresh problem on the board without commentary, a courtesy Camille was grateful for. Given fifteen point zero grams of aluminum and excess bromine, calculate the mass of aluminum bromide formed. Camille wrote the balanced equation, checked it twice, checked it a third time. Twenty-six point nine eight grams per mole of aluminum. She did the arithmetic in the margin, in small, deliberate numbers, the way Priya had taught her years ago for exams. Then across the equation, two aluminum to two aluminum bromide, a ratio of one, almost anticlimactic. Back to grams with the product's molar mass, which she built line by line, adding bromine's mass three times on paper because she did not trust herself to do it in her head.

The answer came out to one hundred forty-seven grams, and Devon, leaning sideways, got the same thing, which they both found more convincing than any single right answer. Camille did not feel certain. That was the part she couldn't explain to anyone who wasn't there: the number sat on her page looking correct and she still couldn't rule out the version of herself who divided where she should have multiplied. But the uncertainty had changed character. Before, the whole subject had been fog; now the fog was localized, a specific corner she could walk into with a flashlight.

When the quizzes came back Thursday, hers had a red circle around the final answer and a small check beside the setup, and Ms. Okafor had written "clean method" in the margin, which was the most trenchant thing she ever said in red ink. Camille read it three times. Then she took out her sandwich at lunch, counted the slices of bread, and said to Priya, "Two sandwiches. Barrel of tuna in the kitchen."

Grandfather's dining table had one leg shorter than the others, so Evan propped his laptop on the dictionary nobody opened anymore and balanced a salt shaker under the dictionary's corner. On the screen was a database he had built himself over three days of summer: two tables, one listing every customer of Grandfather's feed store, the other listing the year's orders. The tutorial had reached the chapter on joins, and the exercise at the bottom of the page asked for something that had seemed, at first, almost philosophical: find the customers who ordered nothing.

He wanted this for a reason. Grandfather was planning a September mailing, the kind with coupons, and he'd been muttering about wasting stamps on people who hadn't bought so much as a bag of scratch grain since the spring before last. Evan had offered, partly to be useful and partly because the alternative was helping reshingle the woodshed, and Grandfather had said, "The boy knows computers," in the tone he reserved for weather he did not trust but could not argue with.

His first attempt used an ordinary join, the INNER kind the chapter had opened with. The result came back as a tidy list of forty-one names, every one attached to at least one order, and Evan stared at it for a long moment before realizing the problem. The people he needed weren't in it at all. They had simply vanished, as if never having ordered anything made a person not exist. Mrs. Pell, who came in every December to beseech Grandfather for burlap and every other month for nothing, was nowhere on the list. He scrolled twice to be sure.

The chapter's next section had a diagram, two overlapping circles with the left circle shaded, and beneath it a sentence Evan read four times. A LEFT JOIN returns every row from the left table, filling the right table's columns with NULL wherever no matching row exists. He typed the new query carefully, left hand hovering, changed one word and one keyword, and ran it.

The list came back longer. Fifty-three names now, and beside some of them, in the columns for order number and order date and total, the word NULL sat in gray. Mrs. Pell was third from the top, NULL across the row like a row of empty chairs. He counted the NULLs. Twelve customers, twelve people the store still considered customers, who had ordered nothing at all.

"There you are," Grandfather said from the doorway, drying his hands on a towel that had once been red. "Your grandmother's been holding dinner hostage. She made the roast."

"She's an epicure, that woman. She'll deny it." He came to look over Evan's shoulder, reading glasses already on, though he pretended they were for later. "What's all this?"

"Everyone who buys from you," Evan said, "and the ones who don't. The ones who don't, the computer fills in a blank. NULL, it's called." He pointed at Mrs. Pell's row. "She's nothing but blanks."

Grandfather leaned in, and Evan watched him read it, watched him recognize the names in order, the way he recognized people at the counter. "Left join," Evan said, tapping the line in his query. "Everything from the left table stays in. Everyone, even the blanks." Grandfather grunted, which could have meant anything, and then said, "Harold Odell. He died in March."

The row for Harold Odell was NULL from one end to the other, which was true in more ways than the computer knew. Evan felt something shift in his thinking, two views of the same table settling against each other: the machine's, where a person was a row that either matched or didn't, and Grandfather's, where a name carried a face and a February conversation about frost. Neither was wrong. The query couldn't tell the difference between a lapsed customer and a dead one, and Evan couldn't decide whether that was the query's flaw or its honesty.
