He laughed, because it was true of the stub too, and of the spreadsheet, and probably of the whole adult ledger he was slowly being admitted into. His mother, in the front seat, said nothing, which he suspected was deliberate. In the back, Austin opened the laptop box on his knees, and Priya leaned over and pressed the power button.

The application closed at six, and at four-thirty Kaitlyn still had six courses on her list. She sat at the corner table of the coffee shop with her laptop open, a flat white going cold beside her, and pressed her thumbnail into the edge of the table until it left a small white crescent.

"You're doing the face," Dev said from across the table. He had come to study for his own exams and had given up pretending an hour ago. "The face you make when you think nobody can see you."

"I have to cut one and I don't know which." She turned the screen toward him. Six rows: three history courses, two archaeology, one joint honours in history and politics. "It lets you pick five. That's it. Five courses, and you don't even get to rank them."

"Rank them how?"

"Like a first choice. There's no first choice. You list five and they all sit there, equal, and the universities can't see which one you actually want." She pulled the screen back. "I read the whole site twice last night to make sure I had it right."

Dev stirred his coffee without drinking it. "So cut the joint honours. You said the personal statement was all history anyway."

"That's the tautological part. The statement is about history because I wrote it about history. If I'd written it about politics, it would be about politics. I can't use my own essay as evidence of what I am. It only proves what I decided to be this autumn."

"Okay," Dev said, "then cut archaeology. You've never even been on a dig."

"That's exactly why I want it." She kept her voice low, though the shop was nearly empty, just the hiss of the machine and a man by the window reading a newspaper. "Everything I can already prove about myself is already on the form. Grades, the statement, the reference. Archaeology is the one thing on the list I can't prove yet. If I cut everything I can't prove, I'm just filing paperwork about a person I already know."

Dev leaned back. "That's the kind of thing you say to sound deep."

"I know." She looked at the table. "But it's also true. Both things."

The barista came over to clear the mug of a customer who had left and, without being asked, said, "Six o'clock deadline, is it?" She had a lanyard with a university name card half tucked into her apron. "Mine closed on a night like this. I sat in here until they locked the doors."

"Did you get in?" Dev asked.

"Deferred, then went, then left." She stacked the mug on her tray. "I picked the sensible one. Still wonder about the other."

Kaitlyn watched her carry the tray to the counter, then looked back at the six rows on her screen. Her mother wanted the politics course, had said so three times on the phone, twice in the tone she used when she wanted Kaitlyn to think an idea was her own. Her history teacher wanted the history courses, the ones with the reputations. Nobody had wanted archaeology, which was partly why it felt like hers, and possibly why it was a bad idea, and she could not find any way to tell those two feelings apart.

"Say something," she said to Dev.

"No. This one's yours."

"Helpful."

"You already know. You keep scrolling to the same row and then scrolling away." He pointed at the trackpad. "You've done it four times since I've been counting."

She scrolled now, deliberately, and stopped where he'd said. The joint honours. The course her mother would call practical and she would call borrowed. She thought of the epigram her father liked, about how you can't step in the same river twice, and how she'd always found it clever and slightly useless, and how tonight it was neither. Deleting it wouldn't cauterize anything. Politics would still be in her, would still show up in every history essay she ever wrote. You couldn't burn off a curiosity like a nerve ending. You could only decide which room to keep it in.

Her cursor hovered over the small grey x. "If I cut this," she said, "and I regret it, that's on me. Not my mum, not you, not the deadline. Me."

"Yup," Dev said.

She clicked. Five courses, listed in no order of preference, none of them first, all of them hers. The submit button turned from grey to green. She checked the clock, 5:12, picked up the cold flat white, and drank the whole thing down like medicine. Then she hit submit.

The blood pressure cuff wheezed like a small animal being sat on, and Simon wrote down the numbers it spat out: 148 over 94. "That's high," said Priya, who was his lab partner mostly because the seating chart was capricious and had decided so on the first day. "For an adult, anyway." Their health teacher, Ms. Okafor, had set up six stations in the classroom, and by the end of the period on Friday they each had to stand up, read a cuff, interpret the numbers, and explain what diet and exercise could do to change them. That was two days away, which sounded like plenty until Simon remembered he also had a calculus test, and his brain did not appear capable of holding both blood pressure and related rates at once.

"Systolic, diastolic," Priya recited at station two, tapping the worksheet. "First number's the push, second is the rest. Your grandpa's is the pushy kind." Simon's grandfather had been drafted into the lesson plan by Ms. Okafor, who wanted them to practice on a real arm rather than the rubber training one, which she called Gerald and which had begun to atrophy in a corner, its bulb cracked, its cuff sagging like something that had given up on being a body part. Simon had gone to his grandfather's apartment on Wednesday with the school cuff and a permission slip, and his grandfather had sat very still for the reading, then announced that he intended to live to a hundred out of spite.

The trouble started on Thursday night, at the same apartment, over soup. His grandfather had opened a can of chicken and rice, and while the old man hunted for a ladle, Simon turned the can in his hand and read the label. Sodium, per serving: 690 milligrams. Two and a half servings per can. He did the arithmetic twice because the first answer seemed rude. "Grandpa," he said, "how much salt are you supposed to have in a day?" His grandfather said he'd never been told a number in his life and considered the whole idea of counting salt a personal insult, though he said it warmly, the way he said most insults.

At school on Friday morning, Simon found Priya at her locker. "Okay, so I looked it up last night," he said. "The World Health Organization says adults should eat less than 2 grams of sodium a day." Priya frowned at him. "Sodium's not the same as salt, is it? Salt is sodium plus, like, the other part." "Less than 5 grams of salt," Simon said. "So the salt number's bigger because salt isn't all sodium. My grandpa's soup can alone had over 1.7 grams of sodium. One can, and he has it with bread." Priya's eyes went wide in a way that suggested she was doing her own rude arithmetic.

Fourth period, they got the message. Ms. Okafor had promised a resource email, and Simon opened it under his desk while his calculus teacher drew a ladder sliding down a wall, an image Simon found deeply unhelpful in two subjects at once. The email contained a photo of a pantry shelf and a note from his grandfather, who had apparently gotten Simon's mother to type it: "Checked the cupboard. Four more cans. I am eating my entire allowance of salt before noon, it seems. Do not tell your grandmother, who believes I eat like a sparrow. Come Sunday. Bring the cuff, bring the shame." Simon read it twice, then held it out to Priya, who was supposed to be finding the derivative of the ladder and instead laughed into her sleeve.

At the station that afternoon, the mock presentation went like this: 148 over 94 was high, and the things a person could change about it were, annoyingly, the things Simon's grandfather liked best. Walking, which his grandfather called "wandering," could lower it; salty canned soup, which his grandfather called "dinner," could raise it. "So the fix is wandering instead of soup," Priya said. "Which sounds like an oxymoron when you put it that way," Simon said, "but the numbers actually work. Move more, pour less." Ms. Okafor, passing behind them, said nothing, which Simon had learned was her version of applause.

There was one thing he could not settle, and he said so when his turn came, standing in front of the class with the cuff and Gerald the deflated arm as his witness. "I don't know if my grandfather's number comes back down in a week or a month or ever," he told them. "I know the direction it should go. I don't know the speed." A boy in the second row asked whether that was going to be on the quiz, and Ms. Okafor said that uncertainty was always on the quiz, which the class received as a threat.

Sunday, Simon rode the bus to the apartment with the cuff in his backpack and a shopping list in his pocket, and found his grandfather at the stove, stirring something in a pot that smelled of actual vegetables. On the counter, the four remaining cans stood in a tidy row, turned so their labels faced the wall. "Two grams of sodium a day," his grandfather said without turning around. "Less than five of salt. I did some reading. I found it insulting and also convincing, which is a new experience for me." He held out the ladle. "Taste this and tell me honestly it needs salt." Simon tasted it, and considered his answer for a long moment, cuff waiting in the bag.

The bank smelled like carpet cleaner and cold coffee, and Vanessa spread the mortgage offers across the little desk the way her economics teacher had taught them to spread arguments, side by side, before deciding anything. Her mother sat beside her with her coat still buttoned, which Vanessa took for impatience until she noticed her mother's hands, folded and still, in her lap.

"Thirty-year fixed," the loan officer said, sliding a sheet toward them. "That's the one most families ask about first."

Vanessa looked at the number at the top of the page and then at the number at the top of the second page, an older offer her mother had kept in a folder at home, and something did not add up, or rather it added up too well, in the wrong direction. "Why is this one so different?" she asked. "From a few years ago, I mean. Mom's old one is way lower."

The officer smiled the way adults smile when they plan to hand you the whole question back. "Why do you think?"

Vanessa had prepared for this, though not on purpose. Three weeks of economics, a notebook with a timeline she'd drawn herself, a teacher who refused to give answers and only gave dates. "The Federal Reserve," she said slowly, testing the sentence as she built it. "They started raising their policy rate from near zero in March 2022. And by July 2023 it was at five and a quarter to five and a half percent." She had checked the figures twice, because getting a number wrong in Mr. Okonkwo's class meant rewriting the whole timeline, and getting it wrong here meant something she couldn't yet name.

"And that makes my rate higher," her mother said. It wasn't a question, but it wanted to be one.

"That's part of it," the officer said, and turned to her screen.

Vanessa sat back and let the two of them talk about points and fees, and while they talked she did what Mr. Okonkwo called holding two ideas at once. On one side was the textbook chain: higher rates made borrowing expensive, expensive borrowing cooled demand, cooled demand eased the pressure on prices, and that pressure was inflation. On the other side was her mother, sitting very straight, who had never once in Vanessa's life refinanced anything. The ideas didn't fit together. Something was pushing on prices from one end and on her mother from the other, and Vanessa could feel the shape of a third thing she couldn't see yet.

"I don't understand the middle part," Vanessa said, interrupting. "Why would the rate being higher slow inflation? Like, actually, for people."

The officer looked up. "You're asking the right question, but you're asking the wrong person. I move the numbers. The Fed decides them."

So Vanessa worked it out herself, out loud, half to her mother and half to the margin of her notebook. If a loan cost more, fewer people took one. If fewer people took one, fewer people bought the things loans bought. If fewer people bought, sellers stopped raising prices just because they could. She wrote it as a chain of arrows and then drew a question mark beside the last arrow, because Mr. Okonkwo had made them all write that same mark: honest about where the chain got thin. It works slowly, she thought. It works on everyone at once. It works whether or not you did anything wrong.

Her mother was quiet the whole time, and it was in that quiet, later, at the counter by the deposit slips while the officer printed something, that the withheld thing surfaced without anyone lifting it. Her mother picked up a pen, put it down, picked it up again. "Your father's hours were cut in the spring," she said to the deposit slip. "We're not refinancing to save money, Vanessa. We're refinancing to have money."

In her mother's car afterward, the folder of offers on the seat between them, Vanessa turned the sentence over. The Fed had lifted its rate from near zero to five and a quarter to five and a half, and somewhere in that climb was a reason prices had stopped climbing so fast, and somewhere in that same climb was the reason her family's old loan, the cheap one, the one signed when money had been practically free to borrow, was now the thing they couldn't afford to keep. She had spent three weeks learning to explain a mechanism, and the mechanism had walked into the car and sat down beside her.

"You were good in there," her mother said, pulling out of the lot. "That teacher of yours, the one who makes you redo everything. He'd have been proud."

Vanessa expostulated that pride wasn't the point, that she'd drawn a question mark where the chain got thin, that anyone who claimed to understand all of it in one sitting was selling a bromide, and then she heard herself and laughed, because she sounded exactly like Mr. Okonkwo. Her mother laughed too, a short, surprised sound, the first one since spring, Vanessa realized, and realized also that she had no way of knowing whether that was true.

"The second offer," Vanessa said, tapping the folder. "The one with the lower fee but the higher rate. We should do the math again, tonight, at the kitchen table, all the way out to year thirty." She took out her pen. "And Mom, when we're done, you're going to explain one thing to me."

"What thing?"

Her hand paused over the folder, the pen's shadow crossing both offers at once. "Why you waited until now to tell me."

The phone repair shop shared a wall with a laundromat, and in August the heat came through both sides. Mackenzie had been hired to replace screens and batteries, but by her second week the owner, Theo, had put her in front of the register's ancient laptop and asked her to figure out who owed him a phone call. He kept two lists, he said. One was customers, one was repair orders, and somewhere in the mismatch between them were people he'd never seen again.

She had finished one year of college and taken a single programming course, the kind where you wrote a query about a fictional library. She knew what a join was in theory. The shop's database was not theory. It was two tables, one called customers and one called orders, and between them a silence she was supposed to interpret.

The shop ran like a theocracy, Desi liked to say, because Theo decided everything from the back room and the rest of them operated on faith. Desi was twenty-six and could peel a diaphanous sheet of tempered glass off a cracked iPhone in one pull, without gloves, without dust. Mackenzie watched his hands while her own hands moved across the keyboard. On her third day she had a query that worked: select the customers whose ids appeared in no order. The screen showed seven names. She printed the list and taped it inside the register.

Then a woman came in with a Samsung that would not charge. Mackenzie took the order, typed the customer's name into the form, and the id field came up blank because the woman had never been entered in the customers table. Mackenzie saved the order anyway, meaning to fix it later, and moved on to the phone.

The next morning Theo asked for the list again before he drove his rounds. Mackenzie ran the query. The screen returned nothing. Not fewer names, not an error, nothing at all, the same seven names erased as if they had never existed. She ran it three times. She checked that she was pointed at the right database. She leaned back and looked at the wall, where the heat shimmered faintly over the laundromat's dryer vents.

She thought of Desi's hands again, the way he lifted a screen in one piece. A query like this had to be whole. If it found one bad row, one blank where a number belonged, the whole thing came apart. She wrote the sentence in her notebook so she would not lose it: a NOT IN query returns no rows at all if the subquery's list contains even one NULL. That was the trap, the common one, the one her professor had never mentioned because his fictional libraries were always perfectly filled in. She did not know yet why it behaved that way. She knew only that it did, and that it had.

She scrolled through the orders table and found the Samsung repair with its blank customer id. She fixed the entry, created the woman properly in the customers table, and ran the query a second time. Seven names again, exactly the same seven, and the eighth still missing because the new customer's order now matched. She tore the old printout off the register and taped up the new one. Then she wrote a second note in the margin of her notebook: the database can be wrong in two directions, the people in it and the people missing from it, and a blank field can hide either kind.

Theo drove off with the list on the passenger seat. Desi came over and looked at the screen, at the seven names and the query above them. "So which ones are real?" he asked.

"All of them now," Mackenzie said. "As far as I know."

Desi picked up her printed list, folded it once, and slid it into his shirt pocket. "Theo's going to call every one of them and offer ten percent off," he said. "Watch. By Friday half of them come back with broken screens they've been saving for a reason." He went back to his workbench, and Mackenzie sat with her hand on the trackpad, running the query once more just to see the seven names hold still.

The essay was due at the end of the period, and Faith had written four paragraphs arguing that ancient women had left no voice, that Roman wives existed in the record only as names attached to fathers and husbands, and Mr. Okafor had walked past her desk three times without saying anything, which she knew was deliberate.

"You're wrong," Marcus said from the next row, not quietly.

"I cited three sources."

"You cited three textbooks that agree with each other." He turned his laptop toward her. On the screen was a photograph of a thin wooden rectangle, ink faded to brown, the edges cracked like something recovered from a fire, though it had not been fire that preserved it. "Vindolanda. It's a fort up on the boreal edge of the empire, near Hadrian's Wall. The ground there is anaerobic. Things don't rot. They found hundreds of letters in the mud."

Faith looked at the photo without touching the screen. "Letters from soldiers."

"That's a birthday party invitation," Marcus said. "From Claudia Severa to Sulpicia Lepidina, written around 100 CE. Sulpicia Lepidina was the prefect's wife. Claudia Severa was inviting her to come celebrate her birthday." He tapped the bottom of the image, where the script changed. "Those closing lines are among the earliest known Latin writing by a woman."

The room went on around them, chairs scraping, someone arguing about citations near the window. Faith read the translation he had pulled up. Claudia Severa hoped her sister would come, to make the day more enjoyable by her presence, and then, in her own hand, she had added a greeting to her absent friend. Faith had written four paragraphs, and the fourth one had used the word "silence" three times.

"How do you know a woman wrote the closing lines?" she said.

"The handwriting changes. Look at it."

She looked. The letters at the bottom were smaller, slanted differently, less practiced. She was not a paleographer. She could not have said what made a hand a hand, and yet the difference was visible even to her, the way you can tell a note on your locker was written by your mother before you see the signature.

"Mr. Okafor," Marcus called across the room. "Can we use primary sources that aren't in the textbook?"

"You can use anything you can defend," Mr. Okafor said, without coming over, and Faith understood that he had heard all of it.

She deleted her fourth paragraph. Then she sat with her cursor blinking at the end of the third and could not write, because the sentence she wanted was that the invitation changed everything, and she suspected it did not change everything, and she did not know how to hold both of those at once. Around her the class was packing up. Rain had started against the windows, thin and sideways, and someone's phone buzzed and was silenced.

"I'm not trying to absolve you," Marcus said, closing the laptop. "You didn't do anything wrong. The books you read were written by people who thought the question was whether women had power."

"And what's the question now?"

He shrugged, shouldering his bag. "Maybe it's whether we've been asking women to prove they existed."

At the door, Mr. Okafor stopped her. "Faith. When you revise, I want you to read these." He handed her two photocopied pages, both about the invitation, both from historians she had cited in paragraph two. She read the first one standing in the emptying room. It argued the tablet proved ordinary Roman women were literate, that Claudia Severa's closing lines were evidence of a lost world of female correspondence. She read the second one standing by the window. It argued that one tablet could not prove anything about ordinary women, that Claudia Severa was an officer's wife, privileged, exceptional, and that historians who inflated her into a representative were doing politics rather than history.

Both had looked at the same wood, the same ink, the same small slanting letters. She turned the pages over as if the backs might take a side, and outside the rain had thickened, and the floodlights on the field came on early against the grey.

She went back to her desk and opened the essay. She wrote a sentence saying that the invitation existed, that a woman named Claudia Severa had invited a woman named Sulpicia Lepidina to a birthday party around 100 CE, and that the closing lines were among the earliest known Latin writing by a woman. She wrote that everything past those facts was interpretation, and that the interpretations disagreed. Then she stopped, because she wanted to say which interpretation was right, and she did not know, and she was not going to pretend.

She sat there a long time, drifting into a kind of reverie, watching the rain, until the room was almost dark except for the light over her desk. In her mind the invitation kept arriving, over and over, a woman writing to a woman: I shall be at your side, and I invite you, so that you may be with me. That part at least was certain. What it meant about the world was still open.

She heard Marcus's voice in the corridor, arguing with someone about football, and she picked up her pen and crossed out her title, "The Silence of Roman Women," and wrote nothing underneath it yet.

Nicholas had never been inside a courthouse before the morning he was assigned to argue both sides. The marble corridor smelled like floor wax and old paper, and his shoes made a sound on the stairs that seemed too loud for the building's hush. In his messenger bag he carried two sets of notes, one for the school district and one for the student, because Coach Reyes had drawn his name for the hardest format: each speaker at the regional mock Supreme Court tournament would have to argue the case twice, once as petitioner, once as respondent, and be credible both times. The case was a real one. A high school student had posted something angry on Snapchat over the weekend, off campus, and the school had punished her for it, and the Supreme Court had taken up whether that punishment was allowed.

He found his team's bench near the windows, where the crepuscular light of the late afternoon would eventually arrive, though right now it was only ten in the morning and everything was flat and bright. Priya was already there, highlighting a printed opinion with a green marker as if green could make the law grow clearer. "You got Mahanoy?" she asked. "Lucky. It's only the most important student speech case in decades."

"That's what I keep reading," Nicholas said, though luck was not how it felt. He had spent the whole week trying to hold two contradictions in his head at once, and instead of clarifying, they had coagulated into something thick that he could not pour into an argument. The school side said adults had to supervise teenagers who were cruel to each other. The student side said a snap sent from a bedroom on a Saturday was nobody's business but the sender's. He believed both, depending on the hour.

Their first round was called at eleven, in a courtroom with a real judge's bench and a retired judge sitting behind it, smiling at them the way people smile at pigeons. Nicholas stood, squared his notes, and argued for the school district. He talked about teams and morale and the way a cheerleading squad was a small biome, its own fragile ecosystem of trust that a toxic post could collapse. The judge nodded once. Priya passed him a note that said "good," which was the highest compliment available.

Between rounds, in the hallway, a girl from another school sat alone on the wide stone steps, scrolling her phone with her thumb moving fast, the way you scroll when you are looking for something and afraid of it. Nicholas recognized her from the pairings sheet. "You okay?" he asked, because it seemed like the thing to ask, and she looked up with the guarded face of someone much younger than sixteen.

"I made a post last weekend," she said. "About my coach. It was stupid, but I didn't think it was illegal stupid. My school suspended me Tuesday." She turned the phone toward him and then pulled it back before he could read anything. "So I looked up whether the Court ever said anything. Mahanoy. Mahanoy Area School District versus B.L., 2021. The Supreme Court ruled eight to one that a school violated a student's free speech by punishing an off-campus Snapchat post. Eight to one. That's basically everybody." She said the case name carefully, like a spell she had memorized in case she needed to say it out loud to an assistant principal.

Nicholas sat down on the step beside her, not too close. He had been carrying the case around all week as an exercise, a tournament problem, a thing to be sliced into arguments, and here it was sitting on a stone stair in the body of a girl with bitten nails. "I have to argue against you in about twenty minutes," he said. "The school's side. It's a mock thing, but I still have to say the words." She laughed, one syllable, surprised out of her. "Then say them," she said. "I want to hear if they're any good."

At one o'clock he stood at the podium again, this time for the student, and the words came differently, or the same words came with different weight, and he could not decide afterward whether the difference was in the argument or in himself. The judge asked him whether schools should have no authority at all over weekend posts, and Nicholas said no, that was not his position, that he did not know exactly where the line was, and that the Court itself had left the boundary unsettled. It was, he understood as he said it, a strange way to win, by admitting the map had blank spaces. When the round ended, Priya squeezed his shoulder, and the girl from the steps was standing at the back of the courtroom, arms folded, waiting for him at the doors with her phone in her hand.

The marble steps of the courthouse were slick from rain, and Sophia climbed them with her binder pressed against her chest, the one holding two sets of notes she had not yet managed to reconcile. Inside, the mock court would convene in forty minutes. She was arguing Tinker v. Des Moines reimagined for the digital age, a fictional case in which a student, suspended for an online post, claimed her First Amendment rights were violated, and Sophia had drawn the unlucky position of preparing both sides.

Her partner for the respondent, Marcus, was already in the lobby, leaning against a radiator that looked like something salvaged from an antiquated ship, all valves and dull brass. "You look like you didn't sleep," he said.

"I didn't. I keep finding holes in my own case." She opened the binder to show him: her petitioner pages argued that the school had punished speech, which the government could not do; her respondent pages argued that the platform hosting the post had removed it first, before the school acted. She had underlined a sentence three times and then crossed it out three times.

"Which side do you actually believe?" Marcus asked, and she hated the question, because last spring she had organized a walkout and then told a younger student, briskly and with total confidence, that the website deleting their event page was a First Amendment violation. She had said it into a microphone. She had been wrong in front of two hundred people, and no one had corrected her, because no one knew.

"Neither," she said. "Both. That's the problem."

They went up to the courtroom, where rows of folding chairs faced a bench borrowed from a real judge's chambers, dark wood, scarred. Other students milled around in blazers that did not quite fit. Sophia found her seat and read her opening lines again, mouthing them.

When her turn came, she stood and argued for the student: schools are arms of the government, the First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech, and punishment for a lawful post was state action, pure and simple. The student judges leaned forward. One of them, a girl with a pen behind her ear, scribbled something. Sophia felt the argument hold, solid and warm, like a wall she could put her back against.

Then the presiding judge said, "Ms. Okafor, the post was also removed by the platform itself. Does your client have a claim against them?"

Sophia opened her mouth to say yes, and the words from last spring rose up, the microphone, her own certainty, and she stopped. Across the room Marcus gave her a look that was almost kind. "No," she said slowly. "The First Amendment limits what the government can do to speech. It does not by itself stop a private company from restricting speech. The platform is private. My claim is against the school alone." The judge with the pen nodded and wrote for a long moment, and Sophia sat down with her heart knocking, because she had just handed the other side a gift.

When they switched, she stood to litigate the respondent's position herself, and it was stranger than she expected, dismantling the wall she had built an hour before. She offered the counterpoint gently: schools may regulate speech that substantially disrupts learning, and the post had caused a hallway confrontation the day after it appeared. She believed it, in this room, under these lights. She had also believed the opposite. Both could not be true, and yet each had felt true while she argued it, and that frightened her a little, the way a smooth floor frightens you when you first feel it give under your shoe.

Afterward, in the corridor, the younger student from the walkout, Priya, was waiting by the water fountain. "I saw the case summary," Priya said. "The part about the private website. Is that why our event page came down last year? Nobody did anything illegal?"

Sophia looked at her, at the binder under her own arm, at the rain streaking the tall windows. "That's not what I said," she answered. "I said nobody could sue over it as a First Amendment claim. There's a difference." Priya's face did something complicated, and Sophia did not know yet whether she had made it better or worse, so she held out the binder, opened to the crossed-out sentence, and let Priya read it for herself.

Zoey's grandmother kept a double boiler in the cabinet above the stove, the way other households kept aspirin. It was dented along one side and older than Zoey's mother, and when Gram finally let her use it, she did so with the ceremony of someone handing over a passport. "Watch the thermometer, not the clock," she said, though she had said it three times already that afternoon, and would say it again before the chocolate was cool.

They were making shells for truffles, the way Gram had done every December for forty years, filling tin boxes for neighbors whose names Zoey only half knew. But this year Gram's hands trembled in a way that had nothing to do with the cold, and she had taken to standing at the counter like a supervisor who no longer remembered the job, only the authority. So Zoey had found the tempering instructions herself, in a flour-smeared notebook with Gram's florid, looping handwriting on every page, the letters so decorative they were almost unreadable. Melt to 115. Cool to 81. Warm again to 88, not one degree past. Seed with a chunk of already-tempered chocolate and stir until the shine comes up.

The shine did not come up. Her first batch set dull and streaked, soft at the edges, and Gram looked at it with something that might have been pity. "You rushed it," she said, which was the one diagnosis she still delivered with full confidence. Zoey scraped the batch back into the bowl, remelted it, and started over, feeling the afternoon narrow to a single question: whether the chocolate would cooperate or whether she would leave for college on Saturday having failed at the only craft this kitchen had ever demanded of her.

That night she called her roommate-to-be, Priya, who was at a campsite in Wisconsin making cake pops for her cousin's birthday. "We just melted these candy melts and dipped everything," Priya said, phone crackling over the sound of a radio. "They hardened in like ten minutes. Snappy and everything. Why are you doing all that thermometer stuff?" Zoey said she didn't know, exactly, and after they hung up she looked it up, sitting on the floor of the guest room with the light from her phone making a small bright country on the wall. The candy melts were compound chocolate, or coating chocolate. It replaced some or all of the cocoa butter with other fats, and it set without tempering. It did not have the same snap.

She read the sentence twice. She thought of her father, who read every contract twice because he distrusted anything that arrived finished. She thought of Priya, who trusted everything, and whose cake pops had looked glossy in the photo she sent. Two ways of moving through the world, and here they were, baked into two kinds of chocolate: the one that demanded patience and gave you, if you were exact, a shell that fractured clean; the one that asked nothing and gave you something almost as good. Almost. That was the word the whole thing turned on, and she could not decide whether it was a small word or an enormous one.

The next morning she tried again. Gram sat at the kitchen table while Zoey stirred, and the stirring was its own kind of attention, so slow and repetitive it desensitized her to everything else, the ticking clock, the neighbor's leaf blower, the fact that Gram had called her by her mother's name at breakfast. She cooled the chocolate to 81, moving it across the slab with a spatula, warming it back to 88 over the water, holding it there the way you hold a note you're afraid to let waver. When she spread a little on wax paper, it set in under three minutes, glossy as lacquer. She broke a test piece and the sound was clean, a small decisive report like a knuckle cracking.

"You got it," Gram said, and Zoey felt the pleasure of it arrive and then immediately go strange, because she could not tell whether Gram understood what she had gotten, or was simply praising the way you praise a child who has drawn the same sun the same yellow as always. In college, Zoey would take a class called Interpretation, or that was the word on the syllabus; her cousin, who had taken something like it, called it hermeneutics, the study of how meaning gets made and whether you can trust the making. Zoey had thought that sounded abstract. Now she wasn't sure. Gram had written the notebook, and the notebook had taught Zoey, and the woman who wrote it sat ten feet away, unreachable by the same words.

She dipped the truffle shells that afternoon, one after another, each one coming out with a skin of light on it. Gram ate two and said they tasted like Christmas, which was the truest thing anyone had said all day, and Zoey packed the rest into a tin, planning to bring them to her roommate, a small proof of what a thermometer and two hours could do. She was taping the lid when she went back to the notebook to check the filling recipe for next time, and there, under Gram's looping script at the bottom of the page, was a note she had skipped the day she was hunting for temperatures. Use the coating chocolate from the restaurant supply, it said. It sets on its own and no one can tell the difference in the boxes.

No one can tell the difference in the boxes. Forty years of truffles, the ones Zoey's mother still described with her eyes closed, the ones the neighbors waited for, and they had been made from something that replaced the cocoa butter with other fats and never needed tempering at all. Everything Zoey had spent two days learning, the cooling and the seeding and the trembling hold at 88, had been for a tradition that had never included it. She sat with the notebook open on the counter for a long moment, the tin warm under her palm, and found she could not decide if she had been faithful to something or had simply replaced it with a harder version no one had asked for.

Gram came in for a glass of water and saw the page upside down in front of her. She put on her glasses, read a few words, and smiled. "That coating chocolate," she said. "Easier. Never bothered tempering, not once." She patted the tin once, twice, like burping an infant, and carried her water out to the porch, leaving Zoey alone with two trays of truffles that shone like nothing Gram had ever made, and a recipe, in that florid hand, for the ones everybody had actually wanted.

Sophia spread the score across the kitchen table and weighted its corners with mugs from the drainer, though nobody was home to disturb it. The printed staves belonged to Mozart's Sonata in C, K. 545, first movement, and her assignment was to mark the exposition, the development and the recapitulation in colored pencil before her lesson on Thursday. She had three colors. She had chosen red, blue and green with what she considered a judicious neutrality, and she had already ruined one photocopy by drawing the blue line in the wrong place, so tonight she was working slowly, headphones on, pencil hovering above measure 28.

"Development," her friend Priya had said that afternoon, leaning over her shoulder in the library, "that's the middle one, the restless one." Priya had said it the way she said everything, as though the world's facts were hers to hand out. "Exposition first, development in the middle, recapitulation at the end. Mr. Alvarez made us memorize it in October." Sophia had nodded and said thanks, but she resented the handout, because she wanted to hear the sections for herself, not be told where they lived.

Her phone buzzed against the table. She turned it face down without looking.

She played the opening again. The first theme dropped down the C major scale, bright and public, almost smug in its simplicity, and then the second theme arrived in G major, more lyrical, like someone changing the subject at a party. She drew the red line at the double bar and wrote exposition beside it in small capitals. So far this was clerical work. The problem began at the double bar, where Mozart stopped being polite.

The middle section did not behave. The left hand churned, the right hand tossed out little broken pieces of tune, and each fragment seemed to land somewhere new before she could name where it had been. She rewound twice, three times, following one short figure with her pencil tip until it slid into another key and she lost it. Then, on the fourth pass, she caught it: four notes in the bass, quick and grumbling, that were unmistakably the opening of the first tune, the bright descending scale, chopped down and buried in the storm. She sat back so fast the headphone cord pulled the phone across the table and she saw, in the half second before she grabbed it, a message from Priya: You need to check the course page. Do it now.

She put the phone in her pocket, unopened, and played the passage again. There it was, the same four notes, transmuted from sunlight into something anxious, hurried out of one key and into the next without apology. That was why the middle sounded restless, she realized, not because Mozart had written new music but because he had broken the old music into fragments and kept moving them, never letting any piece rest long enough in one key to settle. She wrote development beside the blue line, and underneath, in pencil, small enough that only she would read it: he takes the tune apart and runs it through the keys. Then, near the end, the opening theme came back whole, in C major, unharmed, and she drew the green line and wrote recapitulation and felt the strange satisfaction of a room put back in order.

The phone buzzed again in her pocket, twice, and her ennui, which had been sitting on her all evening like weather, sharpened into something closer to dread. Priya did not send messages like that. She carried the phone to the window, the score open behind her with its three colored lines, and opened the thread.

Sophia. The recital requirement moved. It's not Thursday anymore. Submissions close tonight, 11:59. Alvarez posted it at five. You have two hours. You have to record the analysis and upload it, talking through the sections at the piano. I'm so sorry, I only just saw it.

The kitchen clock said 9:41. Sophia stood very still while the facts rearranged themselves, and then she was moving, pulling the phone charger from the wall, dragging the bench out from the piano, propping the score on the rack with the mugs still clipped to its corners. She set the phone against the metronome, camera facing the keys, and pressed record before she could think about whether she was ready, because being ready was no longer among the options.

"Okay," she said to the lens, to Priya, to whoever would watch it later. "First movement, Mozart, K. 545. This is the exposition." She played the opening scale, the smug one, and then the second theme in G, and her hands were steadier than her voice. "And then here, this is where it breaks." She played the churning left hand, and then slowed it down, and pointed with her eyes at the bass. "Listen. That's the opening tune, just a piece of it, and he keeps doing that, breaking the themes into fragments and pushing them through key after key, that's why it sounds restless. And when it comes back whole, at the end, that's the recapitulation." She glanced at the clock. 11:52. The upload bar crawled across the screen, seven percent, twelve, and Sophia watched it with her hands folded in her lap, still warm from the keys.

Ella had been sick for three days with something the campus nurse refused to name, a flu that would have debilitated a less stubborn person, and she had waited until the last hour of voting to drag herself to the fire station on Delancey Street. The line inside was short. Outside, on the curb, two people she knew from the mayoral campaign office were already arguing, and they were arguing loudly enough that a poll worker came to the door and told them to take it to the sidewalk.

"Ella," Marcus said, grabbing her sleeve before she could get in line. "Tell her. The Herald poll has Rivera up two points and the margin of error is four. Two is smaller than four. It's a tie. Dana thinks Rivera's winning."

"I'm not saying he's winning," Dana said. She had a clipboard against her hip and a stack of door-hangers going soft in the drizzle. "I'm saying two points is two points. The number says Rivera."

"The number says nothing. Within the margin of error means tied. That's what it means."

The poll worker leaned out again. "Polls close at eight. It's quarter past seven. If you're voting, get in line. If you're not, move along."

That was the real deadline, and all three of them knew it. The campaign had forty volunteers sitting in cars along Fourth Avenue, waiting for one phone call: either push the last three precincts for Rivera in the final forty-five minutes, or stand down and save the money for the recount fund. Dana had the call sheet in her back pocket. Marcus had the campaign manager's cell number queued on his phone. They had been standing on this curb for twenty minutes going in circles.

Ella pulled her hood up and thought about her statistics elective, which she had taken only because the ceramics studio was full. She thought about the exercise the textbook had made them do twice, and she was careful now, because she did not want to say it wrong in front of both of them.

"Listen," she said. "It's not a tie. I'm pretty sure it's not a tie. When the lead is smaller than the margin of error, the poll can't say with confidence who's ahead. That's all it can't say. It doesn't mean the race is exactly tied. Two points is still two points. The poll just can't tell you it's real."

"So we push," Dana said.

"So you don't know," Ella said. "That's the honest answer. The poll can't tell you Rivera's ahead and it can't tell you he isn't. It's not zero."

Marcus stared at the flyer stapled to the telephone pole above them, one of Rivera's bombastic ones, four exclamation points and a promise to "take back the city by storm." He said, "So what do we do with forty minutes and forty volunteers?"

"You do what you'd do if you didn't have the poll at all," Ella said. "You knock on the doors of people who always vote and always vote for you, and you make sure they got out. That doesn't cost you anything if you're behind, and it doesn't waste much if you're ahead."

Dana was already dialing. Marcus stood there a second longer, working it through, and Ella could see him letting go of the word "tied" the way you let go of a rung you thought was solid. "Okay," he said. "Okay, that's actually not the same as a tie."

Dana got through. "Push the three precincts," she said into the phone. "Yes. Ground game only, no literature drops. Yes, I know it's raining." She hung up and looked at both of them. "Done. Now go vote, both of you, before they lock the doors."

Inside, the line had shrunk to six people. A woman ahead of Ella was reading a voter guide about the county question on laboratory animal standards, out loud, half to herself: "Whereas the party of the first part acknowledges the capacity for sentience in..." She trailed off and flipped the page. Ella checked in at the table, signed her name in the box next to a signature card from six weeks ago, when she had registered on her eighteenth birthday with her mother standing behind her holding the umbrella.

The booth gave her a stubby pencil and a ballot with tiny ovals. She filled in the mayor's race first, then the county question, then the judges she had never heard of, and she thought, briefly, that her single oval was one data point in a pile so large it would never be separable again. At seven fifty-five she fed the ballot into the scanner, which chunked it down with a sound like a mail slot, and the machine displayed a number on its counter, one higher than before.

Outside, Marcus and Dana were gone, and the rain had stopped. She could see the headlights of cars turning onto Fourth Avenue, one after another, all going the same direction.

Hunter paid for two hot chocolates he didn't want, because Marisol had said yes to a football game and a football game meant cold bleachers, and a spartan concession stand offered nothing else. He was eighteen and this was his first real date, a fact his friend Dex had found hilarious for the entire week leading up to it.

They found seats at the top of the visitor side, away from the marching band. For the first quarter it went well. She laughed at his joke about the opposing team's mascot, a costumed antelope with a broken snout, and she explained which players were her cousins. Then the second quarter began and the conversation thinned out like fog burning off, and by the two-minute warning they were watching the scoreboard more than each other, and Hunter understood that silence between strangers is different from silence between friends, though he couldn't have said how.

"So," Marisol said, and the word hung there like a pass with no receiver.

In his pocket his phone buzzed. A text from his sister, Wren, who was home with a broken wrist and her own agenda: "If the date is bad, tell her about your sabbatical from gaming. Girls like reformed boys. Also bring me a pretzel. THIS IS MY ONLY WANT IN LIFE." He typed back "no such thing as reformed" and put the phone away, which Marisol noticed, and which he had to explain, which made her laugh again, which gave him the nerve to try something.

"Can I propose an experiment?" he said. "I read about this study. Arthur Aron, 1997. Pairs of strangers took turns asking each other thirty-six questions that got gradually more personal, and afterward they felt closer than pairs who just made small talk."

"Thirty-six," she said. "At a football game."

"We don't have to do all of them. We could just do some. Trade harder questions."

She pulled her scarf up to her chin, considering. "Fine. But I go first. Question one: why did you actually ask me out? Not the version you told Dex."

He hadn't expected the study to be turned on him so fast. "Because you argued with Mr. Ferreira about the ending of that story and you were wrong, but you were wrong in a way I kept thinking about for a week. Your turn. What do you want that you've never told anyone at this school?"

The game went on below them, small helmets colliding, and neither of them watched it anymore. Her answer involved veterinary school and a mother who thought it was impractical. His next question, borrowed from what he remembered of the study's spirit, was about what she'd want to know about her own future if she could. Hers was about embarrassment, and she answered hers first even though she'd asked it, which he liked. Somewhere in the third quarter the questions stopped being a game and became just talking, though he couldn't locate the exact moment the change happened, the way you can't say when dusk becomes night.

"I have to ask the pretzel question," he said finally. "My sister's want. She's home with a cast on her arm and the emotional leverage of a Victorian orphan."

"Get two," Marisol said. "I'll go with you."

They climbed down through the crowd, and on the walk to the concession stand she asked the last question of the night, the one he turned over all the way home. "Do you think it works," she said, "the study? Do you think we actually feel closer, or we just think we do?"

Below them the band played, and the antelope mascot danced badly near the fence, and Hunter considered the question honestly, because it deserved that. "I don't know if those are different things," he said. "I can't tell yet. Ask me question thirty-seven tomorrow."

She was already writing it down on the back of her ticket stub.

The basement of St. Brigid's smelled of candle wax and instant coffee, and on Sunday afternoons it belonged to whoever needed it most. This afternoon it belonged to Faith, who had spread the score of Mozart's Fantasia and Sonata across the piano bench and was trying, for the third time, to find the exact bar where the exposition gave way to development.

She had until Wednesday. Her audition for the conservatory's theory placement exam included an analysis she would have to talk through out loud, and Ms. Adeyemi had said, in that flat voice she used for serious things, that Faith heard music beautifully but described it carelessly. Faith had been carrying the sentence around for two weeks like a stone in her pocket.

The church was quiet above her. She had started coming here to practice because the piano in the basement was free, the old upright nobody played since the choir director retired, and because her mother's apartment had thin walls and a new boyfriend who watched television at full volume. There was something about playing under a sanctuary, she thought, that made you listen differently, though she couldn't have said how.

She played the first theme again, the stern, dark opening in C minor, and then followed the music as it traveled. She had a theory, or half of one, and it was wrong in a way she was about to discover. In the pieces she'd analyzed all semester, the major-key ones, the second theme had always arrived in the dominant, a fifth above, bright and brash like a raised hand. So she sat with her pencil hovering, waiting for the second theme to show up in G minor, the dominant of C minor, and marking in her head where she'd bracket it.

Instead the music lifted into E-flat major. Three flats where she'd expected two, warmth where she'd braced for more darkness. She stopped playing and sat very still, one hand still resting on the keys.

"No," she said out loud, to nobody. Then, quieter: "Yes."

She found her phone and texted Deshawn, who had placed into the exam last year and who answered, as always, like an epicure of small corrections: "In a minor-key sonata-form movement, the second theme usually moves to the relative major. E-flat in C minor. Didn't you listen to it before marking it?"

She hadn't, not really. She had listened the way she'd been taught to read in middle school, hunting for the answer she already expected. That was the carelessness Ms. Adeyemi meant, she realized, not sloppiness in her handwriting but this: she kept hearing what she assumed instead of what was there. She thought of her father, who used to correct her practicing from the next room without ever coming in, calling out the wrong notes he'd decided she must be playing. She had hated that. She had also, she noticed with discomfort, inherited it.

The sanctuary door creaked overhead and Mrs. Okafor's voice interposed itself down the stairwell before Faith could answer it. "Someone's playing Mozart in my basement."

"Sorry, Mrs. O. I can stop."

"You will not." Mrs. Okafor came down slowly, holding the rail, wearing her Sunday coat though it was four in the afternoon. "My husband used to play that one. The C minor. He said the second part of the beginning was like walking out of a cellar into a garden, and he was a penurious man with compliments, so I believed him." She settled into a folding chair. "Play it. I want to see if he was right."

Faith set her pencil down. She had marked the exposition, and she could mark the development now, the part where Mozart pulled the themes apart and dragged them through keys like a cat worrying a string. She knew the recapitulation would bring the opening back. That was the shape, the promise the form made and kept. But what she hadn't known, what nobody had told her, was that E-flat major in the middle, the garden in the cellar, and she had missed it because she'd been listening for a rule she'd half-remembered.

She played the exposition through, and when the second theme bloomed into E-flat she watched Mrs. Okafor's face change, the loosening around the eyes, the small nod. "There," the old woman said. "The garden."

Faith marked the bar with her pencil, a clean bracket in the margin, and then wrote the key signature beside it in her own shorthand, so she would remember that she had found it rather than guessed it. Maybe that was the position she could take into Wednesday: not that she knew all the rules, but that she knew how to be surprised and could say so precisely. Or maybe that was just a nicer word for guessing late. She couldn't decide, and Mrs. Okafor was still listening, so she went back to the beginning and played it again from bar one.

John had agreed to write the essay only because his grandmother had the poster. It hung above the piano in her front room, a reproduction of The Two Fridas that his grandfather had bought in Mexico City decades before he died, and John's art teacher had assigned exactly that painting for their first formal analysis. He could have worked from the image on his laptop, but his grandmother had said come over, the light is better in the morning, and she had made him eggs before leaving him alone with it.

He began the way the assignment demanded, with a pencil and cheap sketchbook, copying the composition in outline. Two women in chairs, holding hands, seated on a bench under a churned grey sky. The one on the left wore a white European dress, lace at the collar, wedding-style, formal almost to the point of ceremony. The one on the right wore the Tehuana dress, bright colour, and John had to decide what to call that difference in his notes. Costuming as identity, he wrote, and then crossed it out because it sounded like something borrowed. He wrote instead, she painted two of herself and made them opposites, then crossed that out too, because he wasn't sure it was true.

The trouble was the essay itself, which was due Monday and had to argue something. His grandmother drifted in and out with laundry, unapologetic about the interruptions. "You've been staring," she said at one point. "Staring is not looking." She was obstreperous in the mild way of a person who believes her house entitles her to commentary, and John had learned not to argue, only to keep sketching.

The sketch was what changed things. Copying the figures, he had to decide where every line went, and when he reached the chests he stopped. Both women's hearts were exposed, painted outside the body, one whole and flushed, the other cut and bleeding. That was strange enough. But from the torn heart on the left, a single red thread ran down, and John traced it with his pencil, along the arm, through the hand of one Frida to the hand of the other, back up to the intact heart, one blood vessel winding between both hearts, connecting them. He sat back. He had looked at the image for two days and had not seen the line until his own hand had to draw it.

"Did you know this was here?" he asked when his grandmother came through with towels.

She came to the poster and followed his pencil point. "Your grandfather pointed it out to me once," she said. "I said it was morbid. He said it was honest." She folded a towel over her arm. "He was usually right about paintings and wrong about other things."

John worked through the afternoon. Formal analysis wanted him to stay with what he could see: the exposed hearts, the connecting vessel, the scissors in the left Frida's lap, the small portrait the right Frida held, the stormy sky pressing down on both figures equally. Colour supported it, the cold whites and blues on one side, the warm earth tones on the other, and yet the red line crossed the whole divide. He drafted a thesis that the painting's symbols of separation were undercut by its composition, which physically joined the two figures. It was the first idea in the essay that felt like his own.

But something nagged at him. His grandmother's remark sat in his mind while he wrote, and he kept circling back to his own crossed-out notes. Two ways of seeing the painting competed in him: the formal one, where the line was simply a compositional fact linking colour fields, and another, more personal one, where the line insisted that a divided self stays connected by something it cannot sever. He could not fully hold both positions at once, and he was honest enough with himself to write that in the margin, a note to resolve later. The margin note was still there when he finished.

His grandmother read the draft in the kitchen while he washed the dishes he had promised to wash. He watched her over his shoulder, her finger moving down the page, pausing where he had written about the single vessel winding through their hands and hearts. He wanted her to absolve him of the uncertainty he had left in the final paragraph, to say it was fine not to conclude, but she didn't. She set the pages on the table, and he noticed she had set them beside his grandfather's old reading glasses, still kept there, still used for nothing.

"Well," she said. "You saw it. Most people never see the thread."

Lauren had the instructor's confirmation email open on her phone as she stood at the end of the driveway, one shoe on the curb, waiting for a blue automatic Corsa that hadn't appeared yet. Behind her sat her father's manual Golf, faded green, third gear still sticky from the year he'd learned to tow a trailer. The school's booking form had offered automatic lessons at the same price, and she'd ticked automatic without thinking, the way she ticked most boxes, because automatic seemed to subsume everything a beginner needed: steering, mirrors, judgment, all of it minus one pedal and a gearstick. She was eighteen in six weeks and she had a plan she hadn't yet said aloud, a plan involving her grandmother's cottage forty minutes away down lanes the buses didn't serve.

The blue car arrived on time. The instructor, a woman named Pat with reading glasses pushed up into grey hair, got out and walked around to the passenger side. "Lauren? We'll do the cockpit drill, then a few laps of the estate. Quiet this time of morning." She said it kindly, in the tone of someone who had said it four thousand times.

Lauren got in, adjusted the seat, and then didn't touch the seatbelt. "Pat. Can I ask something before we start? If I pass my test in this car, in an automatic, what can I drive after?"

"Automatics," Pat said. "Only automatics. You'd have to pass a manual test to drive a manual car."

Lauren looked through the windscreen at the Golf, at the gearstick she'd watched her father's hand find without looking, at the whole errand of her grandmother's shopping and hospital appointments and the Sunday roast tins that somehow got subsumed under the single word helping. She had assumed a licence was a licence, one genus covering every car on the road. It wasn't. It forked, like the degrees her friends were choosing, and the fork you picked quietly in a booking form turned out to matter.

"I learned in a manual," Pat went on, not lecturing, just filling the silence the way instructors do. "Hated it for three lessons. Then it stopped being a thing I thought about." She checked her mirror, unhurried. "We can swap your bookings, if that's what you're thinking. Same price, same hours. But the first few manual lessons are harder. I won't pretend otherwise. You'll stall it."

From the kitchen window, Pat watched the girl stand very still with her hand on the roof of the car. She had seen this before, though not often, and never this early, before a single lesson. Most learners wanted the easy version and never asked what the easy version left out. The father came out of the house then, still holding his coffee mug, and stood at his own front door like a man uncertain whether he'd been summoned. Pat lowered her window an inch. "She's got a question, Mr. Ahmadi. It's a good one."

Lauren's father came down the driveway slowly, setting the mug on the low wall by the gate. "What question?"

"If I pass in an automatic, I can't drive your car," Lauren said. "Not legally. I'd have to do another test, in a manual, to drive a manual." She heard herself say it and realised she was testing the sentence as much as telling him, checking whether it still sounded absurd in the open air. It didn't. It sounded like something she should have found out in March.

Her father looked at the Golf as if it had said something. "Your uncle drove that car for eight years," he said, which wasn't an answer, and then, quieter, "Your gran asks after you. She thinks you'll come in that car." He said it plainly, without weight, but she understood he'd been thinking about the lanes too, the hospital in Truro, the fact that his own knees were starting to object to the trip. Perhaps he'd even been counting on her, though he'd never have used that word. Grandparents were supposed to be the munificent ones, pressing twenties into card pockets, and her grandmother was, but lately the giving ran in the other direction and nobody had announced the change; it had simply happened, like a season turning.

"I'll swap to manual," Lauren said to Pat. "All the hours. If I stall it, I stall it."

Pat nodded and opened the boot for the L plates, and Lauren, taking one, turned it over in her hands, the white square with its red L, and walked up the driveway to the green car where her father was already fishing the keys out of his jacket pocket. "Not today," Pat called after her, gently. "Bookings first." Lauren stopped, laughed once at herself, and came back, and her father lowered himself into the Golf, started it, and held the clutch down in neutral while he waited, engine running, for his daughter to finish sorting out the paperwork.

Gabrielle counted the bills twice in the aisle by the registers, because counting money in public felt like a confession, and she had exactly eleven dollars and thirty cents. The sneakers on her feet had a hole along the seam that let in water, and the pair she wanted, marked down on the end cap, cost ten ninety-nine. She had done the arithmetic walking here, done it again on the bus, and the margin was thin enough to feel like a dare.

The shoes were on a lower shelf, boxed and heavy, and she carried them to the register like something perishable. Ahead of her a man was buying batteries and a lottery ticket, and the cashier, a woman named Dolores according to the tag, read out his total in a flat, tireless voice. The man's register had a little screen facing the customer, and Gabrielle watched the numbers on it the way she watched chemistry experiments, waiting for the change she could predict.

"Ten ninety-nine," she said when her turn came, laying the box on the belt, "right?" Dolores scanned it and the screen said eleven dollars and seventy-something, and Gabrielle's stomach dropped a small, precise distance. "That's not the price," she said. "The sticker says ten ninety-nine."

"Sticker's before tax," Dolores said. "Sales tax gets added at the register."

Gabrielle stood there with her eleven dollars and thirty cents and understood, in one cold flash, that the number on the shelf had never been the number at the register, that there was a whole category of price that only existed at the last second, after you had already decided. She asked how much the total was with the tax and Dolores told her, and it was more than she had by about forty cents. Forty cents. She looked at the coins in her palm as if they had betrayed her personally.

"Can you put something back?" Dolores asked, not unkindly, and Gabrielle said she couldn't, because the something was the entire purchase. Behind her a boy from school, Marcus, was waiting with a basket, and she felt the particular heat of being watched while failing at arithmetic in public. She took out her phone, opened the calculator, and worked backward from what she had: if she had eleven thirty, what shelf price could she afford once the tax was layered on? The answer came out around ten dollars even, which meant a different, plainer pair of shoes on a different shelf.

She found them, canvas instead of the waterproof ones, and stood a moment in the aisle holding both boxes. It seemed like a strange way to run a country, she thought, a system where every price was a partial truth; other places, she'd heard somewhere, put the real number right on the tag. But that was a rumor, and she had no way to check it here, only the register, which had already told her the truth once. She carried the canvas pair back and let the other box go, and the register's screen said eleven dollars and twenty-one cents, which fit under her money with nine cents of daylight.

"Do you want the receipt?" Dolores asked, and Gabrielle said yes, because she wanted to see the anatomy of it, the line where the shoes ended and the tax began. The receipt showed the subtotal, ten dollars even, then a line for sales tax, then the total, and she folded it into her pocket like evidence.

On the bus home she sat near Marcus, who had been behind her the whole time. "That was slick," he said, meaning the calculator move. "Most people just get short at the register."

"I got short," she said. "I just got short quietly."

He laughed and told her he'd started work at a grocery store in March, and that his first paycheque had shocked him, because he'd done the math on his hours and his wage and arrived at a number that the cheque did not agree with. "They take off income tax before you even see it," he said. "There's a whole deduction section. And then there's another deduction for something called CPP, which nobody explains to you when you're sixteen."

Gabrielle turned that over. So the register took from the top, and the paycheque took from the top, and both of them let you believe in the bigger number first. She wondered whether the deductions were a kind of theft or a kind of promise, whether the money would come back to him someday in some form, and she said so, and Marcus shrugged and said his mother filed a tax return every spring and sometimes got money back, which suggested the system was more like a settling of accounts than a straightforward taking. Neither of them knew, really, and neither pretended to, which felt like its own kind of accomplishment.

Later, in her room, she set the canvas shoes beside the receipt and examined the hole in the old pair, its edges worn to something smooth and almost igneous, like rock that had cooled after heat. Her father came past her door and asked how the shopping had gone, and she said, "Did you know the shelf price isn't the real price?" and he said, "Welcome to adulthood," in the tone of a man who had stopped expecting the world to explain itself.

She put the new shoes on. They were not the waterproof ones, and it was supposed to rain Thursday, and she had nine cents in her pocket, and a paycheque of her own suddenly seemed less like a distant adult thing and more like a door she wanted to walk through, deductions and all. She folded the receipt smaller and put it in the box with the old shoes, and laced up, and stood.

The manager slid a clipboard across the table before Andrew had even sat down, and on it was a form he had never seen before, dense with small boxes, the kind of document that seemed designed to make you feel guilty before you had done anything. "You can't start your shift until this is done," she said. "It's the law. Every new employee has to complete it, no later than their first day of paid work." Andrew turned the clipboard toward the window light of the restaurant, past the mock-mediterranean murals and the igneous black countertop the owner had installed to look expensive, and read the top of the page. Form I-9, Employment Eligibility Verification. Section 1, Employee Information and Attestation. Below that, a smaller line: to be completed by the employee no later than the first day of employment.

"I did the W-4 online," he said. "My mom helped me. Nobody said anything about this one."

"Everyone forgets this one." The manager, whose nametag read DENISE, was already walking a tray of bread to table six. "Fill out Section 1, give me your ID and your social security card, and you're fine. If you didn't bring them, you're not fine."

He had not brought them. He had brought a water bottle and his phone and a folded paper with his availability written on it, because the interview had felt like the hard part and he had assumed the rest was paperwork in the loose, ceremonial sense. He looked at the form again. His date of birth, his address, a citizenship checkbox he could have handled in third grade. Then the attestation, a paragraph in tiny type that he was supposed to certify under penalty of perjury. It asked about his permission to work, which seemed absurd, since he had been staring at the permission to work for two weeks, in the form of a laminated schedule taped to the kitchen door with his name on it.

He found Denise by the drink station. "What happens if I fill this out at home tonight and bring it tomorrow?"

"Then tomorrow's your first day of paid work, and you're on time. Today you're just a person eating free bread." She said it without cruelty, refilling a water pitcher while she talked. "But if you'd shown up for an actual shift without it, we'd have a problem."

He wanted to argue the logic of a law that counted orientation as not-work but required the form for work that had not started. He had spent the whole drive here composing an argument of that kind for his father, who believed that any rule a seventeen-year-old could articulate an objection to was a rule a seventeen-year-old could ignore. His mother held the opposite position with equal force: rules were load-bearing walls, and you did not test them by leaning. For years he had treated their positions as a choice between them, a door with two handles, and lately he had begun to suspect the door might have hinges of its own. The I-9 was not an injustice. It was fifteen minutes and a folder at home. But it was also, his father would point out, the state's way of making a dishwasher prove himself, a small ceremony of subjugation dressed as procedure. His mother would say that a country that could not verify who worked in it could not protect the people who did. Standing at the drink station with a form he could not sign, Andrew found he agreed with both of them, and that agreeing with both of them was not the same as agreeing with nobody.

"I can be back by four," he said. "My house is ten minutes."

"Kitchen tour's at three thirty."

"Then I'll miss the kitchen tour and see the kitchen when I'm in it." He heard his own voice come out clipped, harder than he meant, and Denise looked at him for a moment, sizing up whether he was going to be a problem employee or just a person having one bad half hour.

"That's actually how my last hire did it," she said. "He's at college now. Bring the documents, sign it in front of me, and you start tomorrow at five. That's the whole thing."

He drove home with the clipboard still in his hand, because Denise had said she had copies, and he had said nothing and kept it, and she had said nothing and let him. At the kitchen table he found the folder his mother kept on top of the fridge, his birth certificate, his social security card in its paper sleeve, soft at the corners from years of being handed across counters. His father came through the back door with groceries and saw the form open on the table.

"What's that one?"

"Employment verification. I have to finish it by my first day of work, which is tomorrow at five."

His father set down the bag of oranges. "Section 1's the employee part," he said, tapping the page. "I've filled out fifty of these. Check the box, sign, date it."

Andrew looked up at him. "You've seen this form?"

"Every job since I was nineteen, kid." His father pulled out a chair and sat down across from him, and there was something almost shy in it, a man offering the one inheritance he was sure of. "You want, I'll look it over when you're done."

Andrew took out a pen, printed his full name in the first blank, and began.

Parker had been filing escrow paperwork at Hartwell Realty for six weeks, and by the second week he had stopped reading the documents and started studying them. He was eighteen, and in September he was supposed to move into a two-bedroom apartment above the laundromat on Corbett Street with Dee, who was already counting weeks at her hostess job. The apartment was eight hundred fifty a month, which they would split, but the listing had said "first month, last month, and deposit," and Parker had eleven hundred dollars in a checking account that his debit card kept trying to be honest about. He had done the math on the bus that morning, then done it again as though the numbers might pity him.

At the front desk he sorted the morning's files, and through the glass wall of the conference room he watched Ms. Ruiz walk a young couple through a purchase. He could hear most of it. "The down payment is the part you bring to the table," Ruiz said, tapping the folder. "Twenty percent of the price is ideal. The bank lends the rest, and that loan is the mortgage, and you pay it monthly, with interest, for thirty years if you want." The woman asked what happened if they couldn't pay, and Ruiz didn't soften it. "The bank takes the house. That's the risk. That's the whole arrangement." Parker wrote twenty percent on a sticky note, then the price of a modest house in this town, then the down payment that came out to more than four years of his salary, and folded the note into his pocket like it was evidence of something.

He caught Ruiz at the copier. "Why is it called a mortgage?" he asked. "It's a weird word." She looked at him the way she looked at buyers who asked about schools, deciding whether the question was serious. "I heard a client say once that it means something dark," she said. "I never checked. Ask someone who reads." Then she handed him the listing sheet for the Corbett Street apartment and said, "Your landlord called. He wants the deposit money by the fifteenth or he re-lists."

That night at his grandmother's kitchen table, he ate the pork chops she made without being asked and didn't touch the okra, and he said, "Do you know why a home loan is called a mortgage? It sounds like something died." His grandmother kept cutting. "Old French," she said. "Dead pledge." He waited. She ate a piece of okra he'd pushed to the rim of his plate. "That's what they told your grandfather at the bank in 1979. The pledge dies when the debt is paid." He asked, "And if it isn't paid?" She looked up then. "Or when the property is forfeited." She went back to her plate, and Parker sat with the phrase, dead pledge, turning it over while the refrigerator hummed. Two doors out of the arrangement, and one of them meant losing the house.

On Thursday, Dee's letter came, because Dee wrote letters when the news was bad, having decided that texts made bad news look casual. Parker, it began. They cut my hours to three shifts a week. I have six hundred saved and I can cover maybe a third of the move-in money and my half of rent after that is not guaranteed. My mother says I should stay home and commute and honestly she is right and I hate that she is right. I'm sorry. We can talk Friday. Parker read it twice on the porch steps, then a third time holding it against the railing like a form he had to sign.
