She took out her phone and texted Dax: forty-five okay? and watched him across the street, waiting at the goldfish booth with a paper bag, until he pulled his phone from his jacket, read it, and gave her a thumbs up so large his whole arm moved.

She re-stuffed the envelope with two twenties, a ten, and five ones, then folded it lengthwise and creased it with her thumbnail.

Her grandmother waved her over when the drums started. "Come, the lion is beginning. Bring the envelopes." Maelie crossed the street with the box of oranges and the red stack in her hands, and her grandmother pulled her down into the chair beside her and said, "Hold the money like this, both hands, when you give it. Never one hand."

"Okay," Maelie said, and turned the envelope over twice so the characters faced out.

The synagogue's social hall smelled of coffee and floor wax when Sienna arrived with three grocery bags and her grandmother's Haggadah boxed under one arm. Rabbi Fox had given her the key that afternoon, along with a clipboard listing what the families had signed up to bring, and Sienna had spent the drive rehearsing the order of the blessing over the candles, which she had only ever watched her grandfather recite. He was in hospice now, his voice down to a ribbon, and at Purim he had pressed the old book into her hands and said only, "You know more than you think."

She began by requisitioning the long folding tables from the storage closet, startling Mr. Adler, who was arranging chairs and who insisted on carrying the heavy ends himself. By six the hall had filled. Her parents came with her little brother, and her aunt and uncle, and then, hovering near the sign that said FIRST NIGHT SEDER, WELCOME, came a girl from Sienna's chem class named Priya, who had texted that morning asking if she could come because her roommate was away and the dorm was too quiet.

Sienna poured grape juice into the silver Kiddush cup and its paper-cup companions, and began. She stumbled on the second blessing, recovered, and felt her ears burn, but nobody laughed. Her little brother asked the Four Questions in a monotone that made Priya smile into her sleeve. When they reached the plate at the center of the table, Priya leaned toward it, curious and a little wary of the horseradish root and the shank bone and the pastel heap of charoset.

"That's maror," Sienna said. "Bitter herbs. Horseradish, usually. We eat them on purpose, to recall the bitterness of slavery in Egypt."

Priya looked at the root, then at the faces around the table. "You eat something bitter deliberately. At a party."

"At the exact opposite of a party," Sienna said. "Or the exact same thing. I've been arguing with myself about it all week." She held up the Haggadah, its spine cracked to softness. "My grandfather says the whole night is hermeneutics, that every generation has to read itself into the story, and for years I thought that was just something old men say to sound important. But tonight I keep catching myself doing it."

She distributed the maror, and Priya took her piece with the others, and Sienna watched her cousin Daniel, home from his first year of college and freshly bellicose about every tradition he'd grown up with, glare at the horseradish like it had personally insulted him. "This is performative suffering," he announced. "You can't taste someone else's slavery."

"You're not supposed to taste theirs," Sienna said. "You're supposed to notice what bitterness does in your own mouth, and then notice how fast you want it gone." She hadn't planned to say that. It came out of the week of reading, of the notes her grandfather had left in the margins in his cramped hand, and it landed in the room and sat there.

Daniel chewed his maror with theatrical resentment, eyes watering, and then said, unexpectedly, "Okay. That's actually not stupid." Priya's eyes were watering too, and she laughed while she cried, and Sienna's mother passed the charoset quickly down the table like a rescue line.

Later, after the meal, after the front door had been opened for Elijah and the night air had come in cold and smelling of rain, Sienna stood to lead the grace after the meal and found that her hands were steady. Daniel was humming along with the Chad Gadya under his breath, having declared it capitalist propaganda and then learned all six verses anyway. Priya had taken one of the extra Haggadot and was reading ahead, mouthing the words.

At the sink in the kitchen, washing the silver cup, Sienna thought about texting her grandfather a photo of the table. She typed and deleted three drafts. She didn't know yet whether she believed the way he believed, or whether the bitterness and the sweetness sat in any kind of order she could name, and she suspected she wouldn't know for years. What she knew was the cup in her hands and the sound of her family's voices carrying the last verses from the hall, and that seemed like enough to hold for one night.

She dried the cup, set it upright on the towel, and walked back in as they reached the final line, and she sang it louder than anyone.

Abigail would tell anyone who asked that she had never once been wrong in Mr. Ferreira's physics class, which was true only if you didn't count the midterm, the lab on pendulums, or the time she'd insisted that Venus was closer to Earth than Mars on average, which it is, but not for the reason she'd given. Today she had staked the whole period on being right again. She had asked Ferreira before class if she could present her independent project on the Higgs boson, and he had acceded with a shrug that suggested he expected very little, and that shrug was the thing she intended to make him regret.

The classroom smelled like the dust of chalk and the citrus of the spray they used on the whiteboards, and the radiator under the window ticked in a rhythm Abigail had memorized back in September, when she used to count the ticks instead of listening. Twenty-two desks. Nine students actually present, because it was the last week before exams and half the class had discovered that a signed field trip form was easier to obtain than a grasp of thermodynamics.

"Okay," she said, standing at the front with her laptop open on the demonstration bench. "So the Higgs boson. Discovered at CERN, announced July 4, 2012." She clicked to a slide she had spent two nights building, a photograph of a crowded auditorium with people standing along the walls. "Everyone always shows the particle. I want to show the room."

Rosa Delgado, who sat in the back and sardonic as a matter of policy, raised one eyebrow. "The room."

"The room matters," Abigail said, with more certainty than she felt, because she had only understood why the room mattered forty minutes ago, rereading the same paragraph in her kitchen while her mother asked twice whether she had eaten. "Look, here's what I used to think. I thought some team found a particle, and then there was a press conference, and that was it. Discovery, announcement, done. Like Newton and the apple, except with worse snacks." A small laugh from somewhere near the windows. Ferreira, at his desk, did not look up from his grading, which Abigail chose to interpret as respect.

She clicked again. Two photographs side by side, two enormous machines in underground caverns. "But CERN didn't have one giant detector looking for it. They had two. Two separate teams, completely independent of each other. ATLAS was one. CMS was the other. They weren't allowed to share their results while they worked, because if they compared notes, one team's result would contaminate the other's. You'd just have one answer wearing two coats." She heard herself say it and realized, with a strange double feeling, that she was teaching this to herself at the same time she was teaching it to them.

She remembered, then, her father at the science museum two summers ago, before he moved out, standing in front of a cutaway model of the collider with his arms crossed. A boy near them had asked the guide why CERN needed two giant detectors instead of one, and the guide had started to answer, and her father had said, loudly, "Because they didn't trust themselves, that's why," and laughed at his own joke, and the guide had said something polite about independent confirmation, and Abigail had been fifteen and embarrassed and had not listened. She had spent two years carrying around her father's version, certain of it, repeating it once at a party like it was hers. Standing in front of the class now, she understood that she had been confidently wrong, and that the wrongness had not even been hers. It was borrowed, secondhand, unexamined.

"That's the part that changed how I think about it," she said. "It's not that one experiment succeeded. It's that two teams, not sharing data, found the same new particle. Before July 4, 2012, nobody stood up and said it. Both teams had to get there first. Separately." She paused. "And even then, the announcement was the beginning of checking, not the end. Other physicists got the papers and went after the numbers. That's what the room was full of, in the photograph. People ready to take it apart."

Ferreira put his pen down. "So one result means nothing?"

"I didn't say nothing." She was careful now, slower. "One result means maybe. It means this happened once, in one machine, interpreted by one group of people who could all be making the same mistake together. Two independent results means probably. A hundred replications means we build the next thing on top of it." She looked at Rosa, who was no longer smirking. "I used to think science was a person being right. I think now it's more like a lot of people agreeing to try to prove you wrong, and the idea surviving anyway." She stopped, hearing the pedagogue in her own voice, the lecture-y drawl of someone who had read one book and become insufferable about it, and she added, quieter, "I might still be overselling it. I'm seventeen and my sources are a library database and a YouTube lecture with terrible audio."

Ferreira said, "That caveat is the most scientific thing you've said all period."

After class, Rosa caught her at the door. "My uncle works at a lab in Chicago," Rosa said. "He says they spend half their time trying to repeat other people's experiments and failing, and nobody publishes the failures, so we don't actually know how much falls apart. Does that break your whole speech?"

Abigail stood with her hand on the doorframe, the hallway noise swelling past them, lockers and sneakers and someone's tinny speaker. "No," she said. "It's just the part I can't see yet." Rosa shrugged, almost smiling, and walked off toward the stairwell. Abigail stayed a moment longer, looking at the empty room where two photographs of two machines still glowed on the screen, side by side in the dark, neither one knowing the other was there.

The studio smelled of rosin and radiator dust, and the photocopy of Mozart's Sonata in C, K. 545, lay on the music rack with its margins already crowded. James had exhumed it from the bottom of his backpack that morning, smoothing the creases where his water bottle had flattened it for a week, and now Mrs. Okonkwo tapped the first system with her pencil.

"So. By Friday you hand me this movement with the exposition, the development and the recapitulation marked. Not colored. Marked, with reasons." She sat down in the chair by the window, the ascetic wooden one she never let students use because it threw her back out, and folded her hands. "Show me where you are."

"I found the second theme," James said, and played the run of sixteenths in the right hand, the bright climbing figure he'd been noodling for days. "Here. That's the second theme, so the first theme has to end somewhere before it, right? But I don't know where. The whole first page just sounds like one long idea."

"Then you don't know where the second theme starts either," Mrs. Okonkwo said. "You know where something you like starts."

He hated when she did that, reframed his answer so it became a smaller answer, and he stared at the page as if the barlines might confess. The trouble was that the beginning was cheerful, then more cheerful, then cheerfully busier, and he couldn't point to a moment and say this is new. He had skipped the busy part all week when he practiced, hands leaping over it to land on the tune he liked. The awkward passage was an externality, a debt he kept pushing onto some future James who would have to pay it, and future James had apparently arrived.

"Play from the top," Mrs. Okonkwo said. "Slowly. And listen to your left hand for once in your life."

He played. The opening chords sat under his fingers like home, C major, plain as a kitchen table, and the melody wandered away from them and came back. Then, eight bars or so in, the texture changed. The right hand stopped singing and started working, sixteenths tumbling over each other, nothing you could whistle. And underneath, almost sneaky, the harmonies shifted. He slowed further and the left hand's F natural gave way to F sharp, and something lifted, the whole floor of the music tilting toward G.

"Stop," he said to himself, and did stop, hands hovering. "That's it. That's where it changes key."

"Changes from what to what?" Mrs. Okonkwo asked, and she was not being sarcastic, which somehow made it worse.

"From C to G. The dominant." He traced the bars with his pencil. "So this passage here, the busy part, it's not part of the first theme and it's not the second theme. It's the thing that gets you from one to the other." He hesitated, then remembered the word from a video he'd watched at midnight with his headphones on. "The transition. Some people call it the bridge."

"Mm," said Mrs. Okonkwo, which from her was applause. "And what is it made of, this bridge? What kind of material?"

He looked again at the tumbling sixteenths, the two bars where the melody turned into arithmetic. "Busy stuff," he said. "Not tuneful. It's like he didn't want you to remember it, he just wanted you to end up in the new key and be surprised the tune sounds different there." He wrote TRANSITION in the margin, boxed it, and underneath, smaller: busier, less tuneful, changes key. Then he bracketed the first theme before it, and after the bridge the second theme finally had a birth certificate instead of just a vibe.

"Good. Now the question you should be asking." She stood and came to the piano. "The exposition ends and the development begins, and you will find that easier, because the development sounds unsettled, it wanders. The recapitulation is where he comes home." She turned toward the last page. "Friday. And James, you may not skip the bridge when you practice. You skipped it all week, I could hear the hole in your playing from the waiting room."

He felt his ears go hot. "How did you know I skipped it?"

"Because you played it today like a man walking through a doorway he's afraid of." She laughed once, short, and gathered her coffee mug. "The bridge is the door. Everything interesting happens when you decide to go through it."

At home that night he spread the score across the kitchen table and worked with a ruler and three colors, and the movement organized itself under his hands like a city getting street signs. First theme, bridge, second theme, closing section; then the long unsettled middle; then the return. When he came to the recapitulation he sat back, satisfied, and started bracketing the return of the first theme in the last third of the page. Home again, C major, plain as a kitchen table.

Then he reached the place where the bridge had been before, the busy tumbling passage, and his pencil stopped in the air. He played it. Sixteenths, busier than anything around them, exactly the door he had learned to recognize, and this time he listened hard for the tilt, for the F sharp, for the floor lifting toward a new key.

It never came. The harmonies churned and settled and stayed exactly, stubbornly, in C. He played it three times, then checked the key signature twice, then leaned over the page until his nose nearly touched the print, wondering whether Mozart had made a mistake, whether he had, whether a bridge could still be a bridge if it went nowhere, if the whole point of coming home was that the door could look the same and open onto the same room.

He texted Mrs. Okonkwo, which he never did: "the recap bridge doesn't change key. is that allowed?" He sat with his chin on his fists, staring at the boxed word TRANSITION in the margin of the second half, which now looked less like a label and more like a question, and his phone buzzed once on the table.

She had replied with a single line: "What do you think the second theme sounds like in C instead of G?"

The problem on the worksheet gave the charge on each plate, the area of each plate, and nothing else, and Grace read it three times before she understood that the omission was deliberate. Mr. Okafor had written the voltage on the board for every other problem, a tidy given like a handrail, and now he had taken it away. Across the lab, Dara was already flipping through her notes with the frantic efficiency of someone who intended to find the answer before admitting she had lost it. Grace looked down at her own page, where she had copied the numbers in her small careful hand: so many coulombs, so many square metres.

"You can't get the field without the voltage," Dara said, not looking up. "That's the whole formula. E equals V over d. It's literally the formula."

"Then why would he give us this one?"

"Because he's testing whether we'll admit it's impossible. It's a trick." Dara said this with the certainty of someone who had been tricked before and had decided never to be tricked again, and Grace envied the certainty more than she believed it. Mr. Okafor did not write tricks. He wrote problems that looked impossible until you turned them over.

She turned it over. The plates were ideal, the sheet said, parallel and infinite, which meant the field between them was uniform, which meant the voltage formula was one way of describing something that could be described other ways. She thought of her mother suturing a hem, drawing two edges of fabric together so the seam held without a knot showing; there was always more than one stitch that would hold a thing closed. Charge was given. Area was given. Charge divided by area was something she could compute, a density, the crowding of charge on the plate. And if the crowding of charge was what made the field, then the field ought to come out of that density somehow, divided by some constant of the universe she half remembered seeing in the back of the textbook, unexplained and mysterious as a vestigial organ, printed in a table of constants she had never once used.

She found it in the reference page, between c and h: the permittivity of free space, 8.85 × 10^-12 farads per metre. The symbol was epsilon with a subscript zero, and the table offered no apology for it. Dara leaned over her shoulder.

"What's that?"

"Permittivity of free space," Grace said. "It's in the constants table. About eight point eight five times ten to the minus twelve farads per metre."

"So the field is the charge per area divided by that?"

"That's what I'm going to try." She tried it. She wrote the density first, the charge divided by the plate's area, and then she divided that by the tiny stubborn number, and the answer that emerged was a field strength in newtons per coulomb, plausible and clean, the kind of number that Mr. Okafor's problems always produced when you had done the thing he wanted you to do. She sat back and looked at it and did not trust it, because it had arrived by a road she had never walked before.

Dara did it too, in her own handwriting, and got the same number, and still looked unsatisfied. "But how do we know this isn't just a formula that happens to work for this problem? Like, what if he wants the other way?"

"He can want both ways. They're both true. One uses the voltage, one uses the charge on the plates." Grace tapped the page. "If he'd given us the voltage, we'd never have needed this. Maybe that's why he left it out." She heard how it sounded when she said it, like clemency extended to a man who had withheld the voltage on purpose, as if the omission were not a cruelty but a door, and she decided she meant it that way. She was less sure about the deeper thing, whether the two formulas were two descriptions of one field or two fields that happened to coincide, and she wrote a question mark in the margin next to her answer and let it stand.

Mr. Okafor came by on his slow circuit of the room, looked at her page without touching it, and moved on, which was his version of a nod. Dara erased nothing, copied the answer onto the final line, and snapped her binder shut. At the end of the period, Grace stayed behind a moment to write the question from the margin onto the worksheet itself, below the answer, where he would be sure to see it: how do we know the two methods agree when we can't check both? She left the paper in the center of the bench, squared to its edge, and the question mark inked dark and visible at the bottom of the page.

Tristan had never been wrong about arithmetic, and he told himself this the way other people told themselves they were brave. So when he opened his first envelope from Halvorsen's Hardware and found sixty-eight dollars and change where seventy-three should have been, he assumed the fault lay with the envelope, or with Mr. Halvorsen, or with the wrinkled old man who did the books, and not with the only certainty he owned.

He had worked eleven hours at six sixty-five an hour. He had done the math twice on the walk home, once more at the kitchen table, and a fourth time in the margin of the flyer announcing the store's summer inventory sale, which started Saturday. Saturday was also the deadline to sign the rest of his hiring paperwork, the forms still folded in his backpack, and Mr. Halvorsen had said, in his flat way, that if the papers were not in by then, the job would go to the Rennick boy, who was fifteen and, according to everyone, unemployable.

Tristan's mother said eleven times six sixty-five was seventy-three fifteen, which settled nothing, since he already knew that. His sister said stores steal from kids, which he found too easy. Only Dee, who ran the register on weekends and had worked at Halvorsen's since she was fourteen herself, might know something, so Friday afternoon, with the paperwork deadline a day away and his suspicion calcifying into a grievance, he took his envelope to the register and laid it flat between them.

"Shorted," he said. He said it quietly, the way you say a word you have rehearsed. "Eleven hours. I counted."

Dee did not look impressed. She looked, if anything, tired, and she pulled her own check stub from under the register mat, where she kept it as though it were a bookmark for a book she had stopped reading. "Employers withhold part of your wages," she said. "Six point two percent, for Social Security tax. Up to a yearly wage limit, then it stops for the year."

Tristan looked at the stub, then at his own envelope, then at the ceiling fan turning its slow circles over aisle three. Six point two percent of seventy-three fifteen was four dollars and fifty-three cents, give or take a penny, and seventy-three fifteen minus four fifty-three was sixty-eight sixty-two, which was the number in the envelope down to the last digit. He had been shorted nothing. The ground he had stood on all week, the solid arithmetic ground, had been arithmetic about the wrong thing.

He thought about Mr. Halvorsen, whom he had privately cast as the villain, a man with detractors all over town who claimed he watered down the paint and fired boys for looking at their phones. Tristan had believed them, he realized, because the story fit the number, and the number fit the story, and neither had been checked against the other. It was a profligate way to spend a certainty, handing it out to anyone who would take it, and he had been doing it all week.

"You could have said something," he told Dee, though even as he said it he heard how it sounded, like a boy who wanted the world to apologize for arithmetic.

"You could have asked," Dee said. She rang up a woman buying curtain rods and did not look at him until the receipt was torn. "Most kids don't. They just quit and tell everyone they got robbed, and then the Rennick boy gets the job and the town gets another story about Halvorsen's." She slid the stub back under the mat. "I did that my first month. Told my dad the old man was a thief. He made me sit down with the numbers."

"Was he right to?"

"He made me figure it out myself. That part was right." She straightened the pens by the register, five of them, none of which wrote. "The part where I already knew he'd say I told you so, that part I made up. I'm still not sure which part was worse, what I got wrong or how sure I was while I was getting it wrong."

Tristan picked up his envelope. He did not feel corrected so much as rearranged, as though the store had shifted its aisles overnight and he was still navigating by the old map. Somewhere between his certainty and the town's stories about the old man was a version of things he could actually verify, and it was smaller than either, and slower, and it did not come with the satisfaction of knowing whom to blame.

He walked the three blocks home in the flattening light, took the forms from his backpack, and signed every page at the kitchen table. Then, before he could lose his nerve, he did the math on what Saturday's hours would come to, the gross and the withheld part, both numbers, in pencil, so he could change them.

At the store the next morning he handed the paperwork to Mr. Halvorsen, who looked at it longer than a stack of signatures seemed to require. "Sixty-eight sixty-two," Tristan said. "Last week. It checked out." The old man grunted and filed the papers in a drawer that stuck, and Dee, restocking near the register, said, "Told you nobody robbed him."

Jasmine had worked at the bookstore for three weeks, long enough to acclimate to the smell of old paper and the till that jammed on twenties, but not long enough to stop flinching when the receipt printer spat out a line she could not account for. On Friday her paycheque landed in her account, and she opened the portal on her phone behind the poetry shelf, where Mrs. Okafor never looked. Gross pay: 640.00. Net pay: 558.13. Somewhere between those numbers, eighty-one dollars and eighty-seven cents had gone missing, and she wanted it back.

"CPP, EI, and income tax," said Devi, the other part-timer, when Jasmine showed her the stub during their break. "It's on mine too. Deductions. Everyone gets them." Devi said it the way people said rain in April, as though the withholding were weather rather than a decision, and that was the part Jasmine could not accept. Somebody had chosen those lines. Somebody had a reason.

The same afternoon, a customer with a Manchester United scarf bought a stack of gardening books and asked, watching the register, what the tax was here. "Thirteen percent, HST," Jasmine said, because that was on the placard by the till. He laughed and said he was still converting everything in his head; he'd moved in February. "Our VAT's built into the price, so your tags look cheap and then the machine adds on." She rang him up, printed the receipt, and watched the 6.24 appear beneath the 48.00, that arithmetic of addition she had never thought about until a stranger found it strange.

That night she messaged her cousin Ade, who was doing a gap year in Leeds. Ade, you know tax stuff. UK sales tax, what's the rate? The reply came as a voice note, then a photo: a Boots receipt, tiny print at the bottom. "VAT's twenty percent," Ade's message read. "Has been since the fourth of January, 2011, back when we were kids. Standard rate. It's in the shelf price, you never see it added." Jasmine read it three times. Twenty percent, hidden inside the number on the tag; thirteen percent, bolted on at the register. She thought of arbitrage, a word from her economics unit, buying cheap in one market and selling dear in another, and wondered whether the same book cost the same soul in both countries or whether one of them was quietly more expensive than it looked.

She started keeping a page in the back of her notebook. Column one: the receipt from her own shift, coffee and a muffin, 9.85 total, 1.13 of it tax. Column two: the photo of Ade's receipt. Column three: her pay stub, the 640 shrunk to 558.13. She understood, slowly, that she was comparing unlike things, like weighing fruit against fish, and that the comparison was the point. The sales tax took from her as a buyer. The deductions took from her as a worker. Both took, and both bought something, though she could not yet say what.

On Tuesday she asked Mrs. Okafor for her tax slips, the ones for filing, and Mrs. Okafor printed them from the back office without ceremony. At home, Jasmine entered the numbers into the return and watched the software work a small reversal: her income was low enough, her tuition credit large enough, that the machine declared a refund. Not all of the eighty-one dollars and eighty-seven cents, but most of it, flowing back the other way, from the government to her. She sat very still with that, feeling something tectonic shift in her picture of the world, the deductions not theft but a loan she had not agreed to, or a membership fee for a club whose meetings she had never attended.

She wrote to Ade that night, a real letter, because Ade had complained that nobody wrote letters anymore. "Here's what I figured out. The money they took isn't gone, it's just early. I file and some comes back. The sales tax is different, that one's gone for good, or at least I can't find the door it went through. Yours is higher and invisible, mine is lower and visible, and I keep changing my mind about which I'd rather. At the store I watch people flinch at the add-on and I think, at least they see it. But then I think about the shelf price being a lie, sort of, and I don't know."

The last paragraph of the letter she crossed out and rewrote twice. In the end she kept it simple: "I still don't know if it's fair. I only know how it works, mostly." She sealed the envelope, stamped it, and left it on the hall table for the morning post. Then she set an alarm for her Saturday shift, took her notebook off the desk, and added one more line to the column that had no heading yet: 558.13, in ink, underlined once.

Jake found the card on the fridge on Monday morning, tucked under the sunflower magnet where the hydro bills usually lived. It was addressed to his father, Frank Dooley, and it named a polling place at the elementary school two blocks over. His own name was nowhere on it, which meant, Jake understood with a slow tightening in his stomach, that he had never sent in the registration he'd promised himself he would send in. He had turned eighteen in March, talked all spring about voting in his first federal election, and then finals had swallowed him whole and the form had stayed folded in his backpack like an apology he kept meaning to deliver.

"You're up early," his father said from the kitchen doorway, mug in hand, still in the shirt he'd slept in.

"I'm not on the list," Jake said. "I never registered. So I guess I'm done, right? You have to be on the list before election day."

His father took a slow sip, the way he did when he was deciding whether something was worth correcting. "Where'd you hear that?"

"Everybody knows that."

"Everybody's wrong, then." His father set the mug down. "In a Canadian federal election, if you're not on the voters list, you can register at your assigned polling place on election day."

"That's it? You just show up?"

"You just show up. With ID, proof of address. Don't make that face like I just performed a miracle."

Jake went upstairs not sure whether he felt relieved or cornered. He had wanted the excuse, he could admit that much. All through the spring his father and his grandfather had been conducting their long, cheerful war at the dinner table, his father arguing that the country needed a steady hand and his grandfather, who had voted the other way since before Jake was born, arguing with equal force that a steady hand was exactly the problem. Jake had listened the way he listened to weather reports, assuming it would all be decided somewhere above him. His grandfather called him a dilettante once, half teasing, and the word had stuck in his side all summer.

At the kitchen table he spread out his ID, his health card, a bank statement with the house address, and beside them the folded flyer he'd kept from the candidate who'd come to his school in April. She was young, unproven, from his grandfather's party, and she had talked about tuition in a way that sounded like she'd actually paid some. His father's party had been around long enough that its promises had a congenital caution to them, hedged and reasonable, careful not to promise too much to anyone. Jake had spent weeks telling himself the safe choice was the mature one.

He found his grandfather in the garage, sorting nails into jars with the concentration of a man who considered this a serious occupation. "You voting today?" Jake asked.

"At my age, voting and complaining are the only exercises I get." His grandfather held up a bent nail, judged it, threw it back. "You?"

"I wasn't registered. Dad says I can do it at the polling place." He watched the old man's eyebrows climb. "Today. On election day. He says you just register there."

"Well," his grandfather said, "then you're out of excuses. That must be uncomfortable."

"It is, a little." Jake turned a jar of screws a quarter turn, then back. "Grandpa, can I ask you something? Did you ever vote for a party you didn't agree with? Because it was the safe one?"

His grandfather laughed, a short bark that surprised a wren off the windowsill. "Once. Nineteen years old, scared of wasting my vote. Wasted it anyway, didn't I? Threw it at a man I didn't believe in because I believed in him a little less than I feared the other fellow." He pushed the jar aside and looked at Jake properly. "You're asking the wrong question, though. The question isn't safe or brave. The question is which one you'll still be able to look at in ten years."

Jake walked to the school with his father at ten, the morning bright and cold for April, election signs still standing in front lawns like a crop that had come up unevenly. Inside the gymnasium, the line moved in short shuffles between the floor tape and the folding tables. When his turn came, a poll worker with reading glasses asked for his ID, made a call, and printed something off; a few minutes later Jake was taking an oath and signing a form and being pointed toward a second table, where a ballot slid across to him in a folded square of heavy paper.

The screen was a cardboard tri-fold on a chair, and behind it the pencil felt smaller than he expected. He looked at the names for a long moment. Somewhere behind him his father was waiting, patient, certain of his own choice, and Jake understood that certainty wasn't something he could borrow, not from his father, not from his grandfather, not even from the candidate with the flyer. What he had instead was smaller and harder to hold: his own reading of the whole spring, both men's arguments still loud in his head, weighed once more in the privacy of the cardboard booth. He marked the ballot, folded it along its own creases, and slid it into the box.

Outside, his father asked him nothing, which Jake understood as a kind of respect. They walked home side by side, past the signs, and when they reached the driveway his father said only, "Proud of you for going."

"I almost didn't," Jake said. "I almost let the registration thing be my way out."

"I know." His father pocketed his keys. "Your grandfather's coming for dinner. You can fight about it then."

The notification buzzed against Abigail's thigh during third period, and by lunch the group chat had fifty-one unread messages. The thread was called "senior spring" and it existed mostly for memes and complaints about the calc teacher, but today Marcus had pasted a link to a Washington Post story about a warehouse somewhere in Ohio where drivers were suing over timed bathroom breaks. He had added a single line: "thoughts?"

Abigail read the story under her desk, then read it again at the picnic table outside the cafeteria, the screen glare making her squint. The reporting was detailed, almost gentle toward the drivers, and she found herself nodding along, feeling the small satisfaction of being informed. Then Priya replied to Marcus with a shrug emoji and the words "funny how they never say the quiet part," and when Abigail asked what the quiet part was, Priya sent a screenshot of a headline from a site Abigail had never heard of, one that called the Post "a billionaire's plaything."

"Bezos owns it," Priya typed, fast, the way she typed when she was winning an argument. "Jeff Bezos. Amazon founder. He bought the Washington Post from the Graham family in 2013 for two hundred fifty million dollars." Below it she added, "so yeah, do the math on why the coverage looks like that."

Abigail did not reply right away. She looked up from her phone at the actual picnic table, at Marcus pulling the tab off a can of soda and not drinking it, at Priya across from her wearing the lanyard from the journalism workshop she'd attended in February and hadn't taken off since. Priya wanted the editor-in-chief spot on the school paper next year, wanted it so badly that she had started calling other people's reporting biased the way other people called fouls in basketball, quickly and always in her own favor.

"It's a decent story, though," Abigail said out loud, because some things felt cheaper typed. "They quoted the drivers. They got the documents."

"They quoted the drivers they could afford to quote," Priya said. "That's what owning something means. You set the edges."

Abigail thought about the edges of things, about how her mother described her grandfather's farm and the way the river used to undulate through the low field before the county rerouted it, a slow silver muscle that belonged to no one and then, after the paperwork, to someone. Ownership was like that, she supposed: invisible until it moved.

That night she sat cross-legged on her bed with her laptop open and the group chat pinging on her phone like a small rain. She looked up the purchase herself, not because she doubted Priya, but because repeating a fact felt different from holding it. Two hundred fifty million dollars. It was a strange number, small for a man of that size and large for a newspaper, and she sat with the strangeness of it while her history textbook lay open and ignored beside her. Then she found a Post story about Amazon's working conditions from a few years back, a long investigation, unsparing, and she found another one, and another. She pasted three links into the chat without commentary and watched the typing indicator appear and disappear under Priya's name, appear and disappear, like something surfacing and thinking better of it.

"Fine," Priya finally sent. "They do hard stories on Amazon sometimes. That doesn't mean the ownership doesn't matter. It means we can't tell exactly how it matters."

Abigail read that twice. It was the most honest sentence anyone had typed all day, and it came from the person who had spent all day not being honest in exactly that way. She wanted to say so, but saying so would have cost her something, so instead she typed, "Agreed on the not-telling." Marcus sent a thumbs up, then a message that said he'd been the one who found the article because his cousin drove for the company over the summer and nobody believed him about the bathroom thing, and now a newspaper believed him, or half believed him, or believed him within certain edges.

The chat quieted around eleven. Abigail lay in the dark with her phone on her chest, feeling the day settle into some apportionment she couldn't quite perform, one part of her glad to know the fact about 2013 and the money and the family that sold, one part aware that knowing it hadn't told her what to do with any given headline, one part stubbornly impervious to Priya's certainty and to her own instinct to defend the paper just because Priya had attacked it. Tomorrow there would be another link, another argument, another version of this exact night. Her phone lit once more before she set it face down: Priya had added her to a new chat called "media literacy," created nine seconds ago, with two members and no messages yet.

Maria arrived at the park an hour before anyone else, carrying a binder with a printed schedule taped inside the cover and a soccer ball under her arm. She had been made captain two weeks ago, which meant she was now responsible for things she had never thought about before, and the binder was her attempt to think about them all at once. Monday skills, Tuesday strength, Wednesday rest, Thursday the warm-up plus scrimmage, Friday rest, Saturday match. She had written rest in twice and then, doubting herself, added a question mark beside the second one.

The first person to show up was Devi, who dropped her bag in the shade and squinted at the schedule. "You put rest days on a training plan," she said. "Twice."

"That's the point," Maria said. "Rest is when you actually get stronger. If you train every day you just grind yourself down." She had read that somewhere, or several somewheres, and the more she read the more the reading enraptured her, whole evenings disappearing into forums and studies she only half understood. Her mother had started knocking on her door at eleven to ask whether she was doing homework or homework about soccer.

Devi shrugged, which was not agreement but was also not refusal, and started juggling. Maria did not press her. That was the second thing she was learning, harder than the schedule: which battles could be won by talking and which had to be won by showing up every week with the same plan until it became boring and therefore official.

The others came in ones and twos, and at quarter past five, when there were enough of them, Maria stood on the halfway line and held up the binder. "Ten minutes before we do anything," she said. "There's a warm-up. It's called the FIFA 11+. Running, some strength stuff, some jumping and landing."

Kessie, the fastest girl on the team and the most allergic to standing still, groaned audibly. "Maria, we drive forty minutes to get here. I didn't drive forty minutes to do jumping jacks."

"Then don't take my word for it." Maria had the page dog-eared, and she read it flat, the way she'd practiced in her room so it wouldn't sound like a speech. "There was a trial in Norway, in 2008. Young female players, thirteen to seventeen, who did this warm-up had about a third fewer injuries overall. A third."

Nobody said anything for a moment. A plane went over. Then Amara, who was applying tape to her ankle because she had twisted it in March and it had never fully stopped complaining, said quietly, "A third fewer."

"That's what they found," Maria said, and folded the page back into the binder, refusing to fill the silence. She had learned that too: if she kept explaining, they would argue; if she stopped, they had to decide.

It was Amara who settled it, unlacing her shoe to re-set the tape. "My ankle costs us every third game anyway," she said. "Fine. Ten minutes."

They did it badly the first time. Kessie turned the single-leg squats into a comedy routine, and someone counted the Nordic curls in a falsetto, and Maria had to start the running portion over twice because half of them had missed the cones. It took nineteen minutes, not ten, and by the end she could feel her own plan sitting in the binder like an accusation. When they finally scrimmaged, the light was already going amber at the edges of the field, and they got maybe fifteen minutes of real play before the rec-league parents started claiming the far goals.

Afterward, sitting on the grass pulling her cleats off, Maria felt something she could only call melancholic, though she would not have said the word aloud to anyone. The plan had worked. They had done the warm-up. And the cost was right there in the shortened scrimmage, the lost half hour, Kessie's face during the landing drills. Every gain she could name had a subtraction attached to it, and she had no formula for weighing one against the other. Her phylogeny notebook, borrowed from bio class, sat in the side pocket of her bag where she had stuffed it that morning, its careful branching diagrams of descent reminding her that some things you inherit and some things you build from nothing, and it is not always clear which is which.

Kessie dropped onto the grass beside her, sweating, and looked at the binder lying open between them. "Same thing Thursday?" she asked.

"Same thing Thursday," Maria said, and closed the binder, and held out her hand for Kessie to pull her up.

Edouard found the letter in the mailbox on a Tuesday, folded into a rectangle and addressed in his sister's slanted handwriting. She was two hours away at college, and she wrote the way she talked, as if she were already halfway out the door. "I failed my first bio exam," the letter said. "Not badly, but enough. I have to retake it Friday and I still don't understand how DNA becomes protein. Mom says you're studying the same thing. Explain it to me in a letter, and don't copy the textbook. Explain it like a farm." She had signed it with the doodle of a crow she'd drawn since she was nine.

The problem was that Edouard did not entirely understand it either. He had a test of his own coming, and a week of August afternoons in which the only work was hauling hay and keeping the noxious ragweed out of the soybean rows before it went to seed. His father believed in learning by hand, and when Edouard complained at supper that he couldn't make the chapter stick, his father set down his fork and said, "Then build it where you can see it. Tomorrow, after the windrow's in, use the garden."

The next afternoon Edouard stood at the end of the vegetable rows with a roll of masking tape, a marker, and his cousin Maya, who had agreed to help because he'd promised her the last of the tomatoes. The garden was a square of tilled earth with stakes at each corner, and Edouard had torn the chapter into a plan the night before, writing things down to externalize what was still a fog in his head. First, he taped a long strip of paper along the fence and wrote on it a sequence of three-letter groups, A's and C's and G's and U's, six of them in a row. "That's the messenger RNA," he said. "The copy of one gene that came off the DNA. Each group of three letters is a codon."

Maya squinted at it. "You mean each little three-letter word matches something?"

"That's what I think. Now you're the other side." He handed her a stack of index cards. On each card he had copied a three-letter group of his own invention and, beneath it, a name: Leucine, Valine, Lysine, Arginine. "Each card is a transfer RNA," he said. "Look, I wrote the amino acid at the bottom. Each one carries exactly one amino acid, and the three letters on top, that's the anticodon." Maya turned a card over, checking for some hidden second amino acid, and found only the smell of marker.

She walked the fence line reading her cards against the taped sequence, trying to match each one. At the third codon she hesitated, holding out a card whose letters didn't line up. "This one has the right amino acid but the wrong letters," she said. "Can I just put it there anyway?"

Edouard started to say yes, because it would finish the row faster, and then stopped. He crouched in the dirt and looked at the two sequences, her card and the tape, letter against letter. "No," he said slowly. "That's the whole point. The anticodon has to pair with the codon, three bases to three bases, or the amino acid doesn't go there. The match is what decides the order." He took the card back and set it aside as a mistake he'd made, a card he'd mislabeled when he copied the chart by lamplight. Maya found the right one, matched it, and laid it under the fence strip, and they went on down the line, card by card, until six amino acids sat in the dust in an order that the tape had dictated and nothing else.

"So the long strip is like the order slip at the grain elevator," Maya said, brushing soil from her knees, "and you're the truck that brings one thing at a time."

"Except the truck checks the slip itself," Edouard said. "The matching is the truck's job, not somebody else's." He was quiet for a moment, watching a cabbage white drift over the kale. He knew the chapter left things out, that he had drawn the cell as a garden fence when it was nothing like a fence, and that somewhere between the letters and the living plant there was a distance he couldn't cross yet. What he had was a shape, honest as far as it went, and he decided he could say that much without pretending further.

That night he wrote back. He described the taped strip along the fence and Maya walking the line with her cards, and he told his sister to imagine the order slip at the elevator, the trucks each carrying one amino acid, each one reading the slip by its own three letters. He wrote that he still couldn't picture how the cell keeps the whole thing from tangling, that some of it stayed dark to him, and that he'd borrowed the garden for it because their father said the mind holds what the hands have walked through. At the bottom, before the crow he'd learned to copy from her letters, he wrote, "If you fail anyway, come home and we'll build it in the dirt together. The tomatoes are almost gone."

He walked out before bed to check the tape was still stapled down against the dew. The garden was silver and still, and the row of cards lay where Maya had left them, each one in its place along the fence, spelling out their small protein into the dark.

The community kitchen on Delancey smelled like Thursday, which meant day-old bread warming in the industrial ovens and bleach from the mop bucket someone had left in the corner. Cohen had the big stainless island to himself for once, six chicken thighs laid out on a cutting board, a pot of rice waiting, his mother's spice tin open beside the sink. She was working the late shift at the hospital, his father was two states away on a job, and so dinner for him and his sister had become his job, and he had decided, walking over, that he would do it properly.

He turned the tap on cold, the way his grandmother did every Sunday of his childhood, holding each thigh under the stream while the water hissed and jumped off the pink skin.

"Stop." Priya was eleven and standing on a milk crate to reach the counter, holding his phone out to him like evidence. "Stop, stop, stop."

"What."

"Mom texted." She read off the screen instead of handing it over. "Cohen. Do NOT rinse the chicken. I know Nani always did. CDC says no. Splashing water spreads bacteria all over the sink and counters. I mean it. Use paper towel." Priya looked up. "That was nine minutes ago. She saw your story about cooking tonight."

He kept his hands under the tap a second longer, out of some stubbornness he didn't have a better name for, then shut it off. The water had gone everywhere. He could see the fine spray on the faucet, on the rim of the spice tin, on the handle of the pot.

"How would she even know I was washing it."

"Because you always do. And she always yells. You just never did it where she could see."

He stood there with wet hands and thought about his grandmother, who had cooked for forty people at the temple without ever making anyone sick, as far as anyone said, and who had held chicken under running water with the certainty of a virtuoso, wrist turning each piece at exactly the right angle, no splash escaping her. She was not a careless woman. She had raised him half the time. And now a text message was telling him she'd been doing it wrong, or at least that the government thought so, which was not the same thing, and he couldn't ask her because she had been dead since March.

"Paper towel," he said, mostly to himself. He blotted the thighs dry, one by one, and the towel came away faintly pink, and he threw it in the trash and washed his hands with soap for as long as the hot water took to arrive.

Priya watched him wipe down the whole sink, the faucet, the spice tin, the pot handle, and then wipe the counter again because he had set the towel on it in between. "You're being weird," she said.

"I'm being careful. There's a difference."

"What's the difference."

He didn't answer right away. He salted the chicken, laid it skin-down in the pan his grandmother would have recognized, a wide black skillet that had come from her kitchen and still held a shadow of turmeric in its corners. The fat began to crackle. "The difference is," he said, "she was doing the best she knew how. And now I know something different. That doesn't make her stupid and it doesn't make the CDC stupid. It just means I do it this way now."

"So you're smarter than Nani."

"Nobody's smarter than Nani." He pointed the spatula at the crate. "Get down and make the salad."

She climbed down but didn't go to the fridge. She leaned on the island with her arms folded, the way she did when she was working something out and wanted company while doing it. "If she was wrong about the chicken, what else was she wrong about?"

The rice came to a boil behind him and he turned it down, slid the lid halfway, thought about the question while the steam sublimated off the edge of the pot in a thin white ribbon and vanished. His grandmother had also believed that you should never cook angry, that lentils needed a whisper of asafetida, that a guest who left hungry would carry your bad luck home. Some of that he kept and some of it he would probably let go without ever deciding to, the way you lose things you never meant to lose.

"I don't know," he said. "Some stuff, probably. I still think her chicken was the best chicken anybody ever made."

"So how come you're not washing it."

"Because the water splashes," he said. He flipped a thigh; the skin had gone gold and friable where it hit the pan, and it came up with a crisp sound that made Priya stop sulking and look over. "Because the CDC says not to, and splashing water can spread bacteria to the sink and the counters, and I already did it, so now I get to clean everything twice. Because Mom's working a double and she still texted you about chicken, which means she's thinking about us at nine at night while somebody's vomiting in a bedpan." He heard his own voice get too loud on the last word and pulled it back. "Pick one. They're all true."

Priya went and got the lettuce. She tore it into the bowl the way their grandmother had taught her, no knife, hands only, and she didn't say anything else until the salad was done and the chicken was resting on a plate under foil and the rice had gone quiet.

At home they set the table with two plates and their mother's empty spot facing the door. Cohen texted her a picture of the pan. She replied with three thumbs-up and then, a minute later, a fourth one on its own.

"She's proud of you," Priya said, chewing.

"She's proud of chicken." He put the last thigh on his sister's plate, skin side up, where it gleamed.

"Nani would've washed it," Priya said.

"Yeah," Cohen said, and picked up his fork.

Charles set his work boots under his chair before he sat down, and his mother put the lasagna in the middle of the table without comment, which meant she had something to say and was waiting for an opening. He served himself first because his father always did, and because his father liked it when he did.

"Long shift," his father said. It was not a question.

"Nine and a half hours. We're stocking the new warehouse aisle before the Fourth sale." Charles cut into the lasagna. "Dana stayed late too. Rob left at five on the dot."

His mother passed the salad. "Are those the two you told your uncle about? The ones arguing?"

"Still arguing." Charles had described it to his uncle on the phone Sunday, and now the whole household treated it as a running story. "Dana transferred from Michigan in March. Rob's from Alabama. Dana fills out a dues card her first week, like it's nothing. Rob tells her she's crazy. Says nobody can make him pay a cent to the union if he doesn't want to."

"And can they?" his father asked. "Make him?"

"That's the fight." Charles pushed sauce around his plate. "Dana says yes, Rob says no, and the weird thing is they're both right. About themselves, I mean. Not about each other."

His father set down his fork. "How does that work?"

Charles had worked out how to explain it only on the drive home, talking to himself with the radio off, and he gave it in that order. "The union's still in. We voted it in two years ago, before I got hired. It's the local at the distribution center, everybody on the floor's under the contract. Wages, the overtime after eight hours, the breaks, all of that's in the contract. But the dues are the fight. Dana had to pay dues at her old job in Michigan, so she figures it's the same everywhere. Rob never paid dues in Alabama and figures Michigan people are suckers."

"So who's right?" his sister Ellen asked. She was fifteen and asked questions mostly to keep the table moving.

"Depends on the state." Charles had looked it up on his break, sitting on a stack of pallets with his phone, because he couldn't stand not knowing. "There's this federal law, the Taft-Hartley Act, 1947. Congress passed it over President Truman's veto. It let the states pass what they call right-to-work laws. Those ban contracts that make workers pay union fees."

"Michigan's not one of those states?" his father said.

"Michigan's not. Alabama is. So Dana's used to a contract where paying is required, and Rob's used to one where it isn't, and neither of them knows the state line is what changed." Charles took a bite. The lasagna was good and he had been hungry since four o'clock.

His mother reached for his plate and put more on it without asking. "And there," she said. "Which one is this?"

"Right-to-work." He said it plainly. "So Rob can't be forced to pay. But Dana's from a state where they can make you."

"Then why would anyone pay?" Ellen said.

"Dana says everybody benefits from the contract. The wage scale, the safety stuff, the overtime rules. Rob gets all that without paying, and he says that's the smart move. Dana calls it freeloading." Charles shrugged. "I listened to them for three days. Rob's not stupid. He's got a kid and a car payment, and fourteen dollars a month is fourteen dollars. Dana's not stupid either. She says the contract didn't fall out of the sky, that people before her paid in, and if everyone did what Rob does there'd be nothing left to freeload off of."

His father was quiet for a moment, working through it. "The breaks you get. The overtime after eight."

"I get them either way," Charles said. "That's the part that sits wrong with me, honestly. Rob and I do the same job. He keeps the extra fourteen dollars and I don't have to pay either, but if Dana's the only one paying, then she's carrying it. And if nobody pays, I don't know what happens to the contract. Nobody at the table knows."

"You could ask," his mother said.

"I did ask the steward today. He said the local's been losing checkoffs since the plant opened, people transferring in from right-to-work states who never sign. He didn't have a number. He just said it's slower than it used to be." Charles looked at his plate. He had signed nothing yet. The steward had left a card in his locker on Monday and it was still there, blank, under his jacket.

"Are you going to sign it?" Ellen asked.

"I don't know. Rob's right that the money's real. Dana's right that the contract's real. I keep going back and forth on the drive home." He picked up his fork. "Maybe I'll decide tomorrow."

His father poured more water into Charles's glass, as though filling it settled something, and the screen door banged in the kitchen where the dog had pushed through it.

The gym smelled of floor wax and hot glue, and Sadie's tri-fold board was the only one in the row with a sealed glass tube taped to it instead of a volcano or a bean sprout. The tube held a pale reddish liquid, the color of watered-down cherry juice, and beneath it she had written, in letters she'd inked twice so they wouldn't look shaky, "Predicting Equilibrium Shifts." She had rehearsed her explanation in the car until her little brother told her to stop, and now that the first judge was three booths away, her rehearsal had gone entirely out of her head.

Her problem was simpler than chemistry. Last night, when she'd heated the tube over the stove in her kitchen, the liquid had gone blue, and she had told herself it would stay blue, because blue was what heat made it, and heat was the point. But when the tube cooled on the windowsill while she answered texts, it had faded back to red, then to something in between, a bruised violet, as if the liquid were arguing with itself. She had gone to bed with the tube on her nightstand and woken at six to find it a dull, undecided pink. She had a theory now, half-formed, and a note folded in her skirt pocket to remind her of it.

The judge stopped in front of her board. He was young, maybe a grad student, with a lanyard and a coffee cup he kept switching hands. "So what does the tube do?" he asked.

"Watch," Sadie said, and unhooked it from the board. She had brought a thermos of hot water in her backpack, poured some into a beaker borrowed from the chemistry room, and lowered the sealed tube into it. While the color began to change she talked, gesturing at her data tables, her graphs of temperature against color measured with a phone app, and the judge nodded along. When the liquid had gone deep blue, she lifted the tube out with tongs and set it in a cup of ice water. They both watched.

The blue began, slowly, to give way. The judge glanced at her notebook, where she'd drawn arrows. "Which direction does it go when you heat it?" he asked. "Toward blue, obviously," she said, "but here's the part I got wrong at first. I thought heating it meant blue stays forever. It doesn't. The system was at equilibrium before I touched it, and the heat disturbs it, so the equilibrium shifts to use some of the added heat up, to partly counteract the change. That's the shift toward blue. But it only partly counteracts it. It fights the disturbance, it doesn't erase it." The judge smiled at the word "fights," and she felt her ears go hot.

"Where'd you learn that phrasing?" he asked. "Le Chatelier's principle," Sadie said, and pointed to the citation taped crooked in the corner of her board. "I found it at one in the morning." He laughed, marked something on his clipboard, said the phrase "a proper reactionary system" with what she decided was approval, that the liquid resisted change like an old uncle, and moved on down the row to a potato battery.

Between judging rounds, she sat on the bleachers and read the note in her pocket again, the one her lab partner, Priya, had left in her locker that morning because Priya's flight to her grandmother's had left at dawn. Sadie, it read, I know you wanted me there for the demo, and I'm sorry. Take the tube. If it goes wrong, remember what we argued about: you kept saying the reaction is obsolescent, that once you heat it the red is gone for good, and I kept saying no, it comes back. I think we were both half right and I don't know which half. Don't let the judge see your hands shake. Also you borrowed my ruler in September and I want it back. P.

Priya was the one who had sensitized Sadie to the idea that being wrong in a lab notebook was interesting rather than humiliating, who had written "incorrect but revealing" beside Sadie's first botched data table back in September, and Sadie had carried that phrase around like a coin ever since. But Priya's note had put the argument exactly where Sadie had left it, unresolved. The red came back when the tube cooled, yes. But it never came back all the way, never quite to the color it had been at the start, and Sadie didn't know whether that was the principle doing its work, counteracting the disturbance only partly, or whether something in her solution had changed in a way her tables couldn't see. She had two ways of thinking about it and no way to choose between them yet.

During the final round, a woman judge with gray braids asked her the question she'd been dreading: "If you heated it and kept it hot forever, what would happen?" Sadie looked at the tube, sitting now in its beaker, violet again, neither red nor blue, doing its slow arithmetic of back and forth. "It would shift blue," she said, "and it would stay blue as long as the heat stayed, because the system keeps counteracting the disturbance. But if you took the heat away, it would come back toward red. Mostly. I think mostly." The judge wrote for a long moment. "You think mostly," she repeated.

"I can't prove mostly," Sadie said. "My color app isn't precise enough and I ran out of time. It's what the data points at, and it's what the principle would say, but I haven't earned better than 'I think' yet." The judge looked up at her then, and something in her face changed, the way the liquid changed, gradually and then all at once. "Keep the tube," she said, and moved on.

They announced the awards at four o'clock, after the folding chairs had been stacked and the volcanoes drained down the hallway sinks. Sadie took second place, a ribbon and a gift card, and stood alone by her board while the gym emptied. Priya's ruler was in her backpack; she would return it Monday. She lifted the tube out of the beaker and held it up to the tall windows, where the late sun came through flat and orange, and inside the glass the color was already beginning, grain by grain, to turn.

The folding chairs in the middle school gymnasium had been arranged in crooked rows, and Layla took one near the end, where she could see both the podium and the door. She had come because of the 6:40 bus, the one that had carried her brother Tariq to his job at the greenhouse until the transit authority cut the route in March. She had a speech drafted in her notebook, three paragraphs she had rewritten four times, and a plan to read it during public comment. What she did not have was any clear idea whether a speech at a town hall could become anything more than a speech.

The state senator, Marisol Reyes, opened with a recap of House Bill 214, which would fund rural and small-town transit by redirecting a slice of the state gas tax. She walked them through it the way a jeweler turns a stone. A constituent group had drafted the bill first, she said, with help from a legislative lawyer, and a sponsor had introduced it, and the transportation committee had held hearings in April, taking testimony from riders and drivers and county engineers. The committee had amended it twice, narrowing the funding formula, before voting it out on a nine-to-four tally. Then it had gone to the House floor, where members debated it for two days, and it had passed, barely, with the speaker gaveling through the last objection. Now it was in the Senate, where a committee had just begun its own review, and nothing was guaranteed, because each chamber worked from its own copy of the same bill.

A man in the front row, saturnine in a gray windbreaker, arms crossed the whole time, said the whole thing was theater. "You pass it, the governor line-item vetoes it, we're back at nothing," he said. Senator Reyes didn't flinch. She said the governor's office had signaled cautious openness, which wasn't assent but wasn't opposition either, and that if both chambers passed identical language the bill would reach the governor's desk by June. "After that, the governor signs it, or lets it become law without a signature, or vetoes it," she said. "That's the last gate, and I won't pretend I control it."

During the comment period, a senior from Layla's school named Priya stood up with her phone in her hand. She was there for a civics project, she admitted, and she said she had spent the weekend on a question she couldn't shake. "Last year in the U.S. Senate, a bill had fifty-five supporters, and it still failed," Priya said. "Fifty-five is more than half. It's a majority. Why did it die?"

The gym went quiet in the way rooms do when nobody wants to be the one who answers. Layla felt the question land in her own head and start turning. She knew there was such a thing as a filibuster, or thought she did, mostly from a movie her father liked where a senator talked all night. But the number fifty-five nagged at her. If it took a majority to pass a bill, and a majority wasn't enough to end debate, then debate was the thing that mattered. She pulled out her notebook and wrote, debate is separate from voting, then crossed out separate and wrote, before.

Beside her, an older woman wearing a transit union pin leaned over. "Cloture," the woman said quietly, as if confirming something Layla had nearly remembered. "That's what ending debate is called."

Layla wrote the word down. Ending debate required more than passing the bill did, and she worked the arithmetic in the margin the way she did stoichiometry, converting one thing into another. Fifty-five supporters out of a hundred was fifty-five percent. To end debate you needed more than that. She tried two-thirds and got sixty-seven, which seemed too high, and then she thought about three-fifths, which was sixty percent, which was sixty votes when all hundred seats were filled. Since 1975, the woman beside her murmured, checking her pin as if it held the date, cloture had required three-fifths. Layla looked at her notebook: fifty-five for the bill, sixty to end debate, five votes short of even being allowed to finish. The bill hadn't lost on substance. It had lost on a threshold.

When her turn came, she stood with the notebook shaking slightly in her hand. Her drafted speech suddenly seemed too small, a local complaint beside a national arithmetic. She read the first paragraph anyway, about Tariq walking four miles on Sundays because the replacement shuttle didn't run weekends, about the greenhouse manager saying she'd lost two workers to the cut. Then she set the notebook down on the chair. "I used to think a bill failed because people voted no," she said. "I learned tonight it can fail because it never got to a final vote. And I think HB 214 could fail that way too, in our Senate, if we assume a majority is enough. So I'm asking what the vote count actually is, and who the swing votes are, and what riders like my brother can do besides telling their stories."

Senator Reyes said the count was fluid, that the committee chairman was a farm-district senator whose district had lost two routes of its own, and that testimony like Layla's was exactly what made a chairman's mind fluid. "You've adumbrated the fight better than my caucus memo did," she said, and a few people laughed, warmly. She asked Layla to send the written version to her office so it could go into the committee record, which was, she noted, a thing that actually existed, a binder a senator could point to.

That night Layla sat on her bed and typed a message to Priya, then deleted it twice before sending the version she meant.

You asked the question that made this whole night make sense to me. I did the math: to end debate in the U.S. Senate you need three-fifths of senators, which is 60 votes when all 100 seats are filled, and since 1975 that's been the rule. That's why 55 supporters wasn't enough, five votes short of even getting to a final vote. I used to think majority rules, period. Now I think majority rules sometimes, and other times you need a supermajority just to move. What I still don't know is whether that's a flaw or a feature, honestly, and I'm not going to pretend I settled it in a gymnasium. Come to the Senate committee hearing with me in May? We can count votes in person.

She attached the speech, addressed an email to the senator's office, and pressed send. Down the hall, Tariq's alarm went off for the early shift, and Layla heard him feel along the wall for the light switch.

Gavin crouched on the oil-stained concrete of his uncle's garage, holding a stopwatch he had won at a yard sale and did not entirely trust. The ball launcher, built from PVC pipe and a garage-door spring, pointed at the far wall, where he had taped a measuring tape along the baseboard.

"We need thirty feet by Saturday," Priya said from the workbench, where she was stripping wire with her teeth because the pliers had vanished two weeks ago and neither of them would admit to losing them. "Marcus's team hit twenty-eight on Monday."

"Then we angle it higher." Gavin cranked the barrel up to sixty degrees. "More height, more hang time, more distance."

"That's not how it works."

"It's how it feels like it works."

She came over and stood beside him with her arms crossed, radiating the particular patience of someone who had already done the reading. He fired anyway. The ball climbed, hung, and dropped eleven feet short of his last attempt. The garage smelled like rubber and cold coffee, and somewhere behind the water heater a cricket had been living rent-free since August.

"Congratulations," Priya said. "You've incapacitated your own launcher. It can only go up now. You've turned artillery into a fountain."

He lowered the barrel in increments, firing after each change, and the numbers on the tape told a story his intuition had refused to write. At sixty degrees the ball landed at nineteen feet. At fifty-five, twenty-two. At fifty, twenty-five and change. He kept going, expecting the pattern to collapse, and at forty-five degrees the ball sailed past all its predecessors and bounced off the far wall with a sound like a knuckle on a door. Twenty-nine feet, and that was with the wall in the way.

"Forty-five," he said, mostly to himself.

"Forty-five," she agreed, and wrote it on the back of her hand. "On level ground. Which the gym floor will be, thank God, because if Mr. Okafor made us launch off the bleachers I'd transfer schools."

Gavin sat back on his heels and looked at the tape measure, then at the barrel, then at the notebook where he'd been scribbling. The physics textbook was open on the workbench to a page he'd read four times, the one about splitting a launch into horizontal and vertical components, treating each as its own little problem. He'd understood the words separately the way you can know every ingredient of a cake and still burn it. Now the tape measure had done something the page hadn't. The ball's speed got divided between going far and going high, and every degree past forty-five bought height it paid for out of distance, while every degree below bought speed it paid for out of flight time. Forty-five was the split where neither account was robbed.

"It's not that complicated," Priya said, watching his face. "You're making the face you make when you think you've discovered fire."

"I'm making the face of a putative genius who has just learned he's three hundred and seventy years late." He tapped the textbook. "It was in the assigned reading. I read it. It didn't take."

"So the lesson is do the homework."

"The lesson is fire the homework and measure everything." He stood, brushed concrete dust off his knees, and reset the angle to forty-five exactly, checking it twice against the protractor taped to the hinge. "Saturday we launch at forty-five and we win."

Priya didn't answer right away. She was looking at the garage door, which stood open a hand's width to the October air, and beyond it the driveway where a breeze had just skittered a dry leaf across the chalk mark he used for alignment. "That's outside," she said.

"What's outside?"

"The air. The contest is in the parking lot. All this is clean numbers, no air resistance, perfectly flat ground, the world as physics wishes it were." She shrugged. "There'll be wind."

Gavin looked at his beautiful forty-five degrees, then at the leaf, which had already reached the gutter. He thought about arguing that the breeze was nothing, that twenty-nine feet of margin didn't care about a leaf, and he thought about the sixty-degree shot that had felt so right and landed so wrong. He picked up the notebook instead.

"Then we test outside," he said. "Right now. You hold the tape."

He hauled the launcher to the driveway by himself, wheels squealing, and pointed it down the long flat stretch of cul-de-sac where, he was almost certain, the ground was level and the wind, for the moment, was holding its breath. "Mark where it lands," he called, and pulled the trigger.

The menorah stood on the sideboard between the kugel and a platter of rugelach, and Alex's grandmother had handed him the matches before he could invent an excuse. Four nights already, and every night an uncle or a cousin had supervised the lighting, but tonight the aunts were arguing about the brisket and his father was showing someone a video on his phone, and the silver candelabrum was just waiting there, winking under the dining room light.

He had agreed to it in August, in the parking lot of the community college, when his roommate-to-be, Dev, asked if he was "religious" and Alex had said "not really, cultural, I guess," and then spent the whole drive home wondering what he had meant. His grandmother's Hebrew was better than his. His father's was worse. Somewhere between them was Alex, holding matches and trying to remember which candles went where.

He set the box down and counted the branches of the menorah with his eyes. Nine. Eight in a row, all the same height, and one standing apart, a little taller, set off to the side or raised above the rest. Four nights, he thought. So four candles, but he had a handful of them out of the box already and had lost track of how many he'd actually set in the holders, because his little cousin Rosie had been counting out loud along with him and then had started counting the rugelach instead.

"Five," Rosie announced from the table, mouth full.

"Four," Alex said. "It's the fourth night."

"Five rugelach."

He looked at the menorah. One of the holders had a candle in it, and he couldn't remember putting it there, or whether Rosie had reached up while he was answering a question about his major. If he lit five tonight, his grandmother would notice tomorrow, and his uncle Izzy would make it a joke at the table, the way he made everything a joke, and Alex would smile and feel like a fraud in his own grandmother's dining room.

His grandmother drifted over, drying her hands on a dish towel. She didn't say anything. She watched him count the branches again, tapping the air above each one with a knuckle, like a pianist finding middle C.

"That one," she said at last, nodding at the taller candle, the one set apart. "That's the shamash, the helper."

"The helper," Alex repeated. He'd heard the word his whole life, in songs, in his grandfather's gravelly transliteration, and never once thought about it.
