He took the extra candle out of the holder and set it in the shamash's place instead, and suddenly the arithmetic was simple: four for the four nights, one helper to light them, five flames in total once it was done, and all eight standing in a straight line waiting for the nights still to come. The ninth candle wasn't part of the count at all. It was how you counted.

He struck the match. The room smelled of onion and burnt sulfur and his aunt's perfume, and under that, faintly, the furniture polish his grandmother used to burnish the sideboard every Friday, rubbing the dark wood until it gave back the light of the chandelier. He lit the shamash, and the shamash lit the others, right to left, the way his grandfather had done it, though Alex only knew the direction because Dev had asked him once and he'd had to look it up, embarrassed, at one in the morning.

They sang. Alex knew maybe sixty percent of the words and mouthed the rest, and Rosie banged her spoon, and his uncle's voice slid a third below everyone else's in a way that should have been ugly and somehow wasn't, a consonance Alex felt in his sternum more than heard. His grandmother watched the flames with her hands folded, and when the song ended she didn't say good singing or well done. She said, "Your grandfather did it exactly like that. Sloppy on the words."

Later, at the table, Uncle Izzy piled a second helping of everything onto Alex's plate with an epicurean seriousness, as though the brisket were a matter of principle, and asked him what he was going to study. Undeclared, Alex said, and waited for the joke. Izzy just nodded and said that was honest, that most people lied and picked something.

Alex thought about the helper candle on the way out to the car, holding the tin of leftovers his grandmother had pressed on him. He still couldn't read Hebrew. He still wasn't sure what he believed, or whether Dev's question had a real answer, or whether cultural and religious were two different things or one thing badly divided. But he could count the branches now, and he knew which candle did the lighting, and tomorrow night there would be five in the row and one apart, and he wanted to be the one to set them.

"Next year you do all eight," his grandmother called from the porch.

"Nine," Alex said, and got in the car smiling.

The map had been folded so many times that the creases had gone soft, and Oliver smoothed it across his knees inside the tent, tracing the border of a country he had chosen at random for his geography assignment. His sister Maya leaned over his shoulder, eating a strip of dried apricot, letting the crumbs fall onto the population pyramid printed in the corner of the page. Their father snored in the far corner of the tent, and outside, an early fog was rolling up from the lake, so diaphanous that the pines showed through it like pencil lines half erased.

"Japan," Maya read. "Why Japan?"

"Because it's the example everyone uses," Oliver said. "Narrow at the bottom, wide at the top. The assignment says we have to look at the shape and predict what the country will need to build in thirty years. Schools or nursing homes." He turned the map so the pyramid faced her. Two stacked columns of bars, male on the left, female on the right, thinning out at the base like a candle burning down from the top.

Maya tapped the wide bands near the middle. "All these people in their fifties. In thirty years they'll be the old ones."

"Right. So nursing homes, obviously. But then you have to say whether the population keeps falling, and that part I keep getting wrong." He pulled out his notebook, where he had written a sentence and crossed it out twice. "I wrote that if every family has two children, the population stays the same. Two parents, two kids. Mrs. Ferrante marked it with a question mark and wrote, see me."

The rain began then, a light needling sound on the nylon above them, and Maya reached up to press her palm against a spot where the fabric had gone taut and dark. "Maybe the question mark is the whole point," she said. "Maybe two isn't enough."

"Two has to be enough. It's arithmetic." He said it with more certainty than he felt, because the question mark had been sitting in his stomach for three days, and because the fog outside was thickening and the flashlight was already dimming and he had promised himself he would finish the draft tonight, here, in the tent, where there was nothing else to do and nothing else to want.

Maya unzipped the door flap a few inches and they watched the rain move across the lake in gray sheets. "You know what Priya's mom said at dinner?" she said. "She said our country's birth rate is falling and everybody's arguing about it. Her aunt thinks it's a catastrophe. Her cousin thinks it's a blessing." Then she turned back to him. "Do the assignment properly and you get to have an oratory about it at the dinner table. You love that."

"I don't do oratory," Oliver said, though he had, once, at their grandfather's birthday, a speech about rivers that had apparently beguiled the whole table, or at least made their aunt cry, which he had not intended. He looked back at the pyramid. The bars at the bottom of Japan's chart were shorter than the ones above them, which he had noticed before but never thought through. If each pair of adults truly replaced themselves, the base should match the middle, bar for bar, and it didn't. "Okay," he said slowly. "Wait."

He took out his pencil and wrote: in countries with low death rates, a total fertility rate of about 2.1 children per woman is needed to replace the population without migration. He had found the number buried in a footnote of his textbook and copied it without understanding it, and now, looking at the bars, he circled it. "It's not two," he said. "The book says it's about 2.1 per woman, with low death rates, if there's no migration. So two children per family is close but it isn't enough. I wasn't wrong that it's arithmetic. I was wrong about the number."

Maya frowned. "Two point one. So a country where everyone has exactly two kids still shrinks?"

"Slowly, without migration, yeah. That's what replacement means." He wrote it again in the draft, cleanly this time, and then sat looking at what he had, because a strange thing had happened: the fact had not settled the assignment, it had complicated it. The pyramid still told him nursing homes. But whether the bottom kept narrowing, whether Japan needed schools too, depended on numbers that hadn't happened yet, on choices no graph could show him. He could argue either side. He would have to pick one and admit the rest.

"Here's the twist," Maya said, and her voice changed, went careful. "I looked it up too. Our country is already below that number. Both of them are. So your whole generation, you're the narrow bars." She let that sit while the rain thickened and their father went on snoring and the flashlight guttered out completely, leaving them with the gray light through the wet fabric. Oliver put his pencil down. He folded the map along its soft old creases, once, twice, and put it under the sleeping bag where it would stay dry.

"So what do I write?" he said.

Maya zipped the flap shut against the weather and said, "Start with the bars. Then tell them what you can't know."

The essay was due Thursday, and by Tuesday night Dominic still could not decide whose fault the Cold War was. Mr. Okonkwo had assigned it as a duel: read Gaddis, who leaned toward Soviet paranoia and an autocrat named Stalin refusing to loosen his grip, then read a revisionist who ascribed the whole spiral to American economic ambition, and then weigh both against the documents in the packet. Weigh, Mr. Okonkwo kept saying, as if evidence were something you could hold in two hands.

Dominic spread the packet across his grandfather's dining table, because his own desk was buried under laundry and his grandfather's house was quiet in the afternoons. Grandpa Ray had served in Korea, or near Korea, the story changed depending on the year, and he had opinions. He set down a mug of tea hard enough to slosh the documents.

"You're doing the Cold War," he said. It was not a question.

"For history. I have to compare two historians."

"Which start did they give you? The bomb, or the traitors in the State Department?"

"Neither, actually." Dominic slid a page toward him, the one he had flagged with a torn Post-it. "There's this. A speech from March 1947. The Truman Doctrine. It pledged American support for countries resisting communist pressure, and the first aid went to Greece and Turkey."

Grandpa Ray put on his glasses, which hung from a chain, and read. "I remember my father talking about that. Nobody called it a doctrine at the kitchen table. They called it four hundred million dollars to keep Greece out of Moscow's pocket."

"The packet doesn't give a number," Dominic said. "It just says the aid started with Greece and Turkey."

"Then your packet's smarter than most. Numbers start arguments." He tapped the page. "This is where it began, if you ask me. Before that we were a country, after that we were a cause."

Dominic wrote that down before he could decide whether he agreed with it. That was the problem with Grandpa Ray: he was a primary source and a biased one, all at once, and Dominic had no training for interviewing your own grandfather. The revisionist historian, if he sat at this table, would probably say Truman invented a communist threat to justify markets and the Marshall Plan that followed. Gaddis would say the pressure on Greece was real enough, a civil war with communists on one side, and that Stalin was an autocrat who trusted nobody and expected the same in return. The document just sat there between them, plain as a grocery list.

He built the timeline on butcher paper, because Grandpa Ray insisted timelines belonged on paper you could unroll across a table. February 1946, Kennan's Long Telegram from Moscow, warning that the Soviet Union was expansionist at some atavistic level, hostile by instinct. March 1947, the Truman Doctrine, the pledge, Greece and Turkey. Then everything after. He stood over it with two colors of marker, blue for what supported Gaddis, orange for what supported the revisionist, and found that most events got both colors, which felt like cheating until he realized it might be the honest answer.

"The telegram's the start," Grandpa Ray said over his shoulder. "You don't announce a doctrine without somebody telling you there's something to be doctrinal about."

"But the telegram was secret," Dominic said. "Nobody outside the State Department read it in 1946. The doctrine was public. It's when the country actually chose a side."

"You're telling me the start of the Cold War is when Washington made a speech?"

"I'm telling you the start is when the policy got a name." Dominic drew a hard blue line under March 1947 and then, feeling the grandness of it, an orange question mark beside the line, because he could not prove the line was right, only that the evidence pulled toward it while the revisionist pulled toward money and markets and Gaddis toward fear, and Dominic's considered position was a line with a question mark on it.

Thursday morning he turned it in, seven paragraphs and a photocopied slice of butcher paper. Mr. Okonkwo returned the essays Monday with a single comment at the bottom: "Good weighing. But you never once mention that your grandfather's account and Gaddas overlap almost exactly. Whose voice were you arguing against, exactly?"

Dominic read it three times, then took out his phone to call Grandpa Ray, who answered on the first ring.

"So did I win the argument?" his grandfather asked.

Florence had claimed the carrel by the west window because the afternoon light fell across its desk in a long, honest stripe, and she wanted honesty somewhere in her afternoon even if it was only sunlight. In front of her lay the photocopied story, her pencil, and the assignment sheet on which Mr. Okonkwo had written a single question: How does point of view shape what we trust? She had read "The Tell-Tale Heart" twice already, and twice she had come away with the same unsettled feeling, as though the story had handed her a coin that was faceless on both sides.

She underlined the opening line, the narrator's insistence that he was not mad, and then the details that followed: the old man's eye, the nightly watching, the murder itself, described with terrible calm. Her first instinct had been to take the confession at face value, that the facts were true and only the self-assessment was false. But that felt too easy, the kind of tidy answer a person reaches for when they want to be finished by dinner.

"You're doing the Poe thing too?" A boy she knew slightly, Dara, from her seminar, set his bag down on the edge of her table without quite asking. "Sorry. Every other seat's taken. There's a class in periodicals."

"It's fine," Florence said, and meant it, though she angled her paper slightly, an old habit, preempting the possibility that he would read her half-formed notes and mistake them for her conclusions.

He flipped open his own copy. "You know what got me? He keeps saying he's sane. Over and over. That's the thing that made me doubt him." He tapped the page. "If he'd just told the story straight, I might have believed the parts about the eye and the old man. The protests are what undo him."

Florence looked at her own underlining, the very line she had marked, and felt the small vertigo of someone arriving at a door just as another person opens it from the other side. "So the denials aren't decoration," she said slowly. "They're evidence. The way he tells it is the confession." She wrote in the margin: the form of the telling is the content, then scratched out the second half because it sounded like something borrowed rather than found.

Her eye drifted to the margins of the library's own copy of the anthology, which she had pulled as a second source. Someone had annotated it in green ink, small and confident: notes about the eye as symbol, about guilt, about the heartbeat. The handwriting looked like a girl's from a graduating class some years back. Florence had been reading those notes alongside the story for an hour without quite admitting she was doing it, weighing the stranger's certainty against her own doubt, and preferring the stranger's, which was the problem.

"That's not mine," Dara said, noticing.

"I know. It was in the stacks." She hesitated, then pulled the anthology toward the middle of the table. "Look at this note. Right here by the ending. She writes that the heartbeat is definitely the narrator's own guilt, no other reading possible. Definitely." Florence heard herself say the word and felt it snag. "But how would she know? How would anyone? We only have his account. That's the whole trap of the story. There's no outside view to check him against."

Dara leaned in. "So you're saying the annotator's like him."

"I'm saying she sounds like him," Florence said. "Absolutely certain about something she can't verify. And I was trusting her because the certainty looked like expertise." She thought of herself at fourteen, defending a friend who had lied to her, marshalling every scrap of counter-evidence because the alternative was admitting she'd been played. Recidivism was a word from a documentary she'd watched with her father about parole hearings; the offenders there explained their relapses the way she had explained her trusting: as if it had happened to them, as if there were no choice at any point along the way. She had not thought of that in years, and she did not like thinking of it now, in a library, with a green-ink stranger as the occasion.

"So what's your answer going to be?" Dara asked. "For Okonkwo. If you can't trust the narrator and you can't distrust him completely."

"I don't know yet. Something like: the story makes you a juror with no witnesses, only the defendant, and the defendant is charming." She reread her scratched-out margin note and let it stay scratched out, the crossed words visible, a record of a position she had outgrown in the space of an hour. She would write the essay from the uncertainty itself rather than around it, though she could not yet see the shape of the opening sentence.

Dara stood to leave as the light shifted, the long stripe sliding off her desk onto the floor, taking its borrowed honesty with it. Before he went he nodded at the anthology. "Green ink's in half the Poe copies in here, did you know? Been circulating for years."

Florence turned back the pages and found, on the inside cover, a name in the same green ink, and beneath it a line she had missed: a small, neat claim that the notes were copied, in turn, from an older edition, whose annotator the writer had never identified. She sat very still with her hand flat on the open page, the afternoon emptying out around her, the old man's heartbeat waiting patiently in the paragraph she had stopped on.

Luca had told his grandmother he would lead the Seder this year, and she had looked at him the way she looked at weather she didn't trust, which was to say without any change in her face at all. The family was gathering at Aunt Rena's house, thirteen people counting the twins, and the job had always belonged to Grandpa Sam, who had died in February. Nobody else wanted it. His Uncle David said the words too fast to mean anything, and his mother claimed she only knew the Italian half of the family's habits, which Luca suspected was a lie of convenience. So it was Luca, seventeen, standing in Rena's kitchen on the afternoon before the holiday, holding a photocopied Haggadah that had been Grandpa Sam's, its margins full of handwriting he could barely read.

The trouble had started two weeks earlier, when Rena asked him to book the community hall for the family dinner, since her dining room sat eight and they were now thirteen. He had looked up the date of the first Seder on his phone, seen April 22nd, and booked the hall for the evening of the 22nd. He was proud of the booking. He had even made a little spreadsheet. Then Mrs. Adler from the synagogue office had called him back, and her voice had that gentle pity in it that he hated more than scolding.

"You booked it for tomorrow night, sweetheart," she said. "The 22nd starts at sundown tonight."

Luca stood in the hallway holding the phone, and his cousin Theo, sprawled on the couch behind him, asked what was wrong. Luca said nothing at first, because he was doing the arithmetic in his head and finding it strange. A day that begins at sundown. Not at midnight, not at dawn, but at the moment the sky gives up. He had sat through seventeen years of Seders and somehow never once noticed that they all happened at night, that the holiday arrived in the dark like something arriving by boat.

"The whole day starts in the evening," he said to Theo, half a question. "So tonight is already the 22nd. The whole thing."

"Theo shrugged. "Grandpa Sam always said sundown. I figured it was a Grandpa Sam thing."

The hall was saved; Mrs. Adler moved the booking, and Rena's dining room question dissolved when three cousins caught flu and the number dropped back to nine. But Luca kept the fact in his head all through the afternoon like a coin he kept turning over. He had been so certain of the spreadsheet. He thought about all the other things he had been certain of, the time in ninth grade he had told his history class that his grandfather's stories about the old neighborhood were probably exaggerated, and how Sam had found out, and had never mentioned it, which was worse than mentioning it. Luca had wanted to apologize for that for three years and had never managed it. Maybe, he thought, reading the Haggadah out loud tonight was a way of doing it sideways.

At the table, the candles were lit and his mother touched his arm and said, "Whenever you're ready," and the room went quiet in a way rooms only do for family. Luca began. His voice cracked once on the first blessing and nobody smiled, or everybody was kind enough to pretend not to. He read the four questions with the twins, who had rehearsed in the car and still hiccuped with nerves. He did Grandpa Sam's trick of spilling a drop of wine for each plague, and he found Sam's handwriting in the margin at that exact point, a note that said "slower here" in cramped ballpoint, and Luca slowed, and the twins watched the drops fall with real attention, and something in the room settled.

Uncle David, who had spent the whole ride over complaining that nobody needed a three-hour dinner, asked a question about the middle of the story, an actual question, and Luca answered it by reading Sam's marginal notes almost word for word. He didn't say whose words they were. Later he wondered whether that was theft or inheritance, and couldn't decide, and suspected the difference was smaller than either. Aunt Rena leaned over at one point and murmured that his grandfather would have been beguiled by the whole performance, and Luca didn't know if she meant charmed or fooled, and Rena was the kind of aunt who might have meant both.

The youngest twin, Rosie, asked why they were still eating when it was so late and it wasn't even the holiday yet according to her phone, which said April 22nd began at midnight. Luca opened his mouth and closed it. "For us it's already tomorrow," he said. "It started at sundown." She considered this with the seriousness of an eight-year-old judge, then asked if that meant she could open her birthday presents a day early, since her birthday worked the same way, and the table laughed, and Luca said, honestly, that he didn't know the rules for birthdays.

He thought, while pouring the last cup of wine, about how he had almost done the whole thing on the wrong evening, in a rented hall, on a night that belonged to no one, with everyone fed and satisfied and utterly misplaced in time. He thought about how certainty had felt exactly like knowledge from the inside. He didn't say any of this. He said the closing lines, and his voice held, and his mother's eyes were wet, and Uncle David applauded alone and then looked around defantly, like a man deciding whether to be embarrassed.

Afterward, in the kitchen, rinsing the Kiddush cups, Luca found a page of the photocopied Haggadah he had somehow skipped. It was the section welcoming the stranger, the one about letting all who are hungry come and eat, and Sam had written nothing in that margin at all. Luca stood with the wet page in his hand and thought about his grandfather, destitute of nothing by the end, generous with everything, and about the apology still unsaid, and about whether a ceremony led in a dead man's handwriting counted as a conversation with him or just a very good imitation of one.

Rosie appeared in the doorway in her pajamas. "Is tomorrow still tomorrow when we wake up?" she asked.

"Go to sleep, Rosie," Luca said, and turned off the tap.

The computer lab smelled like floor wax and warm monitors, and the clock over the door read 3:41, which meant Madison had nineteen minutes before the late bus. Her screen held the skeleton of a BankAccount class, the assignment printed beside the keyboard: private fields, getter methods, a test class that proves your object works. She had typed the fields first, because they were easy. Private double balance. Private String owner. Then the constructor, or what she believed was a constructor, a line that read public void BankAccount(double startBalance) with a set of curly braces below it like empty hands waiting for something.

Her test class compiled on the first try, which should have felt like victory and instead felt like the specific silence of a machine that has agreed to nothing. She ran it. The output read 0.0. She had told the constructor, or the thing she had called a constructor, to set balance to startBalance, and she had passed in 250.00 when she created the account in main. The account held nothing. Zero, the shape of a thing never touched.

"Noah," she said, two seats over. He didn't look up. She said it again.

"What."

"It prints zero. I gave it two fifty and it prints zero."

"Balance is private," he said. "You using the getter?"

"Of course I'm using the getter."

He rolled his chair over anyway, the casters catching on the carpet tile, and leaned in. She watched his eyes track down her code the way he read everything, fast, linear, no backtracking. He stopped at her constructor line. He put one finger on the screen, just below the word void.

"There's your problem," he said. "That's not a constructor."

"It's named BankAccount. Same as the class. That's the rule, isn't it?"

"A Java constructor has the same name as its class and no return type," Noah said. "Not even void."

Madison stared at the word void like it had lied to her personally. All semester she had trusted void. It meant this method returns nothing, and a constructor returned nothing, so the logic had seemed airtight, and now the airtight part was the problem. The machine had read her method as a method, some ordinary function that happened to share a name with the class, and had never called it at all. Java had gone on constructing her object its own quiet way, with zero in the balance field, without telling her. It hadn't failed. It had simply ignored her.

From his seat, Noah could see her recalibrate in real time, the way she always did, her mouth firming before her hands moved. She deleted void. She ran the test again. The output read 250.0. She sat back, and he understood the particular relief in her shoulders, because he had hit the same wall in October, on a Student class, and had spent forty minutes blaming the getter before he found the five letters ruining everything. There was something almost funny about it, how the smallest words carried the most weight. He watched her add a second test, a deposit method, a check that would refuse a withdrawal past zero, and he thought about the way she wrote guard clauses, no-nonsense, the same way she argued in seminar.

"Why refuse the withdrawal?" he asked. "Real banks let you overdraft."

"Mine doesn't." She kept typing. "My bank, my rules."

"That's a visceral position on insolvency."

"It's clean. You either have the money or you don't." She stopped, fingers hovering. "Though my mom's card got declined at the grocery store last month, and the cashier just stood there holding the milk. Clean rules don't feel clean from that side."

Noah didn't answer, and Madison was glad, because she hadn't finished thinking it. The class on her screen enforced one version of the world, overdrafts impossible, balances never below zero, and she had built it in ten minutes and believed it in eleven. The store version took longer. She added a comment above her guard clause, the words not appearing in any required output but mattering to her anyway, a note that said only: reconsider after talking to Mom.

The clock read 4:02. The late bus was gone; she would be walking, or calling her mother, whose own account was the thin kind, and whose reaction to a declined card was not something a private field could protect. She saved the file, then saved it again to the flash drive in her backpack, because the school network ate projects the way her family's budget ate surprises. At the door she paused, looking back at the lab, the rows of dark screens, her own still lit with the 250.0 glowing in the console like a small proof that she could build a thing and make it true.

"Coming?" Noah asked, already holding the door.

"In a second." She walked back, opened her test file, and changed the withdrawal amount in her second test, the one that should fail, from 300.00 to 250.01, one cent past everything the account had. She ran it. The method refused, exactly as designed. "Okay," she said, and logged off.

Kate had told everyone at dinner that calculus was going fine, which was true the way a map of a country at war is true. The borders were drawn. The interior was unknown. She sat at the kitchen table with the textbook open to the chapter on integration, a sharpened pencil, and a glass of water she kept forgetting to drink, while her brother Danny, fourteen and unbearably awake for a Sunday evening, dropped into the chair across from her.

"What's that squiggle," he said, pointing at the long slender curve before the x squared.

"That's the integral sign," Kate said. "It's an elongated letter s." Danny looked blank, so she went on, the way she did when she half knew something, which was most of the time lately. "Leibniz introduced it in 1675. He thought of an integral as an infinite sum. That's why it's a stretched s, for sum." Danny nodded slowly, the way people nod at weather.

"And the squiggle does what?"

"It finds the area under a curve." She tapped the graph in the book, the shaded sliver trapped between the parabola and the x-axis. "The area under this curve, from here to here." Danny frowned at it, then at her, then said the thing that undid the whole evening: "How can adding up infinity give you a normal number?"

She should have said she didn't know. Instead she said something about limits that she could not finish, and Danny, who was not cruel but was fourteen, said, "You don't know either," and got up to find a banana. Kate sat with the shaded region and felt the old familiar heat in her face, the one she'd carried out of every math classroom since seventh grade, when Mr. Ruiz had called her method "creative" in front of thirty people and the word had stuck to her like a burr. She had spent years maligning the subject, calling it a sorting machine, calling teachers charlatans with answer keys, and the strange thing was that the insults had never once helped her solve anything.

From the doorway, Danny watched his sister bend over her book and felt a complicated pity he would not have been able to name. He knew she'd told their mother she was "basically tutoring herself," which was maybe true in the way his own claim of having "basically" cleaned his room was true. He also knew that last week he had heard her on the phone with Priya saying she might drop to regular math, and that she'd said it lightly, the way you say a thing you have already decided. He ate his banana and thought that Kate was the smartest person he knew who was also, somehow, the most frightened, and that these two facts lived in her at the same time without either one winning.

She waved him back over, which surprised them both. "Sit. Help me think." He sat. She drew a rectangle under the curve, then another, then a stack of thin slices, each one narrow, each one easy, the area of a rectangle being nothing but base times height. "Leibniz thought of it as an infinite sum," she said again, and this time she heard it. "Like if you cut the area into slices this thin, and thinner, and you never stop cutting, the little errors just vanish." She was not sure that was exactly right. She wrote it anyway. Danny leaned in and said, "So the squiggle is a stretched s because it means sum," and she said yes, and drew the sign long and elegant down the margin of her paper, over and over, until it looked less like a squiggle and more like a letter she was learning to write.

Here is what Kate would tell you afterward: that she sat down that night already understanding integration, and that the evening was ancillary, a pleasant review, and that Danny's questions merely sharpened what was there. The paper tells a different story. The paper shows crossed-out attempts, a torn corner, and then, near midnight, a worked integral with the area under x squared from zero to three computed correctly, the answer circled twice, and beneath it in small handwriting: still not sure why the errors vanish. She left that line in. She could have erased it, and in her retelling of the evening she did erase it, but the paper kept it, honest where she was not, and in the morning Danny found the page and read the circled answer and the small confession underneath.

He carried it to the kitchen where she was eating cereal, and set it down beside her bowl. "You got it," he said.

"I got it," she said. Then, quieter, looking at the small line of doubt in her own handwriting: "Most of it. I still don't know why it works, only that it does."

"That's basically everything," Danny said, and stole the last of her milk.

Justin had been borrowing Mrs. Okonkwo's cello for three weeks, and every Tuesday the A string went flat on him as if it had opinions. He tightened the peg, plucked the string, and watched the clip-on tuner blink red. He wanted, more than he could reasonably explain to anyone at school, to play the Bach minuet his grandfather used to hum while fixing things in the garage, and he wanted it before winter, though nobody had set that deadline but him.

"The A is still low," Mrs. Okonkwo said from the kitchen doorway, holding two mugs. She had the insouciant habit of delivering corrections as if they were weather reports, which made them easier to hear and somehow harder to fix. "But your bow arm is better. You've stopped strangling the frog."

"That sounds like a compliment with a crime in it."

"Drink your tea and tune."

He plucked the A again and the tuner settled at 437, its needle sulking left of center. He eased the peg up until the screen flashed 440 and green. Then, because he was sixteen and curious and Mrs. Okonkwo had gone back to the kettle, he slid his first finger down the string and played the A an octave higher, just to hear it ring.

The tuner read 880.

He stared at it. He plucked the low A, then the high A, then the low again, like a magician checking his own trick. The numbers doubled, exactly, every time. He said it out loud, quietly, because saying things out loud made them real: "A note one octave higher vibrates at exactly twice its frequency." He looked toward the kitchen to see whether anyone would catch him talking to a tuner, but the kettle was shrieking and Mrs. Okonkwo was arguing with it in Igbo.

When she came back, he showed her. "Watch. Low A, 440. High A, 880. The octave is just... double."

She set the mugs down and watched the screen, and something in her face shifted from teacher to player, which he had learned was the better of her two faces. "You found that yourself?"

"The tuner told on the string. I just listened."

For a second he thought she would launch into one of her lectures, the kind his father called "the professor voice," but instead she picked up her own cello and played the two As herself, slow, the low one humming under his collarbone and the high one arriving like a smaller, brighter version of the same voice. Same note, doubled. He heard it differently now that he knew the arithmetic underneath, and that bothered him a little, the way knowing a magic trick's mechanism can bother you.

Here was the problem he chewed on all through the C major scale she made him play twice: his grandfather, who had been dead since Justin was eleven, had hummed that minuet without knowing a single number. To him the octave had been a feeling, a place in the air you could reach. Justin had the tuner and the doubling and the green blinking light, and he had the feeling too, sometimes, late at night, when the string rang and something in his chest rang after it. He was not sure the two ways of knowing could live in the same person, or whether one of them made the other smaller. His friend Dez, an ideologue about analog everything, had told him last week that tuners "kill music," and Justin had defended the tuner without quite believing his own defense.

"Mrs. Okonkwo," he said, setting the bow down. "Did you know about the doubling when you started?"

"Of course. Conservatory makes you memorize frequencies like a drill sergeant."

"Does knowing it ever ruin it?"

She sipped her tea and let the question sit there, and he could see her deciding against an easy answer, the shadows of three different lectures seeming to adumbrate behind her eyes before she chose none of them. "I forget it when I play," she said. "I remember it when I teach. You'll find your own arrangement." Then she tapped the minuet book on the stand. "Again. From the third measure, and this time let the octave at the end open up. Don't press it. Just double it."

He set his fingers, drew the bow, and the low A hummed out at 440, and when he reached up for the octave, he didn't look at the tuner at all.

Hudson had never once been wrong about a number, which was the kind of thing he told people at parties, or would have, if he went to parties. Instead he told Priya Nair, third row, business class, Tuesday morning, that the GST on her calculator receipt was seven percent. He knew this the way he knew his own birthday. The GST, he said, had been seven percent since it started, and anyone who thought otherwise was confusing it with something provincial.

Priya held up the receipt. She had bought a coffee and a muffin at the place across from the school, and the tax line read something smaller than seven percent of the total. She did not say anything. She just turned the paper toward him and let the number sit there in the fluorescent light, and Mr. Okonkwo, who had a rule about never settling an argument for them, wrote "verify" on the board and kept taking attendance.

Hudson worked Thursdays and Saturdays at Frayne's Hardware, where his job was mostly restocking and occasionally the register when Doreen took her break. His paycheque had arrived Monday, and he had stared at it longer than he'd ever stared at any document in his life. The top number, the gross pay, was generous, heroic, a number you could build a summer on. Then came the column beneath it, and the summer shrank. Income tax, it said, in a small black abbreviation. CPP. EI. Deductions, plural, each one taking its share before the money ever reached his hands. He had folded the cheque stub into his wallet like evidence in a case he hadn't decided to bring yet.

That Thursday, a man bought a socket set and a roll of duct tape, and while the receipt printed, Hudson, still stinging from Tuesday, found himself narrating. "See that tax line," he said, pointing. "GST. Seven percent, federally. Hasn't changed." The man said "huh" in the tone of someone buying duct tape, and left, and Hudson looked at the receipt still curling out of the printer and did the arithmetic in his head. Five. The line was five percent of the subtotal, exactly, the way a thing is exactly what it is when you finally bother to look.

He should say something to Priya. He metabolized this over the shift, turning it over the way Doreen turned the CLOSED sign at closing, slowly, and with some resistance. It wasn't that admitting error was impossible; it was that his error had been so confident, so birthday-certain, and he could feel the difference between being right and merely never having been checked.

Friday he looked it up on his phone behind the paint aisle. The GST had come in on January 1, 1991, at seven percent. Since January 1, 2008, it had been five. Both facts sat side by side on the screen, and Hudson had the strange sensation of having been half-right, of holding one true thing from one decade and one true thing from another and having glued them together wrong. His father, he remembered now, had complained about the tax when it arrived, back when complaining was seven-percent sized. That was probably where Hudson's certainty had come from: inherited grievance, passed down like a watch.

In class on Monday, Mr. Okonkwo had them filling out a practice return, the T1 kind, the real shape of the thing. Hudson entered his wages from Frayne's, subtracted his deductions, watched his taxable income become a smaller and more honest number. Priya, beside him, was faster at it. "So the GST," she said, not looking up from her form. "It was seven when it started in ninety-one. Five since the start of 2008. I looked it up." Hudson said, "I know. I found out Thursday." It came out flatter than he intended, and she glanced over, waiting for the rest.

Here was what he hadn't figured out yet, and what he turned over on the walk home: whether a country that keeps a ledger on every coffee, that skims its share off the top of every seventeen-year-old's paycheque before the money is even money, is a technocracy or just a very patient kind of agreement. Maybe both. Maybe the GST at five percent was the government being generous, or being clever, or being tired of arguing at seven. He didn't know, and he noticed that not knowing felt different now, less like a gap and more like a door. He stopped at the coffee place, ordered a muffin, epicurean choice, blueberry, and stood over the receipt doing the math slowly, twice.

"You're blocking the counter," the barista said.

"Five percent," Hudson said, and stepped aside, still holding the receipt.

The cultural festival had taken over the synagogue parking lot, folding tables of baklava and lentil soup and a debate booth that nobody was visiting. Nathan had signed up three weeks ago because Rabbi Sternman said the topic was ancient rules in modern life, and because Priya had dared him to, and because a boy who had nothing to say at his grandfather's shiva needed somewhere to practice having opinions. The topic card he drew from the coffee can read, in the rabbi's cramped hand: corners of the field.

His opponent was Miriam Auerbach, a senior from the day school across town, who was already spreading her notes across the table like she was setting a table for Shabbat. She wore a button that said TEAM MOUNT SINAI, which Nathan suspected she had made herself the night before, and she looked at the topic card over her glasses. "You go to public school," she said. It wasn't a question.

He had prepared, in his way. He'd spent two evenings at the kitchen table with his mother's old chumash, the one with her maiden name in gold on the cover, looking for something he could argue. He'd found it on a page he almost skipped: Leviticus 19:9-10, where farmers are commanded not to reap the corners of their fields but to leave them, and the fallen gleanings too, for the poor and the stranger. He'd underlined it twice, then felt vaguely guilty, as if underlining were a kind of vandalism, and smoothed the page flat again. Before the debate, he'd texted his sister Dalia, away at her first year of college, because she was the only person he knew who would answer honestly.

The message was still on his phone when he sat down. "You're asking the wrong question," she'd written. "It's not whether the rule applies. It's what counts as your field. Figure out what you're a farmer of, and then tell me if you leave the corners." Then, a second bubble: "Also don't interpolate some grand philosophy from one verse. Rabbis hate that. Love, the smarter sibling." He'd read it four times on the bus, and once more now, under the table, while Miriam arranged her index cards in a fanning arc like a card trick.

"Resolved," the rabbi announced to the eleven people who had drifted over, some holding paper plates of kibbeh, "that this law obligates only farmers, and means nothing to the rest of us." Miriam took the affirmative, which meant Nathan had to argue that a rule about not reaping the corners of a field, and leaving the fallen gleanings for the poor and the stranger, could bind a seventeen-year-old who had never grown so much as a basil plant. She opened with the plain meaning of the text, the plain setting, agriculture, and a line about how not everything ancient must be stretched to fit. It was clean and it was reasonable and it landed on the folding chairs like a bromide, something true and useless at once.

Nathan lost the first exchange badly. He tried to talk about charity in the abstract and Miriam asked him, twice, to point at the verse he was using, and he couldn't, because he was using the idea of the verse rather than the verse itself. Eleven people watched him shuffle his notes. Somewhere behind them a band started tuning. He thought about Dalia's text under the fluorescent light of the debate booth. Then he stopped arguing about meaning and started arguing about the shape of the thing.

"The text doesn't say give money," he said, slower now, finding it as he said it. "It says don't reap all of it. The farmer doesn't travel anywhere, doesn't find the poor, doesn't decide who deserves it. The corners stay where they grew. The gleanings stay where they fell." He looked up from the page. "I don't farm. But I have a field. My grades, my time, whatever I'm good at. The rule isn't telling me to be generous. It's telling me not to take everything when I harvest it. Leave the corners for the poor and the stranger, and don't turn it into a ceremony. Just don't reap to the edge."

The judges conferred, and Miriam leaned across the table before they finished. "That's not proof," she said quietly. "That's you deciding the verse means whatever's convenient. Rashi would eat you alive." "Probably," Nathan said. "But you didn't say I was wrong about the corners." She held his eyes a moment, then looked down at her cards, and he understood that she had conceded something small and would never say so out loud.

They gave the round to Miriam on technical grounds, which felt right to him, the way a coin toss feels right. Afterward he found a quiet spot near the falafel stand and typed out a message to Dalia, deleting the part about losing and keeping the part about the corners. Behind him, the band started to play, and someone was dancing badly, and Priya appeared with two paper cups of lemonade and said, "So? Did you leave anything for the poor and the stranger, or did you reap the whole debate?" Nathan took his cup and said, "Ask Miriam. She got the win. I got the corners."

The book club met in the back room of the Lavender Street library, where the radiators clanked all winter and the folding chairs had been arranged in a circle so lopsided that whoever sat at the gap had to crane sideways to see anyone. Ashton took the gap chair because he always arrived last, pedaling from soccer practice with his backpack still smelling of grass and mud. Eleven of them were there, all sixteen or seventeen, no adult in the room. That was the club's one rule, laid down by Priya, who had founded it the previous spring and who guarded the discussion agenda like a fiduciary guarding someone else's money, exactly and a little obsessively.

They had read Jane Eyre. Priya opened her copy with a decisive snap and said they were going to try something new tonight, a critical lens, which meant reading the book through a particular question rather than just talking about whether they liked it. She had written two questions on an index card. "The feminist one asks how gender shapes what the characters can do," she said. "The Marxist one asks how money and class shape it. We'll do both, and then, if we're brave, we'll see whether they can be done at the same time." Ashton noticed she said "if we're brave" and looked directly at him, which he chose not to interpret.

The passage was the one where Jane, a governess, stands in a drawing room full of people above her station. Lena, who wanted to be a poet and said so at every meeting, read it aloud, her finger moving under the words, and the radiator hissed through the pause afterward. Ashton said the first thing that came to him, that Jane was invisible, that nobody saw her because she was a woman and poor and the two things together made her furniture. Priya wrote "woman + poor = furniture" on the whiteboard and underlined it twice.

Then Marcus, who mostly came for the cookies and stayed for the arguments, said the poverty was the real engine, that a rich woman in that room would have been seen perfectly well, so gender was doing less work than they thought. Ashton countered that a poor man could still become a clerk, could sign contracts, could leave. "But Jane does leave," Marcus said. "She leaves and comes back with money, and then everything opens up for her." Nobody had an answer to that, and the circle went quiet in the way that meant thinking rather than boredom. Someone's chair squeaked. Lena tore the corner off a napkin and folded it into a small triangle.

Ashton sat with the silence and found, assembling it piece by piece, that the two lenses were not fighting so much as leaning on each other. Money without the room, the freedom without the means, either one alone was half a door. He was reaching for a way to say this when Marcus, flipping idly through his copy, found something penciled in the margin of an old library sale stamp inside the back cover, a note in faded graphite. He read it out: "Room, own money, 1929, Woolf." He looked up. "What's that supposed to mean?"

"It's A Room of One's Own," Lena said, in the tone of someone who had read it twice. "Virginia Woolf. Published 1929. It argues that a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction." Ashton felt the note click into place like the last piece of something he hadn't known he was building. Here it was, both lenses in one sentence, the money and the room, the Marxist fact and the feminist fact, bound together on a page sixty years before any of them was born. "So the woman who writes the book we're reading," he said slowly, "Brontë, her sisters, all of them, they'd need both first. Before a single word."

Priya turned to the shelf behind her, where the club's year of reading stood in a ragged row, and counted under her breath. Twelve books, one by a woman, Jane Eyre itself. She counted again, as if the count were capricious and might change, and it did not. "We chose these," she said. "We chose them and we didn't notice." Marcus said the list had mostly come from a college syllabus he'd found online, so in a sense the omission had been inherited rather than committed, and Priya said that inheriting a thing does not abrogate your responsibility for it once you see it. They looked at each other across the crooked circle.

What stayed uncertain, Ashton thought but did not say aloud, was whether the old books were worth the rereading or should simply be set down, and whether a lens that explained everything might also flatten it; he liked Jane Eyre, he realized, precisely for what his questions couldn't quite hold. Priya wrote "next term: Woolf" on the whiteboard and boxed it. Lena read the passage again, the invisible woman in the drawing room, and this time Ashton heard it differently, as if someone had moved a lamp and the shadows had shifted.

The radiators clanked. Priya closed her copy and said, "Same chair next month, Ashton," and pointed at the gap.

The crystals were supposed to be blue, and they were, mostly, but they weighed almost nothing. Logan set the jar on the kitchen counter between the toaster and his mother's ferments, three mason jars of cabbage that had been bubbling on the shelf for two weeks like a small, patient chemistry set of their own. His project was due Thursday. He had grown copper sulfate crystals for eleven days, and the scale at school had declared them a disappointment.

He had started with 12.5 grams of copper sulfate pentahydrate, which his lab sheet said had a molar mass of 249.7 grams per mole. That part he could do. Divide the mass by the molar mass and you got moles: 0.0500, a clean number that had felt like a small promise. Then the reaction, simple and smug in the textbook, gave one mole of product for every mole of reactant, so the theoretical yield was 0.0500 moles of crystal. Multiply by the molar mass and he should be holding 12.5 grams of glittering blue. He was holding 8.2.

His little sister Nadia came in for cereal and stood over the jar with the frankness of a fourteen-year-old. "They're pretty," she said, which was the nicest thing anyone had said about the project all week. "Why's there a sticky note that says HELP on the scale?"

"Because the math says I should have more crystal than I do."

"Maybe the math's wrong."

"Maybe the crystal's wrong," Logan said, and then heard himself and frowned. He pulled the calculator toward him, crumbs and all, and started over. The grams went in, the molar mass went under them, the moles came out the same as before. The arithmetic was not the problem. The arithmetic never was. Somewhere between the powder and the jar, eleven grams of ambition had condensed into eight.

He typed a search into his phone: crystals weigh less than theoretical yield. What came back, between a forum post from 2011 and an advertisement for a better balance, was a phrase that stuck its chin out at him: percent yield. He read it twice, then said it aloud, mostly to annoy Nadia, who was still eating cereal at the counter like a spectator at a slow sport.

"Percent yield," he said. "Actual mass of product divided by the theoretical yield, times one hundred." He wrote it on the back of an envelope in ballpoint, pressing hard enough to emboss the counter. The actual mass was 8.2 grams. The theoretical yield was 12.5. He divided, multiplied, and got 65.6, which he stared at for a while. Sixty-five point six percent of a crystal. Thirty-four percent of his science fair had gone somewhere he couldn't point to.

"So it's a bad grade," Nadia said, looking at his face rather than the envelope.

"It's a number. It's not the same thing as a grade." He was surprised by how firmly he believed this. The number was honest in a way his lab sheet wasn't, because the lab sheet only said what should happen, and the number said what did. He had spent two weeks thinking the plan was the real thing and the crystal was a rough draft of the plan. It occurred to him, standing in a kitchen that smelled faintly of soured cabbage, that it might run the other direction. The crystal was the fact. The plan was the story people told about the fact beforehand.

The word itself, he decided, was grandiose for what it described, though he liked it anyway. Yield. He looked up the etymology because he couldn't not, and found it came from an old root meaning to pay, to render up what was owed, which meant the whole term assumed the universe owed you a crystal and was quietly defaulting on two thirds of the debt. He wrote none of this on the envelope, which was already full.

What he wrote instead was the calculation, done a second time with different rounding to see if it held, and under it: where did it go? He didn't have an answer. Some of it might have stayed dissolved in the water he'd poured off. Some might never have reacted. The forums argued about it with more certainty than evidence, and he noticed he trusted the ones that said "unclear" more than the ones that explained everything. He underlined the 65.6 twice, then stopped, because underlining twice was the kind of thing a person did when pretending the underline was data.

Nadia rinsed her bowl and paused at the door with the jar in her line of sight. "Sixty-five is still more than half," she said. "You could put that on the poster. Most of a crystal."

"Most of a crystal," Logan said. He picked up the jar and turned it so the kitchen light caught the biggest one, an uneven tooth of blue, 8.2 grams of the world agreeing with him partially. He set it in the center of the poster board, drew a box around the space where it would sit, and wrote his title above it in careful capital letters.

The community studio smelled of turpentine and old coffee, and Madeline had claimed the stool by the window because she told herself she worked best in the light, though really she worked best wherever Priya wasn't. Priya was already there, of course, leaning over the print Ms. Ro had taped to the easel, the one of the two women holding hands on a bench under a stormy sky. Madeline had said, twice, that she didn't care who got to present first. That wasn't true either, but she was getting good at not checking which of her statements were.

"Formal analysis," Ms. Ro said, walking the rows of easels. "Colour, composition, symbolism. Not whether you like it. What it does." She moved on before anyone could ask her what the painting did, which was the whole problem as far as Madeline could tell.

Ms. Ro was not the problem. Priya was the problem, and also Danny, who had rolled his chair between them like a referee. Danny pointed at the left-hand figure, the one in the pale dress with the lace at the throat, whose exposed heart was being cut by a little pair of scissors. "That one's the real Frida," he said. "The other one's a costume."

"A costume," Priya repeated, in the voice she used when she wanted a fight to seem beneath her. "The one on the left wears the white European-style Victorian dress. The one on the right wears the traditional Tehuana dress." She said the words carefully, the way she'd read them the night before off her phone, though later she would claim she'd known them for years. "So if anything, the Victorian dress is the costume. That's not even controversial."

Madeline had planned to stay quiet. She had a page of notes on the composition, how the two figures sat symmetrically against an empty horizon, how the sky's grey seemed to presage something the figures already knew, holding hands anyway. She had written "shared circulation" and underlined it, because of the vein connecting the two hearts, or the one heart and the surgical absence of one, she couldn't decide which. She looked at her notes and then at the two of them, who were now arguing about whether Frida Kahlo had loved Europe or hated it, as if a person had to do one.

"Both," Madeline said, and hated how much it sounded like a retreat. "That's the whole point of the symbolism. She painted them the same size, same face, holding hands. The composition won't let you pick."

"That's a cop-out," Danny said. "Formal analysis means committing."

Priya turned on him, glad to have an ally against the harder question. "It literally means the opposite. It means describing what's there."

Madeline watched them and understood, with a slow downward feeling, that she was about to lose the argument she'd just entered. Last year she had done this exact thing with her mother, choosing a college two hours from home and calling it independence, and her mother had said, "You always pick the option that lets you feel both things," and Madeline had slammed the door and then, in the hallway, admitted it was accurate. She had told Priya none of this. She and Priya had been close since the printmaking class in fall, close in the way that includes a small ledger of grievances neither of them names, a complicity of silence about who had copied whose colour palette for the portfolio review.

"I'll commit," Madeline said. "The Tehuana Frida holds the locket with the portrait, and the Victorian one is bleeding out because the artery's cut. So the painting argues one side survives on love and the other side dies without it. That's a position."

"Whose love, though," Priya said. "Diego's? That's what the locket is."

"Or self-love. Or heritage." Madeline heard herself hedging and heard Danny hear it too.

Ms. Ro drifted back, arms folded, and said only, "Whose heart is exposed on the right one, and whose on the left?" and then let the question sit there like a stone neither boy would touch. Both hearts were exposed, Madeline realized, which was exactly what she should have said first, and she felt a small hot flare of resentment that Ms. Ro had handed it to her, because now it would look like the teacher's idea. She said it anyway.

"Both hearts are outside. Both. So the painting isn't asking which one is real. It's saying you can't be either one intact."

Nobody answered. Priya was looking at the print with her head tilted, and Danny had started sketching the two figures in the margin of his handout, badly, and outside the window a man was loading clay into the kiln shed, his hands grey to the wrist, as if he'd become impermeable to the cold. Madeline picked up her pencil and wrote, under "shared circulation," a question mark, and left it there.

"So which one do you paint," Priya said at last, "if you're her."

Madeline looked at the stormy sky, the clasped hands, the small portrait in the locket, and turned her notebook to a fresh page.

"Both," she said, "but on a bad day, the one with the scissors."

The auditorium smelled of dust and radiator paint, and Jaxon sat in the third row of the empty hall with a violin that was not his. It belonged to the school, kept in a cabinet behind the stage since the last orchestra kid graduated, and it had arrived in his hands with all four strings slack, the bridge loose in its little paper envelope, and a note from Ms. Ferreira that read, simply, You said you'd open the assembly on Friday. Two days. He had said it, in a moment of bravado he could no longer reconstruct, and now the instrument lay across his knee like a question directed at him personally.

He had wanted this, though the wanting was hard to locate now. His older sister had played cello, and when she left for college the house had gone quiet in a way that felt like a debt he owed. He had told himself it was about music. Possibly it was only about filling her chair-shaped absence. He could not decide, and the undecidedness itself was irritating, so he set the bridge in place, threaded the strings through the tailpiece, and began to tighten pegs.

That was where the trouble started. The strings came out of a paper sleeve in no particular order, identical silver coils, and the packet said nothing. He turned one peg, plucked, and got a sound like a dying moth. He plucked another, tightened, plucked, and spent several minutes cogitating over which string was meant to live where, turning the violin over as if its body might confess. It did not. He tightened the wrong string too far and it snapped with a crack that ricocheted off the back wall of the stage, and he sat very still in the enormous room, ears burning, entirely alone with his culpability.

"Break it already?" The voice came from the wings. Priya, a junior who actually played in the regional youth orchestra, came down the steps carrying her own case. She looked at the snapped string, at the three survivors, and mercifully did not laugh. "You don't know which is which," she said, and it wasn't a question.

"They're all the same. They're just strings."

"They're really not." She took the violin, laid it flat on her palm, and pointed at the pegs one by one, from the side of the instrument nearest his body outward. "Lowest to highest, G, D, A, E. And they're tuned in perfect fifths." She said it the way she'd say the date, flat, ordinary, a thing that was simply the case. Then she took out her phone, played a single pitch, and handed the violin back. "Start from the lowest. You can hear it when you're close."

She left him to it, wandering up onto the stage to mark her blocking for a different piece, and Jaxon worked. He found that he could feel the difference before he could hear it: the G was fat under his finger, almost rope-like, and the E, when he got it near where it wanted to be, was thin as wire and shrank under his touch. Between them the D and A sat in descending order of thickness, and when he had all four roughly singing, he drew the bow across them one at a time, lowest to highest, and heard the interval between each pair open up the same way, again and again, like a staircase where every riser was somehow identical. G up to D. D up to A. A up to E. He had not known that a thing could be built out of the same distance repeated.

He snapped another string at seven that evening, and a third the next afternoon, and on Thursday night his hands ached and his tone still sounded like a petulant animal complaining about weather. Priya found him at intermission of the dress rehearsal, listened to him saw through eight bars, and did not pretend. "It's not going to be beautiful," she said. "Friday. But it will be yours."

Friday morning, the auditorium filled with nine hundred students who did not care about violins and three teachers who had already begun saying his name with a question mark after it. The lights came up too warm. He set the bow on the G string, the fat one, the one he now knew blind, and did not think about his sister or about the debt or about whether wanting something for confused reasons made it less real. He thought only: lowest to highest, then the stairs. He drew the bow.

The gym smelled of floor wax and wet umbrellas, and the voting booths stood in two neat rows like changing rooms at a pool. Charlie had been assigned to hand out ballots for the student mock election, which the civics teacher had insisted be held at the real polling station on the day of the real one, so that students who came to watch their parents vote could practice on their own miniature version. Her job was simple until two boys from her class, Daniel and Yusuf, started arguing in front of her table at ten in the morning, with the mock polls closing at four.

"It's the same everywhere," Daniel said. "The leader loses the parliament, the leader goes home. That's how it works in my country. If the assembly turns against the prime minister, there's a vote, and he's finished by Friday."

"No, no," Yusuf said. "Where I'm from, the president sits there for the whole term no matter what the assembly says about him. They can shout until the ceiling falls. He stays."

Charlie stamped a ballot without looking at it. She had a stack of two hundred mock ballots, a sign-up sheet, and a growing suspicion that she was about to be made a referee. Daniel leaned over her table, and she noticed his hands were shaking slightly, though his voice stayed level. He wanted to win this, she realized, the way some people want to win arguments about their own homeland, as if the country itself were listening.

"Charlie," Daniel said. "Tell him. She takes civics with me, she got the highest mark on the systems test."

"Then she knows I'm right," Yusuf said.

She set down her stamp. What she actually remembered was messier than either of them deserved. The class had spent a week on the difference between a parliamentary system and a presidential one, and she had written an essay about it, but the essay had felt like copying a map without ever walking the streets. "It depends on which system," she said slowly. "In a parliamentary one, like yours, the parliament picks the prime minister, so if the parliament turns against him, he can be removed. That's what you're saying."

"Thank you," said Daniel.

"But in a presidential system," she went on, "the president is elected separately from the legislature. On his own, in his own election. For a fixed term." She was assembling it as she spoke, hearing how the pieces locked together in a way the essay had never made her feel. "So the legislature can't remove him just because they disagree with him. He isn't theirs to remove."

Yusuf pointed at her as if she had produced evidence in court. "Elected separately," he repeated. "Fixed term. Write it down, Daniel."

The line behind them had grown. An old woman waiting to sign the mock registry shifted her weight and said, quietly, that in her day the whole argument would have been settled by whoever brought the best pastries, and this did not ease the tension so much as rearrange it. Charlie stamped three more ballots, and while she stamped she kept turning the two systems over in her mind, one in each hand like unequal stones. In Daniel's country, the leader could fall in a week, which meant the leader always depended on keeping the assembly happy. In Yusuf's, the president could sit through years of open hatred from the legislature because the people, not the assembly, had put him there. Neither one, she decided, was simply better. One moved faster and could shake apart; the other stood firmer and could stand wrong.

The twist came at lunch, and it came from Daniel. He came back alone, holding a paper cup of coffee he hadn't drunk from, and stood at the end of her table while the gym emptied. "My father called," he said. "There's a real vote tonight, back home. A real one. Confidence vote." He turned the cup in his hands. "If it goes the way the radio thinks, we fly back next month, maybe for good."

Charlie looked at the clock above the bleachers. Three hours left in the mock election, and she suddenly understood why his hands had been shaking. "So you weren't arguing about systems," she said.

"I was arguing that my system works," he said. "That it's good that a leader can fall when he loses the parliament. Because if it works tonight, then my father was right to stay, and if it doesn't, then..." He didn't finish. The coffee cup went into the bin with a hollow sound.

She wanted to tell him it would be fine, but she didn't know that, and she was tired of saying things she didn't know. What she had worked out that morning, comparing the two countries like two ways of holding water, was that she still couldn't say which hand held less. "I only know the rule," she said. "In yours, the parliament can remove him. That's the whole of what I know." He almost smiled at that, and she stamped a ballot for a boy in a rain-soaked jacket, and by the time she looked up Daniel had taken a ballot too, and was standing in the booth with his pen hovering, as if the little box could hold something larger than a mock vote.

The restaurant had pushed four tables together in the back room and strung a banner that read CONGRATS MATHIS, though the "M" had begun to peel and curled downward like a wave about to break. Mathis sat with his parents, his aunt Carol, and a handful of classmates who had drifted in from other parties, and he kept noticing the empty chair at the corner, the one they had saved for Dee.

Dee was his cousin, two years older, who had left school in eleventh grade and had said, three weeks ago on the phone, that she would come tonight. "I want to see what a graduation feels like," she'd told him, and he had laughed, and then hadn't.

"Speech," said Priya, raising her water glass. She was going to the state university in the fall and had been talking about it since March, but tonight she kept steering the conversation back to the class itself, to who was where. "Speech, Mathis."

He stood, mostly to have something to do with his hands. "I was going to write something cerebral," he said, "with a thesis and everything, but I left my notes in my other head." His father laughed too loudly at that, and it warmed him, and he sat back down before anyone could demand an actual speech.

It was Priya who counted. She had been thumbing through the photos on her phone from freshman orientation, holding the screen up so the people beside her could squint at it, and she went quiet in the middle of a sentence. "There were, like, three hundred and forty of us," she said. "In the auditorium. I remember because they ran out of programs." She looked around the table, then at the room. "Two hundred and seventy-something crossed the stage."

"Maybe some moved," Mathis's mother offered.

"No, this counts the whole cohort," Priya said. "Anyone who started ninth grade with us, wherever they ended up. That's how they calculate it. I looked it up for my stats project." She scrolled again, as if the phone might disagree with itself.

Mathis did the arithmetic on the paper place mat, in the margin next to a drawing of a fish he'd done earlier without thinking. It came out to about eighty percent, worse than the school had claimed in the newsletter, and he said so, and Priya shook her head. "Our school's different," she said. "The national number's higher. The US average for public high school students, 2021 to 2022, was 87 percent. Adjusted cohort rate. I have it on a flashcard somewhere." The other classmates at the table passed this around without ceremony, the way they passed the bread, and Mathis wrote 87 on the place mat and drew a box around it, and then, without deciding to, wrote 13 beside it.

Thirteen out of a hundred. He tried to make it abstract, because abstract was safer, but the empty chair kept dragging it back down to earth. Dee hadn't moved. Dee hadn't been counted anywhere except in that other number, the one nobody prints on banners.

The restaurant's kitchen door swung open, and a waiter came through with a cake, candles already lit, and the small flames presaged nothing except melted frosting if they didn't hurry, so everyone sang fast and off-key. Mathis blew them out in one breath, and in the dark second before the lights seemed to return, the front bell chimed.

Dee stood in the doorway in her work uniform from the warehouse, hair still flattened from a hairnet, holding a gas station card with a cartoon frog on it. She scanned the room like someone entering a country where the customs were unfamiliar, and Mathis stood up so fast his chair scraped.

"I'm late," she said. "I know."

"You're not," he said, though she was forty minutes late and the cake was already cut.

She sat in the empty chair, and Aunt Carol put a plate in front of her without a word about the past two years, which Mathis understood was its own kind of mercy. Dee looked at the place mat, at the fish and the numbers and the box around 87. "What's that, homework at a party?"

"It's the graduation rate," Priya said. "Nationally. Eighty-seven percent, 2021-22, for public schools. Adjusted cohort, meaning everyone who starts ninth grade together."

Dee turned the place mat toward herself. "So thirteen out of a hundred don't finish," she said, and Mathis couldn't tell whether she said it the way you identify a species or the way you name yourself. He wanted to say something true and not pitying, something that held both facts at once, that most people cross the stage and that the ones who don't are not a footnote, and he found he didn't have the sentence yet. Maybe he would in a year. Maybe college was where people learned to hold two numbers in their head at the same time.

"Thirteen percent," he said instead, "and one of them brought me a frog."

Dee slid the card across the table to him. On the inside, in ballpoint, she had written: For the college kid. Save me a seat at something. He read it twice, then folded it into his shirt pocket and cut her the first slice of cake, the one with most of the frosting still on it, and put it down in front of her like an answer he was willing to start with.

The wood had been stacked in the backyard since noon, a careful pyramid of old branches and broken crates that her father had carried up from the basement in three trips. Lea watched from the kitchen window while her grandmother circled it once, slowly, the way she circled everything before approving it, and then went inside to fill the small brass plate with marigolds and a lump of turmeric.

"Your aunt is coming at seven," her mother said, not looking up from the pot of milk thickening on the stove. "With the boys. So eat something now, because once they arrive you won't sit again until midnight."

Lea had told Priya she would be at the bonfire tonight. She had also told her roommate-to-be, Dana, from the admitted students group chat, that she would call at nine to talk about housing forms. Both could not happen, or not well, and for most of the afternoon she had moved between the two commitments the way her mother moved between the stove and the window, giving each a turn and neither her whole attention. She set her phone face down on the counter and decided that this, at least, was a decision.

When the relatives arrived the yard filled all at once, the way it always did, with noise and bowls and the little cousins who immediately began negotiating over who would get to touch the first match. Her uncle checked the sky. "Good," he said. "Full moon. It should be full tonight, that's the rule. Phalguna's full moon. March, usually." The moon was already up, pale and complete above the neighbor's roof, and it transfixed the little cousins so thoroughly that they stopped negotiating, which Lea noted as a small mercy.

Her grandmother let the youngest boy hold the plate while she said the prayers, her voice low and unhurried, the Sanskrit worn smooth from repetition. Lea stood at the edge of the group and listened without joining in, as she had for the last few years. At college she planned to take a philosophy course; Dana had already declared herself an atheist and once called religion "a fairy tale with better production values." Lea hadn't argued with her. She also hadn't agreed. What she felt, standing in the yard with the smoke beginning to rise, was harder to file under either heading, and she was tired of being asked to choose.

"You know what tonight is called?" her aunt asked, appearing beside her with two cups of chai. "The bonfire. Holika Dahan. It's the night before, and tomorrow morning is the colors, the actual Holi. So don't wear anything you like tomorrow."

"I wasn't planning to."

"That's what you said last year, and then you wore that white kurti and screamed like the powder was acid."

Lea laughed, and the fire chose that moment to catch properly, the flames standing up out of the pyramid in a single tall column. The family stepped back together, an involuntary choreography, and the little cousins were pushed behind the adults' legs. Somebody's phone, not hers, buzzed and was ignored.

Later, when the fire had settled into its long red conversation with itself, Lea sat on the back steps with the chai going cold in her hands. Her father came and sat beside her, smelling of smoke. "Your grandmother was telling the boys the story," he said. "The demoness, the fire, the devotion that survives it. When you were small you asked me if it really happened."

"What did you say?"

"I said I didn't know, and that it mattered anyway." He looked into the fire. "I still think that's true, for what it's worth. And I could be wrong. Both of those at once."

She turned that over while the sparks climbed toward the moon. It seemed to her that Dana would call the story a fabrication, that her grandmother would call it scripture, and that her father had, in eleven words, refused the whole argument without winning it. She picked up her phone and typed to Dana, can we do the housing call tomorrow instead? busy tonight, and then, before she could second-guess it, pressed send. Tomorrow morning she would stand in the yard while her cousins buried her in pink and green, and she would be glad, and she would not be able to say why, and she would keep the philosophy class on her schedule anyway.

"Lea," her aunt called from the fire, "come put on more wood before your father falls asleep on the steps."

She set down the cup and went.

Lea spread the printout on the picnic table and weighted its corners with two pinecones and a jar of screws she had found under the bench. The graph showed a line climbing from left to right, 1960 to now, and beneath the climb the line shivered in little teeth, up and down, up and down, so regular it looked like a sewing machine had made it. Marcus sat across from her with his knees apart and his phone face down on the table, which was his way of showing good faith. She was being paid twenty dollars for this session, money she had already promised to the parking office at the community college, and she had told his mother she could explain the whole thing.

"Okay," she said. "Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, measured in Hawaii, every month for sixty years. It goes up because we burn stuff. That part's easy." She tapped the teeth. "These parts, I used to think they were measurement errors. Like the machine glitching."
