Marcus frowned at the paper. He was seventeen and querulous in the mornings, and their session had started with him asking why he even needed this, since he was going to weld. His mother had answered that already, so Lea let it go.

"The errors wouldn't go in a pattern," he said now, slowly, turning the page sideways as if the angle was the problem. "Errors are random. These are like stairs." He was right, and she felt the small sting of being corrected by her own student. She had read three articles last night and none of them had said it that plainly. Random errors would scatter. These repeated every single year, a saw blade drawn by someone patient.

"So what makes it go down and then back up every year," she said. "That's the part I couldn't get." She pulled the jar of screws closer and set a pinecone on the graph, on one of the dips. Somewhere behind the fence the neighbor's sprinkler came on, ticking across her mother's tomato stakes, and a wasp investigated the jar and left.

Marcus was quiet for a while. He picked up the pinecone, turned it over, and set it back on a peak instead of a dip. "What happens to trees each season?" he said. He said it like he was embarrassed to offer something so obvious. "Like, in spring and summer, all the leaves come out. That's a lot of, what, material. They have to build it out of something."

Lea looked at the pinecone, which was a seed case from a tree, sitting on the graph like an answer. The line dropped every year in the northern half of the world's warm months and rose again in the cold ones. "There's way more land in the Northern Hemisphere," she said. "Way more forest. So when all those plants grow, they take carbon dioxide in, and the whole planet's number dips." She slid her finger along one tooth downward. "And then in fall and winter the leaves die and decay, and it goes back up." She heard herself say it and then said it again in her head to check it, because the check was hers to run. It held. It wasn't a glitch. It was the planet breathing, one breath a year, recorded in ink.

"So the wiggles are trees," Marcus said.

"The wiggles are trees," Lea said, and laughed once, not because it was funny but because she had spent two nights on something a pinecone had settled. She wrote it on the back of the printout in her careful block letters, because tomorrow she had to stand in front of a scholarship committee and explain this graph, and if a woman in a blazer asked about the saw teeth, she would not say measurement error. She would say the wiggles are trees, and then she would say the longer sentence properly: that Northern Hemisphere plants take in carbon dioxide as they grow in spring and summer, and release it as leaves die and decay in autumn and winter.

The wasp came back and landed on the jar of screws, and Marcus watched it instead of her. She let him watch. She was deciding, in the calm way she was learning to adjudicate things now that she was eighteen, between telling him he was good enough to stop and telling him the rest, that the line underneath the teeth never came back down, that the breathing happened on a staircase that only rose. There was uncertainty in her about which he needed. She chose the second one, because tomorrow she would stand in a room and the committee would want to know she could see both things at once, the breath and the climb, and saying it out loud here, in her mother's backyard with the sprinkler ticking, was practice.

"Look at the long line," she said. "Ignore the teeth. The breathing is real, every year, same as ever. But the floor under it keeps rising." She put her finger at the left edge and drew it slowly across the whole century of paper, all the way to the pinecone holding down the right corner.

Marcus picked up the pinecone and held it against the last point on the line, where the paper ended and the fence began. "That's us," he said.

Aaron found the guitar behind the tubas on Monday, leaning against the instrument room's back wall in a case held shut with a strip of electrical tape. It had belonged to Mr. Ferrar's grandfather, the band director said, and if Aaron wanted to borrow it for the semester he could, on the condition that he treat it like something that had outlived three owners already. Aaron carried the case to the practice room at the end of the hall, the one with the foam panels on the walls, and set it on the floor between two chairs.

The tape came off in one long pull. Inside, the strings were dull and slightly rusted at the frets, and when he pressed the low string down at the fifth fret and plucked it, the note wavered somewhere beneath where his ear expected it to land. He had never tuned a guitar in his life. He had come into the school year as a percussionist, a snare player who could read a rhythm chart but not a note on a staff, and the guitar had seemed like a way to learn music from the inside, one string at a time, instead of hitting things from the outside.

He tried tuning by memory, twisting the low string's peg until it felt right, then the next one, matching each string to the one before it by guessing at the interval. The result was a guitar in no key at all, every chord sour in a different direction. He sat with that failure for a while, plucking the strings one at a time, listening to how the wrongness was consistent, a system of mistakes rather than a random one. Whatever he had done, he had done it uniformly.

At lunch, Priya from jazz band found him in the practice room with his phone open to a tuner app he didn't trust. "You tuned it all by ear?" she said, and he admitted he had. She picked up the guitar, plucked the lowest string, and looked at the app. "This is way flat. Do you know what it's supposed to be?" He said he didn't, not really, not in a way he could defend. "E," she said. "From the lowest string to the highest, a guitar in standard tuning goes E, A, D, G, B, E." She said it the way someone recites an address they've walked to a thousand times, and then she handed the guitar back. "You tune it. I'm not doing it for you."

So he did it himself. He plucked the low string and tightened the peg until the app's needle steadied on E, then moved to the next string, A, and the next, D, and G, and B, and finally the thin high string, which was E again, two octaves above the first one, though he only knew that from the sound opening up, not from anything he could prove. When all six were true, he strummed them together and the chord rang out round and complete, nothing clashing, and he strummed it again just to hear it a second time.

He practiced every day after school for a week. The band room was empty by four, and Mr. Ferrar let him stay as long as he locked up. His fingertips hurt in a way he had never experienced, the soft skin at the ends of his fingers pressing into thin wire until it hardened. He learned three chords from a video on his phone and could switch between two of them without stopping. The third chord, F, required barring one finger across all six strings, and he could not make it sound clean no matter how he arranged his hand.

On Friday, Priya came back with a folder of sheet music, a simple melody line transcribed for guitar, and said he should try reading it. This was where his two educations collided. As a percussionist he had learned to read rhythm with total precision, every sixteenth note accounted for, but pitch had been someone else's job, the trumpets', the flutes'. Now the staff meant something different. He could contextualize each note, placing it against the open strings he now knew by name, E and A and D and G and B and E again, finding B on the staff and locating it on the second string, open, no fingers required. The rhythm came instantly and the pitch came slowly, and for the first time he understood that reading music was two skills wearing one costume.

"You're counting it right but you're landing wrong," Priya said, after he mangled the same measure four times. "You trust the rhythm and you guess the pitch." He wanted to argue that guessing was a kind of starting, that his whole percussion education had begun with hedonistic banging on things before it became discipline, but he knew the argument would be a way of defending the wrong note. Instead he slowed down, played the measure at half speed, and made himself find each pitch on the neck before playing it, not after.

Mr. Ferrar came through the band room on his way out and stopped in the doorway of the practice room. He listened for a minute without comment. When Aaron finished the line, badly but recognizably, the old man said, "My grandfather played that in a navy band. He'd have made you tune it before you played a single note." Aaron said he had tuned it, all six strings, and told him the order, low to high, and Mr. Ferrar nodded once, the way a man nods at something that has been passed along correctly. It felt, briefly, like a matter of probity, like the tuning was a small honest account of what the instrument was supposed to be, and Aaron had kept it.

He still could not play the F chord. He still read pitch slower than he wanted to, and he did not know whether the guitar would become his instrument or just the door he walked through to find out what music he actually wanted to make. But on Monday he came back to the practice room, opened the case, plucked the low string, and found it had drifted flat overnight. He put his thumb on the peg and began to turn.

Gabrielle had been staying at her grandparents' house in Yorkshire for a fortnight, and in that time she had parallel parked between her grandfather's compost bins eleven times, clipping the curb on four of them. The test was on Thursday. On Tuesday morning her grandfather, Desmond, lowered himself into the passenger seat of his ancient Vauxhall with the ceremony of a man boarding a lifeboat, adjusted the mirror to watch her face rather than the road, and said, "Right. Today we do the A64. Merging, then. No subterfuge, no pretending you didn't see the lorry."

"It was one lorry," Gabrielle said, starting the engine. "One. And you gesticulated so hard you knocked the satnav into the footwell."

"I was signalling to the lorry," Desmond said, with dignity. "Lorries appreciate a clear gesture."

The problem, as Gabrielle understood it, was that she still did not know what a mistake cost. Tuesday's curb-touch had seemed minor, a soft scuff, but she had watched a boy at the test centre in Leeds fail outright for less, or so her cousin Priya claimed, and Priya claimed many things. That night, unable to sleep, she sat at the kitchen table with her grandmother's reading glasses pushed up on her head and the official booklet open under the lamp. The words were there, plain, and she read them twice because she did not believe them the first time. A candidate passed with no more than fifteen driving faults, and with no serious or dangerous faults at all. Fifteen. She sat back. She had been driving as though every error were a guillotine, when in fact the examiners were counting, and the count went quite a long way before anyone cared. The curb-touch was a fault. Only a fault. It was the dangerous things, the serious things, that ended you in a single stroke.

"So the scuff is nothing," she said to her grandmother the next morning, and Olive looked up from buttering toast and said, "Is that germane to your nerves, dear, or are you just telling me things?"

"It's germane. It's the whole point. I can be imperfect fifteen times. I just can't be catastrophic once."

"That was your grandfather's approach to marriage," Olive said, "and we're fifty-one years in."

Wednesday they merged onto the dual carriageway until Gabrielle's hands stopped shaking, and Desmond's gesticulating diminished from semaphore to a mild waving of the fingers, which she chose to interpret as praise. He noticed, too, that she checked her mirrors a half-second before he could ask, and he said nothing about it, only made them both tea when they got home and let her have the good chair.

At the test centre on Thursday, the examiner was a small brisk woman named Mrs. Okafor who smelled of peppermint and said "Whenever you're ready" in a voice that implied the readiness of the entire Northern Hemisphere. The parallel park came at the end, outside a post office, between a van and a hatchback. Gabrielle reversed, adjusted, reversed again, and felt the rear tyre kiss the curb with a touch so faint it might have been her imagination. Her stomach dropped through the seat. She finished the manoeuvre, straight and centred, and drove back to the centre in a state of glassy calm, certain it was over, certain the scuff had undone three weeks of bins and lorries and her grandfather's flailing arm.

Mrs. Okafor wrote something, then looked up. "You touched the curb on the parking. That's a driving fault." She let the pause sit exactly long enough for Gabrielle's face to do everything it wanted to do. "You've finished with four faults. That's a pass."

Gabrielle laughed, once, an involuntary bark that echoed off the plastic partition, because all Tuesday night she had prepared herself for grief over one scuffed tyre and now she had four faults and a certificate. Four. Eleven bin-clippings of headroom still unspent.

She texted her grandfather from the bus stop, then thought better of it and rang. He answered before the first ring finished.

"I passed," she said. "With faults."

"How many?"

"Four. Out of fifteen."

There was a silence, and then Olive's voice in the background, and then Desmond, sounding slightly strangled: "Your grandmother has a confession. She failed her test in 1971. Three times. She's never actually held a licence."

"I've been driving him to his heart appointments for six years," Olive called out, "and no one has ever asked to see it."

"Grandad," Gabrielle said, "you let her merge onto the A64?"

The field behind the middle school had been Victor's home for eleven summers, and this was the last one. In the fall he'd be two states away, in a dorm, and the league would go on without him, and he found he cared about that more than he'd expected to care about anything all year.

Dex had hit three home runs in the game against Fairlawn, and in the two games after that he'd hit two more, and by Thursday's practice the whole team had organized itself around him. Reyes stood at the cage and called pitches down the middle so Dex could extend. Kirby gave up his spot in the order. When Victor lined into a double play, Dex put a hand on his shoulder in the dugout and said, "Get on for me and I'll cash you in," and it wasn't cruel, which somehow made it worse.

Victor had found the study the way he found most things, chasing a thread past midnight. A 1985 study by Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky had concluded that basketball shooters' streaks were no more common than chance. Five makes in a row were exactly what you'd expect from a decent shooter rolling dice. The authors had called the hot hand a fallacy. Victor read it twice, then a third time, feeling something in him go quiet and stubborn. He didn't want it to be true. He wanted Dex to be a machine for one more month, wanted the season to have a shape, a hero, an ending you could narrate. But wanting wasn't evidence, and the paper sat in his browser tab all week like a signed affidavit against the thing the team had decided to believe.

He brought it up wrong, of course. He brought it up in the dugout with Dex six feet away, sweat still on his neck from his third homer in four days.

"Did you know there was a study," Victor said, "1985, Gilovich, Vallone, Tversky? They looked at pro basketball shooters and the streaks were no more common than chance. The hot hand is a fallacy."

Dex looked at him. "I play baseball."

"It's the same idea. Streaks. I'm not saying you're bad. I'm saying the streak doesn't predict the next pitch."

"So pitch me like normal," Dex said, "and watch."

Reyes laughed from the end of the bench. Kirby said something about spreadsheets that made everyone laugh except Victor, and except Dex, who hadn't actually smiled at all.

The coach pulled Victor aside by the fence. He was a good coach, mostly, a plumber who'd aged out of catching and never stopped squinting at the field like it owed him something. "You want to be right," he said, "or you want to win Saturday?" He didn't wait for an answer, which told Victor the coach thought those were the same thing, or that rightness was some obsolescent luxury the moment had outgrown. Victor said nothing. The conversation had a smell he recognized from arguments with his father: both sides talking about the future, neither saying which future.

Saturday they trailed 2-1 in the sixth. Victor led off with a clean single, and the sign came down from the third base box, small and unmistakable: take. Take until Reyes walked or struck out, take the whole at bat, because if Victor was erased on a bunt the inning belonged to Dex three batters later, and Dex was hot. Victor stood in and let a fastball sail over the inner half, a pitch he could have fouled off or driven. He took it. The crowd made its small approving noise. He took the next one, outside, and the one after, thigh-high, and the count ran to 2-2 before Reyes chopped into a force play that put Victor out at second by four steps. He walked back to the dugout through his own breath. He had done what the fallacy asked of him, or what its refutation asked, and it had cost exactly nothing that a bunt wouldn't have. That was the part nobody had prepared him for, that the evidence didn't portend anything in particular, that it sat there being true while the game ignored it.

Dex came up in the seventh with Kirby on first and the outfield playing shallow, and Victor caught himself leaning forward, wanting it, the same wanting as everybody else. Dex worked the count full and struck out on a slider in the dirt. He came back and sat at the far end of the bench and pulled his helmet down over his eyes. Nobody said anything. In the ninth, with two out and the tying run on third, he singled off the wall to tie it, and the team poured off the bench like something breaking open, and Victor was among them, shouting, pounding Dex's back, and honest enough in the noise to admit he had no idea what any of it proved.

They lost in the tenth on a wild pitch. Afterward, packing the gear bag by himself while the lights hummed and moths bounced off the poles, Victor found Dex sitting against the backstop, cleats off, socks in his hand.

"Three for five," Victor said.

"One for nothing, until I wasn't," Dex said. He looked out at the infield. "That study. It's real?"

"It's real."

Dex nodded slowly, working a knot of clay out of his cleat with his thumb. "Next game, swing when they give you something," he said. "Stop taking pitches for me."

Victor slung the bag over his shoulder. The last light was going off beyond the outfield, and the two of them sat there a moment longer, neither one of them sure.

The last week of July, Juliette was promoted to stroke of the second canoe, which meant she had to tell Marta what to fix. Marta was fifteen, built like a door hinge, and pulled harder than anyone at the camp, but her catch was late, so the boat crabbed sideways at the start of every race and they lost three meters before the buoy. Juliette had watched the older girls do this, deliver criticism, and she had decided the trick was cushioning. You buried the correction under praise, the way you'd wrap a pill in cheese for a dog.

After the Thursday time trial she tried it. She counted on her fingers as she talked, under the tent where the paddles hung in their racks. "Your top arm is beautiful, your rotation is beautiful, your endurance is the best on the water, you call switches perfectly, you never give up, and your catch is about half a second late." Five good things, one bad thing, spread out evenly, like rations.

Marta nodded, re-racked her paddle, and walked toward the mess hall with her shoulders up around her ears. At dinner she said nothing. At breakfast on Friday she said nothing. By the time they carried the boat down to the dock, she was paddling like a woman completing a furlough sentence, technically present, entirely elsewhere, and when Coach Anh asked what was wrong, Marta said, "Juliette thinks I'm slow."

"I said your endurance was the best on the water," Juliette said, but the words arrived too late, the way Marta's blade did.

That night, hiding from the talent show in the staff cabin's screen porch, Juliette found a fat folder of photocopied psychology articles the counselors kept for their CIT training. Most of it was about teamwork, one was about leadership styles, and one, stapled crooked, was a review from 2001 led by a researcher named Roy Baumeister. She read the title twice. "Bad Is Stronger Than Good." The finding inside it was plain: negative events and remarks usually affect people more strongly than positive ones of similar size. Similar size. She thought about her six comments, five of them the size of pennies and one the size of a fist, and about Marta's shoulders, and the whole arithmetic of the dinner table rearranged itself in her head.

Except that couldn't be the whole answer, because the article said nothing about what to do instead, and there were still two races left. If the negative thing always loomed larger, then cushioning just guaranteed the cushion got swallowed. But saying only the good things would leave them crabbing sideways into August. She sat on the porch steps and tried to parametrize the problem, to break it into things she could actually control: the size of the remark, the timing of it, the specificity of it. The timing she couldn't fix, the size she apparently couldn't fix either, but the specificity, that was hers.

On Saturday she asked Marta to walk to the canteen with her, because a girl who'd been hoarding her allowance all summer for the vending machine had a better claim on Marta's attention than a girl with a clipboard. They bought the cheese curl buckets that made the last weekend of camp so quietly hedonistic, and sat on the rail fence behind the boathouse, and Juliette did not count anything on her fingers. "I read something last night," she said. "It's called 'Bad Is Stronger Than Good.' Bad remarks hit harder than good ones, even when they're the same size. So I'm going to try this differently, and you can tell me if it's working."

She set her cheese curls on the fence post. "Your catch is late by about half a second, from the moment the blade passes your knee to the moment it enters the water. Tomorrow, I want you to watch my blade and match it, just at the starts. That's the whole note. There's nothing else." Marta looked at the water, then at the bucket, then at her own hands, which were still enormous and capable, and she said, "Half a second. That's it?" "That's it." Marta ate a cheese curl, considering, and then she said, "I thought you said I was slow." "I said five things and your catch was late. I just said them wrong."

The next morning was the inter-camp regatta, hot and windless, the water flat as a coin. Marta watched Juliette's blade at the line and matched it, and the boat came off the start straight for the first time all summer, and at the second buoy, three meters ahead, Marta called the switch herself, half a second early, just to see what Juliette would do.

The rabbi's study smelled of old paper and the lemon polish someone applied to the bookshelves every Friday, and Alexa sat with her borrowed chumash open to Devarim, chapter twenty-two, because in four days she had to stand in front of the confirmation class and argue that a three-thousand-year-old law could still decide something real. She had picked the verse almost at random, the way you pick a name out of a hat, and now she was stuck with it. "When you build a new house," she read aloud, underlining nothing, "you shall make a parapet for your roof, so that you do not bring bloodguilt on your house if anyone should fall from it." She copied the words into her notebook, then transcribed the Hebrew underneath, letter by careful letter, though her handwriting in the square script still looked like a child's.

The problem was Danny Sorensen, who had already told the class he intended to argue the other side. Nobody owns a flat roof in their neighborhood, he had said; nobody entertains guests up there with wine and oil lamps the way they did in the ancient world; the verse was a museum piece, beautiful and dead. Alexa wanted to beat him more than she wanted to be right, which was the part she did not say out loud to anyone, including herself. She told her mother it was about intellectual honesty. She told herself it was about intellectual honesty. Mostly it was about the way Danny had smiled when he said museum piece, as though her whole tradition were a diorama behind glass.

Her grandmother, of course, had a story. Last spring, before the arthritis got bad, Grandma Ruth had described the flat roof of the house in Rehovot where she had grown up, how her father built the low railing himself, and how the neighbors used the roof for drying figs and sleeping outside in August. Alexa had rolled her eyes at the time. Now she wished she had asked more questions, and this wishing had a shape to it, a specific shape: the railing, the figs, the particular smell of dust that her grandmother always claimed she remembered. Alexa had let herself believe she remembered it too, though she had never been to Rehovot, never seen the roof, never tasted those figs. She had told the story so many times in her own head that it had become hers.

That evening her father found the verse being used somewhere it mattered. He had been reading a responsum on his phone, one of the modern ones, and he read a passage aloud at dinner: the tradition extends the obligation beyond roofs, to any hazard on one's property. A defective ladder, an unguarded pit, a dog known to bite. The rabbis had taken the parapet and widened it, again and again, across centuries. Alexa wrote this down too, and underneath it she wrote, in smaller letters, a question she did not show anyone. If the rule could stretch that far, could it stretch all the way to her own life?

What Alexa could not see, though she believed she saw everything, was how far ahead of her Danny actually was. The day before the debate he sat in the library with a stack of photocopies she had never found, sources she had never thought to search, and he felt something that was not quite pity. He knew her argument was going to be grandiose, all sweeping claims about eternal principles, because that was always her style; she reached for the big abstraction when the small evidence would have served. He considered telling her. He turned the idea over for most of lunch and then let it go, not out of cruelty exactly, but out of something older and less flattering, the wish to win in front of people who mattered.

The debate itself was held after services, in the social hall with its folding chairs and its banner from the Purim carnival still hanging crooked over the stage. Alexa went first. She stood at the little podium and did not use the grandiose opening she had rehearsed. Instead she told them about her grandmother's roof, the parapet her great-grandfather had built, and then she said, "The rule says you build a parapet around a flat roof so that no one falls. And the tradition doesn't leave it there. It extends the rule to other hazards on your property. Any hazard." She paused. "So here is my question. My uncle just bought a trampoline for my cousins and put it up with no net around it, in a yard that slopes. Nobody in that yard is going to fall off a roof. But the falling is the same falling."

Danny, when his turn came, did not attack the verse the way she expected. He said the question wasn't whether the rule applied but who got to decide, that any text old enough to be applied must be interpreted, and interpretation wasn't a science; it was closer to a plebiscite, a vote taken across generations about what a community wanted its book to mean. He said it beautifully. Alexa sat with her hands folded and listened, and part of her understood that he was right about more than he knew, and part of her wanted to knock over the podium.

Afterward the class voted, and it split nearly even, which the rabbi declared a success and which Alexa experienced as a kind of heat in her face. Her grandmother found her by the coat rack. "The roof story," Grandma Ruth said, settling her scarf. "You told it well. But you know you never saw it. I told you about it once, on the phone." Alexa looked at her shoes. "I know," she said. "I know I made some of it up." Her grandmother nodded slowly, the way she did when she was deciding whether to say the next thing, and then she said, "The railing was real, though. I leaned on it every night that summer."

They walked out together into the parking lot, where the evening had gone cold and the first lights were coming on along the street. Alexa took her grandmother's arm at the curb, careful, deliberate, like someone steadying a railing, and did not let go until they reached the car.

Kaylee arrived at Mr. Brandt's studio ten minutes early, which was a mistake, because Mr. Brandt used early minutes to assign extra work. He was copying a page of the Mozart K. 545 first movement onto the grand piano's music stand, and he had already sharpened two pencils and set them beside a ruler like surgical instruments. "Sit," he said, as if she might not have thought of it.

"Are we cutting the music open?" she asked.

"We are marking it. Exposition, development, recapitulation." He tapped each word on the photocopied score with the ruler. "You've played this sonata since you were twelve. Now you're going to know what you played."

The trouble was that Kaylee had played it the way you ride a bike route you've ridden for years, by feel, without street names. Mr. Brandt played the first sixteen measures and stopped. "First theme," he said. "Where does it live?" She looked at the score. The key signature had no sharps or flats. "C major," she said, and he grunted, which from him was applause.

He played on. Somewhere around measure twenty-two a new tune arrived, lighter, almost giggling, and Kaylee's pencil hovered over the page without landing. She knew the moment mattered, because Mr. Brandt had a whole taxonomy of moments, but she could not say why this one did. She stared at the left-hand figure and counted the accidentals stacked along a single measure: F sharp, again, and again.

"G major," she said, mostly to herself.

"Say it again."

"The new tune is in G major. The second theme, or whatever it is."

He put his hands in his lap. "In a major-key movement in sonata form, the exposition's second theme is usually in the dominant key," he said. "So a movement in C major moves to G major. You found it. Now draw the bracket."

"Wait," she said. "I found it because you played it. You basically handed me the answer."

"I handed you sixty measures. You picked out the key change. That's not the same thing." He slid the pencil toward her. "Bracket the exposition. Both themes. Then we find where the development begins, which is where Mozart stops being polite."

She drew the bracket and kept listening. The development took the giggling tune and pulled it apart, running it through minor keys like a rumor passing through a school, each repetition slightly wrong in a new way. She liked this part best, which surprised her, because she had always thought of herself as a melody person, someone who metabolized music in whole tunes rather than in parts. In her physics class last semester she had defended the opposite instinct, arguing in an essay that systems were only collections of appearances and that the underlying structure, the logos of a thing, was a story people told afterward. Mr. Brandt would have hated the essay. Sitting here with the bracketed score, she could see both sides at once: the movement was a single continuous unfolding, and it was also these hinged sections, sedimentary, layer on layer, and neither description swallowed the other.

The recapitulation announced itself when the opening theme returned in the original key, and Kaylee marked it and then sat back. "So the second theme comes back too," she said, "but it stays home this time."

"Stays home," Mr. Brandt repeated. "That's sentimental. Also accurate." He took the score and looked at her brackets for a long time, and she noticed his eyes going to the door, where his four o'clock student, Priya, was already waiting on the porch steps with her viola case, texting. Priya wanted to drop theory entirely and just play, and Mr. Brandt wanted his Tuesday schedule to survive her senior year, and Kaylee was suddenly aware that her lesson existed inside those larger wants, small and fundable and quiet.

"Here's what I still don't get," Kaylee said. "If the form is this regular, why does it feel like it's not regular at all when you play it?"

"Because the map is not the walk." He handed the score back. "Take it home. Mark the development again and tell me where you think Mozart is toying with us versus where he's genuinely lost. There's a difference, and I want your guess, not a book's."

Priya opened the door without knocking. "Mr. Brandt, I've decided I'm quitting theory and becoming famous instead."

"Then you'll need theory more than the rest of us," he said, and stood up to switch on the metronome.

Mathis had forty minutes before the library closed, and the test on the screen was still red. He had come to the public library every Tuesday since September, carrying his mother's old laptop in a canvas bag with a broken zipper, because at home the wifi dropped whenever his stepfather ran the microwave. Here, at the corner table by the geology shelves, the signal held, and nobody asked him why a sixteen-year-old was teaching himself Java from a book with a cracked spine and no provenance he could determine, no name inside the cover, only a coffee ring on chapter twelve.

The chapter wanted him to build a class called BankAccount with a private field for the balance and getter methods to read it. He understood the idea of private. It was like the locked drawer in the kitchen where his mother kept the rent money, except the class was supposed to hand you a key, a small polished method that opened the drawer, showed you what was inside, and closed it again. He typed the class out, then the test, then ran it, and the failure message arrived like a letter addressed to somebody else: expected 50, but was 40. He stared at it. He had written the numbers himself, and still the sentence read like an accusation.

The stakes were not abstract. The coding club at school had a slot for one sophomore at the regional competition in November, and Priya Shah wanted it as badly as he did. She had finished the exercises two weeks early and had a way of mentioning this near his locker, casually, the way people mention weather. Mr. Okafor had said the slot would go to whoever could pass the chapter test unassisted, in his presence, on Thursday. So this red bar on the screen was not just a red bar. It was Priya's name on a form instead of his.

He checked his class first. Private field, yes. Getter, yes. He set the balance to forty in one test and to fifty in another, and when he ran them, the message insisted again: expected 50, but was 40. He pressed his palms against his eyes. On the shelf beside him sat a sample of obsidian, part of a display the librarians had put up for a rock-hunting exhibit, dark and glassy, igneous rock cooled so fast it had no time to form crystals. He turned it over once and set it back. Some part of him was doing the same thing, cooling too fast, refusing to let anything settle into order.

Then he thought about the sentence differently. Expected 50. He had never asked himself what the word expected was doing there. He had written two numbers into a line of test code, and he had assumed the first one was his answer, the thing his class produced. But the message said expected, which meant the first number was the wish, not the outcome. The second number, the actual one, was what his class really did. He scrolled up slowly, the way you slow your steps when you think you hear something behind you, and looked at the line he had typed: the fifty came first, the forty second. He had put them in the wrong order. The test wasn't telling him his arithmetic was broken. It was telling him he had written the wish where the result belonged.

He fixed it, swapped the two, and ran everything again. Green. Both tests green, quiet and unceremonious, the way true things often arrive. He sat back, and for a moment he let himself feel the whole shape of what had happened. He had trusted his instinct that the first number was his answer, and his instinct had been wrong, and the book in front of him had never said otherwise. But the computer had said it, in its flat way, the moment he made the mistake. That was the thing he was starting to love about this work and also the thing that unsettled him: the machine would let you misunderstand it for as long as you liked, and then it would tell you the truth exactly once, in a sentence you had to already know how to read.

Still, honesty pressed on him. The tests were green now, but he had not written them the way the chapter asked. He had skipped the part about testing the getter when the balance was zero, because zero felt like a nothing, and nothings felt safe, and he suspected that was exactly where he was wrong. He wrote the zero test, ran it, and it passed, which somehow told him less than a failure would have. He could not shake the sense that he was memorizing the shape of correctness rather than understanding it, that on Thursday, in front of Mr. Okafor, some small trap would open under him precisely where his confidence had sutured itself over a gap.

Priya came in at eight, ten minutes before close, because of course she did, her own laptop under her arm, heading for the table by the windows. She passed his corner and glanced at his screen, at the two green bars, and stopped.

"That chapter?" she said. "The failure messages messed me up for an hour. I kept thinking my class was wrong."

"What was it?"

"You have to put the expected value first," she said. "The actual value goes second. I had them backwards the whole time."

Mathis looked at her, and something in him resisted, wanting to keep the discovery his, and something else, quieter, wanted to laugh. "Yeah," he said. "I found that out about ten minutes ago."

She studied the green bars on his screen for a moment longer than she needed to, then pulled out the chair across from him and opened her laptop. "You want to try the zero case? That one's tricky."

The library had kept its evening habits even in June: the radiators ticking though the heat was off, the tall windows going from gold to gray, the math club occupying the carrels nearest the atlas shelf because nobody else wanted them. Keira spread her worksheet against the wood grain and weighted the corners with two pencils and her calculator. At the next carrel, Deshawn was muttering at his own paper, and Priya had already finished and was reading a novel with the worksheet face down beside her, which was a kind of showing off Keira chose not to impute to arrogance. Priya was probably just fast.

The problem was the last one on the sheet. Find the area enclosed between the line y equals x plus two and the parabola y equals x squared, between the points where they crossed. Keira had found the crossing points first, setting the two expressions equal and getting x equals negative one and x equals two, and she had drawn the picture carefully, ruler and all. In her sketch the line rode above the curve the whole way across, a chord drawn tight over a sagging bow.

Deshawn leaned over the gap between the carrels. "What did you get?"

"Six." She turned her paper so he could see the columns of algebra.

He frowned at his own result. "I got four and a half. Same interval. Same curves." He slid his work toward her, and she read it the way she read proofs, line by line, expecting to find a dropped sign. There was no dropped sign. He had integrated the parabola and subtracted the integral of the line, top to bottom as it were, and the arithmetic underneath was flawless.

"You subtracted in the wrong order," she said.

"That can't matter."

She looked at her own sketch again. Somewhere in the back of her mind was an inchoate idea about negative area, something a substitute teacher had once said in the fall and she had filed without examining. She didn't want to lean on half a memory, and she didn't want to simply assert that order mattered, because Deshawn was the kind of person who needed to see a thing break before he believed it was fragile. She took a fresh sheet and wrote it out twice: once the line's integral minus the parabola's, once the parabola's minus the line's. Six, then negative six. Same magnitude, opposite sign.

"So one of them is wrong," Deshawn said.

"Or one of them is upside down." She set the two sheets side by side. "On our interval the line is the upper function and the parabola is the lower one. If you subtract the other way, you get the negative of the area. You have to take the upper function minus the lower function over the interval where they're ordered that way."

Deshawn turned back to his diagram, the one he had drawn without a ruler, quick and confident, and looked at it for a long moment. Keira watched him retrace it with his pen, following the line with its steady climb, then the curve hanging beneath it between the crossing points. Down at the reference desk, Ms. Okafor was logging the day's disbursement of loaned calculators into a green ledger, her pencil moving in small unhurried strokes, and the ordinary sound of it made the carrels feel less like a contest and more like a workshop.

"The whole interval, though," Deshawn said. "What if they crossed in the middle somewhere? What if the line went under?"

"Then you'd have to split it." Keira drew a second sketch, a line and a curve braiding through each other, and divided it at the crossing with a dotted vertical. "Upper minus lower on each piece, where they're ordered that way on that piece."

"So the order isn't a rule you memorize. It's just which one's on top."

"That's how it looks to me." She said it plainly, because she was aware of what she hadn't verified. Somewhere past the crossing points, if you extended the interval, the parabola would climb above the line, and she had only checked the ordering between negative one and two, by eye, on a hand-drawn figure. Her certainty was local, and she was willing to say so. "I checked it on the picture. I haven't proved it algebraically for every point between."

Deshawn pulled his worksheet back and began crossing out with single clean strokes, the way he did everything, and Priya lowered her novel to watch the correction travel down his page. "Six," he said, when he reached the bottom.

"Six," Keira agreed. She folded the two comparison sheets together and slid them into her folder, along with the sketch of the braided curves, though nothing on the worksheet had asked for it. Outside the tall windows the streetlights had come on, and the yellow squares lay across the atlas shelf in long parallelograms. Deshawn clicked his pen twice and wrote at the top of his page, in the margin where the teacher would see it, upper minus lower.

The studio smelled of lemon polish and the particular dust that collects under piano keys, and Juliette sat with the score of Mozart's K. 332 flattened on the music stand like a suspect under interrogation. Mr. Barra had given her one week and a stack of colored pencils. "Mark the exposition," he had said. "Mark the development. Mark the recapitulation. And be prepared to defend your borders." She had assumed he was joking. He was not joking.

"You've drawn a green line at measure twenty-three," he said now, tapping the page with a pencil that had been sharpened almost to extinction. "Why there?"

"Because the second theme starts there. New material, new key. It feels like a door opening."

"Feels," he repeated, in the tone of a man who had won this argument many times and was politely bored of winning it. "Juliette, you cannot submit feels to a jury. What is your evidence?"

She looked at the page. The truth was that she had chosen measure twenty-three because her older brother, a pugnacious conservatory student who argued about Mozart the way other people argued about politics, had told her the second theme was "obviously there, are you blind." She had believed him partly because he was usually right and partly because arguing with him was like volunteering for a debate you had already lost. Now, facing Mr. Barra, whose eyebrows had the patience of geological formations, she found she wanted to arrive at her own verdict rather than inherit his.

"I don't have evidence yet," she said. "I have a hunch and a bossy brother."

"Good. A hunch is where analysis starts. Acquittal of a hunch takes longer." He crossed to the piano. "Before we convict anything, let's listen to the middle section. You marked the development starting here." He played the passage, and it wandered, as developments do, key to key like a traveler who had lost the map but not the will to move. Juliette followed along, and something began to happen in her ear, a kind of acclimating, the way a swimmer stops fighting the cold water and lets it become the medium she moves in.

Then, near the end of the development, he slowed down deliberately and let a single harmony ring out, again and again, low in the left hand. The chord sat there and leaned. Juliette, without deciding to, leaned with it, tipping forward on the bench edge, because the music sounded exactly as if the opening tune were about to walk back through the door.

She sat up, caught herself, and heard her own voice arrive before her caution could stop it. "That's a retransition, isn't it. That's the part near the end of the development that keeps hitting the dominant of the home key, so you're waiting for the tonic and the first theme to come back."

Mr. Barra lifted his hands from the keys. For a moment he looked like a man whose birthday had come early. "Where did you learn that word?"

"I didn't learn it. My body learned it just now. My body was leaning."

"Your body," he said gravely, "is a better theorist than your brother." He played the chord once more, let it hang, and then, with the tiny theatrical cruelty available only to pianists, closed the lid over the keys. The chord stayed unresolved in the room like a question addressed to someone who had just left.

"That's horrible," Juliette said, laughing. "You can't just stop there."

"That is precisely what the retransition does to the whole audience," he said. "At concerts I've watched students tip forward in their seats at that chord, certain the opening tune is seconds away, and Mozart makes them wait. You leaned into a dominant. Congratulations. You are now officially suspicious of anything that sounds like a door opening."

She went back to the score with new eyes, or rather new ears attached to old eyes, and found that the retransition worked as a landmark from which she could reason backward. If the recapitulation began at the return of the first theme in the tonic, then she could find it, and having found it, she could measure the development's true borders. Which meant the second theme question could be settled by structure instead of by sibling volume. She picked up the orange pencil, hovered it over measure twenty-three, and then, with a small private smile, moved it four measures later, where the new material actually established itself in the dominant key.

"For the record," she said, handing the page across, "my brother is going to fight me on this."

"Let him," said Mr. Barra, examining her new line. "You've got the retransition on your side. He's only got opinions." He reopened the piano lid, set his fingers over that same leaning chord, and pressed it once, softly, watching her the whole time.

Juliette leaned forward again.

Lucas had the market stall from six in the morning, and by nine the milk chocolate still had not set. He touched the sheet pan again with the back of his knuckle. The surface gave, faintly, the way a candle gives, and left a smudge where his knuckle had been. Behind him the dark chocolate bark, made from the same afternoon of work, sat in clean squares that knocked against each other when he shifted the pan.

The weekend before, his dark chocolate had tempered on the first try. He had seeded it, stirred it, watched the thermometer fall, and poured at the number the supplier's card gave him, and the bark had come out glossy, with a snap he could hear across the kitchen. He had written it in the front of the notebook: dark, 31 to 32, pour. His aunt, whose stall this was, had taken a square to the coffee vendor and come back with an order for forty more, and Lucas had decided, in the flat way one decides something already half decided, that he was good at this.

The milk chocolate was a different matter. He had run the same procedure, the same careful stirring, the same seeding, and poured it at the same reading, 31 degrees on the thermometer, because the number was written in his hand and the procedure was written in his habit. Three hours later the surface was dull in patches and soft everywhere, and the coffee vendor's wife had just asked for a sample of the milk bark for her daughter, who disliked dark.

He carried the pan to the back of the stall, past the jars of honey and the baskets his aunt had bought from a retired potter, and sat on the upturned crate they used as a step. A couple at the next table argued about whether the musician at the far end of the market counted as tangential to the shopping experience or as the reason to come at all. Lucas took out his phone and searched for the supplier, found the page for the milk chocolate coins he had bought, and scrolled past the paragraphs about single-origin cacao and the photograph of a smiling farmer, past all the language that seemed designed to commodify a feeling rather than describe a product.

The specification was further down, in small type under a table. He read it twice. Milk chocolate, it said, working temperature 29 to 30 degrees Celsius. He looked at the thermometer clipped to his cooling bowl, which read 28 and falling, then back at the screen. Under the table, one line: milk fat softens the cocoa butter. He said it out loud, quietly, the way one tests whether a sentence will hold weight. "Milk fat softens the cocoa butter."

His aunt came back from the coffee stand with two paper cups. She looked at the pan, at the smudge his knuckle had left, and said nothing, which was her way of leaving a question in the room. "I poured the milk at dark temperature," Lucas said. "Thirty-one. It wants 29 to 30. I was working it too hot." She handed him a cup and sat on the second crate. "So remake it," she said. "The order's for four o'clock."

He chopped the failed batch back into the bowl, melted it past every number he had trusted, and started again. The market filled around them while he stirred. The musician moved closer, playing something with a repeating figure, and the argument at the next table reignited briefly, the man saying that the man's own maxim about shopping efficiency had ruined more Saturdays than any song ever had. Lucas kept his eyes on the thermometer. At 34 he seeded. At 31 the dark chocolate would have gone onto the marble, and he made himself keep stirring instead, waiting, letting the milk chocolate come down to where it actually wanted to be, somewhere in the low thirties and then under.

At 30 he moved fast, spread it thin on the marble, folded it back, and at 29 he poured. The bark went out in the sunless shade of the awning, and he set a timer and then set a second one on his phone because he did not trust the first. He cleaned the marble while he waited, not watching the pan, and when the timer sounded he touched the surface with the back of his knuckle.

It held. The smudge, when he pulled his hand back, was barely there, a whisper of matte on a field of shine. He broke off a corner, and the piece came away with a clean, high sound, like a knuckle cracking. He took the sample to the coffee vendor's wife, and she bit it, and her daughter, who had been looking at the honey, turned around.

The library smelled like radiator dust and old glue, and Mackenzie had spread her failed quiz across half a table by the window. At the top, in her teacher's green pen, circled twice: minus one, and beside it, "No + C on definite integrals." She had written the same thing on every single problem, four times, proud of her thoroughness, and each one had cost her a mark. Her mother had said it was unfair, marks taken for something so small, but Mackenzie suspected the marks were not the point. The point was that she did not know why.

She flipped back through her notes to the day they had learned antiderivatives. There it was in her own handwriting, underlined twice: always add the constant. Always. So when the definite integrals arrived a week later, she had carried the habit over like a passenger who missed the stop. Now she stared at problem one, the integral from one to three of two x, and tried to see what her teacher had seen.

Dre, two tables away, was not studying. He had a paperback open, but his eyes kept lifting toward the circulation desk, where a girl with a nose ring was checking returns. Mackenzie had known Dre since sophomore year, long enough to know the paperback was a prop. He wanted to ask the girl about the button on her lanyard, some band logo he recognized, and had been circling the question for three weeks the way rain circles a hill before finding a stream.

"Are you actually doing math," he said, without turning his head, "or are you just frowning at it."

"Both," she said. "Come here. I lost four marks and I don't understand it."

He dragged his chair over, keeping the girl at the desk in his peripheral vision like a sailor keeping a lighthouse. Mackenzie copied the problem onto a fresh sheet. The antiderivative of two x was x squared. She knew that much. She wrote it out, from one to three, and then, because the habit was stronger than the correction, she added plus C. Three squared plus C. One squared plus C.

Then she subtracted, the way the notation demanded, top number minus bottom number. Nine plus C minus one plus C. She did the arithmetic. Eight, and the C minus the C, gone, nothing left of it at all. She sat back. The constant was added to both and then subtracted away, and it simply canceled, every time, no matter what C was, no matter how enormous or small. It was not that the constant was forbidden. It was that it could not survive the subtraction. She had been carrying something across the equal sign that the equal sign itself would not let her keep.

"Wait," she said. "It's not a rule I broke. It just doesn't matter. It cancels." She did the problem again without the C, purely to watch it come out to eight again, identical. There was something almost melancholic in it, she thought, a quantity that could be anything at all and still vanish between the two ends of the interval, unremembered by the answer. Then she wondered whether that thought was the kind of thing you were allowed to think about math, or whether her rationalism, her need for everything to reduce to clean reasons, was just going to have to sit beside a stranger fact: that some things you carry are real and still leave no trace.

"So is that why she took the marks?" Dre said.

"Maybe she took them because I wrote something that does nothing. Or because I should have seen it myself." Mackenzie looked at the circled corrections and decided she would ask, tomorrow, before class, not to argue but to check whether she had it right. That was the part she could not do alone: she could see the cancellation on the page, and she believed it, but she wanted one other person to confirm that what she saw was what was there.

Dre had stopped pretending to read. The girl at the desk was closing a drawer, unclipping her lanyard, clearly near the end of her shift. He stood, put the paperback in his back pocket, and Mackenzie watched him straighten his collar in the window's reflection. "If it's still light out," he said, "I'm going to go ask her about the band."

"Go," Mackenzie said, and she was already writing the next problem, interval at the top, C at the ready, curious to watch it disappear again.

The recipe on Alexa's phone said to pull the pork roast at 145 degrees, and at 6:15 the thermometer read exactly that, so she lifted it out of the oven and set it on the cutting board with a sense of ceremony she immediately distrusted. Her mother was due home at seven with the twins, her father was already at the sink washing lettuce with the grim efficiency of a man who believed salad was a moral act, and the whole dinner rested on Alexa because it was her turn, and because her grandmother's recipe card was propped against the backsplash like a small flat judge.

"Done already?" her father said, peering over. "That's fast."

"It hit the number." She showed him the phone screen, where the number sat in bold type beside a photograph of a glistening, improbable roast.

He dried his hands slowly. "Your grandfather pulled things early, always. I thought it was superstition." He paused. "There might be something to it. My brother's a chef now, you know."

She did know. Uncle Marcus was the family's designated argument, the one who'd left a stable job for a kitchen and had been either vindicated or ruined by it depending on which aunt you asked. Alexa had spent years treating the two men as a choice she'd eventually have to make: her father's world of numbers and pensions, or Marcus's world of heat and improvisation. Lately she'd begun to suspect the choice was a false one, a bromide adults repeated so they wouldn't have to think harder, but she hadn't yet found a way to say so without sounding like a college essay.

At 6:40 she sliced into the roast and found the center pale pink and dense, the juices running thin. Not ruined. But the outer inch had gone gray and dry, and she stood there with the knife still in her hand, understanding that the number had been true and the result was still wrong.

"Carryover cooking," her father said quietly, not looking up from the lettuce. "Marcus told me once. It keeps cooking after it comes out. Something that size can climb several degrees while it rests."

"You knew this and you watched me pull it at 145?"

"You didn't ask. And I wasn't sure I believed it." He set down the towel. "I thought it was one of his theories."

She stared at the roast, and at the thermometer, and at the clock, which now gave her exactly thirteen minutes before the minivan full of siblings arrived. Her father's instinct, she realized, had been the same instinct as Uncle Marcus's: pull it early, trust the rest. One had codified it into a rule with a name; the other had simply done it for forty years without a word. She had trusted the printed number over both of them because the number was clean and the men were intransigent in ways that exhausted her, and the roast had paid for it.

"It's still dinner," she said, and carved the rest quickly, piling the pink center slices on the platter and hiding the gray ones beneath the potatoes she'd quartered and roasted hard. When her mother came through the door at 7:02 with the twins shedding backpacks like molting birds, the table was set, the platter was warm, and Alexa was slicing bread with the concentration of someone defusing something.

Her mother took a bite and closed her eyes briefly. "The middle is perfect."

"Pull it early next time," Alexa said to her father, and passed him the platter.

"Six degrees under," he said. "I'll write it on the card."

She watched him actually do it, Grandmother's spidery handwriting getting a small inked line beneath it, an addition rather than a correction, and she decided she would text Marcus in the morning to ask what else he knew that nobody had thought to tell her. For now she ladled applesauce, told the twins to sit, and said, "Plates."

The exam was in nine days, and Hudson's biology grade was a C minus that his mother had described, in the tone she reserved for dead livestock, as "unacceptable." He'd been sent to his grandfather's farm for the summer with a textbook and a threat: bring the grade up or forget the car in September. Now he sat on an overturned feed bucket in the barn loft, trying to memorize the equation for cellular respiration off an index card. C6H12O6 plus 6 O2 yields 6 CO2 plus 6 H2O plus energy. He read it aloud four times, and each time it slid out of his head like water off a tarp.

His cousin Dana found him there at noon, when she came up to throw down hay. "You look like a cow with a math problem," she said.

"I look like a guy who's going to fail biology." He held up the card. "This is supposed to mean something. Glucose plus oxygen becomes carbon dioxide plus water, plus energy. I can say it. I don't get it."

Dana, home from her first year of college, took the card, read it, and handed it back with the indifference of someone who had already survived the course. "Come to the pond tonight," she said. "Bring the card. I have an idea, and if it's wrong, you can throw me in."

That evening, after the chores, they walked out past the lower pasture to the pond, where the frogs were already arguing. Dana lay down on the dock with her chin over the edge and breathed on the water until a small fog bloomed and faded on the surface. "Breathe on it," she said. "Tell me what you're breathing out."

"Air," Hudson said, and breathed on the pond himself.

"You're breathing out carbon dioxide. Six molecules of it for every glucose you burn. So here's my question, and don't look at the card. Where did the carbon come from?"

Hudson stood there while the frogs went on. The carbon had to come from somewhere; nothing in a body is free. He thought about dinner, the corn and pork chops, the toast at breakfast, all of it broken down to glucose, this sugar with six carbons in it, C6, and he thought about his own lungs taking the O2 in and handing CO2 back to the pond. The carbon in the fog on the water had been corn this morning. The equation stopped being a card and started being a route, a map of the food becoming him becoming breath. "The glucose," he said. "The carbon in my breath was in the glucose. In the corn. The whole equation, it's just, glucose and oxygen go in, carbon dioxide and water come out, and the energy's the point."

"And the water?" Dana said.

He worked at it, mouth open, doing the atom bookkeeping on his fingers. "Six waters come out too. It's all right there. In. Out. Plus energy." He was almost laughing. "It's the whole thing. It's what I've been trying to memorize for a week and it's just breathing at a pond."

Later that night he wrote a letter to his lab partner, Reese, who had moved to Ohio in June and whose handwriting was the only thing keeping them both afloat in the class. He wrote it at the kitchen table under the one good bulb, and it went, in part: "Reese. Forget the flashcards. Tonight my cousin made me breathe on a pond and asked where the carbon came from, and I got it. Glucose plus six oxygens, that's what goes in; six carbon dioxides plus six waters plus energy, that's what comes out. The energy is what the mitochondria are for, apparently, like tiny furnaces, and I have been carrying furnaces around my whole body without ever once being introduced to them. I feel like I owe them an apology, or possibly a sacrifice. If you memorize anything, memorize dinner becoming breath. Also I found a snake in the grain room, Grandpa says it's harmless, Grandpa also says tornadoes are harmless. Study. Hudson." He mailed it the next morning at the rural route box, propitiating the biology gods with his one good stamp.

The next afternoon his grandfather found him at the pond again, breathing on the water like a dragon. "You plotting something?" the old man asked.

"Learning respiration."

"From a pond."

"From my breath. It's not solipsism," Hudson added, because Dana had used the word the night before and he'd liked it, "the pond's involved. The CO2 goes into the algae, they make oxygen back." His grandfather grunted, which on this farm could mean anything from approval to a warning, and walked on toward the cattle.

The one thing Hudson couldn't settle, and was honest enough with himself to admit he couldn't, was the energy. He could count carbons and oxygens like coins, but the part of the equation that just said "plus energy," the part that let him climb the loft ladder, that ATP the textbook kept promising in the mitochondria, stayed a kind of promise he couldn't hold. He had two maps now, the card and the pond, and he trusted the pond, and he told himself that was enough for a multiple-choice test even if it wasn't enough for the truth.

On exam day in August, his grandfather drove him the forty miles to the county summer school, and waited in the truck with the radio on. Question fourteen gave the equation with three numbers missing, and Hudson wrote 6, 6, 6 without slowing, and under his breath, so quietly that the proctor never looked up, he was breathing on the desk, watching the faint fog appear and vanish, carbon that had been wheat a day ago, going out into the room.

He came out squinting into the lot, got in the truck, and said, "Corn, oxygen, carbon dioxide, water, energy."

His grandfather put the truck in gear. "Then we'll get you that car," he said, "if you mow the hay first."

Levi had signed up for the language exchange because the form was due at five and everything else was full. Now he sat at a carrel near the library's back window with a photocopied German newspaper article in front of him and a sophomore named Maren across the table, waiting.

The article was short, six paragraphs, about a town voting on whether to close its tram line. His assignment was to read it aloud and then summarise it in his own words, in German, without notes. He had spent forty minutes on the first paragraph the night before and still could not find the verbs.

"Start anywhere," Maren said. She had a coffee she wasn't supposed to have, and she turned the paper sideways to look at it. "You're stalling."

"I'm surveying." He ran his finger along the second line. Half the words began with capital letters, and it wasn't the start of sentences, and it wasn't names. He counted on his fingers: four capitalized words in one short line, then a comma, then three more. "Why is this one big," he said, pointing at a word in the middle. "Fahrzeug. That's not a name."

"German capitalizes every noun," Maren said. "Not just names."

Levi looked at the sentence again. He had assumed the capitals were decoration, or an alphabet with different rules he would never learn, and instead they were doing work. He put his pencil under each capitalized word and the skeleton of the sentence came up out of the page: the nouns, one after another, marked. The little words between them, the lowercase ones, were the connective tissue. He could not translate the sentence yet, but he could see its shape.

He tried the third paragraph, the one with the vote. Two capitalized words sat next to each other, and he recognised the second one from a class handout: Plebiszit. "Plebiscite," he said. "There's a vote. The town is voting on something." Maren made him say it again with the proper stress and wrote the article's actual word on the margin, which turned out to be a different word for the same thing, and she said both were used, the borrowed one in headlines because it was shorter.

The reading aloud went badly for a while. He pronounced one word three ways in three sentences and Maren corrected him each time until he could hear the difference himself. In the fourth paragraph a councillor was quoted calling the tram company's chairman bellicose, and Levi had to stop, because the word looked like a name to him and he had capitalised it in his head as a person. "It's an adjective," Maren said. "It means aggressive, warlike." He underlined it and moved on.

The summary was the real test. He had to put the article down and say what happened in it, out loud, in German. He assembled his sentences in his head and then said them too fast, and one of them came out with the wrong noun capitalized, a verb dressed up as a thing, and Maren laughed and told him to slow down. He tried again. The town had voted on the tram line. The vote was close. A company director had absconded with the maintenance funds two years earlier, which was why the line was losing money, which was why the vote was happening at all, and Levi managed the whole chain of events in five crooked sentences and then sat back.

"Better," Maren said. "Your summary said the director absconded with the funds and then everyone voted. The article says the vote came first." She tapped the paper. "Order matters in news."

He looked at the paragraphs again, following the capitals, and saw that she was right; the vote was announced in the first paragraph, and the absconding didn't appear until near the end, as background, as the thing the town was still angry about. He had flattened the story into a cause-and-effect chain because that was how he would have written it. The German article had arranged the same events in an order he hadn't expected, and he wasn't sure yet whether that was the newspaper's style or something about how the language held information, whether the nouns came first in German the way they had come first for him on the page.

He asked Maren. She thought about it with the coffee halfway to her mouth.

"I don't know," she said. "Read me another one."

The gray would not behave. Kevin had mixed it from titanium white and lamp black, the same two tubes, the same knife, yet the stripe he had laid across the left side of his canvas looked like ash from a warm fire while the stripe on the right looked like February pavement. He scraped the palette clean and mixed again, weighing the pigment on the little spring scale Mr. Okafor kept by the sink, and still the new gray split the same way, warm where it touched the orange field, cold where it crossed the blue.

He was painting his brother Marcus for the senior show, Marcus sitting on the hood of the car their mother was selling, and the whole point of the picture was restraint. Everything else in the room that afternoon was loud. Priya was gluing a hundred paper flames onto a board for a piece about anger, which she described as possibly gratuitous but necessary, and Mr. Okafor was telling anyone who would listen that the district's new schedule would disenfranchise kids who could only take one elective, that art was the first thing pushed out when the choices narrowed.

Dana leaned over from the next easel, brush paused. "Yours looks two different colors," she said.

"It's one color. I weighed it."

"Then your paint is haunted."

Kevin set the knife down and looked at the canvas the way he'd learned to look at proofs in geometry, hunting for the thing he was assuming. The gray was one color. The stripes were identical. What surrounded them was not. He held a fresh chip of the gray against the orange and it went warmer immediately, like it had been sitting near a stove; against the blue it cooled. He moved the chip back and forth, orange, blue, orange, blue, and the chip shifted each time, faithful as a shadow.

Dana was doing something similar with her own painting without noticing, a herd of elephants on a wide green savanna, complaining that the mud on their legs looked purple beside the grass and brown beside the acacia. "Maybe we got a bad batch of gray," she said. "Maybe it's the water."

At the back of the room there was a shelf of books nobody touched, spines faded to the color of weak tea. Kevin found one on color with a cracked cloth binding and sat on the floor with it while Priya's glue gun ticked behind him. The index sent him to a page about a chemist, Michel Eugène Chevreul, who had published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839. The page said that a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it. He read the sentence twice. Orange pushed the gray toward blue, and blue pushed it toward orange, and neither had laid a finger on the actual paint.

"It's called simultaneous contrast," he said to Dana, holding the book open. "Chevreul, 1839. A color shifts toward the complement of whatever's next to it."

"So the paint's fine."

"The paint was always fine."

She came and knelt beside him, still holding her muddy brush away from her jeans, and read the page herself. "So my elephants aren't purple, my green is just shouting at them."

"That's the problem, though," Kevin said. "It's not a problem with the paint, so I can't fix it with paint." He looked at Marcus on the hood of the car, at the gray of Marcus's sweatshirt crossing from the orange late light into the blue shade under the windshield. He had wanted the sweatshirt to be the quiet center of the picture, the one thing that held still. Now he understood that it could never hold still, that the same gray would always be two grays, that this was not a flaw in his mixing but the way eyes worked, and that Chevreul had written it down almost two hundred years ago for a dye works, of all places, because their blacks kept coming out wrong.

He tried three things before the bell. He muted the orange so it would push less. He let the stripe break at the boundary, warm on one side and cool on the other, and found he liked the honesty of it, the way it recorded what actually happened where the light changed. Then he painted a thin band of raw canvas between the fields, and the gray settled somewhere between, undecided, and that was truest of all, because he could not say whether his brother was coming home from the army in June or not, and the picture had been about not being able to say.

Dana cleaned her brush at the sink and looked back at her savanna. "So it's not a mistake," she said. "It's just how it is."

"It's just how it is," Kevin said. He picked up the chip of gray one more time and held it against Marcus's face, and watched it warm.

The usher gave the score in Thomas's hands a suspicious look, as if he might be planning to read along in secret code, but she let him through with his three sticky notes fluttering from the pages: blue, yellow, green. He had a seat at the end of row F, close enough to see the pianist's hands, and forty minutes before the lights dimmed he spread the score across his knees and tried to codify what Mr. Alvarez kept telling him he heard but could not yet hear.

The exam was on Tuesday. Analyse the first movement, mark the form, justify your marks. Thomas had listened to the recording eleven times in his bedroom, headphones on, pencil hovering, and every time the movement dissolved into a bright river of sound that carried him along without ever showing him its floor. His father, querulous from the doorway about the volume, had asked what the point was of studying something you already liked, and Thomas had not had an answer. That was part of what bothered him. He liked it too much to take it apart, and he needed to take it apart to pass.

The blue note went on the first page, because that much was certain. He knew the names now, had copied them from the whiteboard until they stopped feeling like a foreign language: the exposition, which presented the themes. Two of them, in this one, a firm little march and then a softer, singing answer. He had written them out in his own hand and could hum each on command. That was the beginning. Blue for beginning.

The green note was the problem. The recapitulation, the coming back. Somewhere in the last third of the movement, he believed, the march would return and everything would settle, and he had to be able to say where. The yellow note, the development, was the part between, where the themes were worked through other keys, taken apart and reassembled, traveling somewhere else and then, somehow, arriving home. On paper this seemed simple. In sound it was like trying to mark the exact moment a river becomes a lake.

A girl dropped into the seat beside his, saw the score, and leaned over. "K. 331?" she said, reading the number off the cover. "That's tonight's opener."

"Is that cheating, bringing this?" Thomas asked.

"Nobody's checking." She had a scarf pushed back off her hair and a programme folded into a fan she wasn't using. "You a student?"

"Exam Tuesday. I have to mark the whole thing and I can't find where the exposition stops."

"Where the second theme settles in the new key," she said, as if it were obvious, and then looked as if she wished she'd said less. Her mother shushed her from the next seat. The lights went down.

The pianist walked out, sat, and did not pause. The march began, and Thomas followed with his finger, and for the first time the page matched the sound: there was his first theme, there the singing answer, and there, unmistakable, a small cadence, a closing of a door. His hand moved in the dark and pressed the blue note down, its edge just catching the light. The girl beside him nodded once.

Then the development, and he understood immediately why he had failed in his bedroom. It wasn't chaos; it was the same two themes, but restless, each one tugged into a new key like a word repeated until it sounded foreign. He tried to track the march and lost it, found the singing theme wearing a minor key like a borrowed coat, lost that too. The music was doing precisely what his teacher had promised and he could not hold any of it. He felt a familiar despair, the kind that made him want to decide analysis was a fraud, that the music was an animal and the score was immunology, the study of something alive done through things already dead.

He stopped trying to track everything. Instead he waited for the one thing he could wait for: the march, in the original key, at full voice. A return. When it came, it came so cleanly that he laughed out loud, one syllable, quickly smothered, earning a glare from the row behind. He pressed the green note onto the page while the music was still declaring itself, then worked backward and placed the yellow one where the traveling had begun. Three colours. He could see the whole shape of it now, a leaving and a straying and a homecoming, and the fact that the homecoming felt inevitable only after it arrived was, he decided, not a failure of his analysis but the thing itself.

At intermission the girl stood to stretch. "Where'd you put the green?" she asked. He showed her. She studied it, and her mouth twitched. "You're one bar early. Listen to the bass." She hummed the low line, and there it was, the harmony still leaning, arriving home one measure later than the melody pretended to. He moved the note, and his ears agreed with the paper.

On Tuesday, he thought, he would draw the three sections in three colours and write underneath: the return is where the harmony says it is, not where you want it to be. He put the pencil behind his ear and followed the second half of the concert with no score at all.
