The bus smelled of diesel and orange peel, and Alyssa had The Catcher in the Rye open on her knees with a highlighter uncapped and going nowhere. Across the aisle, Dev was failing the same book for the second time, which he announced by dropping his copy on the seat between them like an accusation. "The guy says he's a liar," Dev said. "Page whatever. So why am I supposed to care about anything after that?"

Alyssa found the line and read it aloud, quiet enough that the freshmen up front wouldn't turn around. "I'm the most terrific liar you ever saw in your life." She'd read it four times already that week, and each time it had shifted under her, the way a word repeated too often goes strange in the mouth. "He tells us he lies," she said. "Right at the start. In 1951, when the book came out, that must have knocked people flat."

"So it's all fake?"

"That's the question, isn't it." She tapped the cover. The problem had been circumscribing itself in her notes all week: if he lies, does the lying make everything false, or does admitting it make him honest, or does the honesty itself become a performance she was falling for? Her English teacher had refused to answer, which Alyssa had found obnoxious until she started to suspect the refusal was the whole assignment.

Dev leaned over and flipped to the back, as if the answer were printed there. "Holden," he said. "Where do they get these names. Holden."

"That's actually the interesting part." She had looked it up at midnight instead of sleeping. "The etymology people trace it to 'hold,' like hollow land, or a keeper of something. I don't know if Salinger knew or cared. I might be making that matter more than it does." Dev made a face that said he had stopped listening at the word etymology, so she moved on.

The bus hit the pothole by the credit union, and her highlighter rolled, and Dev caught it without looking, an old habit from years of shared bus seats. "Okay," he said. "Say I believe half of it. How do I know which half?"

"Exactly." This was the part she'd been chewing on. "You don't audit him line by line. You watch what the voice does. When he tells you he's a liar, that's a confession, but it's also a contract. He's saying, you're inside this with me now, you know my rules. It's like..." She searched the bus for it. The seat fabric was old and friable, wearing through to yellow foam at the corners where decades of students had picked at it. "It's like this seat. It's coming apart, and you can see the stuffing, and somehow seeing the stuffing makes you trust it more than a new seat, because at least you know what you're sitting on."

Dev considered the foam. "That's the dumbest analogy I've ever heard," he said, but he wrote it down. He wrote it in the margin of her book, actually, in pen, which she would have killed him for a year ago.

Then the twist, which came from behind them: Priya, who never spoke on the bus, who had earbuds in for the entire four years Alyssa had known her, pulled one out and said, "He's lying about lying. That's the trick. The stuff he calls lies are the true parts, because they're the ones he's ashamed of." The bus went quiet in that way it did when someone unexpected talked. Priya put the earbud back in, apparently finished with public speaking until graduation.

Alyssa sat with that for three more stops. It was a better reading than hers, and it undid her seat analogy entirely, and she found she didn't mind, or minded and wanted it anyway. Maybe Holden's confessed lies were the honest material and his confident parts were the performance. Maybe both were true at once, and the narrator's unreliability wasn't a flaw to correct but the actual weather of the book. She couldn't prove any of it, and the paper was due Friday, and Priya would not elaborate.

"Did you get her number?" Dev whispered, grinning.

"She's been behind us since freshman year, Dev."

"So did you?"

The bus turned onto Marsh Road, and Alyssa marked the liar line in yellow, then, after a second, boxed it. Priya got off two stops early, as always, and walked the rest, and Alyssa watched her go and thought: unreliable narrator, and turned the phrase over until the bus hissed to a stop at her corner. She left Dev her highlighter. He'd need it, and she could get another, and somehow that felt like the first honest thing she'd said all week.
